t: The cloud model: regions, availability zones, edge locations, shared responsibility, IaaS to serverless, and the AWS/GCP/Azure service map
sum: What a cloud provider actually sells and how it is laid out: everything as an API call, control planes versus data planes, regions, availability zones and edge locations as failure and latency boundaries, zonal, regional and global resources, the shared-responsibility model, IaaS, PaaS, containers, serverless and SaaS, and the AWS/GCP/Azure service map, with the 2017 S3 us-east-1 outage as the case.
prereq: net3

A VPC is a private network in the cloud with a CIDR block carved into subnets; route tables decide whether a subnet is public (default route to an internet gateway) or private (default route to a NAT gateway).
k8s1
A virtual machine runs its own kernel on a hypervisor; a container is a process with its own namespaces, cgroups and image, sharing the host kernel.
sc17
Failure domains run from instance to rack to zone to region; RPO is how much data you can lose and RTO is how long you can be down; correlated failures break naive availability arithmetic.
net12
A CDN serves content from points of presence near users, steering them there with DNS or anycast, and caches responses so the origin sees less traffic.
why:
Two engineers start a company. They rent one virtual machine from a cloud provider, install a database and a web server on it, and launch. It works. Six months later they have paying customers, and three things happen in the same quarter.

First, the machine's underlying host fails and the provider retires it. The machine restarts on new hardware, but the database files were on the instance's local disk, which doesn't survive a move, and the last backup is four days old. Second, a security researcher emails them: a storage bucket holding customer uploads is readable by anyone on the internet. They assumed "the cloud is secure" covered that; it doesn't. Third, a big outage in the provider's largest region takes them down for five hours, along with half the internet — and their status page, hosted in the same region, goes down with them, so customers can't even see that they know.

None of these is exotic. Each comes from not knowing the basic shape of what a cloud provider sells. What fails together and what fails separately (an instance, a building, a whole region). Which jobs the provider does and which stay yours. Which services are pinned to one building, which are spread across a region, and which are "global" but secretly managed from one place. The cloud is not one big reliable computer; it is a very large set of rentable parts with carefully defined boundaries, and every design decision in later topics — networks, databases, disaster recovery, cost — is about using those boundaries deliberately.

This lesson builds the map. It explains what "the cloud" is in operational terms (an API in front of pooled hardware, billed by use); the difference between the control plane that changes things and the data plane that runs them; regions, availability zones and edge locations as latency and failure boundaries; zonal, regional and global resources; the shared-responsibility model; the service models from virtual machines to serverless to SaaS; how to choose a region with real numbers; and the AWS, Google Cloud and Azure names for the same building blocks. The case is AWS's 2017 S3 outage in us-east-1, which shows almost every idea in one afternoon.
primer:
The easiest way into the cloud is to think of it as renting from a very large, very automated landlord.

Imagine a company that owns hundreds of warehouses full of identical shelving and machinery, spread across a few dozen cities. You never visit. You send a form — "I'd like four machines of this size, a locked storage room of 500 GB, and a private corridor connecting them" — and seconds later they exist, and a meter starts running. Send another form and they disappear, and the meter stops. That form is an API call (a request to the provider's web service), the machines are virtual machines, the storage room is a disk or a bucket, and the corridor is a virtual network.

The landlord groups its warehouses deliberately. Each city where it operates is a region: "US East (N. Virginia)", "Europe (Frankfurt)". A region is not one building. It is several separate sites, each called an availability zone (AZ), placed kilometres apart, each with its own power supply, cooling and network links, so a fire, a flood or a substation failure in one doesn't reach the others. The sites are linked by fast private fibre, so a machine in one zone can talk to a machine in another in a millisecond or two. On top of this, the landlord has hundreds of small kiosks — edge locations — in many more cities, which don't rent machines but run network services close to people: caching web content, answering DNS queries, filtering attacks.

Two more ideas complete the picture. First, the landlord and the tenant split the work, and the split is written down: the landlord guards the buildings, the machines and its own software; you guard what you put inside and who you give keys to. This is the shared-responsibility model, and most cloud security failures happen on the tenant's side of it. Second, you can rent at different levels of finish. You can rent bare machines and install everything yourself (IaaS, infrastructure as a service); rent a managed database or runtime and just use it (PaaS and managed services); hand over a function and pay per run (serverless); or rent finished software (SaaS). The more finished the thing you rent, the less you operate and the less you control.

Where the analogy breaks: a real landlord's building is either standing or not. Cloud services fail in subtler ways. The software that runs a whole region is shared across its zones, so a bad deployment or a software bug can take out every zone at once even though the buildings are fine. And the forms you send — the API — are themselves a service that can fail while everything already running keeps working. Those two facts, regional software as a shared failure domain and the split between the API that changes things and the systems that run them, are the two ideas in this lesson that matter most for senior-level design.
body:
1. What a cloud provider actually sells

The most-cited definition is NIST's (the US National Institute of Standards and Technology, special publication 800-145, 2011). It lists five essential characteristics, and each one is worth reading as an engineering fact rather than marketing:

  • On-demand self-service. You get resources by calling an API, not by raising a ticket. A virtual machine typically takes tens of seconds to a couple of minutes to boot; a bucket exists the moment the call returns.
  • Broad network access. Everything is reached over the network through standard protocols — HTTPS APIs, SSH, database wire protocols.
  • Resource pooling. Many customers share the same physical hardware, separated by virtualisation and access control. You don't know or care which server you are on, which is why the provider can move you when hardware fails.
  • Rapid elasticity. You can add or remove capacity quickly, often automatically. "Quickly" has limits: the provider's spare capacity in a zone is finite, and your account has quotas.
  • Measured service. Usage is metered and billed: per second of instance time, per gigabyte-month stored, per million requests, per gigabyte transferred. Every architecture decision in the cloud is also a billing decision, which is why cl12 exists.

NIST also names deployment models: public cloud (a provider's shared infrastructure, sold to anyone), private cloud (the same style of self-service infrastructure run for one organisation), community cloud (shared by a group with common requirements), and hybrid (a combination connected together). This track is about public clouds, with AWS as the main example.

2. Everything is an API call: control plane and data plane

When you click "launch instance" in a web console, the console calls the same public API that the command-line tool and the SDKs call. A launch looks like this with the AWS CLI (this needs an AWS account; it's shown so you can see the shape):

aws ec2 run-instances --region us-east-1 \
  --image-id ami-0abc1234example --instance-type t4g.small \
  --subnet-id subnet-0123example --count 1

That request goes to the EC2 control plane: the set of services that authenticate you, check your permissions and quotas, choose a physical host in the zone your subnet lives in, allocate a network interface and an IP address, attach a disk built from the image, and start the virtual machine. It returns an instance ID like i-0a1b2c3d4e5f67890 long before the machine has finished booting. From then on, the running instance's network traffic, disk reads and CPU are handled by the data plane: the hypervisor on the host, the virtual network fabric, the storage servers behind the disk.

The split exists in every service. For S3, CreateBucket and PutBucketPolicy are control plane; GetObject and PutObject are data plane. For DNS (Route 53), creating a hosted zone or changing a record is control plane; answering a DNS query is data plane. The general term for control-plane actions is CRUDL: create, read, update, delete, list.

Why this matters: the two halves are built differently on purpose. Control planes are complex (many steps, many dependencies, workflow engines, databases of configuration) and run at low request rates. Data planes are simpler, handle vastly more traffic, and are engineered to keep working when the control plane is down — an instance keeps running and serving traffic even if nobody can launch a new one. AWS's fault-isolation whitepaper puts it bluntly: data planes are designed to be more available than control planes. So the rule senior engineers apply is: during an incident, depend only on data planes. Have capacity already running, DNS records already in place with health checks that flip them automatically, and credentials already issued. Don't plan to fix an outage by launching, creating or reconfiguring things.

A second consequence: control-plane APIs are often eventually consistent. The EC2 API documentation warns that right after you create a resource, a following call that describes or uses it may briefly fail with "not found", because the change hasn't propagated to every part of the control plane yet. Scripts and infrastructure tools retry with backoff for this reason (cl9 returns to this).

3. Regions

A region is a named geographic area where the provider runs a full, largely independent copy of its services: its own EC2 control plane, its own S3, its own DynamoDB, its own deployments of each service's software. On 7 October 2026 AWS listed 39 regions with 124 availability zones (and announced two more regions, in Saudi Arabia and Chile); Google Cloud listed 43 regions with 130 zones; Azure lists its regions and which of them have zones in its documentation. Each region has a code — us-east-1, eu-central-1, ap-south-1 — that you pass on every API call. Calling the API in one region doesn't show you resources in another: an instance in Frankfurt is invisible to describe-instances in Virginia.

Region independence is the reason regions are the unit of disaster recovery. Because each region runs its own copy of the software, a bad deployment or a software bug in one region's DynamoDB should not affect another region's. Providers deploy changes to one region (and inside it, one zone) at a time precisely so a bad change hits a limited area. It also means data does not leave a region unless you, or a service you configured, move it — which is what makes regions the unit of data residency, the legal requirement that certain data stay in certain countries.

There is one level above regions on AWS: the partition. The commercial regions form the aws partition; China's regions (aws-cn) and the US government's GovCloud regions (aws-us-gov) are separate partitions with separate accounts, separate control planes and separate identity systems. Nothing is shared across partitions, which is why resource names (ARNs, covered below) include the partition.

4. Availability zones

An availability zone is one or more physical data centres inside a region with separate, redundant power, networking and connectivity. AWS's fault-isolation whitepaper says zones in a region are "meaningfully distant from each other, up to 60 miles (~100 km)", far enough that a utility failure, flood, fire or earthquake shouldn't hit two at once, but close enough for synchronous replication "with single-digit millisecond latency". Generators and cooling are not shared, and zones are fed from different power substations. Azure's documentation gives the same picture: zones typically several kilometres apart and usually within 100 km, with a target inter-zone round trip of under about 2 ms.

That latency is the whole point. Synchronous replication means a write is acknowledged only after it is stored in two places. If the places are 2 ms apart, every write costs about 2 ms extra — acceptable for a database. If they were 65 ms apart (Virginia to Frankfurt), every committed transaction would wait 65 ms, which is why cross-region replication is almost always asynchronous (the write is acknowledged locally and copied later, so a region loss can lose the last few seconds of writes — the RPO you met in sc17).

Zones change how you deploy everything. A managed database in "Multi-AZ" mode keeps a standby in a second zone and fails over to it automatically. A load balancer has nodes in each zone you enable. An autoscaling group spreads instances across zones. The EC2 service-level agreement shows the provider's own view of the arithmetic: on 7 October 2026 it promised 99.5% monthly uptime for a single instance, but 99.99% for the region-level case of instances deployed across two or more zones.

Two practical details trip people up. First, zone names are per account. AWS maps the physical zones to the letters us-east-1a, -1b and so on randomly for each account, so everyone's "a" isn't the same overloaded building. The stable name is the AZ ID, like use1-az1, which means the same physical zone for every account. You need AZ IDs whenever two accounts must agree on a location. Second, cross-zone traffic costs money on AWS: $0.01 per GB in each direction between zones in the same region on 7 October 2026 (from the AWS price list), so a chatty service sending 50 TB a month across zones pays about $1,000 for the privilege. Azure, by contrast, states that it does not charge for data transfer between zones in a region. cl3 and cl12 return to this.

5. Edge locations, Local Zones and other extensions

Regions are few and large; users are everywhere. Providers fill the gap with smaller sites. Edge locations (points of presence, PoPs) run network-facing services close to users: the CDN cache (CloudFront on AWS), authoritative DNS (Route 53), web application firewalls and DDoS protection, and lightweight edge compute. AWS listed more than 750 CloudFront PoPs plus 15 regional edge caches on 7 October 2026; Google listed more than 200 network edge locations. You don't run virtual machines there; you configure services that run there. net12 covers how traffic is steered to them.

Between the two sit extensions of a region. A Local Zone (AWS had 46) places a small set of services — instances, disks, some databases — in a metropolitan area for single-digit-millisecond latency to users there; it hangs off a parent region and depends on it for its control plane. Wavelength Zones sit inside telecom operators' 5G networks. Outposts are racks of AWS hardware installed in your own data centre, managed from a parent region. Each extension trades breadth of services and independence for proximity.

6. Zonal, regional and global resources

Every resource you create has a scope, and the scope tells you what fails with it and what you must do for resilience. This is the single most useful table to memorise:

ScopeExamples (AWS)Fails withWhat you do for resilience
ZonalEC2 instance, EBS volume, subnet, NAT gateway (zonal mode), RDS single-AZ instanceits zonerun copies in several zones; replicate data
RegionalVPC, S3 bucket, DynamoDB table, SQS queue, Lambda function, ALBits region (the service spreads it across zones)copy or rebuild in another region
GlobalIAM roles and policies, Route 53 hosted zones, CloudFront distributionsdata plane: rarely; control plane: its home regionavoid needing control-plane changes in an incident

The scope also differs between providers, which matters when you translate a design. On AWS a subnet lives in exactly one zone, so "three zones" means three subnets per tier. On Azure and Google Cloud a subnet is regional and spans zones; you choose zones per resource instead. A Google Cloud VPC network is global — one network can have subnets in many regions — whereas an AWS VPC or an Azure virtual network is regional. Same concepts, different boundaries.

"Global" deserves care. Global services still separate control and data planes, and AWS's whitepaper lists where their single control planes live. In the aws partition, IAM's control plane is in us-east-1, as are those of AWS Organizations, Route 53 (public and private DNS), CloudFront, and the certificate service used by CloudFront; Route 53 Application Recovery Controller and Global Accelerator keep theirs in us-west-2. The data planes — checking a request's signature and permissions, answering DNS queries, serving cached content — are distributed to every region or edge location. So a us-east-1 problem shouldn't stop your eu-west-1 application from authenticating requests, but it could stop you creating a new IAM role or editing a DNS record anywhere. Even some regional-looking actions have a global dependency: creating or deleting any S3 bucket checks global name uniqueness in us-east-1, and SDKs historically defaulted to the global STS (temporary-credential) endpoint, which is in us-east-1, unless configured to use a regional one.

7. Naming things: accounts and ARNs

Resources belong to a container that is also the unit of billing and of security isolation. On AWS that container is an account (a 12-digit number); on Google Cloud it is a project; on Azure it is a subscription holding resource groups. Many organisations run dozens or hundreds of accounts — one per environment and team — under an organisation; cl13 covers that structure. Every AWS resource has an ARN (Amazon Resource Name) that encodes the partition, service, region, account and resource:

arn:aws:s3:::invoices-prod-eu                         (S3: no region or account in bucket ARNs)
arn:aws:ec2:eu-central-1:123456789012:instance/i-0a1b2c3d4e5f67890
arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/payments-api           (IAM: global, so no region)

Notice the empty region field for IAM — the name itself tells you the resource is global. ARNs matter because permissions (cl2) are written against them.

8. The shared-responsibility model

AWS's wording is the standard one. The provider is responsible for "security of the cloud": "protecting the infrastructure that runs all of the services offered in the AWS Cloud" — facilities, hardware, the hypervisor, the network, and the software of its managed services. The customer is responsible for "security in the cloud", and that responsibility "will be determined by the AWS Cloud services that a customer selects".

The phrase "determined by the services" is the key. For EC2, the customer owns "the guest operating system (including updates and security patches), any application software or utilities installed by the customer on the instances, and the configuration of the AWS-provided firewall (called a security group)". For abstracted services such as S3 and DynamoDB, AWS runs the infrastructure, OS and platform, and customers "are responsible for managing their data (including encryption options), classifying their assets, and using IAM tools to apply the appropriate permissions". Some controls are explicitly shared: AWS patches the infrastructure, you patch your guest OS and applications; AWS configures its devices, you configure your OS, databases and applications; AWS trains its staff, you train yours.

The single most important consequence: identity and access configuration is always yours. A bucket made public by a policy, an access key committed to a repository, a role that any account in the world can assume — none of these are provider failures, and cl2 and cl13 spend most of their time on them.

9. Service models: from virtual machines to SaaS

The same small web application — an HTTP API, a PostgreSQL database and a nightly report job — can be run at five levels of "finish". Walking it through each makes the trade-offs concrete:

  • IaaS. Rent three virtual machines (EC2, Compute Engine, Azure Virtual Machines). Install the OS packages, the runtime, PostgreSQL, a cron daemon. You patch, back up, monitor disks, fail the database over by hand or with your own tooling. Most control, most work. Cost: about $0.0168 an hour for a t4g.small in us-east-1, so roughly $12 a month per machine, plus disks.
  • Managed services (PaaS-style). Keep the API on a VM or container, but rent PostgreSQL as a managed service (RDS, Cloud SQL, Azure Database for PostgreSQL). The provider installs, patches, backs up and fails over the database; you choose size, parameters and who can connect. A db.t4g.micro PostgreSQL instance was $0.016 an hour single-zone and $0.032 multi-zone on 7 October 2026 — you pay double for the standby, which is the honest price of zone failover.
  • Containers as a service (CaaS). Package the API as a container image (k8s1–k8s3) and run it on Fargate, Cloud Run or Azure Container Apps: no servers to manage, you choose CPU and memory per task. Or run Kubernetes (EKS, GKE, AKS), where the provider runs the control plane and you run what's on it.
  • Serverless functions (FaaS). Turn the report job into a function (Lambda, Cloud Run functions, Azure Functions) triggered by a schedule. It runs a few minutes a night and costs cents; when idle it costs nothing. Maximum run time, cold starts and concurrency limits now become your design constraints — cl5 is about exactly this.
  • SaaS. Replace the reporting with a hosted analytics product. You configure it and give it data; the vendor runs everything. You inherit its availability, its data location and its security posture, which you now have to assess as a vendor risk.

"Serverless" is used more broadly than functions: any service where you never size servers and pay for use — S3, DynamoDB on-demand, SQS — is often called serverless. The useful test is: do I provision capacity, and do I pay when idle? If no and no, it's serverless in the sense that matters for cost and operations.

10. The service map across AWS, Google Cloud and Azure

Every concept in this track exists on all three major providers under different names. Interviewers often ask "what's the GCP equivalent of…", and teams increasingly work with more than one. Names below were checked against each provider's current product pages on 7 October 2026 — note two recent renames: Google's Vertex AI became Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform (announced at Cloud Next 2026, with the old name removed from the console in May 2026), and Azure AI Foundry became Microsoft Foundry (Microsoft's product terms from January 2026), which includes Azure OpenAI.

Equivalents are rarely identical. DynamoDB, Firestore and Cosmos DB have different consistency options and pricing units; SQS and Pub/Sub have different delivery semantics. Use the table to translate vocabulary, then read the specific service's documentation before translating a design.

11. Choosing a region, worked with numbers

A company in London is launching a product whose customers are mostly in the UK and Germany, with a growing group in India. Walk the decision in the order of what's hardest to change.

Step 1: hard constraints. Contracts with German enterprise customers require personal data to stay in the EU. That removes us-east-1 as the primary and points at an EU region: Frankfurt (eu-central-1), Ireland (eu-west-1) or others. (London, eu-west-2, is in the UK, which is outside the EU, so check whether contracts say "EU" or "EEA or adequate country" — a legal question, not a technical one.) Then check the services: if the product needs a particular GPU instance type or managed model, confirm it is offered in the candidate region. Instance families launch region by region; on 7 October 2026, for example, the p5.48xlarge (8 × H100) appeared in the on-demand price lists for us-east-1, us-west-2, Mumbai, Tokyo and São Paulo but not for Frankfurt.

Step 2: latency. Light in optical fibre travels at about two-thirds of its speed in a vacuum, roughly 200,000 km/s, so every 100 km of fibre adds about 0.5 ms one way, 1 ms round trip. Real paths are longer than great circles and pass through routers, so measured round trips are typically 1.5–2× the floor. Great-circle distances give the floors:

PathDistanceMinimum round trip
London ↔ Frankfurt~640 km~6 ms
London ↔ N. Virginia~5,900 km~59 ms
Mumbai ↔ Frankfurt~6,560 km~66 ms
Mumbai ↔ N. Virginia~12,900 km~129 ms

A page that needs four sequential round trips to the API (a TLS handshake, an auth call, two data calls) costs about 25 ms of pure physics from London to Frankfurt and about 260 ms or more from Mumbai to Frankfurt. Frankfurt is fine for the UK and Germany; Indian users will notice, and the mitigations are a CDN for static content, fewer round trips, and — if the business grows there — a second regional deployment in Mumbai (ap-south-1).

Step 3: price. From the AWS price list on 7 October 2026, an m7i.large Linux instance cost $0.1008/hour in us-east-1, $0.12075 in Frankfurt (+20%), $0.10605 in Mumbai (+5%), $0.1302 in Tokyo (+29%) and $0.16065 in São Paulo (+59%). For a fleet of 40 such instances running all month (730 hours), Frankfurt costs 40 × 730 × 0.12075 ≈ $3,526 against $2,943 in Virginia — a real but secondary difference next to residency and latency. Data transfer prices differ by region too.

Step 4: quotas and capacity. New accounts start with modest per-region quotas, for example on the number of vCPUs of on-demand instances, and GPU quotas often start at zero. Request increases well before launch. Large instance types can be scarce in a particular zone; spreading across zones and keeping a second instance type as a fallback helps (cl4).

Decision: primary region eu-central-1 across three zones; backups copied to a second EU region for disaster recovery; CDN in front; revisit a Mumbai deployment when Indian traffic justifies the operational cost.
deep:
Static stability is the design principle behind zones

AWS's Builders' Library describes how EC2 itself is built to be statically stable: when a zone fails, the instances in the other zones keep running without anything needing to happen — no new launches, no configuration changes, no control-plane calls. The same principle applies to your systems. A service running at 60% utilisation in each of three zones loses a third of its capacity when one zone fails, and the remaining two must run at 90%: survivable. A service running at 85% in each zone would need 127% in the remaining two, so it must scale up during the incident, which means calling the EC2 control plane at exactly the moment thousands of other customers are trying to do the same in the same region. Pre-provisioning enough capacity to absorb a zone loss costs money every day; it buys you not depending on the most contended resource during an incident. For N zones, the steady-state utilisation ceiling is (N−1)/N: 67% for three zones, 75% for four.

Zones are independent for hardware, not for software

Zones are built so that physical events don't correlate: different substations, separate cooling, separate buildings. But every zone in a region runs the same build of the same regional services, configured by the same automation. A bad configuration push, a latent bug triggered by load, or a dependency that every zone shares (DNS automation for a regional endpoint, a regional metadata store) fails them together. Providers reduce this with zone-by-zone deployments and cell-based architectures, but they can't eliminate it, and the largest incidents in AWS's public history — S3 in 2017, the internal network event in December 2021, DynamoDB's DNS race in October 2025 — were regional, not zonal. For a senior design, this is the reason "multi-AZ" and "disaster recovery" are separate line items.

Capacity is finite, and it's per zone

"Rapid elasticity" is a statistical promise, not a guarantee. Each zone has a finite number of hosts of each type. When demand for a type spikes — a popular GPU, or everyone failing over after an incident — launches fail with an insufficient-capacity error even though your quota allows them. That's why providers sell capacity reservations (pay to hold capacity whether you use it or not) and why autoscaling groups are configured with several instance types and all zones. For GPU work, capacity is often the binding constraint rather than price, and cl14 treats it as a first-class design input.

Data gravity and lock-in are mostly about data and identity, not compute

Moving a stateless service between regions or providers is a deployment exercise. Moving 500 TB of data is not: at $0.09/GB for internet egress from AWS, that's about $46,000 in transfer charges alone (AWS and the other major providers have announced waivers of egress charges for customers leaving entirely, under conditions — check current terms), plus weeks of copy time and a cutover plan. Identity is the other anchor: hundreds of IAM roles, trust relationships and policies written in one provider's language. Managed services add a third: an application built on DynamoDB's API and semantics doesn't run on Cosmos DB without changes. A senior answer to "how do we avoid lock-in" is to be deliberate about which of these you accept in exchange for what, not to avoid managed services wholesale.

Partitions and sovereign regions are separate clouds

China (aws-cn) and GovCloud (aws-us-gov) are separate partitions: different accounts, separate IAM, separate control planes, service sets that lag the commercial partition. Providers are building more such separations for sovereignty requirements — clouds operated by in-country staff, with control planes inside a jurisdiction. Designs that assume "one AWS" (cross-account roles, a single organisation, global services) don't extend across partitions. If a product must serve such a market, plan it as a second deployment with its own identity and tooling.

The provider's abstraction has a shape you will hit

Every managed service exposes limits that come from its internals: maximum object sizes, request rates per key prefix or partition, connection limits, maximum function durations, API rate limits on the control plane. These are documented per service as quotas (some adjustable, some fixed). Senior engineers read the quota page before choosing a service, because a design that needs 10× a hard limit is a redesign, not a support ticket. cl10 returns to quotas as a reliability risk.

Pricing follows the architecture of the provider

Prices reveal what's expensive for the provider. Inbound data is free because it fills otherwise idle capacity; outbound internet traffic is billed because it consumes transit. Cross-zone traffic on AWS costs $0.01/GB each way because it crosses metro fibre between buildings. Standby replicas cost as much as primaries because they occupy the same hardware. Reading a price sheet as a description of the provider's costs helps you predict which designs will be cheap — and is the theme of cl12.
prod:
Characteristic failures

The single-zone production system. Everything works until a zone has a power or network event; then the database, which nobody configured as Multi-AZ, is unreachable for hours. Symptom: a zone-specific event on the provider's health dashboard and 100% errors. Prevention: an inventory of every stateful component and its zone placement, and a rule in infrastructure-as-code reviews that production data stores are multi-zone.

The multi-zone design with a zonal single point. Compute spans three zones, but there's one NAT gateway in one zone, or one cache node, or a self-managed database primary. When that zone fails, the "multi-AZ" system fails. NAT gateways are a classic case because they are created per zone and cost money each, so teams create one (cl3).

Gray failure in a zone. A zone doesn't fail cleanly; it gets slow, or loses a fraction of packets. Health checks pass, but latency and errors rise for requests routed there. The mitigation is zonal observability (metrics broken down by zone) and the ability to shift traffic away from a zone — AWS offers zonal shift for load balancers in Route 53 Application Recovery Controller for this reason.

Hidden regional dependencies. The application runs in eu-west-1, but the CI/CD system, the container registry, the secrets store, the status page or the identity provider is in us-east-1. A us-east-1 event then blocks deploys, sign-ins or communication even though production is fine. Inventory where your tooling runs.

Control-plane dependent recovery. The runbook says "launch replacement instances" or "update the DNS record". During a large regional event, those APIs are throttled or failing. Prefer pre-provisioned capacity and health-check-driven DNS failover.

Quota and capacity surprises. A launch day or a failover hits the per-region vCPU quota, or a zone has no capacity for the chosen instance type. Monitor quota utilisation (Service Quotas exposes it as metrics), request headroom ahead of events, and configure instance-type diversity.

What to watch

The provider's own signals: the AWS Health Dashboard (with account-specific events for your resources), Google Cloud Service Health and Azure Service Health. Your own: error rate and latency broken down by zone and region, quota utilisation, and the inventory of resource scopes. Many teams subscribe health events to their alerting so a provider notice reaches on-call before customers do.

The case: Amazon S3 in us-east-1, 28 February 2017

At 9:37 AM PST, an S3 team member was debugging a slow billing system and ran an established playbook command to remove a small number of servers from one S3 subsystem. One input was entered incorrectly, and a much larger set of servers was removed — including servers supporting two other subsystems: the index subsystem, which manages the metadata and location of every object in the region, and the placement subsystem, which allocates storage for new objects. Both had to be fully restarted, which they hadn't been in years, and the restart and safety checks took longer than expected because of the region's growth. The index subsystem began serving requests again at 12:26 PM and was fully recovered at 1:18 PM; placement finished recovering at 1:54 PM.

Because S3 is a dependency of other services, the impact spread: the S3 console, new EC2 instance launches, EBS volumes that needed data from S3 snapshots, and Lambda were impaired. AWS's own Service Health Dashboard couldn't be updated until 11:37 AM because its administration console depended on S3, so AWS communicated through Twitter and a banner. AWS changed the tool to remove capacity more slowly and to refuse to take any subsystem below its minimum capacity, audited other tools for the same risk, and prioritised splitting the index subsystem into smaller cells to cut recovery time.

Read as an engineer, the event shows the ideas of this lesson in order. The failure was regional software, so all zones were hit at once. Recovery took much longer than the fault (seconds to type, hours to restart) because rarely exercised restart paths are slow. Dependencies chain: services you didn't know used S3 failed with it. A monitoring system that shares fate with what it monitors goes dark exactly when needed. And human operations on a control plane need guard rails proportional to blast radius.
myths: Moving to the cloud means the provider is responsible for security.

The provider secures the facilities, hardware, hypervisor and its own managed software ('security of the cloud'). Your identities, permissions, network rules, data classification, encryption choices and, on virtual machines, the guest operating system and everything installed on it remain yours ('security in the cloud'). Almost every well-known cloud breach — public buckets, leaked access keys, over-broad roles — happened on the customer's side of that line.
Running in two availability zones means you survive a region outage.

Zones protect against a building-scale failure: power, cooling, a fibre cut, a fire. They share the region's software: the same control planes, the same regional service deployments, the same DNS automation. The 2017 S3 event and the 2025 DynamoDB DNS event both hit every zone in us-east-1 at once. Surviving a region needs a second region, with a failover path that does not depend on the broken one.
us-east-1a is the same building for everyone.

AWS maps zone names to physical zones randomly per account, so your us-east-1a may be someone else's us-east-1c. That spreads load across buildings. When you coordinate across accounts — sharing a subnet, comparing latency, reading an incident notice — use zone IDs such as use1-az1, which are the same everywhere.
Serverless means there are no servers and nothing to operate.

There are servers; you just never see, patch or size them. You still own the code, its dependencies, its permissions, its timeouts and retries, its cost, and the limits of the platform — concurrency quotas, cold starts, maximum run time. Serverless moves operational work to the provider; it doesn't delete it.
All cloud prices are the same everywhere, so region choice is only about latency.

Prices differ by region, sometimes a lot: on 7 October 2026 an m7i.large Linux instance cost $0.1008 an hour in us-east-1, $0.12075 in Frankfurt and $0.16065 in São Paulo — 59% more. Services and instance types also launch region by region, quotas are per region, and data-residency rules can force the choice before price or latency are considered.
A global service like IAM can't be affected by one region's problems.

Global services keep their data planes in every region, so signing requests and checking permissions keep working, but several have a single control plane — IAM's, Route 53's and CloudFront's live in us-east-1. If that region is impaired you may be unable to create a role, change a DNS record or update a distribution anywhere in the world. Failover plans that need those changes are fragile.
lab:
Goal: build a small model of regions, zones and resource scopes, and use it to answer "what survives this failure?" and "how much headroom do I need?" — Python 3.12 standard library only. About 15 minutes. No cloud account needed.

  1. Inventory. Write a list of dicts describing a system: {"name": "api-1", "scope": "zonal", "region": "eu-central-1", "az": "euc1-az1", "tier": "api"}, plus two more API instances in az2 and az3, a database primary in az3 and a standby in az2, one NAT gateway in az1, an S3 bucket (regional) and an IAM role (global, home region us-east-1 for its control plane).
  2. Failure function. Write survivors(inventory, failed), where failed is a set of zone IDs or region names. A zonal resource dies if its zone or region failed; a regional one if its region failed; a global one survives (note separately whether its control plane's region failed).
  3. Tier check. For each tier, report whether at least one member survives. Fail zone euc1-az1: which tier loses all members? (Expect the NAT tier.) Fail eu-central-1: everything regional and zonal is gone.
  4. Headroom. Write max_util(n_zones) returning (n−1)/n, and needed_util(load, per_zone_capacity, n, lost=1). With 3 zones of 100 units and total load 210, what utilisation do the survivors run at after one loss?
  5. Latency floor. Write a haversine function and compute minimum round trips (2 × km ÷ 200,000 km/s) for London–Frankfurt and Mumbai–Virginia.

What to look for: step 3 shows that "multi-AZ" is a property of every tier, not of the system — one zonal NAT gateway breaks it. Step 4 gives 105% for the survivors, so 210 units of load is too much for three zones of 100: the ceiling is 200 (67% each). Step 5 should give about 6 ms and 129 ms, matching the table in the body.

Needs an AWS account (optional): aws ec2 describe-availability-zones --region eu-central-1 --query "AvailabilityZones[].[ZoneName,ZoneId]" --output table lists your zone names next to their AZ IDs; compare with a colleague's account to see the mapping differ.
recap: A cloud provider rents pooled compute, storage and networking on demand, through an API, metered by use; NIST's five characteristics are on-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity and measured service.

Every action is an API call: the control plane creates, changes and deletes resources, and is complex and less available; the data plane serves the running resource and is simpler and built to keep working when the control plane doesn't.

A region is a geographic area with its own independent copy of most services; an availability zone is one or more data centres in that region with separate power, cooling and networking, up to about 100 km from its neighbours and a few milliseconds away.
Resources are zonal (an instance, a disk, an AWS subnet), regional (a VPC, a bucket, a managed queue) or global (IAM, Route 53 DNS, CloudFront); the scope tells you what a failure takes with it.
Global services usually have globally distributed data planes but a single control plane, several of them in us-east-1, so recovery plans should never depend on changing them during an incident.

Under the shared-responsibility model the provider secures the cloud itself and the customer secures what they put in it; the line moves up as you go from virtual machines to managed services to SaaS, but identity, permissions and data are always the customer's.

IaaS rents machines, PaaS and managed services rent a runtime or a database, containers-as-a-service runs your images, serverless runs functions per event and bills per use, and SaaS rents finished software; each step up trades control for less operational work.
Region choice is driven by data residency, latency to users (bounded by the speed of light in fibre, about 1 ms of round trip per 100 km), service and instance availability, price and quotas.

Concepts map across providers but details differ: AWS subnets live in one zone while Azure and GCP subnets span zones, GCP VPCs are global, and AWS charges for traffic between zones where Azure does not.
glossary: ALB (Application Load Balancer)
AWS's managed HTTP(S) load balancer; it is regional and places nodes in each zone you enable.
ARN (Amazon Resource Name)
The unique name of an AWS resource, encoding partition, service, region, account and resource, e.g. arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/payments-api.
Availability zone (AZ)

One or more data centres inside a region with their own power, cooling and network connections, placed far enough from the region's other zones to fail independently but close enough for millisecond latency.
AZ ID
AWS's account-independent name for a physical zone, such as use1-az1. Zone names like us-east-1a are mapped to physical zones differently in each account; AZ IDs are not.
CaaS (containers as a service)
A service that runs your container images without you managing the servers underneath, such as AWS Fargate, Google Cloud Run or Azure Container Apps.
Control plane
The part of a service that creates, configures and deletes resources: the APIs behind 'launch an instance' or 'create a bucket'. More complex and less available than the data plane.
CRUDL
Create, read, update, delete, list: the configuration operations a control plane offers.
Data plane

The part of a service that does the work of a running resource: a running instance's network, reads and writes to an existing bucket, DNS answers. Designed to keep working when the control plane is impaired.
Data residency
A legal or contractual requirement that certain data be stored, and sometimes processed, only in particular countries or regions.
EBS (Elastic Block Store)
AWS's network-attached disks for EC2 instances; each volume lives in one availability zone.
EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud)
AWS's virtual machine service; an EC2 instance is one virtual machine.
Edge location (point of presence)
A small site, much more numerous than regions, that runs network-facing services such as a CDN cache, DNS servers or a web firewall close to users.
FaaS (functions as a service)

A serverless model where you upload a function and the provider runs a copy per event, scaling to zero when idle and billing per request and duration. AWS Lambda, Cloud Run functions, Azure Functions.
Global resource
A resource that is not tied to one region, such as an IAM role or a Route 53 hosted zone.
IaaS (infrastructure as a service)
Renting virtual machines, disks and networks; you manage the operating system and everything above it.
IAM (Identity and Access Management)
The service that defines who (users, roles) may do what to which resources; covered in cl2.
Local Zone
An AWS extension of a region placed in a metropolitan area for single-digit-millisecond latency to nearby users, with a subset of services.
Managed service
A service where the provider runs the software for you — a database, queue or cache — so you configure and use it rather than install, patch and fail it over.
PaaS (platform as a service)
Renting a managed runtime: you deploy code or configuration and the provider runs the operating system, runtime and scaling.
Partition
A completely separate group of AWS regions with its own control planes and accounts: aws (commercial), aws-cn (China) and aws-us-gov (GovCloud).
Quota (service limit)
A per-account, usually per-region ceiling on how much of a resource you may use, such as vCPUs of on-demand instances; some can be raised on request.
RDS (Relational Database Service)
AWS's managed relational databases (PostgreSQL, MySQL and others); Multi-AZ mode keeps a standby in another zone.
Region
A separate geographic area where a provider runs a full, largely independent copy of its services, made of several availability zones.
Regional resource
A resource that lives in one region and is spread or replicated across its zones by the service, such as an S3 bucket or an SQS queue.
S3 (Simple Storage Service)
AWS's object storage: buckets of objects addressed by key, regional and replicated across zones.
SaaS (software as a service)
Renting finished software used through a browser or API, such as email or a CRM; the provider runs everything except your data and user settings.
Serverless
A style of service with no servers for you to see or size, automatic scaling (often to zero), and billing for actual use rather than for provisioned capacity.
Shared-responsibility model
The division of security and operational duties between provider and customer: the provider secures the cloud itself, the customer secures what they run and store in it.
Static stability
A design property: the system keeps working through a failure without needing to make changes (launch capacity, update DNS, call a control plane) during it.
STS (Security Token Service)
The AWS service that issues temporary credentials, for example when a role is assumed.
VPC (Virtual Private Cloud)
A private, isolated virtual network in a cloud region with its own IP range, subnets and route tables (net3, cl3).
Zonal resource
A resource that lives in exactly one availability zone, such as an EC2 instance or an EBS volume, and fails with it.
drill:
Review: "we're highly available"

A team describes its production system in us-east-1: an Application Load Balancer across three zones; six API instances in an autoscaling group across three zones, running at about 80% CPU at peak; a PostgreSQL database on RDS in single-AZ mode with daily snapshots; one NAT gateway; a Redis cache on one node; the status page and CI runners on a VM in the same region. Their runbook for a zone failure says: "the autoscaling group will launch replacements; restore the database from the latest snapshot if needed." Identify the risks in priority order and propose changes.

Answer

1. Single-AZ database (highest). A zone failure takes the only database down, and restoring from a daily snapshot means up to 24 hours of lost data and an hour or more to restore. Switch to Multi-AZ (synchronous standby, automatic failover in about a minute or two), and enable point-in-time recovery so RPO is minutes for logical errors too.

2. Zonal single points: one NAT gateway, one Redis node. Losing the NAT gateway's zone cuts outbound internet for all private instances; losing the Redis node either stalls the API or stampedes the database. Use one NAT gateway per zone with per-zone routes, and a replicated cache with automatic failover — or make the API survive a cold cache.

3. Not statically stable. At 80% utilisation across three zones, losing one puts the survivors at 120%. The runbook relies on launching replacements during a regional rush on capacity. Run at most ~65% at peak (or add capacity so that two zones carry peak), and treat autoscaling as a bonus.

4. Shared fate for tooling. The status page and CI in the same region go dark in a regional event, exactly when needed. Move the status page off the provider or to another region; make sure deploys and break-glass access don't depend on us-east-1 alone.

5. Missing disaster recovery. Nothing survives a regional event. Decide RTO/RPO with the business (sc17); at minimum copy backups to another region and rehearse a restore (cl10).

6. Test it. Run a zone-evacuation game day (shift traffic away from one zone, fail the database over) and measure.
qa: E
What is the difference between a region and an availability zone?

A region is a geographic area — northern Virginia, Frankfurt — where the provider runs a largely independent copy of its services. An availability zone is one or more data centres inside a region with their own power, cooling and network, placed far enough from the others (AWS says up to about 100 km) not to share disasters but close enough for single-digit-millisecond latency, so data can be replicated synchronously between zones. Zones protect you from a building failing; regions protect you from a whole region's infrastructure or software failing.

Follow-up: why not just put zones 500 km apart for more safety? — Because synchronous replication across them would add several milliseconds to every write and transactions would slow down; that distance is what a second region is for, with asynchronous replication.
E
Explain the shared-responsibility model with an example.

The provider is responsible for security of the cloud — data centres, hardware, the hypervisor, the network, and the software of its managed services. The customer is responsible for security in the cloud — what they deploy and how it is configured. On an EC2 instance you patch the guest OS, configure security groups and manage your application; on S3 or DynamoDB AWS runs the OS and platform, and you still own your data, its encryption settings, its classification and the IAM permissions that guard it. A public bucket is the customer's mistake, not AWS's.

Follow-up: where does the line sit for a managed database? — The provider patches the OS and database engine (in a maintenance window you choose) and runs backups and failover; you own users, network exposure, parameter choices like TLS enforcement, and who can read the data.
E
What do IaaS, PaaS, serverless and SaaS mean, and what does each make you responsible for?

IaaS rents virtual machines and disks: you manage the OS, runtime, scaling and application. PaaS rents a managed runtime: you deploy code and the provider handles the OS, runtime and much of the scaling. Serverless (functions or containers that scale to zero) goes further: no capacity to size, billing per request and duration. SaaS is finished software you configure and use. Each step up gives away control and gains less operational work, and the shared-responsibility line moves up with it.

Follow-up: where does Kubernetes on EKS sit? — In between: the provider runs the control plane, but you own the worker nodes (unless you use Fargate or a managed node mode), the cluster add-ons, and everything you deploy.
M
What is the difference between a control plane and a data plane, and why does it matter during an outage?

The control plane is the configuration API — create an instance, change a DNS record, attach a policy. The data plane is the running thing — the instance's network, DNS answers, reads and writes to a table. Providers design data planes to be simpler, more distributed and more available, and to keep working when the control plane is impaired. So a resilient design depends only on the data plane during an incident: capacity already running, DNS records already present with health checks, credentials already issued. A plan that needs to launch instances or edit Route 53 records in the middle of a regional event leans on the part most likely to be broken.

Follow-up: give an example of a recovery plan that violates this. — 'On failure, a script creates a new load balancer and updates the DNS record to point at it.' Both steps are control-plane calls, and Route 53's control plane is in us-east-1. Better: pre-create both load balancers and use health-checked failover records.
M
IAM is a global service. What happens to your application in eu-west-1 if us-east-1 has a major outage?

Probably nothing for running workloads: IAM's data plane — authenticating and authorising requests — runs in every region, so calls in eu-west-1 keep being signed and checked. What you might lose are control-plane operations, because IAM's control plane is in us-east-1: creating or changing roles and policies could fail. You might also hit hidden dependencies: SDKs that use the global STS endpoint by default, an identity provider hosted in us-east-1, CI pipelines or dashboards that live there. The fix is regional STS endpoints, pre-created roles, and break-glass access that doesn't route through us-east-1.

Follow-up: how would you find such hidden dependencies? — Read your recovery runbooks for control-plane calls, check SDK endpoint configuration, list where your tooling runs, and run a game day that blocks us-east-1 endpoints from a test environment.
M
How would you choose a region for a new product?

First apply hard constraints: data-residency law or customer contracts, and whether the services and instance types you need exist there (GPU families launch region by region). Then latency to your users: physics gives about 1 ms of round-trip per 100 km of fibre, so a European user base wants a European region. Then price, which varies by region — an m7i.large was 20% more in Frankfurt and 59% more in São Paulo than in us-east-1 in October 2026 — and quotas. Finally, operational concentration: us-east-1 is the largest, cheapest and first to get features, but it hosts several global control planes and has had the most widely felt incidents, so some teams deliberately choose another primary.

Follow-up: what if your users are split between the US and India? — Serve static and cacheable content from a CDN everywhere; then either accept ~130 ms minimum round trips for one group, or run regional deployments with data partitioned by user home region, which adds real complexity.
M
What is the difference between zonal, regional and global resources? Give examples.

A zonal resource lives in one availability zone and fails with it: an EC2 instance, an EBS volume, an AWS subnet. A regional resource lives in one region and the service spreads it across zones for you: an S3 bucket, an SQS queue, a DynamoDB table, a VPC. A global resource isn't tied to a region: IAM roles, Route 53 hosted zones, CloudFront distributions. The scope tells you what you must do for resilience — zonal resources need you to deploy copies in several zones, regional ones are already multi-zone, and for regional and global ones you must think about the region or the control plane failing.

Follow-up: is an Azure subnet zonal? — No: Azure and GCP subnets are regional and span zones, unlike AWS subnets, which are each in one zone. The concept is the same, the boundary is in a different place, which matters when you translate designs between providers.
M
Your team says 'we're multi-AZ, so we're highly available.' What questions do you ask?

Is every tier multi-AZ — load balancer, compute, database with a standby in another zone, caches, NAT gateways — or is one piece pinned to one zone? Is there enough capacity in the surviving zones to take the load if one zone disappears, already running rather than planned to scale up? Do clients and health checks actually move traffic away from a degraded zone, including partial failures? Is anything still single-region or single-control-plane, such as DNS changes during failover? And has anyone tested it with a zone evacuation exercise?

Follow-up: how much extra capacity do you need for zone failure with three zones? — If each zone runs a third of the load and must absorb a lost zone, each of the remaining two must carry half, so you need 50% headroom over steady state: run at most about 67% utilisation per zone.
M
Why does AWS map zone names like us-east-1a differently per account, and when does it bite?

To spread customers across physical zones; otherwise everyone would pick 'a' first and that building would fill up. It bites when you coordinate across accounts: sharing subnets with AWS RAM, placing a client in the same zone as a service in another account for latency or to avoid cross-zone charges, or reading an incident note that names a zone. Use AZ IDs such as use1-az1, which mean the same physical zone in every account.
Follow-up: where do you look them up? — aws ec2 describe-availability-zones returns ZoneName and ZoneId together; subnets also expose their AZ ID.
H
Walk me through what the 2017 S3 us-east-1 outage teaches about cloud architecture.

An operator ran a capacity-removal command with a mistyped input and removed far more servers than intended, including S3's index and placement subsystems in us-east-1. Those had to be fully restarted; S3 in the region was impaired from 9:37 AM PST until about 1:54 PM. Every zone was affected because the failure was in regional software, not a building. Services that depend on S3 — EC2 launches from snapshots, EBS volumes needing snapshot data, Lambda — were impaired too, and AWS's own status dashboard couldn't be updated because its admin console used S3. Lessons: zones don't protect against regional software failure; hidden dependencies (your status page, your deployment pipeline) share fate with what they monitor; and operational tooling needs rate limits and minimum-capacity guards, which is what AWS added.

Follow-up: how would you design your status page after reading that? — Host it on a different provider or at least a different region from production, with no dependency on the systems it reports on, and update it through a path that doesn't need your main identity provider.
H
Design the regional and zonal layout for a B2B SaaS with customers in the EU and US, an 99.95% availability target and EU data-residency requirements for EU customers.

Residency forces at least two independent deployments: an EU stack (for example eu-central-1) holding EU customers' data, and a US stack. Each is multi-AZ across three zones with a load balancer, stateless compute spread across zones with 50% headroom, and a database with a synchronous standby in another zone. 99.95% allows about 22 minutes of downtime a month, which multi-AZ with automatic failover can meet without multi-region, so each stack does not need a hot secondary region; backups are copied to a second region within the same jurisdiction (eu-west-1 for the EU stack) for disaster recovery. A thin global layer routes each tenant to its home stack by tenant ID; it must never hold EU data. Identity and billing either run per region or are designed to hold no residency-bound data.
Follow-up: what breaks first in this design? — The global pieces: routing, sign-in and anything shared. They need their own multi-region design or the two 'independent' stacks fail together.
H
When would you choose serverless functions over containers or VMs for a new service, and when would you avoid them?

Serverless fits spiky or low, event-driven work — webhooks, file processing, scheduled jobs, glue between managed services — where scale-to-zero saves money and you want no capacity planning. Avoid it for steady high throughput, where per-request pricing exceeds a right-sized container fleet; for long-running work beyond the maximum duration (15 minutes on Lambda); for latency-critical paths that can't tolerate cold starts; and for workloads needing GPUs, large memory or special networking. Containers are the middle ground: portable, long-running, cheaper at steady load, but you size and scale them. cl4 and cl5 work the break-even numbers.

Follow-up: what single metric would make you revisit the choice later? — Cost per request against a container equivalent at current volume, tracked monthly; when steady load grows, the crossover arrives quietly.
H
Is multi-cloud a good resilience strategy?

Usually not as the first step. Running the same workload active on two providers doubles the platform work — two IAM models, two networks, two sets of managed services, or a lowest-common-denominator design that gives up the managed services that make a cloud worth using. Most outages that matter are regional, and multi-region on one provider covers them more cheaply. Multi-cloud makes sense for specific reasons: regulatory demands for exit plans, using a particular provider's unique service (a model API, a data warehouse), negotiating leverage, or a portable tier such as Kubernetes with data replicated outside the provider. A cheap middle ground is keeping backups and a status page outside the primary provider.

Follow-up: what do regulators ask for here? — Increasingly an exit strategy and concentration-risk assessment for critical third parties (for example the EU's DORA for financial firms); that is usually satisfied by tested data export and a documented, rehearsed migration path rather than active-active across clouds.

t: Cloud identity and access management: principals, roles, policies, policy evaluation, least privilege, assumed roles and the classic IAM mistakes
sum: How a cloud decides whether an API call is allowed: principals (root, users, roles, sessions, service principals), the JSON policy language, identity- versus resource-based policies, guardrails (permissions boundaries, SCPs, session policies), AWS's evaluation logic worked by hand for an allow plus an explicit deny, assumed roles and temporary credentials, least privilege in practice, GCP and Azure equivalents, and the IAM mistakes behind real incidents — with the 2022 AppSync confused-deputy bug as the case.
prereq: cl1
Every cloud action is an API call to a regional or global service; IAM is global with its control plane in us-east-1 and its data plane in every region; resources are named by ARNs.
au1
Authentication proves who is calling, authorisation decides what they may do, accounting records it; principals include humans, services, machines and agents.
au8
RBAC grants permissions through roles, ABAC through attributes of the subject, resource and request; policy engines evaluate rules with default deny and explicit deny precedence.
au10
Workloads should get short-lived cloud credentials by exchanging a signed identity token (workload identity federation) instead of holding static keys; IMDSv2 protects instance credentials from SSRF.
why:
A machine-learning team needs a training job to read a dataset bucket and write checkpoints. The quickest way to make it work is to give the job's role AdministratorAccess. It works on the first try, the deadline is met, and nobody revisits it. Eight months later a dependency in the training container is compromised. The attacker's code runs with the job's credentials, and those credentials can do anything in the account: read every bucket, including the one with customer PII; create new users with access keys for persistence; switch off the audit trail. The incident write-up says the root cause was a malicious package. The real root cause was a permission that was never needed.

The opposite failure is just as common. A careful engineer writes a tight policy; the job fails with AccessDenied; they add an Allow and it still fails, because a Deny they didn't know about in an organisation-wide guardrail blocks it, or because they put an object action on a bucket ARN. After an afternoon of guessing, someone adds a wildcard "temporarily".

Both failures come from not understanding the machine that sits in front of every cloud API: the identity and access management system. Every one of the billions of API calls made to a cloud each day — read an object, start an instance, publish a message — is checked against a set of policies, by fixed rules, before anything happens. If you understand those rules you can grant exactly what is needed, predict the answer to "why is this denied?" without guessing, and spot the configurations that turn a small compromise into a total one. Most cloud breaches are, at bottom, IAM failures: credentials that lived too long, roles that could do too much, trust that extended too far.

This lesson teaches IAM the way the evaluation engine sees it, using AWS as the concrete system (it's the most detailed and the one interviews probe most), with Google Cloud and Azure compared at the end. It covers principals, the policy language, identity-based and resource-based policies, the guardrails that cap them, the evaluation logic worked by hand for a request with an allow and an explicit deny, assumed roles and temporary credentials, how least privilege is achieved in practice, and the classic mistakes — with a real confused-deputy bug in an AWS service as the case.
primer:
Think of IAM as the security desk of a large office building that never sleeps and never makes exceptions.

Every time anyone wants to do anything — open a door, use a printer, take a file from a cabinet — they must present a badge at the desk and state exactly what they want: "I'm badge 4417, I want to open the file cabinet in room 3B, it's Tuesday at 14:00, and I came in through the main entrance." The desk has a binder of rules. Some rules are clipped to people ("badge 4417 may open cabinets on floor 3"). Some are taped to the objects themselves ("this cabinet may be opened by anyone from the finance department"). And some are building-wide notices from management ("nobody may remove files from the building after 18:00", "floor 9 is off-limits to contractors"). The desk applies them the same way every time: if any rule says no to this exact request, the answer is no. Otherwise, if management's notices permit it and some rule says yes, the answer is yes. If no rule says yes, the answer is no.

Map that to the cloud. The badge is a principal — the identity making the request, proven by a cryptographic signature on the API call. "Open" is the action (s3:GetObject). "The cabinet in room 3B" is the resource (arn:aws:s3:::acme-ml-datasets/train/part-0001.parquet). Tuesday at 14:00 and the main entrance are the request context: time, source IP, whether TLS was used, tags on the caller and the resource. Rules clipped to people are identity-based policies, rules taped to objects are resource-based policies, and management's notices are guardrails such as service control policies. The fixed procedure is policy evaluation.

Two more ideas complete the mental model. First, the safest badges are temporary. Instead of giving a program a permanent key, you create a role — a set of permissions with no key of its own — and let the program assume it, which returns credentials that expire after an hour or so. Stolen temporary credentials stop working on their own. Second, the goal is least privilege: each principal can do what its job needs and nothing else, so a compromise of one component stays small.

Where the analogy breaks: a human security desk might use judgement, notice something odd, or let the CEO through. IAM does none of that. It applies the rules exactly, including the rules you didn't mean to write, and it evaluates every one of billions of requests in milliseconds. That precision is its strength — you can reason about it like code — and the reason a single wildcard can be catastrophic. (One exception to "no VIPs": the account's root user, covered below.) Keep the desk in mind through the rest of the lesson: every question of the form "why was this denied?" is answered by replaying the desk's procedure, rule by rule, against the exact request that was made.
body:
1. Principals: who can make a request

A principal is whatever signs an API request. AWS requests are signed with a secret key using the Signature Version 4 scheme: the client computes an HMAC (a keyed hash, au4) over the request using its secret access key, and AWS recomputes it to prove the caller holds the key. The access key ID in the request tells AWS which principal that is. The kinds of principal are:

  • The root user. Created with the account, signs in with the account's email address. It has full access that identity policies can't limit (AWS's evaluation documentation states that all requests are implicitly denied "with the exception of the AWS account root user, which has full access"). In an organisation, SCPs can restrict member accounts' root users. Use it only for the handful of tasks that require it, protect it with MFA (au7), and never create access keys for it.
  • IAM users. Long-lived identities with an optional console password and up to two long-term access keys (IDs beginning AKIA). They were the original model and are now the main source of leaked credentials; modern practice avoids them.
  • Roles and role sessions. A role has permissions but no credentials. A principal that the role's trust policy allows calls STS (the Security Token Service) to assume it and gets temporary credentials: an access key ID beginning ASIA, a secret, and a session token, all expiring together. The principal that then makes requests is the role session, with an ARN like arn:aws:sts::111122223333:assumed-role/ml-training/job-8812, where the last part is a session name chosen at assumption time.
  • Federated principals. Humans authenticated by an external identity provider (Okta, Entra ID, Google Workspace, IAM Identity Center) or workloads authenticated by an OIDC issuer (a Kubernetes cluster, GitHub Actions) exchange that proof for a role session. au10 traced this for workloads.
  • Service principals. AWS services acting on your behalf, named like lambda.amazonaws.com or ec2.amazonaws.com. When you create a Lambda function you give it an execution role whose trust policy allows lambda.amazonaws.com to assume it.

Groups exist (collections of IAM users to attach policies to) but are not principals — you can't name a group in a resource policy.

2. The policy language

A policy is a JSON document with a Version (always "2012-10-17", the current language version; omitting it falls back to an older version without policy variables) and a list of statements. Each statement has:

  • Effect: Allow or Deny.
  • Action (or NotAction): API operations as service:Operation, with * and ? wildcards — s3:GetObject, s3:Get*, ec2:Describe*.
  • Resource (or NotResource): ARNs the statement applies to, with wildcards. Some actions don't support resource-level scoping and need "*" — for example many Describe/List calls. The Service Authorization Reference lists, for every action, which resource types and condition keys it supports.
  • Principal: only in resource-based policies — who the statement is about.
  • Condition: optional tests on the request context.

Here is the identity-based policy we will evaluate later, attached to a role named ml-training:

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    { "Sid": "ReadDatasets",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["s3:GetObject"],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::acme-ml-datasets/*" },
    { "Sid": "ListDatasets",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": "s3:ListBucket",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::acme-ml-datasets" },
    { "Sid": "WriteCheckpoints",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["s3:PutObject"],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::acme-ml-checkpoints/runs/*" },
    { "Sid": "NoPiiWithoutClearance",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": "s3:GetObject",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::acme-ml-datasets/pii/*",
      "Condition": { "StringNotEquals": { "aws:PrincipalTag/data-clearance": "pii" } } }
  ]
}

Notice the two ARN forms for S3: the bucket (arn:aws:s3:::acme-ml-datasets) for bucket-level actions like ListBucket, and objects (arn:aws:s3:::acme-ml-datasets/*) for object-level actions like GetObject. Mixing them up is the commonest reason a policy "should work but doesn't". The Sid is just a label.

Conditions use an operator, a condition key and values. Operators include StringEquals, StringLike (with wildcards), StringNotEquals, ArnLike, IpAddress, Bool, NumericLessThan, DateGreaterThan, and ...IfExists variants. Global keys available on most requests include aws:PrincipalTag/key (tags on the calling role or user), aws:ResourceTag/key, aws:RequestTag/key (tags being set in this request), aws:PrincipalOrgID (the caller's AWS organisation), aws:SourceIp, aws:SourceVpce (the VPC endpoint the request came through), aws:SecureTransport (whether TLS was used), aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent, aws:RequestedRegion, aws:SourceAccount and aws:SourceArn (for requests made by a service on behalf of a resource). Services add their own, such as s3:prefix. Multiple keys in one condition block are ANDed; multiple values for one key are ORed. A key that's absent from the request makes ordinary operators evaluate to false — except the negated ones like StringNotEquals, which evaluate to true when the key is missing, which is why the Deny above also blocks sessions with no clearance tag at all.

Policies can include variables: "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::home-dirs/${aws:username}/*" gives each user their own prefix with one policy.

3. Where policies live: identity-based, resource-based and guardrails

Policies come in kinds, distinguished by where they are attached and whether they can grant:

KindAttached toCan grant?Typical use
Identity-based (managed or inline)user, group, roleyeswhat this workload or person may do
Resource-basedbucket, queue, KMS key, role (trust policy)…yeswho may use this resource, including other accounts
Service control policy (SCP)organisation root, OU, accountno — caps principalsorganisation-wide rules: regions, logging, leaving the org
Resource control policy (RCP)organisation root, OU, accountno — caps resources"our buckets can never be read from outside the org"
Permissions boundaryuser or roleno — caps that identitysafe delegation of role creation
Session policyone role sessionno — caps that sessionnarrowing a broad role for one task

Managed policies are standalone documents you can attach to many identities (up to 20 per role by default, raisable to 25, as of October 2026; each at most 6,144 characters, not counting whitespace). Inline policies are embedded in one identity (a role's inline policies together can be up to 10,240 characters). AWS also publishes AWS managed policies like ReadOnlyAccess — convenient, but broad, and AWS adds actions to them when services launch features.

A role has two policies with different jobs. Its permissions policies (identity-based) say what the role can do. Its trust policy (resource-based, with the role as the resource) says who can become the role:

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Principal": { "Service": "sagemaker.amazonaws.com" },
    "Action": "sts:AssumeRole",
    "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "aws:SourceAccount": "111122223333" } }
  }]
}

This one lets the SageMaker service assume the role, but only when acting on behalf of resources in account 111122223333 — the condition that blocks the cross-service confused deputy described in the deep section.

4. The evaluation logic, step by step

AWS's documentation describes evaluation as a fixed sequence. For a request within one account:

  1. Start at deny. Every request is implicitly denied unless something allows it.
  2. Explicit deny check. Look through every applicable policy — RCPs, SCPs, the resource-based policy, identity-based policies, the permissions boundary, the session policy — for a Deny statement matching this request. If there is even one, the final answer is Deny. Stop.
  3. RCPs. If the organisation uses resource control policies, they must contain an Allow for this action on this resource (AWS attaches a default RCPFullAWSAccess that allows everything, so this step mostly matters via Denies). Otherwise Deny.
  4. SCPs. The SCPs on every level from the organisation root down to the account must each allow the action (the default FullAWSAccess SCP allows everything; teams either keep it and add Deny SCPs, or replace it with allow-lists). Otherwise Deny.
  5. Resource-based policy. If it grants the action to this principal, it can be enough on its own in the same account. If it names the exact IAM user or role session, the answer is Allow even if identity policies, boundaries or session policies are silent. If it names the role's ARN (rather than the session), the session is still limited by any boundary and session policy.
  6. Identity-based policies. Otherwise, some identity-based policy must allow it. If none does: implicit Deny.
  7. Permissions boundary. If the identity has one, it must also allow the action. Otherwise Deny.
  8. Session policy. If this is a role session created with a session policy, it must also allow the action. Otherwise Deny.
  9. Allow.

Cross-account requests are evaluated twice: in the caller's account (identity-based policies plus that account's guardrails must allow) and in the resource's account (the resource-based policy plus that account's guardrails must allow). Both must say Allow. That's why sharing a bucket with another account needs a bucket policy naming the other account and an identity policy in the other account letting its role use the bucket. Two resource types are strict even within an account: a role's trust policy and a KMS key policy must explicitly allow the principal; an identity policy alone is not enough.

5. Worked example: an allow and an explicit deny

Set the scene in account 111122223333, part of an AWS organisation. The ml-training role has the identity policy from section 2 and no permissions boundary. It carries the tag data-clearance=none. The account's OU has two SCPs: the default FullAWSAccess and a region guardrail:

{ "Effect": "Deny",
  "NotAction": ["iam:*", "sts:*", "organizations:*", "support:*", "cloudfront:*", "route53:*"],
  "Resource": "*",
  "Condition": { "StringNotEquals": { "aws:RequestedRegion": ["eu-central-1", "eu-west-1"] } } }
