(NotAction exempts global services, whose requests are routed to us-east-1 and would otherwise be blocked.) The bucket acme-ml-datasets has a bucket policy that denies any request not made over TLS:

{ "Effect": "Deny", "Principal": "*", "Action": "s3:*",
  "Resource": ["arn:aws:s3:::acme-ml-datasets", "arn:aws:s3:::acme-ml-datasets/*"],
  "Condition": { "Bool": { "aws:SecureTransport": "false" } } }

Now evaluate five requests made by a session of ml-training:

#RequestExplicit deny?SCP allows?Grant?Result
1GetObject acme-ml-datasets/train/part-0001.parquet, HTTPS, eu-central-1none matchyesReadDatasetsAllow
2GetObject acme-ml-datasets/pii/users.parquet, HTTPS, eu-central-1NoPiiWithoutClearance: key under pii/ and tag ≠ "pii"—(ReadDatasets would)Deny (explicit)
3GetObject train/part-0001.parquet over plain HTTPbucket policy: SecureTransport = false——Deny (explicit)
4PutObject acme-ml-datasets/train/new.parquetnoneyesno statement allows PutObject hereDeny (implicit)
5GetObject train/part-0001.parquet, endpoint in us-east-1SCP region deny: s3 not in NotAction, region not listed——Deny (explicit)

Trace request 2 slowly, because it's the one interviewers ask about. The engine collects the SCPs, the bucket policy and the role's identity policy. It scans for Denies. The SCP region Deny: the condition aws:RequestedRegion not in the list is false (eu-central-1 is in the list), so it doesn't match. The bucket's TLS Deny: aws:SecureTransport is true, so Bool false doesn't match. The NoPiiWithoutClearance Deny: action s3:GetObject matches, resource arn:aws:s3:::acme-ml-datasets/pii/users.parquet matches .../pii/*, and StringNotEquals aws:PrincipalTag/data-clearance "pii" is true because the tag is "none". All three parts match: explicit Deny, final answer, no further steps. ReadDatasets is irrelevant even though it matches too.

Request 4 shows the other kind of no: nothing denies it, but nothing allows it either. The error message is the same AccessDenied, but the fix is different — an Allow would fix request 4, while nothing short of changing the Deny or the tag fixes request 2. Many services now say which kind of policy blocked a request in the error message ("explicit deny in a service control policy", "no identity-based policy allows"), which shortens debugging a lot.

Two variations sharpen it. If an engineer is given a session of the same role with the tag data-clearance=pii (for example passed as a session tag by the identity provider), request 2 becomes an Allow: the Deny's condition is now false, so the Deny doesn't match, and ReadDatasets grants. And if the role had a permissions boundary allowing only s3:ListBucket, request 1 would become an implicit Deny at the boundary step, despite ReadDatasets.

6. Assumed roles and temporary credentials

Assuming a role is an API call to STS. With the CLI (needs an AWS account):

aws sts assume-role \
  --role-arn arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/ml-training \
  --role-session-name job-8812 --duration-seconds 3600

The response, per the STS API reference, contains Credentials (an AccessKeyId beginning ASIA, a SecretAccessKey, a SessionToken and an Expiration time) and an AssumedRoleUser ARN of the form arn:aws:sts::111122223333:assumed-role/ml-training/job-8812. STS checks two things: that the role's trust policy allows the caller, and (for a caller in the same account that isn't named directly in the trust policy, or any caller in another account) that the caller's own identity policy allows sts:AssumeRole on that role.

The numbers worth knowing (from the STS API reference and IAM quotas page, October 2026): DurationSeconds ranges from 900 (15 minutes) to the role's maximum session duration, which can be set from 1 to 12 hours; the default is 3,600 seconds. Role chaining — using one role session to assume another role — caps the new session at one hour. A session policy passed at assumption (one inline JSON document plus up to 10 managed policy ARNs, together at most 2,048 characters) narrows the session to the intersection of the role's permissions and the session policy. Session tags (up to 50) become aws:PrincipalTag values for that session — that's how an identity provider's "department" attribute reaches policies. SourceIdentity records the original human through a chain of role assumptions, so CloudTrail logs can show who was behind assumed-role/deploy/…. The account-wide STS request quota was 600 requests per second per region for calls like AssumeRole, which matters for systems that assume roles per request instead of caching credentials until shortly before expiry.

Third-party access uses the same mechanism with one extra field. A monitoring vendor's account assumes a role in yours; your trust policy names the vendor's account and requires "sts:ExternalId": "<value the vendor gave you>". The external ID is the vendor's per-customer identifier; it prevents another of the vendor's customers from getting the vendor to assume your role by giving the vendor your role ARN (a confused deputy, explained in the deep section).

7. Least privilege in practice

Least privilege is easy to state and hard to do, because nobody knows the exact list of actions an application uses. The working method is a loop:

  1. Start scoped, not perfect. Write by resource and purpose: this service reads this bucket prefix and writes to this queue. Avoid AWS managed policies like AmazonS3FullAccess for workloads.
  2. Cap the blast radius. Guardrails make mistakes survivable: SCPs that deny unused regions and dangerous actions, permissions boundaries on roles developers create, resource policies that deny access from outside the organisation (an aws:PrincipalOrgID condition).
  3. Observe. CloudTrail (cl11) records every API call with the principal and outcome. IAM's "last accessed" data shows which services and actions a role has used and when. IAM Access Analyzer can generate a policy from a role's CloudTrail history, reports unused roles, keys and permissions, and reports resources and roles accessible from outside your organisation.
  4. Trim and repeat. Remove what wasn't used in, say, 90 days; review whenever the service changes.

Two tactics scale this beyond hand-written policies. One role per workload, never shared, so its permissions and its logs describe one thing. And ABAC (au8): instead of listing resources, compare tags — allow ec2:StopInstances when aws:ResourceTag/team equals ${aws:PrincipalTag/team}. New resources are covered automatically when tagged, at the cost that tagging becomes a security operation that must itself be restricted.

8. The classic IAM mistakes

These come up in nearly every cloud security review, and each has a mechanism behind it:

  • Long-lived access keys. IAM user keys in code, CI variables, laptops and container images are the most common initial access in cloud breaches. Replace with roles, federation (au10) and, for humans, single sign-on.
  • "Action": "*", "Resource": "*" on workloads. Turns any code execution in that workload into account takeover.
  • iam:PassRole on *. Lets a principal launch compute with any role, including admin, and read its credentials — privilege escalation without ever being granted admin. Scope it to specific roles and add iam:PassedToService.
  • Self-modifying permissions. iam:CreatePolicyVersion, iam:AttachRolePolicy, iam:PutRolePolicy or iam:UpdateAssumeRolePolicy on your own role or a more powerful one is admin with extra steps.
  • Trust policies that trust too much. "Principal": {"AWS": "*"} without conditions, an entire foreign account without an external ID, or an OIDC trust without a sub condition (au10).
  • Missing service-side conditions. Roles assumable by a service principal without aws:SourceAccount/aws:SourceArn, and resource policies granting a service principal without them.
  • NotAction with Allow. "Allow everything except IAM" also allows every action of every future service.
  • Using the root user for daily work, or leaving it without MFA.

9. The same ideas on Google Cloud and Azure

ConceptAWSGoogle CloudAzure
Workload identityIAM role (assumed)Service account (attached or impersonated)Managed identity (in Entra ID)
GrantPolicy document on identity or resourceRole binding in an allow policy on a resourceRole assignment: principal + role definition + scope
InheritanceNone (guardrails via Organizations)Organisation → folders → projects → resourcesManagement group → subscription → resource group → resource
DenyDeny statements anywhere, SCPs, RCPsIAM deny policiesDeny assignments; Azure Policy for configuration
Long-lived key to avoidIAM user access keyService account keyClient secret on an app registration

The shapes differ. On Google Cloud you rarely write policy documents; you grant a role — a bundle of permissions such as roles/storage.objectViewer — to a principal on a resource, and the grant is inherited by everything below that resource. On Azure, identity lives in Microsoft Entra ID and authorisation is Azure RBAC: role assignments are additive and inherit down the scope hierarchy, and deny assignments override them. The habits carry over: no long-lived keys, one identity per workload, grant at the narrowest scope, guardrails at the top.
deep:
The confused deputy, and why it keeps reappearing

A confused deputy is a program with authority that can be tricked into using it for someone else. In clouds the deputy is usually a service or a vendor that acts across many customers. Suppose a log-analysis vendor assumes a role in each customer's account from its own account. If customer A's trust policy only says "the vendor's account may assume this role", then customer B can register with the vendor, type in customer A's role ARN as "their" role, and the vendor — a deputy with access to every customer's trust — will fetch A's data for B. The external ID fixes this because the vendor assigns it, per customer, and sends it on every AssumeRole for that customer; B can't make the vendor send A's ID. When the deputy is an AWS service (S3 delivering to SNS, a service assuming your role), the equivalent is conditions on aws:SourceAccount and aws:SourceArn, which the service populates with the account and resource it's acting for. The pattern reappears whenever a new service accepts a role ARN or a resource ARN from its caller.

The case in miniature: AppSync, 2022

AWS AppSync lets developers create data sources that AppSync accesses using a role ARN the developer supplies; the role's trust policy allows appsync.amazonaws.com. AppSync checked that the supplied role belonged to the caller's own account. Datadog's researchers found that the API accepted the parameter name in mixed case, and that the lowercase spelling servicerolearn skipped the check, so a data source could reference a role in another account. Any role trusting AppSync without source conditions was then usable by any AWS customer — in their demonstration, to read a DynamoDB table across accounts. It was reported on 1 September 2022, fixed by AWS on 6 September, and disclosed on 21 November; AWS said it confirmed the issue had not been used against other customers. The lessons for your own designs: trust policies for service principals should carry aws:SourceAccount/aws:SourceArn conditions, because they turn a bug in the deputy into a denied request; and validation done in one layer (the API) is fragile compared with a check the authorisation system enforces.

Why default deny plus explicit deny is the right algebra

The evaluation rules make the permission set a simple function: (union of grants) minus (union of denies), intersected with each guardrail. That has useful properties. Adding an Allow can never remove access; adding a Deny can never add access; guardrails compose by intersection, so a platform team can add one without reading every team's policies. It also makes analysis tractable. AWS uses an automated-reasoning engine (described in its Zelkova research) to answer questions like "can anyone outside this organisation read this bucket?" over all possible requests, which powers Access Analyzer's external-access findings. The cost is expressiveness: there's no "allow unless" except by pairing an Allow with a Deny.

Policy size, sprawl and the tagging trade-off

Hard limits shape designs: 6,144 characters per managed policy, 10,240 for a role's inline policies combined, 20–25 managed policies per role, 2,048 characters for a session policy, a default trust policy length of 2,048 characters (raisable to 8,192). A platform with 300 buckets can't list every ARN in one policy. Teams respond with naming conventions and wildcards (arn:aws:s3:::acme-team-search-*), which are cheap but trust the naming discipline, or with ABAC on tags, which scales but moves security into tag management. Neither is free; a senior answer names the trade-off and the control that makes it safe (prefix ownership enforced by SCPs, or tag changes restricted and tags required at creation).

Revocation of temporary credentials

Issued STS credentials can't be recalled; they're validated cryptographically until they expire. Revocation is therefore done by policy: attach a Deny for sessions whose aws:TokenIssueTime is before now (the console's "revoke active sessions" does this), or remove the role's permissions. For long-lived IAM user keys, deactivate and delete them. This is why session lifetime is a security parameter: with one-hour sessions, a stolen credential has an expected useful life of half an hour after theft unless the attacker can mint more — and preventing that minting (the trust policy, the source identity) matters more than shaving minutes off the duration.

The perimeter, expressed in IAM

"Data perimeter" policies are a modern pattern that uses three condition keys to state "only our identities, on our resources, from our networks". Resource policies (or RCPs) deny access unless aws:PrincipalOrgID is your organisation; identity policies (or SCPs) deny access to resources outside your organisation (aws:ResourceOrgID); and network conditions (aws:SourceVpce, aws:SourceIp) deny use of credentials from outside your networks. Together they turn leaked credentials or a misconfigured bucket from a breach into a denied request, at the cost of carefully exempting AWS services that act on your behalf.

Human access is a different problem from workload access

Workloads have stable, narrow needs, so tight policies and long-term stability are realistic. Humans have broad, changing needs and make mistakes under pressure. Good human access design leans on federation with MFA, broad read access, narrow standing write access, and just-in-time elevation for the rest — a time-limited grant with approval and logging. The failure mode to avoid is the opposite: tight human policies that cause so much friction that someone creates an IAM user with admin keys "for emergencies" and keeps it forever.
prod:
Failure modes you will see

AccessDenied in production after a change. Causes, in rough order of frequency: a new code path calls an action the role doesn't allow; the wrong ARN form (bucket vs object); a new SCP or RCP from the platform team; a KMS key policy that doesn't include the role (S3 objects encrypted with a customer-managed key need kms:Decrypt on the key and the key policy must allow it); a condition key that isn't present for that action. Read the error message for the policy type, then check CloudTrail for the denied event with its errorCode and request parameters.

Leaked access keys. Keys pushed to a public repository are typically found by automated scanners within minutes. AWS scans public GitHub and notifies the account and can attach a quarantine policy, but attackers often move first: crypto-mining instances in every region, or enumeration and data access. Response: deactivate the key, review CloudTrail for its activity across all regions, remove any persistence the attacker created (new users, keys, roles, trust policy edits), then fix the pipeline that leaked it (au11's playbook).

Privilege escalation inside the account. A compromised low-privilege role uses PassRole, policy-version or function-update permissions to become admin. Detection: CloudTrail alerts on IAM write events from workload roles, which should almost never happen.

Over-trusting roles. Cross-account roles that trust whole accounts without external IDs, OIDC trusts missing a subject condition, roles assumable by *. Access Analyzer reports the external ones; reviews catch the rest.

STS throttling. A service that calls AssumeRole for every request hits the per-account STS quota (600 requests per second per region for these calls, October 2026) and starts failing under load. Cache credentials until close to expiry; SDK credential providers already do.

What to measure

Number of IAM users and active access keys (target: trending to zero), age of the oldest key, roles with administrator-equivalent permissions, roles unused for 90 days, externally accessible resources and roles, IAM write events by non-admin principals, denied API calls by role (a sudden rise often means an attack or a broken deploy), and root user sign-ins (should be essentially never, and always alerted).

Knobs

Maximum session duration per role (shorter for powerful roles), session tags from the identity provider for ABAC, SCPs for regions and protected services, permissions boundaries on developer-created roles, Access Analyzer's unused-access and external-access analysers, and IAM Identity Center permission sets in place of IAM users.

The case, read as an engineer

The AppSync bug (Datadog Security Labs, November 2022) is worth retelling in an interview because it ties together several ideas. AppSync is a deputy: it acts with roles customers give it. The protection was a validation check in the API layer rather than something IAM itself enforced. A parsing quirk — accepting servicerolearn as well as serviceRoleArn but validating only one spelling — opened a cross-account path. AWS fixed it within five days of the report and found no use against customers. What you control: every role trusting a service principal should say for which account and resource the service may assume it, so that if the service is confused, IAM still says no.
myths: An Allow in a policy means the request will succeed.

An Allow is necessary but not sufficient. The request also has to survive every explicit Deny in every applicable policy, and every guardrail in its path — service control policies, resource control policies, permissions boundaries and session policies — must also allow it. Guardrails never grant anything; they only cap what other policies grant. A role with AdministratorAccess in an account whose SCP denies everything outside two regions cannot launch an instance in a third.
IAM policies are evaluated in order, so put the important statement first.

Statement order doesn't matter. AWS gathers every applicable statement from every applicable policy and applies fixed rules: any matching explicit Deny wins; otherwise the request needs a matching Allow and must pass every guardrail; otherwise it is implicitly denied. Reordering statements never changes a decision.
A role is a kind of user with a password.

A role has no long-term credentials at all. It is a set of permissions plus a trust policy that says who may assume it. Assuming it returns temporary credentials — an access key ID, a secret and a session token — that expire, by default after one hour. That expiry is the main reason roles are safer than IAM users with access keys.
If my bucket policy doesn't mention someone, they can't access the bucket.

Within the same account, an identity-based policy alone is enough for most services: a role with s3:GetObject on arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket/* can read the bucket even if the bucket policy never names it. Bucket policies matter on their own for cross-account access (where both sides must allow), and for Deny statements that apply to everyone. Only some resource policies — role trust policies and KMS key policies — must explicitly allow the principal even within the account.
Least privilege means writing the perfect policy before launch.

Nobody knows the exact set of actions an application needs on day one. Least privilege is a loop: start from a reasonably scoped policy, run the workload, use access logs and tools such as IAM Access Analyzer's policy generation and last-accessed data to see what is actually used, then remove the rest — repeatedly. Guardrails (SCPs, boundaries) cap the blast radius while the loop runs.
Wildcards are always a mistake.

Wildcards are a tool: arn:aws:s3:::acme-ml-checkpoints/runs/* is exactly the right resource for 'all checkpoints'. The dangerous ones are wildcards on actions that change permissions (iam:*), on the principal of a trust or resource policy ("Principal": "*" without conditions), and Action "*" with Resource "*". Read each wildcard as 'what is the largest thing this could match, now and after the next service launch?'
lab:
Goal: build a toy policy evaluator that follows AWS's order, and use it to reproduce the five requests in section 5 — Python 3.12 standard library only (json, fnmatch). About 20 minutes.

  1. Matching. Write matches(stmt, req): actions and resources match with fnmatch.fnmatchcase (AWS action names are case-insensitive, resource ARNs case-sensitive — lowercase the actions); support NotAction; support conditions StringEquals, StringNotEquals (true when the key is missing) and Bool over a req["context"] dict.
  2. Evaluate. Write evaluate(req, scps, resource_policy, identity, boundary=None) returning ("Allow"|"Deny", reason): explicit deny in any policy → Deny; every SCP list must contain a matching Allow → else Deny; identity or resource Allow → else implicit Deny; boundary must allow if present.
  3. Load the scenario. Paste the identity policy, the SCPs (FullAWSAccess plus the region deny) and the bucket policy from the lesson as Python dicts.
  4. Run the five requests from the table, with context keys aws:SecureTransport, aws:RequestedRegion and aws:PrincipalTag/data-clearance.
  5. Variations. Set the tag to "pii" and rerun request 2; remove the tag entirely; add a boundary allowing only s3:ListBucket and rerun request 1.

What to look for: requests 2, 3 and 5 return explicit denies with different reasons and request 4 an implicit deny; request 1 is the only Allow. With pii, request 2 flips to Allow; with no tag it stays Deny (the negated operator treats a missing key as a match); with the boundary, request 1 becomes an implicit Deny. Shuffle the statement order: no result changes.

Needs an AWS account (optional): the IAM policy simulator (aws iam simulate-principal-policy --policy-source-arn <role-arn> --action-names s3:GetObject --resource-arns arn:aws:s3:::acme-ml-datasets/pii/users.parquet) returns an EvalDecision of explicitDeny, implicitDeny or allowed with the matching statements; compare it with your evaluator.
recap: IAM answers one question for every API call: may this principal perform this action on this resource under these conditions; the default answer is no.
Principals are the root user, IAM users, roles (assumed into temporary sessions), federated users and AWS services; prefer roles with temporary credentials over users with long-lived access keys.

A policy is JSON statements of Effect, Action, Resource, optional Principal and Condition; identity-based policies attach to principals, resource-based policies attach to resources and name principals.
Guardrails — SCPs and RCPs from AWS Organizations, permissions boundaries and session policies — never grant; they cap what identity and resource policies grant.

Evaluation: any applicable explicit Deny wins; then every guardrail must allow; then an identity- or resource-based Allow is needed (both, for cross-account); otherwise implicit deny. Statement order is irrelevant.
AssumeRole returns credentials valid for 15 minutes to 12 hours (one hour by default, and at most one hour when chaining roles), and the trust policy decides who may assume the role.

Least privilege is an iterative loop of scoping, observing actual use and trimming, with guardrails limiting damage while it runs; conditions on tags, organisation IDs, source accounts and network context make policies precise.
The classic mistakes are long-lived keys, wildcard admin, iam:PassRole on *, trust policies that trust too much, missing confused-deputy conditions, and treating the root user as an everyday account.

GCP binds roles to principals on resources in a hierarchy that inherits downward; Azure assigns role definitions to principals at a scope; both add deny mechanisms, but the AWS evaluation model is the one most interviews probe.
glossary: ABAC (attribute-based access control)
Granting access by comparing attributes, such as a tag on the principal with a tag on the resource, instead of listing every resource by name.
Access key
A long-term credential for an IAM user: an access key ID (starting AKIA) and a secret access key used to sign API requests.
Action
The API operation a statement is about, written service:Operation, such as s3:GetObject or ec2:RunInstances.
ARN (Amazon Resource Name)
The unique name of an AWS resource that policies use in Resource and Principal elements (cl1).
AssumeRole
The STS operation that returns temporary credentials for a role, if the role's trust policy allows the caller.
Condition
The optional part of a statement that must be true for it to apply, for example a tag value, the caller's organisation, or whether TLS was used.
Condition key
A named value in the request context that conditions test, such as aws:PrincipalTag/team, aws:SourceIp or aws:SecureTransport.
Confused deputy
A privileged service that is tricked into using its authority on behalf of someone who shouldn't have it.
Explicit deny
A Deny statement that matches the request; it overrides every Allow.
External ID
A value a third party must pass when assuming a role in your account, used in the trust policy to stop other customers of that third party from using the same role.
IAM (Identity and Access Management)
The cloud service that defines principals and the policies deciding what each may do; on AWS it is global.
Identity-based policy
A policy attached to a user, group or role that says what that principal may do.
Implicit deny
The default outcome when no statement allows a request.
KMS (Key Management Service)
The managed service that holds encryption keys and performs encrypt and decrypt operations under its own key policies (au11).
Least privilege
Granting only the permissions a principal needs for its task, and no more.
Managed policy
A standalone, reusable policy that can be attached to many principals; AWS managed policies are written by AWS, customer managed by you.
Permissions boundary
A managed policy set on a user or role that caps the maximum permissions its identity-based policies can grant.
PII (personally identifiable information)
Data that identifies a person, such as names, emails or account numbers; often subject to legal protection.
Policy
A JSON document of statements that allows or denies actions on resources under conditions.
Principal
The entity making a request: the root user, an IAM user, a role session, a federated user or an AWS service.
RCP (resource control policy)
An AWS Organizations guardrail attached to accounts or OUs that caps what can be done to the resources in them, whoever the caller is.
Resource
The thing an action is performed on, named by its ARN in a policy.
Resource-based policy
A policy attached to a resource, such as a bucket policy or a role trust policy, that names which principals may act on it.
Role
An IAM identity with permissions but no long-term credentials; principals allowed by its trust policy assume it to get temporary credentials.
Role chaining
Using a role session's credentials to assume another role; sessions created this way last at most one hour.
Root user
The identity created with an AWS account, which has full access that ordinary policies cannot restrict; use it only for the few tasks that require it.
SCP (service control policy)
An AWS Organizations guardrail attached to accounts or OUs that caps what principals in those accounts can do.
Service principal
An AWS service acting as a principal, named like lambda.amazonaws.com, for example when it assumes a role you created for it.
Session policy
A policy passed when assuming a role that narrows the permissions of that one session.
Statement
One rule inside a policy: an Effect (Allow or Deny), Actions, Resources, and optionally a Principal and Conditions.
STS (Security Token Service)
The AWS service that issues temporary credentials, for example when a role is assumed.
Temporary credentials
An access key ID (starting ASIA), secret key and session token issued by STS that expire after a set time.
Trust policy
The resource-based policy on a role that says which principals may assume it, and under what conditions.
drill:
Diagnose: "I added the permission and it's still denied"

A data engineer's Glue job runs as role etl-orders in account 444455556666. It needs to read s3://partner-drop/orders/2026-10-07.csv, a bucket owned by a partner in account 777788889999, objects encrypted with the partner's customer-managed KMS key. The engineer added s3:GetObject on arn:aws:s3:::partner-drop/* to the role. The job fails with AccessDenied. The partner says "we added your account to our bucket policy". List the possible causes in the order you'd check them and how you'd confirm each.

Answer

1. The error text. Read the full AccessDenied message: S3 now often says whether a bucket policy, an identity policy, an SCP or a KMS key policy blocked it, which shortcuts everything below.

2. Cross-account needs both sides. The role's identity policy now allows GetObject (side one). Confirm the partner's bucket policy really grants s3:GetObject on arn:aws:s3:::partner-drop/* (object ARN, not the bucket ARN) to arn:aws:iam::444455556666:role/etl-orders or the account root principal.

3. KMS. With a customer-managed key, reading also needs kms:Decrypt: the partner's key policy must allow your role or account, and your role's identity policy must allow kms:Decrypt on the key's ARN. This is the most commonly missed piece; CloudTrail in your account shows a denied Decrypt event if it's the cause.

4. Guardrails on either side. An SCP in your organisation might deny access to resources outside your organisation (an aws:ResourceOrgID data-perimeter rule), or the partner's RCP or bucket policy might deny principals outside their organisation. Either is an explicit deny that no Allow fixes; it needs an exception.

5. Object ownership. If objects were uploaded by a third account and the bucket's ownership setting doesn't make the bucket owner own them, the bucket policy doesn't apply to those objects. Ask the partner to check the bucket's Object Ownership setting.

6. Network conditions. The bucket policy may require aws:SourceVpce or an IP range that your Glue job doesn't come from.

Confirm with CloudTrail in both accounts (the partner sees the data event if they log it), and the policy simulator for your side.
qa: E
What is the difference between an IAM user and an IAM role?

A user is a long-lived identity that can have a password and long-term access keys. A role has permissions but no credentials of its own: principals that its trust policy allows assume it and receive temporary credentials that expire, one hour by default. Workloads, cross-account access and humans signing in through single sign-on should use roles; IAM users with access keys are a legacy pattern kept only where nothing else works.

Follow-up: how do humans get roles without IAM users? — Through federation: IAM Identity Center or an external identity provider authenticates the person (with MFA) and hands them a role session in the account they choose.
E
What does 'explicit deny overrides allow' mean, and why is it designed that way?

If any applicable statement in any applicable policy says Deny for this request, the request is denied, no matter how many Allows exist elsewhere. It's designed that way so that guardrails are reliable: a security team can write a Deny ('nobody may disable CloudTrail', 'nothing outside the EU') knowing no team can override it by adding an Allow somewhere. Without it, permissions would depend on the order or number of policies.

Follow-up: what's the difference between an explicit and an implicit deny? — Implicit deny is the default when nothing allows the request; adding an Allow fixes it. Explicit deny is a matching Deny statement; no Allow can fix it, only changing the Deny.
E
Write a policy that lets a role read objects in one S3 bucket.

Two resources are needed because bucket-level and object-level actions have different ARNs: {"Effect":"Allow","Action":"s3:ListBucket","Resource":"arn:aws:s3:::acme-ml-datasets"} and {"Effect":"Allow","Action":"s3:GetObject","Resource":"arn:aws:s3:::acme-ml-datasets/*"}. Putting GetObject on the bucket ARN, or ListBucket on bucket/*, matches nothing, which is one of the most common reasons such policies 'don't work'.
Follow-up: how would you restrict listing to one prefix? — Add a condition on ListBucket: "StringLike": {"s3:prefix": ["train/*"]}, and scope GetObject to arn:aws:s3:::acme-ml-datasets/train/*.
M
Walk through how AWS evaluates a request in a single account.

Gather every applicable policy: SCPs and RCPs from the organisation, resource-based policy, identity-based policies, permissions boundary, session policy. Step one: if any has a matching Deny, deny. Step two: the RCPs and SCPs in the path must contain a matching Allow, else deny. Step three: an Allow must come from an identity-based policy or a resource-based policy. Step four: if there's a permissions boundary it must also allow, and if it's a role session with a session policy, that must allow too. Otherwise allow. One subtlety: a resource-based policy that names the exact user or role session can grant access even without an identity-based Allow, and isn't limited by the boundary or session policy in that case.

Follow-up: how does cross-account change it? — The request is evaluated in both accounts: the caller's account must allow it through identity-based policies (and guardrails there), and the resource's account must allow it through the resource-based policy (and guardrails there). Both must say allow.
M
What is a confused deputy in IAM, and how do you prevent it for a third-party integration?

A third-party SaaS that monitors many customers' accounts uses a role in each, assumed from the vendor's account. If your role's trust policy only checks 'the vendor's account', another vendor customer could give the vendor your role ARN and make the vendor read your account on their behalf. The fix is an external ID: a unique value the vendor generates per customer, which your trust policy requires via sts:ExternalId, so only requests made for you carry it. For AWS services acting as a deputy, the equivalent is conditions on aws:SourceAccount or aws:SourceArn.

Follow-up: who should generate the external ID? — The vendor, per customer, and the customer must not be able to choose it; otherwise an attacker can set their own account's external ID to match yours.
M
What are SCPs and permissions boundaries, and when would you use each?

Both cap permissions without granting any. An SCP attaches to accounts or organisational units and limits every principal in those accounts (except the management account), set centrally by the platform team: region restrictions, 'never leave the organisation', 'never disable logging'. A permissions boundary attaches to a single user or role and caps what its identity policies can grant; its classic use is delegated administration — letting developers create roles for their Lambda functions, but only roles whose boundary prevents them from exceeding the developers' own scope.

Follow-up: why doesn't an SCP protect against the management account? — SCPs don't apply to the management account's principals at all, which is why the management account should run nothing but organisation administration.
M
Why is iam:PassRole dangerous, and how should it be scoped?

PassRole lets a principal hand a role to a service — 'launch this instance with role X', 'create this Lambda function running as role Y'. If a developer can pass any role, they can launch an instance with the admin role attached and read its credentials from inside, escalating to admin without ever being granted admin permissions directly. Scope PassRole to specific role ARNs (or a path like role/app/*) and use the iam:PassedToService condition so a role can only be passed to the service it was made for.

Follow-up: name another escalation path. — iam:CreatePolicyVersion with --set-as-default on a policy attached to yourself; lambda:UpdateFunctionCode on a function that runs as a powerful role; iam:UpdateAssumeRolePolicy on a privileged role.
M
How does attribute-based access control with tags work on AWS, and what are its risks?

Instead of listing resources, you compare tags: allow ec2:StopInstances when aws:ResourceTag/team equals ${aws:PrincipalTag/team}. New resources tagged team=search are automatically covered for the search team's roles; no policy edit needed. The risks: tags become security attributes, so whoever can change tags can change access — you must restrict ec2:CreateTags and tag changes (aws:RequestTag, aws:TagKeys conditions) and require tags at creation. And not every action supports every condition key, so check the service authorization reference.

Follow-up: where do principal tags come from for humans? — From the identity provider as session tags when they sign in, so a department attribute in the directory becomes aws:PrincipalTag/department in every session.
M
How long do temporary credentials last, and what are the trade-offs in choosing the duration?

AssumeRole sessions last 15 minutes to 12 hours, one hour by default, capped by the role's maximum session duration; a session obtained by chaining from another role session is capped at one hour. Shorter sessions limit how long stolen credentials work and make revocation faster; longer ones help long-running jobs and humans who don't want to re-authenticate. SDKs refresh credentials automatically for workloads, so short sessions cost little; for long batch jobs, make sure the job refreshes rather than raising the maximum.

Follow-up: how do you revoke an active role session? — You can't delete issued credentials, but you can add a deny for sessions issued before now (an aws:TokenIssueTime condition, which the console's 'revoke active sessions' does for you), then fix the root cause.
H

Evaluate this: a role's identity policy allows s3:GetObject on arn:aws:s3:::acme-ml-datasets/*, a second statement denies s3:GetObject on acme-ml-datasets/pii/* unless the principal tag data-clearance is 'pii', the bucket policy denies any request without TLS, and an SCP denies everything outside eu-central-1. What happens to GetObject of pii/users.parquet over HTTPS in eu-central-1 by a session tagged data-clearance=none?

Gather policies, then look for an explicit Deny first. The SCP's region deny doesn't match (the request is in eu-central-1). The bucket policy's TLS deny doesn't match (aws:SecureTransport is true). The identity policy's pii deny does match: the key is under pii/, and StringNotEquals aws:PrincipalTag/data-clearance 'pii' is true for 'none'. One matching explicit Deny ends evaluation: denied, even though the first statement allows the object. The same session reading train/part-0001.parquet passes all Denies, the SCP allows (default FullAWSAccess plus no matching deny), the identity Allow matches, there's no boundary or session policy: allowed.

Follow-up: what if the session had no data-clearance tag at all? — StringNotEquals with a missing key evaluates to true, so the Deny still applies. That's the safe default; using StringEquals in an Allow would also fail closed. Be careful with ...IfExists operators, which flip missing keys to 'match'.
H
Design the IAM setup for a team of 40 engineers across dev, staging and prod accounts, plus CI/CD and 30 services.

Humans sign in once through IAM Identity Center federated to the company IdP with MFA, and get permission sets per account: broad in dev, read-mostly in staging and prod, with a separate break-glass admin set that pages security when used. No IAM users. CI/CD deploys via OIDC federation (au10): one deploy role per account trusting only the main branch or protected environment of each repository. Each service gets its own role with least-privilege policies generated from observed use, attached via EKS pod identity or the compute service's role. Guardrails: SCPs denying unused regions, disabling CloudTrail or leaving the organisation; permissions boundaries on any role that developers may create. Access Analyzer for external and unused access; quarterly review of permission sets.

Follow-up: how do you handle an urgent prod fix needing write access? — Just-in-time elevation: a time-bound permission set granted through an approval workflow, logged and expiring automatically, rather than standing write access.
H
A security review finds 'Principal': {'AWS': '*'} in a role trust policy. How bad is it, and what would you check?

It means any AWS principal in any account can attempt to assume the role, so the only protection is whatever Condition block is present. With no conditions it's a full public backdoor: anyone with any AWS account gets the role's permissions. Check the conditions (an aws:PrincipalOrgID restricting to your organisation, or an sts:ExternalId, makes it far narrower), check CloudTrail for AssumeRole events from unknown accounts, check the role's permissions, and use IAM Access Analyzer, which reports roles assumable from outside your zone of trust.

Follow-up: why would anyone write it intentionally? — To let every account in a large organisation assume a role without listing hundreds of account IDs; the correct form is Principal '*' plus a condition aws:PrincipalOrgID equal to the organisation ID.
H
Compare AWS IAM with Google Cloud IAM and Azure RBAC.

AWS attaches JSON policies to identities and resources and evaluates them with explicit-deny-wins logic, with guardrails from Organizations. Google Cloud binds roles (bundles of permissions: basic, predefined or custom) to principals in allow policies on resources in a hierarchy — organisation, folders, projects, resources — and bindings inherit downward; deny policies and IAM Conditions were added later. Azure separates identity (Microsoft Entra ID) from authorisation (Azure RBAC): a role assignment ties a principal to a role definition at a scope (management group, subscription, resource group or resource), assignments are additive and inherit down, and deny assignments override. The practical difference: on GCP and Azure you mostly think 'which role at which scope'; on AWS you also write policy documents and reason about evaluation.

Follow-up: what's the GCP equivalent of an IAM role assumed by a workload? — A service account, which workloads impersonate or attach; service account keys are the GCP version of long-lived access keys and should be avoided in favour of attached accounts and workload identity federation.
refs: Policy evaluation logic (AWS IAM User Guide)
The authoritative order of evaluation: explicit deny, RCPs, SCPs, resource-based, identity-based, boundaries and session policies, with the same-account subtleties.
AWS AppSync vulnerability disclosure (Datadog Security Labs, November 2022)
The case: a case-sensitivity bug let AppSync assume roles in other accounts — a cross-tenant confused deputy, fixed in five days.
Why cross-account requests need an Allow on both sides, with a worked bucket example.
Session durations, role chaining, session policies (2,048 characters, up to 10 ARNs), external IDs, source identity and session tags.
The confused deputy problem (AWS IAM User Guide)
External IDs for third parties and aws:SourceArn / aws:SourceAccount for cross-service confused deputies.
Policy size limits, managed policies per role, trust policy length and the STS request quota.
Principals, roles, allow policies and the resource hierarchy, for comparison.
What is Azure role-based access control (Azure RBAC)?
Security principal, role definition and scope; how role and deny assignments combine.

t: Cloud networking: VPCs, public and private subnets, route tables, internet and NAT gateways, security groups vs NACLs, peering, transit gateways, PrivateLink and data-transfer cost
sum: How a cloud network is built and what it costs: a VPC CIDR plan for three zones worked with real numbers, reserved addresses, route tables and how each gateway behaves (internet, NAT zonal and regional, egress-only), security groups versus network ACLs in depth, VPC DNS, peering versus Transit Gateway versus PrivateLink and gateway endpoints, the price of every traffic path, and GCP and Azure differences — with Slack's January 2021 Transit Gateway outage as the case.
prereq: net3

CIDR notation and subnet maths, private ranges, NAT, route tables with longest-prefix match; in a VPC a subnet is public if its default route points at an internet gateway and private if it points at a NAT gateway.
net14

Security groups are stateful allow-only firewalls on network interfaces that can reference other groups; network ACLs are stateless ordered rules on subnets; private connectivity uses endpoints, peering and transit gateways.
cl1
Regions contain availability zones; AWS subnets are zonal, VPCs are regional; cross-zone traffic is billed on AWS; control-plane changes are best avoided during incidents.
cl2
IAM decides which API calls a principal may make; resource policies can add conditions such as aws:SourceVpce to require that requests arrive through a particular VPC endpoint.
why:
A team moves a monolith to the cloud. They accept the console's defaults: one VPC with a 10.0.0.0/16 range, a couple of subnets, everything in a public subnet "for now" because it's easier to SSH in. Over two years the company grows to 30 accounts. Then four things happen.

A partner integration needs a private connection, and the partner's network is also 10.0.0.0/16 — the two can't be routed together. An acquisition brings another set of VPCs with the same overlap. The finance team asks why the AWS bill has a $14,000 line for "NAT Gateway" when the product barely talks to the internet; the answer is that terabytes of S3 reads from private subnets were going through the NAT gateway, at $0.045 a gigabyte, for no reason. And during a zone outage, all private instances lose outbound internet access, because the single NAT gateway lived in the zone that failed.

None of these was a bug. Each was a networking decision made by default, early, and expensive to reverse: address ranges are almost impossible to change once workloads use them, and routing mistakes hide in the bill. Cloud networking looks like it's taken care of — there's no hardware to rack — but the provider only gives you building blocks. You decide the address plan, which subnets can reach the internet and how, which firewall rules apply, how VPCs connect to each other and to your offices, and, through all of that, what every byte costs.

This lesson goes beyond net3 and net14, which introduced VPCs, subnets, route tables, NAT, security groups and NACLs. It plans a real three-zone address layout with numbers, follows packets through each gateway, compares security groups and NACLs at the level that interviewers probe, explains the options for connecting many VPCs (peering, Transit Gateway, PrivateLink, endpoints) and their failure and cost behaviour, prices every traffic path from the official price list, and compares AWS with Google Cloud and Azure. The case is Slack's January 2021 outage, which began in a Transit Gateway.
primer:
Picture a cloud network as a gated business park that you design on an empty plot of land.

The VPC is the plot, with its own address scheme: you choose a block of addresses, say 10.20.0.0/16 (65,536 addresses), and every building you put on the plot gets an address from it. The plot sits in one region. Inside it you lay out subnets, which are like separate fenced lots; on AWS each lot is in one availability zone (one physically separate data centre campus, cl1). You'll normally build the same three lots in each of three zones: one facing the street for things the public must reach (load balancers), one behind it for application servers, and one at the back for databases.

Route tables are the signposts at each lot's exit. Every signpost says "anything for the park's own addresses, stay inside" (the local route). The street-facing lot's signpost adds "everything else: out through the main gate" — the internet gateway, which is what makes the lot public. The application lot's signpost says "everything else: through the courier office" — a NAT gateway, which sends parcels out on the application servers' behalf and brings replies back, but never lets a stranger walk in. That is what makes the lot private. The database lot may have no exit to the outside at all.

Every building has a guard at its own door — a security group — who has a list of who may come in ("the application servers, on port 5432") and remembers whoever went out so their replies are let back in. Each lot can also have a gate guard — a network ACL — who checks every person in both directions against a numbered list and remembers nothing.

Two things make this more than a diagram. First, almost nothing about the address plan can be changed later without moving workloads, so the plan is a long-lived decision. Second, every arrow has a price. Bytes that stay in a zone are free; bytes that cross zones, pass through a NAT gateway or a transit hub, cross regions or leave for the internet are each billed per gigabyte. A cloud network is therefore designed twice: once for reachability and safety, and once for cost.

Connecting several parks is the next layer. Two parks can build a private road between them (peering), but a road only joins those two; with dozens of parks you build a central interchange that every park connects to once (a transit gateway). And when a park only needs to use one service in another park — not reach everything there — the other park can open a private service window directly into your lot (PrivateLink), with no road at all.

Where the analogy breaks: the "gates" and "courier office" are not buildings with a fixed capacity you can see; they're distributed software that scales automatically — usually. When they don't scale fast enough, or when a single "office" lives in one zone, they become hidden single points of failure. That's what Slack learned in 2021.
body:
1. The address plan, worked

On AWS a VPC gets a primary IPv4 CIDR block between /16 (65,536 addresses) and /28 (16), and up to five blocks in total by default (raisable to 50) through secondary CIDRs. Each subnet takes a slice of a VPC block, lives in exactly one zone, and must also be between /16 and /28. In every subnet AWS reserves five addresses. In 10.20.0.0/19, they are 10.20.0.0 (network address), 10.20.0.1 (the VPC router), 10.20.0.2 (DNS — strictly, the DNS server is at the VPC's base plus two, and the base plus two of every subnet is reserved), 10.20.0.3 (reserved for future use) and 10.20.31.255 (broadcast, reserved even though VPCs don't support broadcast). So a /24 gives 251 usable addresses, not 254.

Now plan a production VPC for an ML-serving platform in three zones. Requirements: an EKS cluster whose pods get VPC addresses (the default AWS VPC CNI behaviour), up to about 6,000 pods per zone at peak; databases and caches; load balancers and NAT gateways; and room to grow.

Step 1: choose a block that won't collide. Pick 10.20.0.0/16 from a central plan (IPAM, below) so that no other VPC, office or likely partner uses it.

Step 2: size each tier per zone for its largest consumer. 6,000 pods plus nodes need more than 4,091 (a /20's usable count) and fit in 8,187 (a /19's), so application subnets are /19s. Databases and caches need tens of addresses; /22s (1,019 usable) leave plenty of headroom for read replicas and managed services that create several interfaces. Public subnets only hold load-balancer nodes and NAT gateways; /24s are ample.

Step 3: lay the blocks out in order, biggest first, so they stay aligned:

TierAZ 1AZ 2AZ 3Usable each
Private app10.20.0.0/1910.20.32.0/1910.20.64.0/198,187
Data10.20.96.0/2210.20.100.0/2210.20.104.0/221,019
Public10.20.108.0/2410.20.109.0/2410.20.110.0/24251
Free10.20.111.0 – 10.20.255.255 (145 /24s, ~37,000 addresses)—

The plan uses 28,416 of 65,536 addresses and leaves the top of the range for a fourth zone, a dedicated tier for interface endpoints, or a second cluster. You can check every line with Python's ipaddress module — that's the lab.

Why plan centrally. Two VPCs with overlapping ranges cannot be peered or routed through a Transit Gateway, and changing a VPC's addresses means moving every workload in it. Organisations with many accounts use an IP address manager (Amazon VPC IPAM, or a spreadsheet in small shops) that hands out non-overlapping blocks: for example a /12 per region (16 /16s) split into a /16 per account-VPC. Leave ranges aside for on-premises networks and for the Kubernetes service CIDR (k8s8), which also must not overlap anything pods talk to.

2. Route tables and the gateways they point at

Each subnet is associated with one route table; a route table can serve many subnets. A route says "destination CIDR → target", and the most specific match wins (longest-prefix match, net3). Every route table starts with a local route for each VPC CIDR, which can't be removed, so all subnets in a VPC can reach each other unless security groups or NACLs say otherwise. The targets you'll meet:

  • Internet gateway (IGW). One per VPC, horizontally scaled and redundant by AWS, with no bandwidth limit of its own. It does one-to-one translation between an instance's private IP and its public IP (an auto-assigned public IPv4 or an Elastic IP). An instance without a public IP can't use it, even in a public subnet. Since February 2024 AWS charges for every public IPv4 address, in use or idle — $0.005 per hour (about $3.65 a month) in October 2026 — which is one reason to keep instances out of public subnets.
  • NAT gateway. Covered in detail next.
  • Egress-only internet gateway. For IPv6, where every address is globally routable and there's no translation; it allows outbound-initiated IPv6 traffic and blocks inbound.
  • VPC endpoints, peering connections, Transit Gateway attachments, virtual private gateways (VPN) and network interfaces of appliances (for routing through a firewall).

Trace one packet. An application pod at 10.20.5.17 in AZ 1 calls api.partner.example, which resolves to 203.0.113.50. The pod's subnet route table has 10.20.0.0/16 → local, pl-s3 → vpce-s3 (a prefix list of S3's address ranges, added by the gateway endpoint) and 0.0.0.0/0 → nat-az1. 203.0.113.50 matches only the default route, so the VPC router delivers the packet to the NAT gateway in AZ 1's public subnet. The NAT gateway rewrites the source to its own private IP (10.20.108.9, say) and source port, tracks the mapping, and forwards it; the public subnet's route table sends it to the IGW, which translates 10.20.108.9 to the NAT gateway's Elastic IP, 198.51.100.7. The partner sees a connection from 198.51.100.7:43120. The reply follows the same path backwards. A read from S3 by the same pod matches the more specific prefix-list route and goes straight to S3 through the gateway endpoint.

3. NAT gateways: limits, placement and price

From the VPC documentation (October 2026): a NAT gateway supports TCP, UDP and ICMP; starts at 5 Gbps and scales automatically to 100 Gbps; processes 1 million packets per second, scaling to 10 million, and drops packets beyond that; and each of its IPv4 addresses supports up to 55,000 simultaneous connections to each unique destination (destination IP, port and protocol), with up to 8 addresses per gateway. It uses source ports 1024–65535. You can't attach a security group to it, and you can't route traffic to it through a peering connection.

The 55,000 figure matters more than the bandwidth. A fleet calling one external API endpoint (one IP, port 443) through one NAT address can hold at most 55,000 connections to it at once; beyond that, new connections fail with errors the NAT gateway reports as ErrorPortAllocation. Connection pooling and keep-alive in clients, or more NAT addresses, are the fixes.

Placement. A standard (zonal) NAT gateway lives in one zone. AWS's documentation states the consequence plainly: if resources in several zones share one NAT gateway and its zone goes down, resources in the other zones lose internet access. So production designs put one in each zone and give each zone's private subnets a route table pointing at the local one — which also avoids paying $0.01/GB each way for traffic crossing zones to reach a remote NAT. In November 2025 AWS added a regional availability mode: a single NAT gateway ID, no public subnet needed, that expands to each zone where you have network interfaces (taking up to 60 minutes to expand to a new zone, during which traffic is processed in an existing zone) and supports up to 32 addresses per zone. It's billed per zone it is active in, so it doesn't save the hourly charge; it saves configuration and the single-zone mistake.

Price, worked. In us-east-1 a NAT gateway costs $0.045 per hour plus $0.045 per GB processed (October 2026 price list). Three zonal gateways: 3 × 730 h × $0.045 = $98.55 a month standing cost. Suppose private workloads send and receive 2 TB a month to external APIs and package registries, and read 30 TB a month from S3:

DesignNAT hoursNAT processingMonthly total
Everything through NAT$98.5532,768 GB × $0.045 = $1,474.56$1,573.11
S3 via gateway endpoint$98.552,048 GB × $0.045 = $92.16$190.71

(Internet egress for bytes leaving AWS is billed separately in both cases.) One free route-table entry removes about $1,380 a month. Gateway endpoints exist only for S3 and DynamoDB; for other AWS services, interface endpoints (section 6) do the same job for a fee.

4. Security groups in depth

net14 introduced security groups as stateful, allow-only firewalls attached to network interfaces, with rules that can reference other groups. Three further details matter in practice.

Connection tracking. "Stateful" is implemented by tracking connections: when an allowed packet starts a flow, the flow is recorded so return traffic is allowed regardless of rules. Tracking has limits per instance (an allowance that depends on instance size), and an instance can hit them under huge numbers of short connections; the ENA network driver exposes a conntrack_allowance_exceeded counter. Some flows are untracked — for example when a rule allows all traffic in both directions — which is one reason a very broad security group behaves differently under load.

Limits. By default a security group can have 60 inbound and 60 outbound rules (separately for IPv4 and IPv6), and an interface can have 5 security groups (raisable to 16, but rules per group × groups per interface can't exceed 1,000). Referencing a prefix list counts as its maximum number of entries. Large allow-lists of IP ranges therefore hit limits; referencing groups instead of addresses avoids most of them.

Changes apply immediately to new and, for most rule changes, existing tracked connections are not torn down — removing a rule doesn't necessarily cut a connection that's already established. When you need to cut traffic now, a NACL deny (stateless) does.

5. Network ACLs in depth

A network ACL applies to every packet entering or leaving a subnet. Rules are numbered; evaluation starts at the lowest number and stops at the first match; a final * rule denies anything unmatched. The default NACL in a VPC allows everything; a custom NACL starts by denying everything. Default quotas are 20 inbound and 20 outbound rules per NACL (raisable to 40 each).

Because NACLs are stateless, every flow needs rules in both directions. Work through a web server in a public subnet:

DirectionRule #Protocol / portsSource / destinationActionWhy
Inbound100TCP 4430.0.0.0/0Allowclients connecting
Inbound110TCP 1024–655350.0.0.0/0Allowreplies to the server's own outbound calls
Inbound90all192.0.2.0/24Denyblock a known-bad range (lower number, so it's checked first)
Outbound100TCP 1024–655350.0.0.0/0Allowreplies to clients' ephemeral ports
Outbound110TCP 4430.0.0.0/0Allowthe server's own HTTPS calls

The ephemeral range is wide on purpose: Linux clients use 32768–60999 by default, Windows 49152–65535, and NAT gateways and load balancers use 1024–65535. Forgetting one of these rules is the classic NACL outage: everything works from some clients and fails from others. Most teams therefore keep NACLs simple — subnet-to-subnet separation and explicit denies — and do fine-grained control with security groups.

6. Connecting VPCs and reaching services privately

VPC peering links two VPCs (same or different account or region) so their address spaces route to each other; each side adds routes to the other's CIDR via the peering connection. It has no hourly charge; traffic within one zone over a peering connection is free, across zones is charged like any cross-zone traffic, and across regions at inter-region rates. It's not transitive — no routing through a peer to a third VPC, an on-premises network, or the peer's internet or NAT gateway — and the ranges must not overlap. For n VPCs, a full mesh needs n(n−1)/2 peerings: 45 for 10 VPCs, 1,225 for 50.

Transit Gateway (TGW) is a regional hub. Each VPC attaches once (through small subnets in each zone where you want the attachment), as do VPNs and Direct Connect links; TGW route tables decide which attachments can reach which, so you can let prod reach shared services but not dev. TGWs in different regions can peer. It costs $0.05 per attachment-hour and $0.02 per GB processed in us-east-1 (October 2026). Fifty VPC attachments cost 50 × 730 × $0.05 = $1,825 a month before data; 100 TB processed adds 102,400 × $0.02 = $2,048.

PrivateLink solves a different problem: offering one service to many networks without connecting the networks. The provider puts the service behind a Network Load Balancer and creates an endpoint service; each consumer creates an interface endpoint, which appears as network interfaces with private IPs in the consumer's own subnets. Traffic is one-directional (consumer to service), address overlap doesn't matter, and the provider approves which accounts may connect. AWS's own services are offered the same way: interface endpoints for STS, Secrets Manager, ECR, CloudWatch, Bedrock and most others let private subnets reach them without NAT. An interface endpoint costs $0.01 per hour per zone plus $0.01 per GB (us-east-1, October 2026), so one endpoint in three zones is about $21.90 a month before data.

Gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB are the exception: free, implemented as route-table entries pointing at a prefix list, and regional (they reach the service in the same region only).

Endpoints also strengthen IAM (cl2). A bucket policy can deny requests unless aws:SourceVpce equals your endpoint's ID, so even valid credentials used from outside your network are refused; endpoint policies can restrict which buckets can be reached through the endpoint, so a compromised instance can't upload data to an attacker's bucket.

7. DNS inside the VPC

Every VPC has a DNS resolver, Route 53 Resolver, at the VPC's base address plus two (10.20.0.2 here) and at the link-local 169.254.169.253; instances get it by default. It answers for public names, for private hosted zones associated with the VPC (internal names like orders.internal.example), for instance hostnames, and for interface endpoints — with private DNS enabled, secretsmanager.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com resolves to the endpoint's private IPs inside the VPC. Each network interface can send at most 1,024 packets per second to the resolver, a limit that can't be raised, so busy services must cache DNS. For hybrid networks, resolver endpoints forward queries between the VPC and on-premises DNS servers.

8. What every path costs

Data transfer is where cloud network design shows up on the bill. Prices below are us-east-1 from the AWS price list on 7 October 2026:

Put numbers on a typical mistake. A service in AZ 2 sends 10 TB a month to the internet through a NAT gateway in AZ 1: cross-zone 10,240 GB × $0.02 = $204.80 (a cent as it leaves AZ 2 and a cent as it arrives in AZ 1), NAT processing 10,240 × $0.045 = $460.80, internet egress (after the free 100 GB) 10,140 × $0.09 = $912.60. A NAT gateway in AZ 2 removes the $204.80; nothing removes the egress except sending fewer bytes or putting a CDN (net12) in front, whose own egress pricing is usually lower at volume.

9. The same network on Google Cloud and Azure

Firewallsecurity groups (stateful, allow) + NACLs (stateless)VPC firewall rules and policies (stateful, allow and deny, priorities; implied deny ingress, allow egress)network security groups (stateful, allow and deny, priorities)
