The habit that changes most is per-zone plumbing: on Google Cloud and Azure you don't create one subnet and one NAT per zone. Two others: Google Cloud's global VPC means instances in two regions can talk privately without peering, and Azure's network security groups have deny rules with priorities, so they mix the roles AWS splits between security groups and NACLs.
deep:
Why address exhaustion hits Kubernetes first

With AWS's VPC CNI, every pod gets a real VPC address from its node's subnet, and nodes pre-allocate "warm" addresses so pods start quickly. A cluster can therefore consume addresses far faster than its pod count suggests, and a /24 per zone runs out at a few hundred pods. When it does, pods sit in ContainerCreating with IP-allocation errors while the nodes have spare CPU. The ways out are all disruptive: add a secondary CIDR (often from 100.64.0.0/10, the carrier-grade NAT range, which is non-routable on most corporate networks) and configure custom pod networking; enable prefix delegation, which assigns /28 blocks to nodes and changes fragmentation behaviour; or move to IPv6 for pods. The lesson for design reviews is to size application subnets from the pod count, not the node count, and to keep spare space in the VPC.

The hidden capacity of "infinitely scalable" network components

Internet gateways, NAT gateways, Transit Gateways and load balancers are described as scaling automatically, and they do — over minutes, along curves tuned for typical growth. A step change (a holiday reopening, a launch, a failover of a whole region's traffic) can arrive faster than the scaling. NAT gateways drop packets above their current packet rate; load balancers return 5xx while they add capacity (AWS offers pre-warming of load-balancer capacity units for known events); Slack's TGW dropped packets. The senior responses are to know which components sit on the critical path, to watch their drop and error metrics (NAT PacketsDropCount, TGW PacketDropCount*), to request capacity ahead of known surges, and to avoid putting monitoring on the same path.

Zone affinity is a design principle, not a tweak

Cross-zone charges ($0.01/GB each way on AWS) and cross-zone latency (a millisecond or two) both reward keeping a request inside one zone from load balancer to database replica. Doing that consistently is a property of the whole stack: load balancers with cross-zone load balancing off (at the cost of uneven distribution if zones have unequal capacity); Kubernetes topology-aware routing so Services prefer endpoints in the caller's zone; Kafka consumers fetching from the nearest replica; caches and read replicas per zone. It also improves failure isolation: a degraded zone affects only requests that started there, and evacuating it becomes a load-balancer change. The cost is complexity and the need to keep capacity balanced across zones.

Egress control is a security boundary

Most data exfiltration needs an outbound connection. A private subnet with a NAT gateway allows outbound connections to anywhere on the internet, which is convenient and is also the channel an attacker uses. Tighter designs route egress through an inspection point — AWS Network Firewall with domain allow-lists, or a proxy — so workloads can reach their package registries and partner APIs and nothing else, and use VPC endpoints with endpoint policies for AWS services so even S3 uploads are limited to your buckets. DNS is a covert channel too: Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall can block or allow domains at the resolver. The trade-off is operational: every new dependency needs an allow-list change, so teams usually start with logging (to learn the real destinations) before enforcing.

Hub-and-spoke concentrates both control and risk

A central Transit Gateway with inspection gives a platform team one place to enforce segmentation and egress policy for hundreds of VPCs. It also makes that place a shared dependency in two senses: capacity (every byte between VPCs crosses it and pays $0.02/GB) and configuration (one wrong route-table association can connect prod to dev or blackhole a region's traffic). Mature designs keep the hub's configuration in code with review and automated reachability tests (AWS's Reachability Analyzer can check whether a path exists between two endpoints before and after a change), and route heavy, low-risk flows around it.

IPv6 changes the shape of the problem

With IPv6, addresses are plentiful (AWS gives a VPC a /56 and each subnet a /64) and globally unique, so exhaustion and overlap mostly disappear, and NAT is replaced by the egress-only gateway's stateful filtering. Public IPv4 charges ($0.005/hour per address in October 2026) give a cost reason to move public endpoints to dual-stack or IPv6. The obstacles are dependencies that remain IPv4-only — some partners, some AWS service endpoints, older libraries — which NAT64 with DNS64 (supported by NAT gateways and the resolver) bridges at the cost of NAT processing charges.
prod:
Failure modes and their symptoms

IP exhaustion. New instances, pods, Lambda functions in the VPC or load-balancer nodes fail to launch with "insufficient free addresses in subnet". Watch available-IP counts per subnet and alert at 20% remaining.

NAT port exhaustion. Outbound calls to one popular destination fail intermittently under load while bandwidth is fine. The NAT gateway's ErrorPortAllocation metric rises. Fix with connection pooling and keep-alive, more NAT addresses, or an endpoint if the destination is an AWS service.

Zone-dependent NAT. During a zone event, private subnets in healthy zones lose internet access because their default route points at the dead zone's NAT gateway. Fix with per-zone NAT or regional mode, and test with a zone evacuation.

NACL asymmetry. Some clients work and others time out after a NACL change; flow logs show REJECT on return traffic to high ports. Fix the ephemeral-port rules.

Security group drift. Someone adds 0.0.0.0/0 on port 22 "temporarily". Detect with config rules or a policy-as-code check in the infrastructure pipeline, and use Systems Manager Session Manager instead of SSH so port 22 needn't be open at all.

Surprise data-transfer bills. The bill grows faster than traffic. Break down the Cost and Usage Report by usage type (DataTransfer-Regional-Bytes, NatGateway-Bytes, TransitGateway-Bytes, DataTransfer-Out-Bytes) and join VPC flow logs with zone IDs to find the talkers.

DNS throttling. Bursts of SERVFAIL or timeouts from busy hosts because of the 1,024 packets per second per interface limit. Cache DNS locally.

Tools

VPC flow logs (accept/reject records per interface, with fields such as source and destination zone IDs in custom formats), Reachability Analyzer (can A reach B, and which rule blocks it), Network Access Analyzer (which paths exist from the internet to sensitive subnets), CloudWatch metrics for NAT, TGW and load balancers, and the Cost and Usage Report for transfer.

The case: Slack, 4 January 2021

Slack's engineering write-up describes the first working day of 2021. Over the holidays traffic is low; on the first Monday back, client caches are cold and clients download more than usual, so Slack goes overnight from its quietest time of year to one of its biggest days. Slack's VPCs were connected through AWS Transit Gateways. The TGWs are meant to scale transparently, but one did not scale fast enough and began dropping packets. Error rates crept up; at 6:57 AM PST, 99% of messages were being sent successfully against a normal rate above 99.999%. The packet loss made web servers wait longer on their backends, and the 7:00 AM traffic peak saturated the web tier: Slack became unavailable.

The recovery tools shared the failing path. Dashboards and alerting depended on the TGWs, so the team's visibility was degraded. Autoscaling tried to add 1,200 servers to the web tier between 7:01 and 7:15 AM, but the provisioning service hit its own limits (the Linux open-files limit and AWS quotas) while talking to its dependencies over the degraded network, so most never came into service. By around 9:15 AM Slack was degraded rather than down. AWS engineers manually increased TGW capacity; by 10:40 AM PST the change had rolled out across all zones and error rates and latency returned to normal. Slack's follow-ups included moving dashboard services into the same VPC as their data so they don't cross the TGW, load-testing the provisioning service regularly, and asking AWS to pre-scale TGWs ahead of holidays; AWS said it was reviewing the TGW scaling algorithms for large packet-per-second increases.

For a designer, the incident shows four things from this lesson at once: managed network components have scaling curves; a hub every VPC depends on is a shared failure point; monitoring and recovery tooling must not share fate with what they fix; and scaling up during a network problem multiplies load on the network.
myths: A private subnet is private because it uses private IP addresses.

Every subnet in a VPC uses the VPC's addresses, which are usually private RFC 1918 ranges. What makes a subnet public or private is its route table: a public subnet's default route points at an internet gateway, a private one's doesn't. Put a public IP on an instance in a 'private' subnet and it still can't be reached from the internet, because there's no route; put a public IP on an instance in a public subnet and it can, subject to its security group.
One NAT gateway is enough; it's a managed, redundant service.

A zonal NAT gateway is redundant within its zone, but it lives in one zone. If that zone fails, every private subnet routing through it loses outbound internet access, and while it works, traffic from other zones pays cross-zone charges to reach it. The fixes are one zonal NAT gateway per zone with per-zone routes, or the regional NAT gateway mode AWS added in November 2025, which spreads itself across zones where you have workloads.
Security groups and network ACLs do the same job, so use both everywhere.

They work at different levels with different semantics. Security groups are stateful, attach to network interfaces, can only allow, and can reference other groups, which makes them the right tool for 'the app tier may reach the database on 5432'. Network ACLs are stateless, attach to subnets, have numbered allow and deny rules, and need explicit rules for return traffic on ephemeral ports. Most designs rely on security groups and use NACLs sparingly for coarse subnet-wide denies.
Traffic inside the cloud is free.

On AWS, traffic between instances in the same zone over private IPs is free, but crossing zones costs $0.01/GB in each direction, going through a NAT gateway adds $0.045/GB, through a Transit Gateway $0.02/GB, through an interface endpoint $0.01/GB, between regions $0.02/GB from us-east-1 to us-west-2, and to the internet $0.09/GB after the first 100 GB a month (October 2026 prices). A chatty microservice architecture can spend more on moving bytes than on computing them.
VPC peering lets everything reach everything once you peer the hub.

Peering is a one-to-one relationship and is not transitive: if A peers with B and B with C, A can't reach C through B, and a VPC can't use its peer's internet or NAT gateway. Many VPCs need either a full mesh of peerings (n(n−1)/2 of them) or a hub such as Transit Gateway that does route between attachments.
S3 traffic from private subnets has to go through the NAT gateway.

A gateway VPC endpoint for S3 (or DynamoDB) adds a route for the service's address ranges to your route tables, so traffic to S3 in the same region goes directly, never touches the NAT gateway and costs nothing extra. Without it, a training job reading 50 TB of data through NAT pays about $2,300 in NAT processing alone.
lab:
Goal: build a subnet planner and a transfer-cost calculator with Python 3.12's standard library (ipaddress), and check the lesson's numbers. About 20 minutes; no cloud account needed.

  1. Planner. Write plan(vpc, tiers, azs) where tiers is a list like [("app", 19), ("data", 22), ("public", 24)]. Allocate biggest tier first, one subnet per zone, each starting at the next aligned address (use ipaddress.ip_network(f"{cursor}/{prefix}") and move the cursor to broadcast_address + 1). Print each subnet, its usable count (num_addresses - 5), first usable (net[4]) and last usable (net[-2]).
  2. Validate. Assert no two subnets overlap (a.overlaps(b)), all are inside the VPC (a.subnet_of(vpc)), and print the free space left.
  3. Pods. Write prefix_for(n_ips), the smallest prefix whose usable count covers n_ips. What does 6,000 pods per zone need? What about 9,000?
  4. Costs. Encode the October 2026 us-east-1 prices from section 8 and write monthly_cost(gb, path) for paths such as ["cross_az", "nat", "internet"]. Reproduce the NAT table in section 3 and the 10 TB example in section 8.
  5. Mesh vs hub. Print peering counts n(n−1)/2 and TGW attachment-hour costs for n = 5, 10, 50.

What to look for: the planner should reproduce the table in section 1 exactly (10.20.0.0/19 … 10.20.110.0/24, next free 10.20.111.0); 6,000 pods → /19 and 9,000 → /18. The everything-through-NAT design costs about $1,573 against $191 with the S3 endpoint. The peering count passes 1,000 at n = 50, which is the whole argument for a hub.

Needs an AWS account (optional): aws ec2 describe-subnets --filters Name=vpc-id,Values=<vpc> --query "Subnets[].[CidrBlock,AvailabilityZoneId,AvailableIpAddressCount]" --output table shows each subnet's zone ID and free addresses — the number to alert on.
recap: A VPC is a regional private network with one or more CIDR blocks; on AWS each subnet lives in one zone, can be /16 to /28, and loses five addresses (network, router, DNS, reserved, broadcast).

Plan addresses once and generously: non-overlapping with every network you may ever connect to, a subnet per tier per zone sized for the largest consumer (pods take addresses), and spare space for new zones and tiers.
Route tables decide where traffic goes by longest-prefix match; a subnet is public when 0.0.0.0/0 points at an internet gateway and private when it points at a NAT gateway or nowhere.

A zonal NAT gateway lives in one zone, scales from 5 to 100 Gbps, allows 55,000 connections per destination per IP and costs $0.045/hour plus $0.045/GB in us-east-1; deploy one per zone or use regional mode, and keep heavy service traffic off it with endpoints.
Security groups are stateful, allow-only, per interface and can reference groups; network ACLs are stateless, ordered allow/deny rules per subnet that must permit return traffic on ephemeral ports.

Peering connects two VPCs privately but isn't transitive; Transit Gateway is a regional hub with route tables that scales to many VPCs and on-premises links at $0.05/attachment-hour plus $0.02/GB; PrivateLink exposes one service privately across VPCs and accounts.

Gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB are free route-table entries; interface endpoints are network interfaces per zone billed per hour and per GB, and both let resource policies require traffic from your network.

Every byte has a price that depends on its path: free in a zone, $0.01/GB each way across zones, $0.02/GB across US regions, $0.09/GB to the internet, plus NAT, Transit Gateway or endpoint processing.
Network components are shared dependencies: Slack's 2021 outage started with a Transit Gateway that didn't scale fast enough for a traffic surge, and its own monitoring depended on the same path.
glossary: AZ (availability zone)
A physically separate group of data centres inside a region (cl1); AWS subnets each live in one.
CIDR block
A range of IP addresses written as a base address and prefix length, such as 10.20.0.0/16 (65,536 addresses); see net3.
CNI (Container Network Interface)
The Kubernetes plugin interface that gives pods their network; AWS's VPC CNI assigns pods real VPC addresses (k8s8).
ECR (Elastic Container Registry)
AWS's managed container image registry, reachable privately through interface endpoints.
Egress-only internet gateway
An AWS gateway for IPv6 that lets instances start outbound connections to the internet but blocks inbound ones, the IPv6 counterpart of a NAT gateway (without address translation).
Elastic IP
A static public IPv4 address you allocate to your account and attach to an instance or NAT gateway; billed per hour like every public IPv4 address.
ENI (elastic network interface)
A virtual network card in a subnet with private IPs and security groups; instances, load balancers, endpoints and Lambda functions in a VPC all use them.
Ephemeral port
A temporary source port chosen by a client's OS for an outgoing connection, which replies come back to; Linux uses 32768–60999 by default.
Gateway endpoint
A free VPC endpoint type for S3 and DynamoDB that works by adding routes for the service's prefix list to route tables.
Interface endpoint
A VPC endpoint implemented as network interfaces in your subnets with private IPs, used to reach AWS services or PrivateLink services privately; billed per hour per zone and per GB.
Internet gateway (IGW)
The horizontally scaled, redundant VPC component that connects a VPC to the internet and translates between instances' private IPs and their public IPs.
IPAM (IP address management)
A system, such as Amazon VPC IPAM, that allocates and tracks non-overlapping address ranges across accounts and regions.
Longest-prefix match
The routing rule that picks the most specific matching route, so 10.20.0.0/16 → local beats 0.0.0.0/0 → NAT for an address in the VPC.
NAT gateway
A managed network address translator that lets instances in private subnets start outbound IPv4 connections while staying unreachable from outside.
NAT64 / DNS64
Mechanisms that let IPv6-only clients reach IPv4-only servers: DNS64 synthesises IPv6 addresses for IPv4 names and NAT64 translates the packets.
Network ACL (NACL)
A stateless, numbered list of allow and deny rules applied to all traffic entering or leaving a subnet.
Prefix list
A named set of CIDR blocks that route tables and security groups can reference; AWS publishes managed prefix lists for services such as S3.
Private subnet
A subnet with no route to an internet gateway; outbound internet access, if any, goes through a NAT gateway.
PrivateLink
AWS's technology for exposing a service behind a Network Load Balancer to other VPCs as interface endpoints, without peering or routing between the networks.
Public subnet
A subnet whose route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to an internet gateway.
Route 53 Resolver
The DNS resolver built into every VPC, reachable at the VPC base address plus two (e.g. 10.20.0.2) and at 169.254.169.253.
Route table
A set of rules (destination CIDR → target) associated with subnets that decides where traffic leaving the subnet goes.
Security group
A stateful, allow-only virtual firewall attached to network interfaces; rules can reference IP ranges, prefix lists or other security groups.
Stateful / stateless
A stateful firewall remembers connections and allows their replies automatically; a stateless one judges every packet on its own, so replies need their own rules.
Transit Gateway (TGW)
A regional AWS network hub that VPCs, VPNs and Direct Connect attach to, with its own route tables, replacing a mesh of peerings.
VPC (virtual private cloud)
A logically isolated virtual network in a region with your chosen address range, subnets, route tables and gateways.
VPC peering
A private, non-transitive connection between two VPCs, in the same or different regions and accounts, with non-overlapping address ranges.
VPN (virtual private network)
An encrypted tunnel over the internet connecting a VPC to another network, such as an office or data centre.
drill:
Estimate and fix: the network line on the bill

An ML platform in us-east-1 runs a training cluster in private subnets across three zones with a single NAT gateway in AZ 1. Each month it reads 80 TB of training data from S3, pulls 3 TB of container images from a public registry, and writes 6 TB of checkpoints to S3. Its inference service sends 4 TB a month of responses to users over the internet through an Application Load Balancer, and replicas in different zones exchange 20 TB a month of feature-store traffic. Estimate the monthly network-related charges, then propose changes and the new estimate. (Use 1 TB = 1,024 GB; ignore load-balancer capacity units.)

Answer

Current state. NAT hours: 730 × $0.045 = $32.85. NAT processing: S3 reads and writes plus images go through NAT: (80 + 6 + 3) × 1,024 = 91,136 GB × $0.045 = $4,101.12. Cross-zone to reach the single NAT: two-thirds of the cluster is in other zones, so about 2/3 × 91,136 ≈ 60,757 GB crosses zones, billed $0.01 leaving one zone and $0.01 arriving in the other: 60,757 × $0.02 ≈ $1,215.14. Feature-store cross-zone: 20 × 1,024 = 20,480 GB × $0.02 (out and in) = $409.60. Internet egress for responses: (4,096 − 100) GB × $0.09 = $359.64. Total ≈ $32.85 + $4,101.12 + $1,215.14 + $409.60 + $359.64 ≈ $6,118 a month.

Changes. (1) Add an S3 gateway endpoint: 86 TB of S3 traffic leaves the NAT gateway and stops crossing zones — free. (2) One NAT gateway per zone (or regional mode): image pulls stay zone-local. (3) Better still, mirror the images into a private registry (ECR) reached via an interface endpoint, or a pull-through cache, which also removes the dependency on a public registry. (4) Make feature-store reads zone-local where possible; replication across zones remains for durability.

New estimate. NAT hours: 3 × $32.85 = $98.55. NAT processing for 3 TB of images: 3,072 × $0.045 = $138.24. Cross-zone for NAT: ~$0. Feature store, if half the traffic becomes zone-local: $204.80. Internet egress unchanged: $359.64. Total ≈ $801 a month, a saving of about $5,300 a month, almost all from one free endpoint.
qa: E
What makes a subnet public or private?

Its route table. A public subnet has a route sending 0.0.0.0/0 (the default route) to an internet gateway, so instances with public IPs can be reached and can reach the internet directly. A private subnet has no such route; if it needs outbound access its default route points at a NAT gateway, which lets instances start connections but never accept inbound ones from the internet. Both kinds use addresses from the VPC's own range.

Follow-up: an instance in a public subnet has no public IP. Can it reach the internet? — No. The internet gateway only translates for instances that have a public IP; without one, outbound packets have nothing to be translated to. It would need a NAT gateway or a public IP.
E
What's the difference between a security group and a network ACL?

A security group is a stateful firewall on each network interface: it has only allow rules, return traffic for allowed connections is automatically allowed, and rules can reference other security groups. A network ACL is a stateless firewall on a subnet: it has numbered allow and deny rules evaluated lowest number first, and because it doesn't track connections, you must allow return traffic on ephemeral ports explicitly. Security groups do most of the work; NACLs are a coarse subnet-wide backstop.

Follow-up: when would you use a NACL? — To block a known-bad range across a whole subnet, or to enforce a hard separation between subnets that application teams can't override with their own security groups.
E
Why can't you peer two VPCs that both use 10.0.0.0/16?

Routing would be ambiguous: a packet to 10.0.4.7 could belong to either network, and each VPC's route table already has a local route for 10.0.0.0/16 that would always win. AWS refuses to create peerings between overlapping ranges for that reason. It's why address planning across all accounts and future partners matters on day one; fixing an overlap later means renumbering or adding translation (private NAT or PrivateLink).

Follow-up: what if you must connect them anyway? — Expose specific services with PrivateLink, which needs no routing between the networks, or put a private NAT gateway in between to translate one side into a non-overlapping range.
M
Plan the subnets for a production VPC in three zones with public, private application and data tiers.

Give the VPC a /16 that doesn't overlap anything, for example 10.20.0.0/16. Size application subnets for the largest consumer — with Kubernetes using VPC IPs for pods, a /19 per zone (8,187 usable addresses after AWS reserves five) — so 10.20.0.0/19, 10.20.32.0/19, 10.20.64.0/19. Data subnets for databases and caches are small: /22 each at 10.20.96.0, .100.0 and .104.0. Public subnets for load balancers and NAT gateways: /24 each at 10.20.108.0, .109.0 and .110.0. That uses 10.20.0.0 to 10.20.110.255 and leaves over half the VPC free for a fourth zone, new tiers or endpoints.

Follow-up: what fails first if you size the app subnets as /24? — Pod IP exhaustion: 251 usable addresses per zone run out at a few hundred pods, and new pods sit Pending with IP allocation errors; the usual escape is adding a secondary CIDR and custom pod networking, a painful migration.
M
A private subnet's instances need to call an external API and read from S3. How do you set up the routes, and what does it cost?

Add a gateway endpoint for S3 to the private route tables: S3 traffic follows the S3 prefix-list route directly, free. Put a NAT gateway in each zone (or one regional NAT gateway) and point each private subnet's 0.0.0.0/0 at the NAT in its own zone, so external API calls leave through NAT. In us-east-1, three zonal NAT gateways cost 3 × 730 h × $0.045 ≈ $99 a month before data, plus $0.045/GB processed and normal internet egress for responses leaving AWS's network, not for inbound responses. Routing S3 through NAT instead would add $0.045/GB for nothing.

Follow-up: how do you notice the S3-through-NAT mistake in production? — Cost and Usage Report lines for NatGateway-Bytes growing with data volume, and VPC flow logs showing NAT traffic to S3's address ranges.
M
Compare VPC peering, Transit Gateway and PrivateLink.

Peering connects two VPCs' whole address spaces, one-to-one, non-transitively, with no hourly fee and data charged like normal cross-zone or cross-region traffic (free within a zone). Transit Gateway is a regional hub: every VPC and on-premises link attaches once, route tables decide who reaches whom, and it costs $0.05 per attachment-hour plus $0.02/GB — simple at scale, a central component and a cost per byte. PrivateLink exposes one service (behind a Network Load Balancer) as interface endpoints in consumers' VPCs: no routing between networks, overlapping ranges are fine, access is one-directional, and you pay per endpoint-hour per zone and per GB. Choose peering for a few VPCs with heavy traffic, Transit Gateway for many VPCs and hybrid, PrivateLink for offering a service to many consumers or across trust boundaries.

Follow-up: why might a team keep heavy east-west traffic on peering even with a Transit Gateway in place? — Cost: 100 TB a month through TGW is about $2,048 in processing alone, while peered traffic within a zone is free and across zones is $0.01/GB each way.
M
What breaks when a NACL allows inbound 443 and outbound 443 only?

Responses. A client connecting to your server on 443 uses an ephemeral source port, say 51544, so the server's reply goes to port 51544 — and the outbound NACL rule only allows destination port 443, so the reply is dropped. Likewise, your instances' outbound calls on 443 get replies on their own ephemeral ports, which the inbound rule drops. Because NACLs are stateless, you need inbound and outbound rules for ephemeral ports (1024–65535 to cover NAT gateways, load balancers and different operating systems).
Follow-up: why don't security groups have this problem? — They're stateful: once a connection is allowed in one direction, the return packets are matched to it and allowed automatically.
M
How does DNS work inside a VPC, and what can go wrong?

Every VPC has a resolver (Route 53 Resolver) at the VPC base address plus two, e.g. 10.20.0.2, and at 169.254.169.253; instances use it by default via DHCP options. It resolves public names, private hosted zones attached to the VPC, AWS's instance hostnames, and interface endpoint names, returning private IPs for endpoints when private DNS is on. Things that go wrong: per-interface query limits (1,024 packets per second to the resolver, not raisable) hit by services that don't cache DNS; hybrid setups that need inbound and outbound resolver endpoints to forward between on-premises DNS and the VPC; and endpoint private DNS overriding a public name you didn't expect.

Follow-up: how would you fix resolver throttling? — Cache DNS on the host (for example a local caching resolver or the runtime's DNS cache), reduce lookups per request, and confirm with the resolver query metrics.
H
Design the network for 40 AWS accounts across three regions, with an on-premises data centre and central egress inspection.

Allocate address space centrally with IPAM: a /12 per region carved into non-overlapping /16s per account-VPC. In each region, a Transit Gateway shared to all accounts via Resource Access Manager; each VPC attaches from dedicated small attachment subnets in every zone. Separate TGW route tables segment environments: prod VPCs can reach shared services and on-premises but not dev. An inspection VPC with a firewall (AWS Network Firewall or appliances behind a Gateway Load Balancer) sits in the path for egress and inter-environment traffic; central NAT gateways in an egress VPC, one per zone. Direct Connect (with VPN backup) to the on-premises network terminates on the TGWs; TGW peering connects regions. Keep high-volume east-west flows that don't need inspection on direct peering or PrivateLink to avoid per-GB charges, and put gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB in every VPC.

Follow-up: what's the main risk of this design? — The hub is a shared dependency: a TGW route-table mistake or capacity event affects every account, so changes go through infrastructure as code with review, route tables are tested, and critical flows have monitored alternatives.
H
Your bill shows $18,000 a month in data transfer for a service that 'only talks to itself'. How do you find and cut it?

Break down the Cost and Usage Report by usage type: DataTransfer-Regional-Bytes (cross-zone), NatGateway-Bytes, TransitGateway-Bytes, inter-region and internet egress lines, and by resource. Each gigabyte that crosses zones is billed twice — $0.01 leaving one zone and $0.01 arriving in the other — so $18,000 of cross-zone charges is about 900,000 GB, roughly 880 TB crossing zones a month. Use VPC flow logs with the zone IDs of source and destination to find the talkers. Typical causes: load balancers with cross-zone load balancing sending half of requests to other zones, Kafka or database replicas and clients in different zones, service meshes ignoring zone, and NAT gateways in one zone. Fixes: zone-aware routing (topology-aware routing in Kubernetes, rack-aware Kafka consumers), keeping replicas where clients are, one NAT per zone, endpoints for AWS services, and compression for what must cross.

Follow-up: why not put everything in one zone? — You'd save the transfer charges and lose zone failure tolerance; the right answer keeps redundancy across zones but makes steady-state traffic zone-local, crossing zones only for replication and failover.
H
Walk through Slack's January 2021 outage and what it teaches about cloud networking.

On 4 January 2021, the first workday after the holidays, Slack's traffic jumped from the year's quietest period to one of its busiest, with cold client caches. Slack's VPCs were connected through AWS Transit Gateways, which are meant to scale transparently but did not scale fast enough, and one dropped packets. Packet loss slowed the web tier until the 7:00 AM PST traffic peak saturated it and Slack became unavailable; autoscaling tried to add 1,200 web servers, but the provisioning service hit its own limits and depended on the same degraded network; dashboards and alerting also crossed the TGWs, so engineers were partly blind. AWS manually raised TGW capacity, completed across all zones by 10:40 AM PST. Lessons: managed network components have scaling behaviour you must understand and sometimes pre-warm; monitoring must not share fate with what it monitors; and scale-up paths need to be load-tested under the conditions that trigger them.

Follow-up: what would you change in a design that has every VPC talking through one TGW? — Keep latency-critical, high-volume paths (web to database, monitoring to its data) inside one VPC or on peering, request capacity ahead of known surges, and alert on TGW packet-drop metrics.
H
How does Google Cloud's or Azure's network model change the AWS design you'd normally draw?

On Google Cloud a VPC network is global: one network has regional subnets in many regions, and instances in different regions talk over Google's backbone without peering or a transit hub; firewall rules belong to the network and target instances by tags or service accounts, with implied deny-ingress and allow-egress; Cloud NAT is a software-defined regional service rather than a gateway instance per zone. On Azure, a virtual network is regional and its subnets span zones; network security groups are stateful but have priority-ordered allow and deny rules and attach to subnets or NICs; NAT Gateway provides outbound access; and for new virtual networks created with API versions after 31 March 2026, subnets are private by default with no implicit outbound internet access. So per-zone subnet triplets and per-zone NAT are AWS-specific habits; the concepts — segmentation, explicit egress, private service access, hub-and-spoke — carry over.
Follow-up: what's GCP's equivalent of PrivateLink? — Private Service Connect, which exposes a producer's service as an endpoint IP in the consumer's VPC.
refs: The case: a Transit Gateway that didn't scale fast enough for a post-holiday surge, a provisioning system that depended on the same network, and dashboards that went dark.

NAT gateway (zonal and regional), public IPv4, Transit Gateway, PrivateLink and data-transfer references.

t: Compute choices: VMs and instance families, spot capacity, autoscaling groups, containers (ECS, EKS, Cloud Run) and serverless functions, with the decision table
sum: How to choose where code runs in the cloud: reading instance names and families, vCPUs that are threads or cores, burstable credits, Arm versus x86, spot capacity and its two-minute notice, autoscaling groups traced through a scale-out, containers on ECS, Fargate, EKS and Cloud Run, functions in one paragraph before cl5, a fleet sized and priced by hand, and the decision table — with Honeycomb's 2026 Graviton4-to-Graviton5 A/B migration as the case.
prereq: cl1
IaaS rents machines, CaaS runs your images, FaaS runs functions per event; capacity is finite per zone and static stability means surviving a zone loss without launching anything.
k8s1
A VM runs its own kernel on a hypervisor; a container is a process with namespaces and cgroups sharing the host kernel, packaged as an image.
k8s11
The HPA adjusts replica counts from metrics, node autoscalers (Cluster Autoscaler, Karpenter) add and remove nodes, and KEDA scales on queue depth, including to zero.
sc15
Kubernetes reconciles desired state; requests drive scheduling; autoscaling happens at the pod, node and cluster level; deployment strategies include rolling, blue-green and canary.
why:
A team building a document-processing product needs somewhere to run four things: an HTTP API with steady traffic, a nightly job that re-indexes everything, a webhook receiver that is idle for hours and then gets ten thousand calls in a minute, and an OCR model that needs a GPU. Asked "where should this run?", the team picks what it knows. It puts everything on a handful of large virtual machines, sized for the webhook burst and the GPU model, running all month.

The bill arrives. The GPU sits at 4% average utilisation because inference only happens during business hours. The API servers idle at 15% CPU because they were sized for a peak that happens twice a year. The nightly job takes six hours because it runs on the same machines and has to share them. The webhook burst still drops requests because the burst arrives faster than anything was sized for. The team is paying for capacity that does nothing most of the time while still failing at the moments that matter.

Cloud compute isn't one product. It's a menu that runs from renting a specific machine by the second, to renting spare machines at a steep discount that can be taken back with two minutes' notice, to handing over a container image and letting the platform decide how many copies to run, to handing over a function and paying per call. Each option prices a different shape of load well and another shape badly. Choosing well is mostly about matching the option to the shape of each workload — steady, spiky, interruptible, long-running, GPU-bound — and knowing the mechanics underneath well enough to predict what happens at the peak.

This lesson builds that judgement. It explains how to read an instance type and what a vCPU really is, how burstable instances and Arm processors change the arithmetic, how spot capacity works and how to survive its interruptions, how autoscaling groups react to load and how long that takes, what container platforms (ECS, Fargate, EKS, Cloud Run) take off your hands, where functions fit (cl5 goes deep), and how to size and price a real fleet by hand. It ends with the decision table, and with a 2026 case where Honeycomb measured the gain from one instance generation to the next.
primer:
Think about how a city moves people. You can buy a car: it's yours, always available, you choose everything, and it costs money even when parked. You can lease one for three years at a discount. You can rent from a company's surplus fleet at a fraction of the price, on the condition that they can take the car back with two minutes' warning. You can take a taxi, paying only per trip but more per kilometre. Or you can ride a bus that runs on its own schedule. No one option is best; a delivery business, a commuter and a tourist each choose differently, and a sensible household combines several.

Cloud compute has the same structure. A virtual machine (an instance on AWS) is the car: you pick its exact type, run anything on it, and pay per second while it runs. Commitments (savings plans, reserved instances) are the lease. Spot capacity is the surplus fleet: the same machines at a large discount, reclaimable with short notice. Containers on a managed platform are closer to a chauffeur service: you say what to run and how much CPU and memory it needs, and the platform finds the machines. Functions are the taxi: per trip (per request), nothing when idle, more per unit of work at high volume.

Two forces decide which option fits a workload. The first is the shape of the load: steady load favours capacity you keep and fill (VMs or containers with commitments); spiky or rare load favours capacity you pay for only while used (functions, scale-to-zero containers); interruptible load favours spot. The second is what you'd rather spend: engineering time on running platforms, or money on the provider doing it for you. A team of four usually should spend money; a company running ten thousand cores usually should spend engineering time.

One number ties the whole menu together: cost per unit of work — dollars per million requests, per thousand documents, per training step. Hourly prices can't be compared across models (an instance-hour, a vCPU-hour of Fargate and a GB-second of Lambda measure different things), but every option can be turned into cost per unit once you know how much work one unit of capacity does at your target latency. The rest of this lesson is about measuring that work, predicting how capacity follows load, and choosing the option whose cost per unit is lowest for each load shape — while still surviving the failures from cl1.

Where the analogy breaks: unlike a car park, cloud capacity isn't infinite. When everyone wants the same GPU, or every customer fails over into the same zone, launches fail with "insufficient capacity" even though you're willing to pay. Owning (reserving) capacity matters more in the cloud than the "rent everything on demand" story suggests, especially for scarce instance types.
body:
1. Reading an instance type

AWS names instance types like m7g.xlarge. The parts:

  • Family letter. m general purpose (4 GiB of memory per vCPU), c compute-optimised (2 GiB per vCPU), r memory-optimised (8 GiB per vCPU), x and u very large memory, i and d local NVMe storage, t burstable, p and g NVIDIA GPUs (p for training-class, g for graphics and inference-class), inf and trn AWS's Inferentia and Trainium chips.
  • Generation. 6, 7, 8, 9. Newer generations bring newer processors, usually better price-performance.
  • Attributes. g Graviton (Arm), i Intel, a AMD, d local NVMe disks, n enhanced networking, e extra memory or storage, flex a cheaper variant that doesn't guarantee full CPU all the time.
  • Size. medium, large (2 vCPUs), xlarge (4), 2xlarge (8)… each step doubles vCPUs, memory and usually network bandwidth; metal is the whole physical server.

So an m7g.xlarge is a 7th-generation general-purpose Graviton instance with 4 vCPUs and 16 GiB; a c7i.large is a 7th-generation compute-optimised Intel instance with 2 vCPUs and 4 GiB. Prices in us-east-1 on 7 October 2026 (Linux, on-demand, from the AWS price list):

TypevCPU / GiBProcessor$/hour$/month (730 h)
t4g.small2 / 2Graviton2, burstable0.016812.26
c7g.large2 / 4Graviton30.072552.93
c7i.large2 / 4Intel Sapphire Rapids0.0892565.15
m7g.large2 / 8Graviton30.081659.57
m7i.large2 / 8Intel Sapphire Rapids0.100873.58
m8g.large2 / 8Graviton40.0897665.52
m9g.large2 / 8Graviton50.0978471.42
r7g.large2 / 16Graviton30.107178.18

Underneath, modern AWS instances run on Nitro, AWS's virtualisation system that moves networking, storage access and security functions onto dedicated cards, so almost all of the host's CPU is available to instances and performance is close to bare metal. Network bandwidth and disk (EBS) bandwidth scale with size; small sizes have "up to" figures that they can burst to briefly, which matters for network-heavy services on small instances.

2. What a vCPU is, and why Arm changes the arithmetic

A vCPU is what the instance sees as a CPU. On most Intel and AMD instance types it is one hardware thread: physical cores run two threads each through simultaneous multithreading (Intel calls it Hyper-Threading), and AWS's documentation states that each vCPU is a thread of an Intel Xeon or AMD EPYC core, except on T2 and Graviton types. On Graviton, each vCPU is a whole physical core. Two threads on one core share its execution units, so two x86 vCPUs do less than two cores' worth of work on CPU-bound code — the gain from the second thread is workload-dependent and often 10–30%, not 100%.

That's why per-vCPU prices mislead. An m7g.large costs 19% less per hour than an m7i.large ($0.0816 vs $0.1008) with the same 2 vCPUs and 8 GiB, but the real question is cost per unit of your work. The only reliable answer is to measure: run the same service on both under the same traffic and compare requests per second at the same latency, then divide price by throughput. Software must be built for arm64: most languages' runtimes and container base images support it, but native extensions, vendor binaries and code with x86-specific optimisations may not.

3. Burstable instances and CPU credits

Burstable instances (the t family) give a baseline share of CPU and let you bank unused time. The unit is the CPU credit: one vCPU at 100% for one minute (or one vCPU at 50% for two minutes). Each size earns credits at a fixed rate. From AWS's credit table (October 2026): a t4g.micro earns 12 credits an hour (10% baseline per vCPU), a t4g.small and t4g.medium 24 (20%), a t4g.large 36 (30%). Below baseline, credits accumulate up to a day's worth; above it, they're spent.

Work through a t4g.small (2 vCPUs, 24 credits an hour). At baseline it can use 24 vCPU-minutes per hour: 2 vCPUs × 20% × 60 minutes. A small web app idles at 5% on both vCPUs for 20 hours (spending 2 × 0.05 × 60 = 6 credits an hour, banking 18 an hour, capped at 576) and then runs at 70% for 4 hours (spending 84 an hour, earning 24, a net 60 an hour, 240 over four hours). The bank covers it: no throttling, no extra charge. Change the pattern to 50% for 24 hours (60 credits an hour spent, 24 earned) and the bank drains. In standard mode the instance falls to baseline when the bank is empty, which looks like a sudden slowdown; in unlimited mode (the default for T3 and T4g) it keeps running and, if its 24-hour average exceeds baseline, the surplus is billed at a flat rate per vCPU-hour. Burstable instances are excellent for spiky, low-average work and a trap for steady work.

4. Pricing models in brief (cl12 goes deep)

The same instance can be bought three ways. On-demand: the list price, per second for Linux with a one-minute minimum, no commitment. Commitments: a one- or three-year promise in exchange for a discount; for example the m7g.large's one-year, no-upfront reserved rate was $0.054 an hour against $0.0816 on demand (34% off) on 7 October 2026. Spot: spare capacity at a variable discount — AWS says up to 90% off on-demand — which AWS can reclaim. A typical production pattern covers the steady baseline with commitments, the daily swing with on-demand, and interruptible work with spot.

5. Spot capacity and interruptions

Spot instances are the provider's unused capacity. Prices move slowly with long-term supply and demand in each capacity pool (an instance type in a zone), and when the provider needs the capacity back it interrupts spot instances in that pool. On AWS you get an interruption notice two minutes before the instance is stopped or terminated, delivered as an EC2 Spot Instance Interruption Warning event in EventBridge and as an instance-action item in instance metadata (/latest/meta-data/spot/instance-action, which returns 404 until an interruption is scheduled; AWS recommends checking every five seconds). Notices are best effort. A rebalance recommendation can arrive earlier, signalling elevated risk.

Other providers differ in detail. Google Cloud's Spot VMs have no maximum runtime and, per the current documentation, a configurable preemption notice of 0 seconds (the default) or 120 seconds, followed by a best-effort shutdown period of up to 30 seconds; Google advertises discounts of up to 91%. Azure Spot VMs give a short eviction notice through Scheduled Events.

Designing for spot comes down to four habits:

  1. Diversify. Allow many instance types (say m7g, m7i, m6i, c7g, c7i, r7g in two or three sizes) in all zones. More pools means more available capacity and fewer simultaneous interruptions.
  2. Choose capacity over price. Use a capacity-optimised allocation strategy (on AWS, price-capacity-optimized), which launches from pools with the most spare capacity, not merely the cheapest.
  3. Handle the notice. On notice: deregister from the load balancer, stop pulling new work, checkpoint or finish in-flight work within two minutes. Kubernetes node termination handlers and Karpenter do this for pods.
  4. Keep a floor. Run enough on-demand capacity for what must not be interrupted and to absorb a spot shortfall.

6. Autoscaling groups, traced

An autoscaling group (ASG) manages a fleet of instances from a launch template (image, instance types, network, security groups, IAM role, user data). You set a minimum, maximum and desired count, and the subnets (zones) to use. The group:

  • launches or terminates instances to match the desired count, balancing across zones;
  • replaces instances that fail EC2 status checks or, if configured, load-balancer health checks (after a health check grace period);
  • changes the desired count through scaling policies: target tracking (keep average CPU at 50%, or requests per target at 1,000), step (add 4 instances when CPU exceeds 70%, 8 above 85%), scheduled (set desired to 30 at 08:00 on weekdays) and predictive (forecast from history and scale ahead);
  • runs lifecycle hooks that pause launches or terminations so you can warm caches or drain connections;
  • supports mixed instances (several types, on-demand base plus spot), warm pools (pre-initialised stopped instances that start in seconds) and instance refresh (rolling replacement to a new launch template).

Trace a spike. A target-tracking policy keeps average CPU at 50% on a group of 10 instances. At 12:00:00 traffic jumps 60%; CPU climbs to 80%. CloudWatch's alarm (created by the policy) needs its evaluation periods to breach — with one-minute metrics, typically by about 12:02. The group raises desired capacity to 16 and calls RunInstances. Instances boot by 12:03, user data installs the agent and pulls the application image by 12:04, the load balancer marks them healthy after two passed health checks at 12:04:30, and their metrics count after the warm-up period. From 12:00 to about 12:05 the original 10 instances carried 160% of the old load at 80% CPU — fine, because the target left 50% headroom. Had the target been 75%, they'd have been at 120% demand: queueing, latency and errors.

Scaling in is deliberately slower (to avoid flapping), and instances should drain: the load balancer's deregistration delay lets in-flight requests finish before termination.

7. Containers on managed platforms

Containers (k8s1–k8s3) package an application with its dependencies as an image. The cloud question is who runs the machines and the scheduler.

Amazon ECS is AWS's own orchestrator. A task definition lists containers, CPU and memory, ports, an IAM task role and log configuration; a service keeps N tasks running behind a load balancer, does rolling deployments and integrates with autoscaling. Capacity comes from capacity providers: your own EC2 autoscaling groups, Fargate, or Fargate Spot. There's no fee for ECS itself.

Fargate runs each task (or EKS pod) in its own isolated micro-VM sized to what you request, billed per second for vCPU and memory. In us-east-1 on 7 October 2026: $0.04048 per vCPU-hour and $0.004445 per GB-hour on x86, $0.03238 and $0.00356 on Arm. A 1 vCPU, 2 GB x86 task costs $0.04048 + 2 × $0.004445 = $0.04937 an hour, about $36 a month. You never patch a host or scale a cluster, and each task is isolated from others by a VM boundary rather than a shared kernel. The trade-offs: a premium over equivalent EC2 capacity, slower task start than a container on a warm node (image pulls on every start), no GPUs, no privileged containers or daemonsets.

Amazon EKS, GKE and AKS are managed Kubernetes: the provider runs the control plane (API server, etcd, scheduler) and you supply worker capacity — managed node groups, self-managed autoscaling groups, Karpenter-provisioned nodes, Fargate, or provider "auto" modes where the provider also manages the nodes for an extra per-instance fee. EKS charged $0.10 per cluster-hour (about $73 a month) in October 2026. Kubernetes is worth it for its ecosystem, portability across clouds, and fine-grained scheduling (k8s6–k8s14); it costs upgrade work every few months and add-ons to run.

Request-driven container platforms — Google Cloud Run, Azure Container Apps, and on AWS App Runner — sit closest to functions. You deploy an image; the platform runs instances in response to requests, each instance handling many concurrent requests (Cloud Run's per-instance concurrency is configurable, with a default of 80), scales out with load, and can scale to zero when idle, with a cold start when traffic resumes. Billing is per instance time, by default only while handling requests. They're excellent for HTTP services with uneven traffic and small teams.

8. Functions, briefly

Functions as a service — AWS Lambda, Google Cloud Run functions, Azure Functions — run your code once per event (an HTTP request, a queue message, a file upload, a schedule), each execution environment handling one request at a time on Lambda, scaling out by adding environments, and billing per request plus per GB-second of memory-time. In us-east-1 on 7 October 2026, Lambda cost $0.20 per million requests and $0.0000166667 per GB-second on x86. A function with 512 MB running 100 ms costs 0.5 × 0.1 × $0.0000166667 ≈ $0.00000083 per call plus $0.0000002 for the request — about $1.03 per million calls. Functions are the right default for glue and spiky event handling and the wrong one for steady heavy traffic, long jobs (Lambda's maximum is 15 minutes) and latency-critical paths sensitive to cold starts. cl5 is entirely about this execution model; here it just takes its place in the table.

9. Sizing and pricing a fleet by hand

An internal search API is load-tested on m7g instances: each request uses 12 ms of CPU. Traffic peaks at 3,000 requests per second for about four hours on weekdays, averages 1,800, and falls to 400 at night. It must survive the loss of one of three zones without needing to launch anything.

CPU demand. At peak: 3,000 × 0.012 s = 36 vCPU-seconds per second — 36 vCPUs fully busy. Average: 1,800 × 0.012 = 21.6. Night: 4.8.

Zone-loss sizing (static stability, cl1). If one zone disappears at peak, the other two must carry 36 vCPUs of work. Allowing 85% utilisation in that emergency: 36 / 0.85 ≈ 42.4 vCPUs across two zones, so at least 21.2 per zone. In m7g.xlarge units (4 vCPUs): 6 per zone (24 vCPUs), 18 instances, 72 vCPUs. In normal operation at peak they run at 36 / 72 = 50%.

Price the options (us-east-1, 7 October 2026, 730 hours a month):

OptionFleetMonthly
A. Static, on-demand18 × m7g.xlarge × $0.1632$2,144.45
B. Static, 1-year no-upfront reserved18 × $0.108$1,419.12
C. 12 reserved (2 zones' worth at 75%) + autoscaled on-demand for the 4 h weekday peak12 × $0.108 × 730 + 6 × $0.1632 × 4 h × 22 days$946.08 + $86.17 = $1,032.25
D. Fargate Arm, same 72 vCPU, 2 GB per vCPU, all month72 × ($0.03238 + 2 × $0.00356) × 730$2,076.12

Option C is cheapest but gives up part of static stability: after a zone loss at peak, the survivors carry 36 vCPUs on 32 (eight reserved instances) until scale-out arrives a few minutes later, so they're overloaded briefly. That's a business decision, not an engineering one. Option D costs about the same as on-demand EC2 and removes host management; it wins if the team is small or traffic falls to zero for long periods (Fargate tasks can scale down further at night than an instance fleet bound to zone minimums). The point of the exercise isn't the exact numbers, which change; it's that the cheapest option depends on load shape, availability requirements and what you'll commit to.

deep:
Capacity is a market with physical limits

On-demand capacity in a zone is finite per instance type. When demand for a type exceeds the free hosts — a new GPU, a regional event shifting traffic, a big customer's launch — RunInstances fails with an insufficient-capacity error regardless of your quota. Three tools manage this. Flexibility: accept several types and sizes and all zones, so the scheduler can find something. Reservations: on-demand capacity reservations hold capacity in a zone whether you use it or not (you pay for it either way), and capacity blocks reserve GPU clusters for fixed windows. Static stability: run what you'd need after a failure before the failure, because during a regional event everyone is launching at once. For GPU workloads, capacity rather than price is often the binding constraint (cl14).

Why spot interruption rates vary so much

Interruptions happen when the provider needs a pool's capacity for on-demand or reserved customers. A pool that is a popular type in a busy zone is reclaimed often; an older generation in a quiet zone rarely. Running a single type in one zone concentrates your risk in one pool, so a demand spike there interrupts your whole fleet at once — the worst case for a service. Spreading across 15–20 pools makes simultaneous interruption of a large fraction unlikely and lets capacity-aware allocation steer launches away from stressed pools. This is the same diversification argument as in finance, and it's why "spot is unreliable" usually means "spot with one instance type is unreliable".

Bin-packing and the hidden cost of orchestrators

Containers promise efficiency through packing many small workloads onto large nodes. The promise is kept only if requests are accurate and the node autoscaler can find good fits. Real clusters lose capacity to fragmentation (a node with 1.5 free vCPUs can't place a 2-vCPU pod), per-node overheads (kubelet and system reservations, daemonsets for logging, metrics and networking on every node), zone minimums and pods that block consolidation. Measured "requested over allocatable" ratios of 50–70% are common. Karpenter-style autoscalers improve this by choosing instance types to fit pending pods and actively consolidating underused nodes, at the cost of more node churn — which interacts with long-running pods and disruption budgets.

Fargate isolation is a security property, not just convenience

On a shared node, containers share a kernel; a kernel exploit from one pod can reach the others (os13, k8s1). Fargate runs every task or pod in its own micro-VM (AWS built Firecracker for Lambda and Fargate-style isolation), so the isolation boundary is a hypervisor rather than namespaces. For multi-tenant platforms running customer code — notebooks, agents executing code — this boundary is often worth the price premium by itself, or worth reproducing with sandboxed runtimes (gVisor, Kata Containers) on your own nodes.

Arm migration is mostly a build-system problem

Moving to Graviton rarely needs application changes in Go, Java, Python or Node. The work is in the pipeline: multi-architecture container images (one tag pointing at amd64 and arm64 variants, k8s5), CI runners for both architectures, native dependencies with arm64 builds, and observability that can compare architectures side by side. Honeycomb's 2021 retrospective describes the change as transparent to developers once CI produced multi-architecture artifacts. Once that's in place, every future generation — and every switch between providers' Arm and x86 offerings — becomes a scheduling decision rather than a project.

Graceful shutdown is part of the compute contract

Every elastic option removes capacity as well as adding it: scale-in, spot interruptions, deployments, instance refreshes, Fargate task replacements, node consolidation. Each sends a termination signal and then, after a grace period, kills the process. Services that ignore SIGTERM drop in-flight requests every time capacity shrinks, which on an autoscaled fleet is many times a day. The contract is the same everywhere: on SIGTERM stop accepting new work, let the load balancer deregister you (deregistration delay), finish or hand off in-flight work, flush buffers, then exit — within the platform's window (two minutes for spot, 30 seconds by default for Kubernetes pods, configurable for ECS tasks). Getting this right is what makes cheap, elastic capacity safe to use.

Right-sizing is continuous because software changes

The instance size that was right at launch drifts: new features add CPU per request, a library upgrade changes memory use, traffic mix shifts. Treat sizing as a measured loop like least privilege (cl2): collect CPU, memory and network per instance and per request, use provider recommendations (AWS Compute Optimizer, GKE's recommendations, VPA in Kubernetes) as input, and test changes as canaries. Over-sizing wastes money quietly; under-sizing shows up only at peak.
prod:
Failure modes

Insufficient capacity at launch. Scale-out or a deploy fails with InsufficientInstanceCapacity for a type in a zone. Symptoms: ASG activity history full of failed launches, pods pending in Kubernetes. Fix: more instance types and zones in the launch template or node pool, capacity reservations for critical baselines.

Quota limits. The account's vCPU quota for on-demand or spot instances in a region stops scaling. AWS quotas for EC2 are per instance family group in vCPUs; GPU families often start at zero. Monitor usage against quotas and raise them ahead of growth.

Scale-out too slow. Latency and errors during traffic ramps despite autoscaling. Typical causes: boot-time installation, large images, long health check intervals, target utilisation set too high. Fix with baked images, warm pools, predictive or scheduled scaling, lower targets.

Mass spot interruption. Many instances interrupted together because the fleet used one pool. Fix by diversifying and keeping an on-demand floor.

Burst credit exhaustion. A t-instance service slows to a crawl after a long busy period (standard mode) or the bill shows surplus credit charges (unlimited). Alert on CPUCreditBalance.

Noisy deploys. Instance refresh or a rolling deployment drops capacity below what peak needs. Set minimum healthy percentages, deploy outside peaks, and check the deployment's effect on capacity before starting.

Image and AMI drift. Instances launched months apart from different images behave differently; a scale-out brings up machines with an old kernel or agent. Rebuild images on a schedule and use instance refresh to roll fleets onto them.

What to measure

CPU, memory and network per instance and aggregated per service; cost per thousand requests (the number that tells you whether a change helped); scale-out latency (time from alarm to healthy capacity); launch failures by reason; spot interruptions per day by pool; cluster efficiency (requested/allocatable and used/requested); quota utilisation.

The case: Honeycomb moves from Graviton4 to Graviton5 (June 2026)

Honeycomb, an observability company, published per-service results of moving shared production compute from m8g.8xlarge (Graviton4) to m9g.8xlarge (Graviton5). The method is the lesson: both generations ran concurrently in the same Kubernetes namespace for 60 days, serving the same traffic, and Honeycomb compared per-pod metrics. Every measured service used between 11% and 26% less CPU on Graviton5; compute-bound services 16–22%. Ingest P99 latency dropped 28%; one metrics-ingest pipeline's P99 halved from 880 to 440 microseconds; tail-based sampling queues were 44–73% shorter at P95. The post doesn't give cost figures.

Price it yourself. On 7 October 2026 the AWS price list showed $1.56544 per hour for an m9g.8xlarge and $1.43616 for an m8g.8xlarge in us-east-1, a 9.0% premium. If a service's fleet is sized by CPU and needs 20% less, the cost ratio is 1.09 × 0.80 ≈ 0.87: about 13% cheaper for the same work, with better tail latency. For a service whose CPU fell only 11%, it's 1.09 × 0.89 ≈ 0.97, a smaller saving; for a memory-bound service, the newer instance may simply cost more. That spread is why per-service measurement on real traffic beats a single benchmark. The same company's 2021 Graviton2 retrospective shows the enabling work: multi-architecture CI and standardised service tooling made the move "push-button" for most services.
myths: A vCPU is a CPU core.

On most Intel and AMD instance types a vCPU is one hardware thread, and two vCPUs share one physical core through simultaneous multithreading; on AWS Graviton (Arm) instances each vCPU is a full physical core. So 4 vCPUs of an m7i are two cores with two threads each, while 4 vCPUs of an m7g are four cores. For CPU-bound work this changes how much throughput a vCPU buys — measure per vCPU rather than assuming.
Burstable t-instances are just cheaper general-purpose instances.

They're priced for a baseline: a t4g.small earns credits for 20% of each vCPU, and running above that spends credits. In the default unlimited mode, a sustained average above baseline is billed extra per vCPU-hour; in standard mode the instance is throttled to baseline when credits run out. For steady CPU-heavy services, an m- or c-family instance is usually cheaper and always more predictable.
Spot instances are unreliable, so they're only for toys.

Spot capacity can be reclaimed with two minutes' notice on AWS, but large production fleets run on it: stateless web tiers behind load balancers, batch and CI workers, and checkpointed training jobs. The design requirements are diversification (many instance types and zones), graceful handling of the notice, and a baseline of on-demand capacity for what can't be interrupted.
Autoscaling means I never have to think about capacity.

Autoscaling reacts to metrics with delays: a metric period, an alarm evaluation, an instance launch, boot, warm-up and health checks — often three to six minutes for VMs. Spikes faster than that hit the capacity you already have. It also depends on the provider having capacity of your instance type in your zones, and on quotas. You still choose headroom, step sizes, warm pools or scheduled scaling for known peaks.
Containers are always cheaper than VMs.

Containers make packing and deploying easier; they don't make CPU cheaper. Fargate charges per vCPU-hour and GB-hour at a premium over the equivalent EC2 capacity in exchange for not managing hosts, and a Kubernetes cluster adds a control-plane fee and the cost of nodes that are rarely fully packed. Containers become cheaper when they let you bin-pack many small services onto fewer, larger, well-utilised instances.
Newer instance generations always cost more.

Newer generations usually cost about the same or a little more per hour but deliver more work per hour. On 7 October 2026 an m9g.8xlarge (Graviton5) cost about 9% more per hour than an m8g.8xlarge (Graviton4) in us-east-1, while Honeycomb measured 11–26% less CPU on the newer one for the same work. If the fleet is sized by CPU, the newer generation is cheaper overall.
