t: Cloud storage: object storage (S3 classes, consistency, lifecycle, multipart), block (EBS) and file (EFS, FSx), and choosing between them for datasets, checkpoints and model weights
sum: The three shapes of cloud storage and how each really works: S3's object model, durability, strong consistency and conditional writes, storage classes with their minimum durations and retrieval fees, lifecycle rules, request-rate and multipart mechanics; EBS volumes, snapshots and instance store; EFS and FSx for Lustre; and the ML choices worked with numbers — a 70B-parameter checkpoint, a 40 TB dataset of small files, and loading model weights — with Canva's 130-petabyte move to Glacier Instant Retrieval as the case.
prereq: sc8
Object stores hold immutable blobs addressed by key, cheaply and durably, and underpin data lakes; databases, search and analytics stores each fit different access patterns.
k8s9
PersistentVolumes and StorageClasses provision disks dynamically; block volumes attach to one node in one zone; shared file systems allow many readers but have their own consistency rules.
os10
File systems map names to inodes and blocks, journal metadata, and offer POSIX operations like rename, append and fsync that applications rely on.
cl1
Zonal resources fail with their zone; regional services spread data across zones; prices differ by region and per request.
why:
An ML team trains its first large model. The dataset — 400 million images — sits in a bucket as 400 million separate files, because that's how it arrived. Checkpoints go to a shared network file system because the training script expects a path. The trained weights are copied onto each inference server's disk by hand.

Three weeks later the problems pile up. Data loading is the bottleneck: the GPUs sit idle 60% of the time waiting for images, and the bucket returns "503 Slow Down" errors. The shared file system bill is larger than the GPU bill's rounding error should allow, because it charges per gigabyte read and the job rereads the dataset every epoch. A job crashes halfway through writing a checkpoint, and the next run resumes from a corrupted file nobody noticed was incomplete. Someone's cleanup script deletes the "old" checkpoints prefix — which was the only copy of the best run. And when traffic grows, new inference servers take twenty minutes to start because they copy 140 GB of weights over a slow path.

Each of these comes from treating storage as one thing. Cloud providers offer three different shapes — object, block and file — each built for a different access pattern and priced differently, and inside object storage a ladder of storage classes with rules that can save or waste millions. Getting the shape right decides whether the GPUs are fed, whether checkpoints are safe, and whether the storage bill is a rounding error or a line item.

This lesson explains how each shape works underneath: S3's object model, durability and consistency, storage classes and lifecycle rules, request-rate and multipart mechanics; EBS volumes, snapshots and local NVMe; EFS and FSx for Lustre. It then works the ML cases with real numbers — a 70B-parameter checkpoint, a dataset of small files, model weights for serving — and closes with Canva's move of 130 petabytes to a colder class, which shows how to decide with data rather than instinct.
primer:
Picture three ways of keeping things for a company.

The first is a huge warehouse run by someone else. You hand over a sealed box with a label ("datasets/v3/shard-00042"), get a receipt, and later ask for it back by label. You can't open a box in the warehouse and change one page; to change anything you send a whole new box with the same label. The warehouse is enormous, cheap per box, keeps copies in several buildings so it practically never loses one, and serves thousands of people at once — but every trip costs a small fee and takes a moment. That's object storage: S3, Google Cloud Storage, Azure Blob Storage.

The second is a filing cabinet bolted to your desk. You can open any drawer, change one page, add a note to a folder, instantly. Only you can use it, and it's in your office — if the building burns, so does the cabinet, unless you photocopied it to the warehouse. That's block storage: an EBS volume attached to one instance in one zone, on which the operating system puts a normal file system.

The third is a shared office library. Everyone on the floor can open the same folders, edit the same files, see each other's changes. It's convenient, but it costs more per shelf than the warehouse, and when a hundred people rush in at once the librarian becomes the bottleneck. That's file storage: EFS (shared NFS) or a parallel file system like FSx for Lustre built for many readers.

The prices tell the story: in us-east-1 in October 2026, a gigabyte-month cost $0.023 in S3 Standard, $0.08 on a gp3 volume and $0.30 in EFS Standard — about 13 times S3. So a sensible default for large data is the warehouse, with block for things a single machine must change quickly, and file only where many machines genuinely need a shared tree.

For ML work the mapping is usually simple. Training data and checkpoints belong in the warehouse, packed into large boxes. Each training node's scratch work — unpacking a shard, staging a checkpoint before upload — happens on the desk cabinet or, faster still, on the node's own local NVMe disks. A shared library is worth paying for only when a framework insists on file paths and many machines must read the same files at very high speed; then a parallel file system that fronts the warehouse gives the best of both. Getting this mapping right is most of the work; the rest of the lesson explains the mechanics and the numbers that justify it.

Where the analogy breaks: the warehouse isn't slow in aggregate. One request takes a hundred milliseconds or so, but you can send thousands at once, and large jobs routinely pull tens of gigabits per second per instance from S3. Throughput comes from parallelism, not from any single trip — which is the key to using it well for ML.
body:
1. The object model

S3 stores objects in buckets. A bucket lives in one region and has a globally unique name. An object is identified by its key — any UTF-8 string up to 1,024 bytes, such as datasets/v3/shard-00042.tar — and consists of data (up to 48.8 TiB) plus metadata (content type, user-defined headers, tags). The namespace is flat: the slashes are just characters, and "folders" in consoles are a display trick. LIST operations can group keys by a delimiter and a prefix, which is how directory-like browsing works.

The operations are few: PUT (create or replace a whole object), GET (read all of it or a byte range), HEAD (metadata), DELETE, LIST, COPY, and multipart upload. There's no append, no partial overwrite, no atomic rename (a "rename" is a copy plus a delete, which for a large prefix is many requests and not atomic). Each operation is an HTTPS request, authorised by IAM and bucket policies (cl2), and billed: in us-east-1 in October 2026, $0.005 per 1,000 PUT, COPY, POST or LIST requests and $0.0004 per 1,000 GETs on S3 Standard.

With versioning enabled on a bucket, a PUT to an existing key creates a new version rather than replacing the old one, and a DELETE adds a "delete marker" that hides the object while keeping its versions. Versions are billed as storage, so versioned buckets need lifecycle rules that expire noncurrent versions.

2. Durability and availability, and what they don't cover

S3 Standard is designed for 99.999999999% (eleven nines) durability and 99.99% availability, storing data across at least three availability zones (from the storage-class comparison table, October 2026). Eleven nines is a statement about hardware loss: if you store ten million objects, you can on average expect to lose one every 10,000 years. AWS achieves it with redundancy across devices and zones (erasure coding — fragments plus parity spread so that missing pieces can be rebuilt) and constant background checking and repair.

Durability is not protection from yourself. A lifecycle rule with the wrong prefix, a script with aws s3 rm --recursive, a compromised credential, ransomware that overwrites objects with encrypted copies — S3 will durably store the result. The protections are layered: versioning (undo overwrites and deletes), Object Lock (make versions immutable for a retention period; in compliance mode not even the root user can shorten it), restrictive delete permissions, and replication to a bucket in another account and possibly another region (cl10 covers backups and RPO). The classes ending "One Zone" store data in a single zone and are not resilient to losing that zone.

3. Consistency and conditional writes

Since December 2020, S3 has provided strong read-after-write consistency: after a successful PUT or DELETE of an object (new or overwritten), every subsequent GET, HEAD or LIST reflects it, in every region. Werner Vogels described the engineering behind this in 2021: S3 added a replicated, strongly consistent witness that tracks the latest version of each object's metadata and lets caches know when they're stale, so reads can be both fast and current. Before that, overwrites and LISTs were eventually consistent, and big-data tools needed extra consistency layers.

Strong consistency doesn't make concurrent writers safe. Two clients writing the same key at the same time both succeed and the last write wins. Conditional writes fix this. If-None-Match: * makes a PUT succeed only if the key doesn't exist (otherwise 412 Precondition Failed); If-Match: <ETag> makes it succeed only if the object still has the version you read. That's enough to build create-once semantics (a checkpoint manifest that must not be overwritten), optimistic concurrency (read, modify, write-if-unchanged) and simple locks — Terraform's S3 backend now uses this for state locking (cl9).

4. Storage classes and lifecycle, with numbers

Every object has a storage class. The classes trade a lower price per GB for rules that penalise the wrong data. Figures for us-east-1 from the AWS price list and storage-class documentation, October 2026:

Read the rules as costs. A 10 KB object in Standard-IA is billed as 128 KB — 12.8 times its size — so at $0.0125 per GB it costs more than in Standard at $0.023. An object deleted from Glacier Instant Retrieval after 30 days is billed for 90. Moving an object between classes with a lifecycle rule is itself a request: Canva paid $0.02 per 1,000 objects to transition into Glacier IR. And reading cold data costs retrieval fees per GB on top of request fees.

Work a break-even. Moving a 1 MB object from Standard to Glacier IR saves (0.023 − 0.004) × 0.001 GB = $0.000019 per month, and costs $0.00002 to transition — paid back in about a month, then pure saving, provided it isn't read often (each full read costs $0.00003). For a 20 KB object, billed as 128 KB in Glacier IR: storage goes from 0.023 × 0.00002 = $0.00000046 to 0.004 × 0.000128 = $0.000000512 a month — more expensive, before the transition fee. That's why Canva found a break-even near 20 KB and why lifecycle policies should filter by object size (lifecycle rules support size filters).

Lifecycle rules automate this per bucket: by prefix, tag or object size, transition objects after N days, expire them after M days, expire noncurrent versions, and abort incomplete multipart uploads. Intelligent-Tiering does it per object based on observed access (30 days without access to the infrequent tier, 90 days to the archive-instant tier) for a monitoring fee — attractive for large objects with unknown patterns, costly for billions of small ones.

5. Performance: request rates, latency and parallelism

AWS's performance guide (October 2026) gives the numbers to design with. S3 supports at least 3,500 PUT/COPY/POST/DELETE and 5,500 GET/HEAD requests per second per partitioned prefix, and there's no limit on the number of prefixes; it scales gradually, and while it scales you may see 503 Slow Down errors, which clients should retry with backoff. Latency for small objects, and time to first byte for large ones, is roughly 100–200 ms. Throughput comes from concurrency: a single instance can drive up to 100 Gb/s from S3 with enough parallel requests, and fleets reach terabits per second.

Multipart upload is how large objects are written fast and safely. You initiate an upload, send parts (5 MiB to 5 GiB each, up to 10,000 parts, numbered so order doesn't matter) in parallel, then complete it, at which point S3 assembles the object atomically: readers see either the old object or the whole new one. Failed parts are simply retried. The arithmetic: a 125 GB object needs parts of at least 125 GB ÷ 10,000 = 12.5 MB; with 64 MiB parts it's about 1,863 parts, each a separate PUT. Until completed or aborted, uploaded parts are stored and billed but invisible in normal listings — a classic hidden cost, fixed with an AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload lifecycle rule. On the read side, byte-range GETs let many connections download different parts of one large object in parallel.

For latency-sensitive access there's S3 Express One Zone: "directory buckets" in a single zone you choose, designed for consistent single-digit-millisecond access, at a higher storage price ($0.11/GB-month) but much cheaper requests ($0.00113 per 1,000 PUTs, $0.00003 per 1,000 GETs). It suits hot intermediate data near compute — shuffle data, a training job's cache — not the primary copy of anything.

6. Block storage: EBS volumes, snapshots and instance store

An EBS volume is a network-attached disk in one availability zone that attaches to one instance (or, for io1/io2, several with multi-attach). The instance's operating system formats it with a file system and gets ordinary POSIX semantics. Volume types, from the EBS documentation (October 2026):

io2 Block Express4 GiB–64 TiB256,0004,000 MiB/s99.999%$0.125/GB-mo + $0.065/IOPS-mo (tiered)

gp3's design is worth noticing: performance is provisioned separately from size, so a 100 GB volume can have 16,000 IOPS, which wasn't possible with gp2. io2 Block Express is for latency-critical databases, designed for average latency under 500 µs. And every instance type has its own EBS bandwidth limit, so a large volume on a small instance can't reach the volume's numbers.

Snapshots are point-in-time copies of volumes, stored in S3 (at $0.05/GB-month in October 2026) and incremental: the first copies all used blocks, later ones only changed blocks. New volumes can be created from them in any zone of the region, and snapshots can be copied to other regions — the basic block-level backup and migration tool. A volume restored from a snapshot loads blocks lazily from S3 on first access, so first reads are slow unless you pre-warm.

Instance store is different: NVMe SSDs physically in the host (the d in names like m7gd, and standard on GPU training instances), with very high throughput and low latency, and no durability — the data disappears when the instance stops, terminates or its host fails. It's the right place for caches, scratch space, shuffle data, and staging checkpoints before upload, never for the only copy.

7. File storage: EFS and FSx for Lustre

EFS is a managed NFS (v4.1) file system: regional by default (data stored across zones, with mount targets in each zone's subnets), growing and shrinking automatically with no provisioning. Many instances, containers and functions can mount it at once with full POSIX semantics — rename, append, locks. The price in us-east-1, October 2026: $0.30/GB-month in Standard, $0.025 in Infrequent Access, $0.008 in Archive, plus, in the default elastic throughput mode, $0.03 per GB read and $0.06 per GB written. A training job that reads a 10 TB dataset 20 times through EFS elastic throughput pays 200 TB × 1,024 × $0.03 ≈ $6,144 in read charges on top of $3,072 a month for storage — against $235 a month to store it in S3 Standard and read it without per-GB fees inside the region.

FSx for Lustre is a managed parallel file system: data is striped across many storage servers so that hundreds of clients can read and write at aggregate throughputs of hundreds of GB/s, with POSIX semantics. Persistent SSD deployments are priced by throughput tier — for example $0.145/GB-month for 125 MB/s per TiB and $0.60 for 1,000 MB/s per TiB (us-east-1, October 2026). It can be linked to an S3 bucket: files appear in the file system and are loaded lazily from S3 on first access, and results can be exported back. It's the standard answer when an HPC or ML framework insists on a POSIX path and needs very high throughput. Other FSx flavours (NetApp ONTAP, OpenZFS, Windows File Server) serve enterprise file workloads.

8. Choosing storage for datasets, checkpoints and weights

Datasets: shard them. Take an image dataset of 400 million files averaging 100 KB (about 40 TB). Stored as-is in S3, one epoch is 400 million GETs: $160 in request charges per epoch, and at 5,500 GETs per second per prefix about 20 hours per prefix — you'd need dozens of prefixes and thousands of concurrent connections just to keep up. Packed into 1 GB shards (tar files or a record format such as WebDataset, TFRecord or Parquet), it's 40,000 objects: 40,000 GETs per epoch ($0.016), read sequentially with large range requests, limited by network bandwidth rather than request rates. Shuffling happens in a buffer across several shards. Storage cost is the same either way: 40 TB × 1,024 × $0.023 ≈ $942 a month in Standard.

Checkpoints: parallel, atomic, tiered. A checkpoint of a 70B-parameter model trained with mixed-precision Adam holds bf16 weights (2 bytes per parameter), FP32 master weights (4) and two FP32 Adam moments (4 + 4): 14 bytes per parameter, about 980 GB. (gpu9 explains why each piece exists.) With 64 GPUs on 8 nodes, each node writes about 122.5 GB. The pattern:

  1. Copy GPU state to host memory or local NVMe (instance store), then let training continue — only this copy pauses the GPUs.
  2. Upload each node's shard with multipart upload, 64–128 MiB parts, many in parallel.
  3. When every shard is complete, write a small manifest — step number, shard keys, checksums — with If-None-Match: *. Readers load only checkpoints that have a manifest, so a crash mid-upload leaves no half-checkpoint that looks valid.
  4. Lifecycle: keep recent ones hot, move daily ones to Glacier Instant Retrieval, expire the rest, abort incomplete uploads after a day.

Price the retention policy: the last five hourly checkpoints in Standard are 4,900 GB × $0.023 ≈ $112.70 a month. One checkpoint per day for 90 days is 88,200 GB: $2,028.60 a month in Standard, $352.80 in Glacier Instant Retrieval. Requests are negligible (about 15,000 part PUTs per checkpoint ≈ $0.08). Milestone checkpoints and the final model go under Object Lock and are replicated to another account.

Model weights for serving: stage close to the GPU. A 70B model in bf16 is 140 GB. New inference instances need it fast, because cold start time is capacity lost during scale-out (k8s14). Options in order of speed: weights already on local NVMe (from a warm pool or a previous run); pulled from S3 with highly parallel range GETs at several GB/s per instance (140 GB at 5 GB/s ≈ 28 seconds); a shared cache (FSx for Lustre or a node-local cache) so many instances don't each pull from S3; worst, a single-stream copy at a few hundred MB/s (several minutes). Container images with the weights baked in are convenient for small models and slow for large ones, because image layers are pulled and unpacked sequentially.

9. The same shapes elsewhere

ShapeAWSGoogle CloudAzure

FileEFS, FSx (Lustre, ONTAP, OpenZFS, Windows)Filestore, Managed Lustre, ParallelstoreAzure Files, NetApp Files, Managed Lustre

The rules transfer: minimum durations on cold classes (Google's are 30, 90 and 365 days for Nearline, Coldline and Archive), per-operation charges, zonal disks, and parallelism for throughput. The main design difference is where redundancy is chosen — per object class on S3, per bucket location on Cloud Storage, per storage account on Azure.
deep:
Why object storage scales where file systems struggle

A POSIX file system promises a single, consistent tree: rename is atomic, a directory listing reflects every create and delete, appends from several writers interleave correctly. Keeping those promises across many servers requires coordinating metadata on every operation, which is why shared file systems have metadata servers that become bottlenecks and why their prices are higher. Object storage drops the promises that need coordination — no rename, no partial writes, no hierarchy — so each key can be handled independently, partitioned by key range across a fleet, and scaled by splitting partitions. That's the origin of the per-prefix request rates: S3 partitions its index by key, and a "partitioned prefix" is one slice of it. Hot slices are split as load grows, which is why scaling is gradual and why bursts against one prefix see 503s first.

How strong consistency was added without a global lock

S3's metadata is cached heavily for speed; the old eventual consistency came from caches that could briefly serve stale metadata after an overwrite. Vogels's 2021 description of the change: S3 introduced a replicated, highly available component that tracks the order of writes per object, and caches consult it cheaply to learn whether their view is current, with a protocol designed so that the common case stays fast and the system remains available when parts fail. The point for designers is that strong consistency became a property you get for free per object, not a transaction across objects: there's still no multi-object atomic commit, which is why checkpoint and table formats (Iceberg, Delta Lake) use a manifest or log written last.

The small-files problem is a cost and a latency problem

Every object carries fixed overheads: a request fee, 100-plus milliseconds of latency, index entries, and in colder classes minimum billable sizes and per-object metadata. When objects are small, those overheads dominate the bytes. Small files also hurt everything downstream: LIST operations return 1,000 keys per call, so a prefix of 100 million objects takes 100,000 LIST calls to enumerate; lifecycle transitions cost per object; inventory and replication scale with object count. The remedies are always some form of packing — shards, record files, columnar formats with large row groups — plus an index when random access is needed.

Data loaders are distributed systems

Feeding 64 GPUs at, say, 2 GB/s each means 128 GB/s from storage. That needs thousands of concurrent requests spread across many prefixes, retries for 503s and timeouts, prefetching far enough ahead to hide 100–200 ms latency, and shuffling that doesn't require random access to individual samples. Libraries built for this (streaming dataset loaders, S3 connectors for PyTorch, Mountpoint for Amazon S3 for sequential file access) package these patterns. When the framework can't stream from S3, a parallel file system linked to the bucket provides POSIX paths at the cost of provisioning throughput.

Checkpoint frequency is an optimisation problem

Checkpointing costs GPU time (the pause to copy state) and storage; not checkpointing costs the work lost when a failure happens. With mean time between failures M for the whole job and checkpoint cost C (in time), the classic first-order result (Young's formula) puts the optimal interval near √(2 × C × M). For a large job whose fleet sees a failure every 6 hours on average and whose checkpoint copy pauses training for 2 minutes, that's √(2 × 2 × 360) ≈ 38 minutes. Faster checkpointing (async upload, in-memory replicas on peer nodes) lowers C and so allows more frequent checkpoints and less lost work — which is why large training systems invest in it.

Replication has its own consistency and cost model

Cross-region and same-region replication copy new objects asynchronously to another bucket, usually within minutes; S3 Replication Time Control adds an SLA-backed target of 15 minutes for most objects. Replication doesn't copy objects that existed before it was enabled unless you run a batch job, doesn't by default replicate deletes (a protection against propagating mistakes), and bills inter-region transfer per GB plus storage in the target. For disaster recovery that makes the RPO for objects minutes rather than zero, and it makes replication a cost line proportional to write volume — relevant when checkpoints write a terabyte an hour.

Encryption choices have cost consequences

All new S3 objects are encrypted at rest by default with S3-managed keys. Using customer-managed KMS keys (SSE-KMS) adds control and an audit trail of key use (cl13, au11), but each object operation can call KMS, which has request quotas and charges; S3 Bucket Keys cut those calls by deriving a bucket-level data key. For high-request workloads — millions of small reads — forgetting bucket keys shows up as KMS throttling and a surprising KMS line on the bill.
prod:
Failure modes and their symptoms

503 Slow Down. A new workload hammers one prefix faster than S3 has partitioned it. Symptoms: bursts of 503s and retries, rising latency. Fix: spread keys across prefixes, ramp up gradually, retry with exponential backoff and jitter (SDKs do), and reduce request counts by packing.

Accidental deletion. A cleanup job, a mistyped prefix or an over-eager lifecycle rule removes data. With versioning, restore by deleting delete markers or copying old versions back; without it, the data is gone. Prevention: versioning, Object Lock for critical data, delete permissions limited to a few roles, lifecycle rules reviewed like code.

Hidden storage growth. Noncurrent versions, incomplete multipart uploads and forgotten replication targets grow quietly. Storage Lens and inventory reports show them; lifecycle rules fix them.

Transitions that lose money. Lifecycle rules move billions of small objects to IA or Glacier classes: transition fees and minimum sizes exceed savings. Filter rules by object size; model the break-even first.

EBS performance ceilings. A database on gp3 hits its provisioned IOPS or throughput (or the instance's EBS bandwidth): latency climbs, VolumeQueueLength grows. Raise gp3 IOPS/throughput or move up an instance size.

Snapshot restores are slow at first. A volume created from a snapshot fetches blocks lazily; a database restored this way runs slowly until warmed. Pre-warm by reading the volume, or use fast snapshot restore for critical volumes.

Shared file system bottlenecks and bills. Many clients on EFS hit throughput or per-operation limits, or elastic throughput charges balloon. Measure bytes read per job; move bulk data to S3.

What to watch

Per bucket: storage by class and version state, object count and average size, requests by type, 4xx/5xx rates, first-byte latency, replication lag; per volume: IOPS and throughput against provisioned, queue length, burst balance on older types; per file system: throughput, metadata operations, per-GB access charges. Storage Lens gives organisation-wide views of most of these.

The case: Canva moves 130 PB to Glacier Instant Retrieval (May 2023)

Canva's engineering blog describes an S3 estate of about 230 petabytes and more than 300 billion objects, with the largest bucket at 45 PB. Much of it was user-uploaded media, already partly in Standard-IA. Using S3 Storage Class Analysis, the team found two patterns: in Standard, retrieval "falls drastically after the first 15 days" — Standard held about 10% of the bytes but 60–70% of the accesses; Standard-IA held about 90% of the bytes and a flat 30–40% of accesses over time. That's the signature of data that's rarely read but must still load in milliseconds when a user opens an old design: a fit for Glacier Instant Retrieval.

The decision turned on object size and transition fees. Glacier IR bills at least 128 KB per object and charges $0.02 per 1,000 objects to transition in, so moving tiny objects costs more than it saves; Canva calculated a point around 20 KB below which Standard is cheaper, and limited the move to buckets whose average object size was 400 KB or larger, where payback would come within six months. Moving roughly 80 billion objects cost $1.6 million once; the result is about $300,000 a month saved ($3.6 million a year), with about 130 PB now in Glacier IR.

The engineering lesson is the method: measure access by age, measure object size distribution, compute the transition cost and the payback period per bucket, and only then write the lifecycle rule. The same three numbers decide every storage-class question, from a team's log bucket to a 45-petabyte media store.
myths: S3 is a file system in the cloud.

S3 is a key-value store of whole objects behind an HTTP API. There are no directories (a slash in a key is just a character that list operations can group by), no partial writes or appends, no atomic rename, and every operation is a billed network request with tens to hundreds of milliseconds of latency. Tools that mount buckets as file systems translate POSIX calls into these operations, which works for sequential reads and writes of large files and badly for anything that rewrites small parts of files.
Eleven nines of durability means my data can't be lost.

S3's design target of 99.999999999% durability protects against losing objects to hardware failure. It does nothing against you or an attacker deleting or overwriting them, a lifecycle rule that expires the wrong prefix, or ransomware re-encrypting them. Versioning, Object Lock, replication to another account and backups protect against those, and they're your job.
S3 is eventually consistent, so I must wait after writing.

Since December 2020 S3 provides strong read-after-write consistency for all PUT and DELETE operations, including overwrites, and for LIST: once a write returns success, every subsequent read sees it. What S3 doesn't provide by default is coordination between concurrent writers — two PUTs to the same key race and the last one wins — unless you use conditional writes.
Moving data to a colder storage class always saves money.

Colder classes trade storage price for minimum storage durations, minimum billable object sizes, retrieval fees and per-object transition fees. Canva found that below about 20 KB per object it was cheaper to stay in S3 Standard, and only moved buckets whose average object was 400 KB or more. Millions of tiny objects moved to Glacier Instant Retrieval can cost more in transition requests and 128 KB minimum billing than they ever save.
EBS volumes are as durable as S3.

A gp3 volume is designed for 99.8–99.9% durability, an annual failure rate of 0.1–0.2%, and lives in one availability zone; io2 Block Express is designed for 99.999%. S3 Standard is designed for eleven nines across at least three zones. A volume is a fast disk for one instance, not an archive: protect what matters with snapshots, which are stored in S3.
A shared file system is the natural place for training data and checkpoints.

General-purpose NFS (EFS) is convenient but priced at about 13× S3 Standard per GB in us-east-1 and, in elastic mode, charges per GB read and written; at ML scale it's usually the wrong default. Large training jobs read sharded datasets directly from S3, or through a parallel file system such as FSx for Lustre linked to S3 when they need POSIX semantics and very high throughput, and write checkpoints to S3.
lab:
Goal: build a storage cost and layout calculator in Python 3.12 (standard library only) and use it to make the lesson's decisions. About 20 minutes; no cloud account needed.

  1. Price table. Encode the October 2026 us-east-1 figures from section 4: price per GB-month, minimum billable size, minimum duration, retrieval fee per GB, transition fee per 1,000 objects (use $0.02 for Glacier IR, $0.01 for Standard-IA as an assumption to vary).
  2. Per-object cost. Write monthly_cost(cls, size_bytes, reads_per_month) applying the minimum billable size and retrieval fees. Find the object size at which Glacier IR becomes cheaper than Standard for an object read never, and for one read once a quarter.
  3. Payback. Write payback_months(size, from_cls, to_cls) = transition fee ÷ monthly saving. Reproduce Canva's rule of thumb: what's the payback at 20 KB, 100 KB and 400 KB?
  4. Multipart. Write parts(object_bytes, part_bytes) that enforces 5 MiB ≤ part ≤ 5 GiB and ≤ 10,000 parts, and min_part(object_bytes). Check a 122.5 GB shard and a 48 TiB object.
  5. Shards. For 400 million samples of 100 KB, compute GET requests, request cost and hours at 5,500 GETs per second per prefix, for raw objects and for 1 GB shards.
  6. Checkpoint retention. Compute the monthly cost of the retention policy in section 8 for a 980 GB checkpoint, then for a 7B model (≈98 GB).

What to look for: step 2 shows Glacier IR losing below roughly 20–25 KB for never-read objects (the 128 KB minimum at $0.004 equals Standard at about 22 KB) and the break-even rising with reads; step 3 shows payback of months at 400 KB and never at 20 KB; step 4 gives a minimum part of 12.25 MB for 122.5 GB; step 5 gives $160 and about 20 hours per epoch for raw objects against cents and seconds of request time for shards; step 6 reproduces about $113 + $353 a month.

Needs an AWS account (optional): aws s3api list-multipart-uploads --bucket <bucket> lists invisible incomplete uploads you're paying for; aws s3api put-object --bucket <b> --key lock/test --body empty.txt --if-none-match "*" run twice shows the second attempt failing with 412 PreconditionFailed.
recap: Cloud storage comes in three shapes: object (whole immutable blobs by key over HTTP, regional, cheap and durable), block (a network disk for one instance in one zone, fast and POSIX through a file system) and file (a shared POSIX file system over the network).

S3 Standard stores objects across at least three zones, is designed for 99.999999999% durability and 99.99% availability, and has been strongly consistent for writes, deletes and lists since December 2020; conditional writes let concurrent writers coordinate.

Storage classes trade price per GB against minimum durations (30, 90 or 180 days), a 128 KB minimum billable size for IA and Glacier IR, retrieval fees and transition fees; lifecycle rules move or expire objects by age, and Intelligent-Tiering does it per object for a monitoring fee.

S3 scales to at least 3,500 writes and 5,500 reads per second per prefix, first-byte latency is roughly 100–200 ms, and throughput comes from parallelism: multipart uploads (5 MiB–5 GiB parts, up to 10,000, objects up to 48.8 TiB) and concurrent range reads.

EBS volumes are zonal network disks: gp3 gives 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s baseline and up to 80,000 IOPS and 2,000 MiB/s, io2 Block Express up to 256,000 IOPS with sub-millisecond latency; snapshots are incremental and stored in S3; instance store is fast but vanishes with the instance.
EFS is a regional, elastic NFS file system at about $0.30/GB-month plus per-GB access charges in elastic mode; FSx for Lustre is a parallel file system for HPC and ML that can front an S3 bucket.

For ML: keep datasets in S3 as large shards, not millions of small files; write checkpoints to S3 with parallel multipart uploads and an atomic manifest, and tier old checkpoints with lifecycle rules; stage model weights on local NVMe or a cache for fast loading.
Many storage costs come from requests and lifecycle mistakes: small objects, incomplete multipart uploads, unexpired noncurrent versions and transitions that never pay back.
Canva moved about 130 PB and 80 billion objects to Glacier Instant Retrieval for a one-time $1.6 million transition cost, saving about $300,000 a month, after measuring access by age and object size.
glossary: Block storage
Storage presented as a raw disk of fixed-size blocks to one machine, which puts its own file system on it; EBS on AWS.
Bucket
A named container of objects in one region; bucket names are globally unique on S3.
Conditional write
A write that succeeds only if a precondition holds, such as the key not existing (If-None-Match) or the object still having a given ETag (If-Match).
Durability
The probability that stored data isn't lost over a period, usually a year; distinct from availability, which is whether you can reach it right now.
EBS (Elastic Block Store)
AWS's network-attached block volumes for EC2 instances, each in one availability zone.
EFS (Elastic File System)
AWS's managed NFS file system, regional, growing and shrinking automatically.
Erasure coding
Splitting data into fragments plus parity fragments so that the original can be rebuilt from any sufficient subset, giving high durability with less overhead than full copies.
ETag
An identifier S3 returns for each object version, usually a hash of its content, used for caching and conditional writes.
FP32 / bf16
Number formats: 32-bit floating point (4 bytes) and bfloat16 (2 bytes); model weights and optimiser state are stored in these (gpu4).
FSx for Lustre
AWS's managed Lustre parallel file system for high-throughput workloads, optionally linked to an S3 bucket.
Glacier IR
Short for S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval, the archive class with millisecond access, a 90-day minimum and per-GB retrieval fees.
HPC (high-performance computing)
Large parallel computing jobs, such as simulations or model training, that need very high aggregate storage throughput.
Instance store
NVMe or SSD disks physically attached to an instance's host; very fast, but erased when the instance stops or fails.
IOPS
Input/output operations per second: how many reads or writes a disk can do each second, the key metric for small random I/O.
Key
The full name of an object in a bucket, such as datasets/v3/shard-00042.tar; slashes are just characters.
Lifecycle rule
A bucket rule that transitions objects to other storage classes or deletes them based on age, prefix, tags or version state.
LRS / ZRS / GRS
Azure Storage redundancy options: locally redundant (one data centre), zone-redundant (across zones) and geo-redundant (to a paired region).
Minimum storage duration
The period a storage class bills an object for even if you delete or move it sooner: 30 days for Standard-IA, 90 for Glacier Instant and Flexible Retrieval, 180 for Deep Archive.
Multipart upload
Uploading one object as up to 10,000 parts in parallel, then completing it so S3 assembles the parts atomically.
NFS (Network File System)
A protocol for mounting a remote file system over the network; EFS speaks NFS v4.1.
Object Lock
An S3 feature that makes object versions immutable for a retention period (write once, read many).
Object storage
Storage of whole objects (data plus metadata) addressed by key over an HTTP API, with no in-place modification.
POSIX
The Unix standard for file system behaviour — open, read, write at offsets, append, rename, locks — that applications expect from a file system.
Prefix
The leading part of a key (for example datasets/v3/); S3 scales request capacity per partitioned prefix.
Snapshot
A point-in-time, incremental copy of an EBS volume stored in S3, from which new volumes can be created.
SSE (server-side encryption)
Encryption of objects at rest by the storage service, with S3-managed keys (SSE-S3), KMS keys (SSE-KMS) or customer-provided keys (SSE-C).
Storage class
The S3 tier an object is stored in (Standard, Standard-IA, One Zone-IA, Intelligent-Tiering, Express One Zone, Glacier Instant, Flexible, Deep Archive), each with its own price and rules.
Throughput
Bytes per second a storage system delivers, the key metric for large sequential I/O.
Versioning
An S3 bucket setting that keeps every version of every object, so overwrites and deletes can be undone.
drill:
Design and estimate: storage for an ML platform

A team runs: (1) a 25 TB training corpus of text, currently 50 million JSON files of ~500 KB; (2) fine-tuning jobs on 8-GPU nodes that checkpoint a 13B-parameter model (mixed-precision Adam) every 30 minutes over 2-day runs, about 20 runs a month; (3) an inference fleet that scales from 4 to 40 instances, each loading the 26 GB bf16 weights; (4) application logs of 2 TB a month, mostly 8 KB objects, needed for 30 days and kept a year for audit. Propose storage for each, estimate monthly storage cost in us-east-1 with the lesson's prices, and name the main risk.

Answer

1. Corpus. Repack into ~1 GB shards (Parquet or JSONL compressed — often 3–5× smaller); keep in S3 Standard. Uncompressed: 25 × 1,024 × $0.023 ≈ $589/month; compressed 4× ≈ $147. Requests become trivial (25,000 objects). Risk: losing the corpus — enable versioning and replicate the canonical copy to another account.

2. Checkpoints. 13B × 14 bytes ≈ 182 GB per checkpoint. Each run writes 96 over two days; keep only the last 3 per run hot plus the final one. Stage to local NVMe, multipart upload, manifest last. Hot set across concurrent runs (say 3 runs at a time × 3 checkpoints): ~1.6 TB in Standard ≈ $38/month; final checkpoints, 20 a month × 182 GB = 3.6 TB per month added, moved to Glacier IR after 7 days at $0.004 ≈ $15 per month for each month's batch, growing. Lifecycle: expire intermediate checkpoints after 2 days, abort incomplete uploads after 1 day. Risk: hidden growth from not expiring intermediates — 96 × 182 GB × 20 runs ≈ 349,000 GB a month if kept, ~$8,000/month in Standard.

3. Weights. One copy in S3 (26 GB, pennies). Instances pull with parallel range GETs to local NVMe at startup (26 GB at a few GB/s ≈ 10 s), or from a warm pool. Risk: 36 instances scaling out simultaneously each pulling 26 GB — fine for S3, but check startup scripts parallelise and don't serialise on a single stream.

4. Logs. 8 KB objects make IA and Glacier classes a loss (128 KB minimum; per-object transitions on 2 TB ÷ 8 KB ≈ 268 million objects a month ≈ $5,400 at $0.02 per 1,000). Instead batch logs into larger objects (for example hourly compressed files per service) before storage, then lifecycle to Glacier Flexible Retrieval at 30 days and expire at 365. If batching is impossible, keep them in Standard for 30 days, then export a compacted archive and delete the originals. Risk: transition and request fees exceeding storage costs.
qa: E
When would you use object, block and file storage?

Object storage (S3) for anything written once and read many times by many clients: datasets, logs, backups, media, model artefacts, checkpoints — it's regional, very durable and cheap per GB, but accessed through an HTTP API with no in-place updates. Block storage (EBS) for one instance's disk: operating systems, databases you run yourself, anything needing low-latency random I/O and a normal file system. File storage (EFS, FSx) when several machines need the same POSIX file system at once: shared home directories, legacy applications, and HPC or ML jobs that need a parallel file system.

Follow-up: why do databases run on block storage rather than S3? — They do small random reads and in-place writes with fsync for durability and need sub-millisecond latency; S3 offers whole-object writes with tens of milliseconds of latency.
E
What does S3's strong consistency guarantee, and what doesn't it?

Since December 2020, after a successful PUT or DELETE (including overwrites), any subsequent GET, HEAD or LIST sees the result. That means a job can write an object and immediately tell another job to read it. It doesn't coordinate concurrent writers: two simultaneous PUTs to the same key both succeed and the later one wins. For coordination use conditional writes — If-None-Match: * to create only if absent, or If-Match with an ETag to update only if unchanged.

Follow-up: how would you use that for a lock? — Write lock/job-42 with If-None-Match: *; the first writer gets 200, everyone else gets 412 Precondition Failed; delete it to release, with an expiry convention for crashed holders.
E
What are S3 lifecycle rules, and give an example for logs.

Rules on a bucket that act on objects by age, prefix, tags or version state: transition to a cheaper class or expire (delete). For application logs: keep in Standard for 30 days (frequent debugging), transition to Standard-IA at 30 days, to Glacier Flexible Retrieval at 90, delete at 400; also expire noncurrent versions after 30 days and abort incomplete multipart uploads after 7. Check minimum durations and object sizes first so transitions actually save money.

Follow-up: what if most log objects are 4 KB? — Standard-IA bills a 128 KB minimum per object, so tiny objects cost more after transition; batch logs into larger objects before storing, or leave them in Standard.
M
A training job reads 400 million 100 KB images from S3 every epoch. What problems will it hit and how would you fix them?

Requests: 400 million GETs at $0.0004 per 1,000 is $160 per epoch, before any compute. Rate: a single prefix supports at least 5,500 GETs per second, so 400 million objects would take about 20 hours per epoch through one prefix; spreading keys across prefixes helps but per-request latency (100–200 ms) still means you need thousands of concurrent requests. Fix the shape instead: pack images into shards of about 1 GB (tar or a record format), 40,000 objects in total; read shards sequentially with parallel range requests and shuffle within a buffer. Requests drop by 10,000×, throughput is limited by network rather than request rates, and the cost per epoch is cents.
Follow-up: what about random access for evaluation? — Keep an index of byte offsets per sample in each shard and use range GETs, or keep a small evaluation set separately.
M
How do you write a 1 TB checkpoint to S3 quickly and safely?

Shard it: each training node writes its own part, in parallel. Each part is uploaded with multipart upload using many concurrent part uploads; parts must be 5 MiB–5 GiB and at most 10,000, so a 125 GB shard needs parts of at least 12.5 MB — 64 or 128 MB is typical. Completing a multipart upload is atomic, so a reader never sees half an object. Then write a small manifest (checkpoint step, list of shard keys and checksums) last, with a conditional write; readers trust only checkpoints with a manifest. Set a lifecycle rule to abort incomplete uploads, which otherwise accrue storage charges invisibly.
Follow-up: how do you avoid stalling training while uploading? — Copy state to host memory or local NVMe first, resume training, and upload asynchronously; only the copy pauses the GPUs.
M
Compare S3 Standard-IA, Intelligent-Tiering and Glacier Instant Retrieval for data that is rarely read.

Standard-IA: $0.0125/GB-month in us-east-1 (October 2026), 30-day minimum, 128 KB minimum billable size, $0.01/GB retrieval — good for backups read about monthly. Glacier Instant Retrieval: $0.004/GB-month, 90-day minimum, 128 KB minimum, $0.03/GB retrieval, millisecond access — good for data read about quarterly. Intelligent-Tiering: Standard price at first, moves objects not accessed for 30 days to an IA tier ($0.0125) and 90 days to an Archive Instant tier ($0.004), no retrieval fees, but $0.0025 per 1,000 objects monitored per month and objects under 128 KB aren't tiered — best when access patterns are unknown and objects are large.
Follow-up: which would you pick for 10 billion 50 KB objects? — Probably none of them: the 128 KB minimum and per-object fees dominate; pack them into larger objects or leave them in Standard.
M
What are the performance characteristics of gp3 and when would you use io2?

gp3 volumes (October 2026) give a baseline of 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s regardless of size and can be provisioned up to 80,000 IOPS and 2,000 MiB/s, paid separately from capacity; durability is 99.8–99.9% and latency is single-digit milliseconds. io2 Block Express provisions up to 256,000 IOPS and 4,000 MiB/s with average latency under 500 µs and 99.999% durability, and supports multi-attach. Use gp3 for most databases and boot volumes; io2 for latency-critical, I/O-heavy databases. Remember the instance's own EBS bandwidth caps what any volume can deliver.

Follow-up: a database on gp3 shows high latency at 3,000 IOPS. What do you check? — Whether it's hitting the provisioned IOPS or throughput limits (VolumeQueueLength, throughput metrics), the instance's EBS bandwidth limit, and the I/O size; raise IOPS or throughput on gp3 before switching type.
M
How would you protect an S3 bucket of training data and checkpoints against accidental deletion and ransomware?

Enable versioning so overwrites and deletes keep previous versions, with lifecycle rules to expire noncurrent versions after a window. Restrict delete permissions to a few roles and require MFA delete or deny deletes via bucket policy for most principals. For critical artefacts use Object Lock in compliance or governance mode for a retention period. Replicate to a bucket in a separate account (and ideally region) that production credentials can't write to. Alarm on unusual delete or PutObject volumes in CloudTrail data events.

Follow-up: why a separate account? — An attacker or bad script with admin rights in the production account can delete versions and replication targets in that account; a different account with its own credentials breaks that blast radius.
H
Design storage for a team that pre-trains a 70B-parameter model on 64 GPUs, checkpointing hourly.

Checkpoint size with mixed-precision Adam: bf16 weights 2 bytes, FP32 master weights 4 and two Adam moments 4 each — 14 bytes per parameter, about 980 GB per checkpoint. Each of 8 nodes writes its ~122 GB shard to S3 in parallel with multipart uploads after staging to local NVMe; a manifest written last makes the checkpoint visible. Retention: keep the last 5 hourly checkpoints in Standard (4.9 TB ≈ $113/month at $0.023/GB) and one per day for 90 days, transitioned to Glacier Instant Retrieval (88 TB ≈ $353/month at $0.004/GB, against about $2,029 in Standard); final and milestone checkpoints locked with Object Lock and replicated to another account. Dataset as large shards in S3 Standard, read through a streaming loader; if the framework needs POSIX, FSx for Lustre linked to the bucket.

Follow-up: how long does a restore take? — Reading 980 GB from S3 across 8 nodes in parallel is bounded by per-node network throughput; at a few GB/s per node it's on the order of a minute or two, which is why restore time should be measured, not assumed.
H
Your S3 bill jumped 40% with no increase in stored data. Where do you look?

Break the bill down by usage type and bucket (Cost and Usage Report, S3 Storage Lens). Common causes: request charges from a new workload doing many small GETs or LISTs; noncurrent versions accumulating because versioning was enabled without lifecycle expiry (storage you don't see in the current-version view); incomplete multipart uploads from failed jobs; lifecycle transitions of many small objects (per-request transition fees and 128 KB minimums); early-deletion charges from deleting IA or Glacier objects before their minimum duration; data transfer out or cross-region replication; KMS request charges if SSE-KMS without bucket keys.
Follow-up: how do you find incomplete multipart uploads? — ListMultipartUploads per bucket or Storage Lens metrics; fix with an AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload lifecycle rule.
H
Walk through Canva's 2023 move to Glacier Instant Retrieval as a decision process.

Canva had about 230 PB in S3 and over 300 billion objects. Storage Class Analysis showed that access to user content fell sharply after about 15 days — S3 Standard held 10% of bytes but 60–70% of accesses, while Standard-IA held 90% of bytes and a flat 30–40% of accesses. Glacier Instant Retrieval keeps millisecond access at a much lower storage price, but has a 128 KB minimum billable size, a 90-day minimum, retrieval fees and a transition fee per object ($0.02 per 1,000). They worked out that below about 20 KB per object it was cheaper to stay in Standard and chose buckets averaging 400 KB or more, where payback was within six months. Moving about 80 billion objects cost $1.6 million once; it saves about $300,000 a month, and around 130 PB now sits in Glacier IR.

Follow-up: what would have happened if they'd used Intelligent-Tiering on everything? — The per-object monitoring fee on hundreds of billions of objects, and small objects that it never tiers, would have eaten much of the saving; the per-bucket analysis was the point.
H
How do the storage options on Google Cloud and Azure map to AWS, and what differs?

Google Cloud Storage has Standard, Nearline, Coldline and Archive classes (minimum durations of 30, 90 and 365 days for the colder ones), regional, dual-region and multi-region buckets, and strong global consistency; block storage is Persistent Disk and Hyperdisk; file storage is Filestore, with managed Lustre and Parallelstore for HPC. Azure Blob Storage has hot, cool, cold and archive tiers, redundancy options from locally redundant to geo-zone-redundant chosen per storage account; block storage is Managed Disks (Premium SSD v2, Ultra Disk); file storage is Azure Files and Azure NetApp Files, plus Azure Managed Lustre. The same rules apply everywhere — minimum durations, retrieval fees, per-request costs, zonal disks — with different numbers.

Follow-up: what's the most important difference for designs? — Redundancy choices: on Azure you pick replication per account (LRS, ZRS, GRS), so a 'storage account' may be single-zone unless chosen otherwise; on GCS, location type decides it; on S3, the class decides (One Zone classes are single-zone).
refs: How Canva saves millions annually in Amazon S3 costs (Canva Engineering, May 2023)
The case: 230 PB, access by age, the 20 KB break-even, $1.6M to move 80 billion objects and ~$300k a month saved.
Understanding and managing Amazon S3 storage classes
Durability, availability, zones, minimum durations and minimum object sizes for every class.
Best practices design patterns: optimizing Amazon S3 performance
3,500/5,500 requests per second per prefix, 503 Slow Down while scaling, parallelism and 100–200 ms latency.
48.8 TiB objects, 10,000 parts of 5 MiB to 5 GiB.
Diving deep on S3 consistency (Werner Vogels, All Things Distributed)
How S3 added strong read-after-write consistency without giving up performance or availability.
gp3, io2 Block Express, st1 and sc1: sizes, IOPS, throughput and durability.
If-None-Match and If-Match preconditions for coordinating concurrent writers.
Amazon FSx for Lustre: linking a file system to an S3 bucket

t: Managed databases and caches: RDS and Aurora, DynamoDB partition keys and capacity modes, managed Redis/Valkey, read replicas, and managed vs self-hosted
sum: What a managed database service actually does and what it leaves to you: RDS Multi-AZ failover traced through DNS, read replicas and their lag, Aurora's shared six-copy storage, DynamoDB's partitions, capacity units and the provisioned-versus-on-demand decision worked for a real read/write rate, hot keys and adaptive capacity, ElastiCache with Valkey or Redis, connection management from serverless and containers, and the price and control trade of managed versus self-hosted — with DynamoDB's September 2015 metadata-service outage as the case.
prereq: sc6
Leader-follower replication: synchronous replication waits for a follower, asynchronous doesn't and can lose recent writes on failover; followers serve reads with lag.
sc7
Partitioning splits data by key range or hash; a bad key concentrates load on one partition (a hot spot); rebalancing moves partitions between nodes.
db11
Key-value and wide-column stores model data around access patterns, with a partition key that decides placement and a sort key that orders items within it.
sc3
Cache-aside reads the cache first and fills it from the database on a miss; TTLs and invalidation bound staleness; stampedes happen when many misses hit the database at once.
cl5
Every concurrent Lambda environment is separate, so N concurrent executions open N database connections unless something pools them.
why:
A startup runs PostgreSQL on a virtual machine it set up on day one. It works for two years. Then, on one Saturday, the disk fills with WAL files because a replica fell behind; the database stops accepting writes; the person who set it up has left; nobody knows whether last night's backup script still runs (it stopped eight months ago when a credential rotated). The team spends a weekend recovering and on Monday decides to "move to a managed database".

They pick the managed service, click through the defaults, and feel safe. But the defaults were single-zone, with seven days of backups. Their Lambda functions open a new connection per request, and during the next traffic spike the database hits its connection limit. They add a read replica for analytics, and customers start seeing their own updates "disappear" for a few seconds because some reads now go to the lagging replica. They add DynamoDB for a new activity feed, partitioned by date, and every write for today goes to one partition, which throttles while the table shows plenty of unused capacity. And they put a cache in front of everything, which works beautifully until a cache failover sends every read to the database at once.

Managed databases remove the work of running database software — installing, patching, backing up, replacing failed hardware, failing over. They don't remove the need to understand the database. Each service has a model underneath: how it replicates, how it fails over and what clients see during it, how it partitions data, what it counts as a unit of capacity and how it charges for it. Those models decide whether the system is available, correct and affordable.

This lesson takes the main managed data services in turn, using AWS as the concrete case: RDS and its Multi-AZ and replica options, Aurora's separated storage, DynamoDB's partitions and capacity modes (with a capacity calculation for a real workload), managed Redis and Valkey caches, connection management from serverless and containers, and how to decide between managed and self-hosted. The case is DynamoDB's 2015 outage, which shows a managed database failing in a way no customer could have configured away.
primer:
A managed database is like moving from owning a car to a full-service lease. The leasing company handles servicing, replaces parts when they fail, keeps a spare car ready, and keeps the logbook. You still choose the model, decide who's allowed to drive, decide how much luggage it must carry, and — crucially — you still drive. If you drive into a wall, the lease doesn't undo it; if the spare car takes two minutes to arrive, your passengers wait two minutes.

The cloud offers several kinds of managed data service, each with a different model underneath:

  • Managed relational databases (RDS for PostgreSQL, MySQL and others; Cloud SQL; Azure Database for PostgreSQL) run a normal database engine on a dedicated instance with attached storage. The provider adds automated backups, patching, a standby for failover, and read replicas. It's the same PostgreSQL you'd run yourself, operated for you.
  • Cloud-native relational databases (Aurora, AlloyDB, and distributed SQL such as Spanner) change the architecture: compute is separated from a shared, replicated storage layer, so replicas and failover don't need full copies of data.
  • Managed key-value and document stores (DynamoDB, Firestore, Cosmos DB) are built as distributed services from the start: data is spread across many partitions by key, capacity is bought in request units, and there are no servers to see.
  • Managed caches (ElastiCache and MemoryDB on AWS, Memorystore, Azure Cache for Redis) run in-memory stores — Valkey, Redis or Memcached — on nodes you size, with replication and failover.

Whatever the service, three questions decide most designs. How does it fail over, and what do clients see while it does? How does it scale — up (bigger instance), out for reads (replicas) or out for everything (partitions)? And what is the unit of capacity you pay for — instance-hours, request units, gigabytes of memory? The rest of the lesson answers those three questions for each service.

A good first pass at choosing among them follows the data's access patterns rather than fashion (sc8). If the data is relational — many entities joined in flexible queries, with transactions across them — start with managed PostgreSQL or MySQL, and reach for Aurora when you need faster failover, many low-lag replicas or storage that manages itself. If every access is "get or update the items for this key" at very high or very spiky rates, a key-value store like DynamoDB scales without servers, provided you can design keys that spread load. If the same few objects are read far more often than they change, put a cache in front of whichever store holds the truth. Most real systems use two or three of these together, each for the access path it serves best, and the hard work is keeping them consistent enough with each other.

Where the analogy breaks: the leasing company's spare car is yours alone. A managed database's control systems — the metadata that says which server holds which data, the automation that runs failovers — are shared by every customer in the region. When they have a problem, every customer has it at once, and nothing in your configuration can opt you out. That's what the 2015 DynamoDB case shows.
body:
1. What "managed" covers, precisely

For RDS, AWS runs: provisioning the instance and storage, installing the engine, minor-version patching in a maintenance window you choose, OS patching, automated daily snapshots plus continuous transaction-log backup (enabling point-in-time recovery within a retention window you set, up to 35 days), failure detection and failover in Multi-AZ deployments, storage autoscaling if enabled, and metrics. You own: instance class and storage type, Multi-AZ and replica topology, engine parameters (via parameter groups), major version upgrades (you schedule them), schema and queries, users and grants, network placement and security groups, encryption choices, backup retention and copy-to-another-region, and how your application behaves during failover.

The split matters most in incidents. A runaway query, a missing index, a migration that locks a table, a connection storm, a disk filled by a forgotten replication slot — all happen on a managed database just as on your own, and the provider won't fix them.

2. RDS Multi-AZ failover, traced

In a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment, RDS keeps a synchronous standby in another zone: the primary writes each transaction to its own EBS storage and to the standby's before acknowledging the commit. The standby serves no traffic. Your application connects through a DNS name such as orders.c9akciq32.eu-central-1.rds.amazonaws.com, which resolves to the primary's IP.

When RDS detects a failure — the primary host unhealthy or unreachable, its storage failed, the zone impaired, or during OS patching or an instance modification — it promotes the standby and changes the DNS record to point at it. The documentation gives typical failover times of 60–120 seconds, longer with large transactions to recover. Trace what the application sees:

  1. T+0: the primary stops responding. Existing connections hang or reset; queries in flight fail; uncommitted transactions are lost (committed ones are safe on the standby).
  2. T+0 to ~T+60–120 s: RDS detects, promotes and flips DNS. New connection attempts fail or time out.
  3. After the flip: clients that re-resolve DNS connect to the new primary. Clients that cached the old IP keep trying the dead host. AWS specifically warns that some JVM configurations cache DNS forever and recommends a DNS TTL of no more than 60 seconds.
  4. Applications must retry failed transactions — idempotently, since a transaction might have committed just before the failure without the client seeing the acknowledgement.

The cost is double the instance price: a db.m7g.large PostgreSQL instance was $0.168 an hour single-AZ and $0.337 Multi-AZ in us-east-1 on 7 October 2026, and gp3 storage $0.115/GB-month single-AZ against $0.23 Multi-AZ. Commit latency rises slightly because every commit crosses zones. A Multi-AZ DB cluster variant runs a writer and two readable standbys across three zones with faster failover — useful when you want both read scaling and quicker recovery.

3. Read replicas and lag

A read replica is a separate instance kept up to date by asynchronous replication (PostgreSQL streaming replication, MySQL binlog replication). It serves read-only queries and can be in another zone or region; it can be promoted to a standalone primary for disaster recovery. Because replication is asynchronous, replicas lag — usually milliseconds to seconds, more under write bursts or when a long-running query on the replica holds back replay.

Lag creates anomalies (sc6): a user updates their profile and the next page, read from a replica, shows the old value; two consecutive requests hit different replicas and see time go backwards. The fixes are routing rules: reads that must reflect the user's own recent writes go to the primary (for a few seconds after a write, or always for that session); dashboards and analytics go to replicas; replicas lagging beyond a threshold are taken out of rotation. RDS exposes ReplicaLag per replica.

4. Aurora: separating compute from storage

Aurora (MySQL- and PostgreSQL-compatible) keeps the engine's query processing but replaces its storage. The database instances don't write data pages to their own disks; the writer sends redo log records to a distributed storage service that maintains the cluster volume. The Aurora paper (SIGMOD 2017) describes six copies of each 10 GB segment of data, two in each of three zones, with writes acknowledged when four of six copies have them and reads needing three of six — so the volume survives losing a whole zone plus one more copy for reads, and keeps accepting writes after losing a zone. The storage nodes apply log records to pages themselves, which is why Aurora writes far less across the network than a database shipping full pages.

Consequences for design: replicas (up to 15) read the same volume, so adding one doesn't copy data, and they lag only by the time to apply log records to their caches, typically tens of milliseconds; failover promotes a replica that already sees all committed data; storage grows automatically (up to 256 TiB on recent engine versions) and you pay for what's used. In us-east-1, October 2026: a db.r7g.large Aurora PostgreSQL instance was $0.276 an hour, storage $0.10/GB-month plus $0.20 per million I/O requests in the Standard configuration, or $0.225/GB-month with no I/O charges in I/O-Optimized (AWS's guidance: choose it when I/O is 25% or more of the Aurora bill). Aurora Serverless v2 adjusts instance capacity in fine increments for variable load.

5. DynamoDB: partitions and keys

DynamoDB stores items (up to 400 KB each) in tables. Every item has a primary key: a partition key alone, or a partition key plus a sort key. DynamoDB hashes the partition key to choose a partition — a replicated unit of storage and throughput — and keeps items with the same partition key together, ordered by sort key. A query reads one partition key's items, optionally a range of sort keys; a scan reads everything and is expensive.

The rule that drives every design, from the developer guide: each partition delivers at most 3,000 read units and 1,000 write units per second (and holds roughly 10 GB). A table with 20,000 write units of capacity spread over 20 partitions can absorb 20,000 writes per second only if the writes spread across partition keys; if 30% of writes share one partition key, that key's partition caps them at 1,000 per second and they throttle while the table looks under-used.

Two mechanisms soften this. Burst capacity lets a provisioned partition briefly use capacity it didn't use in recent minutes. Adaptive capacity moves unused throughput from cold partitions to hot ones and splits partitions whose keys are hot, isolating frequently accessed items (the 2022 DynamoDB paper describes how this evolved). Neither lets a single item exceed one partition's limits: a single item read 600 times per second with strong consistency at 20 KB per read (5 read units each) already uses all 3,000 read units of its partition. Hot single items need caching (DynamoDB Accelerator or ElastiCache) or a redesign.

Global secondary indexes (GSIs) let you query by another key. Each is effectively another table, maintained asynchronously from the base table, with its own partitions and its own write capacity: every write that changes indexed attributes costs write units in the GSI too. A GSI whose key is low-cardinality (say status) becomes a hot partition, and a throttled GSI can throttle writes to the base table.

6. DynamoDB capacity, worked

Capacity units (from the developer guide): one read capacity unit (RCU) is one strongly consistent read per second of an item up to 4 KB, or two eventually consistent reads; one write capacity unit (WCU) is one write per second of an item up to 1 KB. Sizes round up. Transactional reads and writes cost double. On-demand mode bills the same units per request (read and write request units) rather than per hour.

A personalisation service needs 12,000 reads per second of 6 KB user-profile items (eventually consistent is fine) and 1,500 writes per second of 2.5 KB items, with one GSI that projects all attributes.

  • Reads: 6 KB rounds up to two 4 KB units = 2 RCU strongly consistent, 1 RCU eventually consistent. 12,000 × 1 = 12,000 RCU.
  • Writes: 2.5 KB rounds up to 3 WCU per write. Base table 1,500 × 3 = 4,500 WCU; the GSI another 4,500. 9,000 WCU in total.
  • Partitions: the base table needs at least max(12,000 ÷ 3,000, 4,500 ÷ 1,000) = 4.5, so five or more partitions, with keys spread evenly; the GSI likewise.

Now price it with us-east-1 rates from the price list on 7 October 2026 (provisioned: $0.00013 per RCU-hour, $0.00065 per WCU-hour; on-demand: $0.125 per million read request units, $0.625 per million write request units; a 730-hour month is 2,628,000 seconds):

ModeReadsWritesMonthly
Provisioned at a 70% utilisation target (17,143 RCU, 12,857 WCU)17,143 × $0.00013 × 730 = $1,626.8612,857 × $0.00065 × 730 = $6,100.71$7,727.57
On-demand, steady at this rate12,000 × 2,628,000 ÷ 10⁶ × $0.125 = $3,942.009,000 × 2,628,000 ÷ 10⁶ × $0.625 = $14,782.50$18,724.50

At steady load, on-demand costs 2.4 times provisioned. But on-demand charges only for what's used, so if traffic is diurnal and averages 40% of this peak, on-demand costs about $7,490 — roughly the same as provisioned sized for peak; at a 15% average it's about $2,809. The break-even is where the average-to-peak ratio is about 7,728 ÷ 18,725 ≈ 41%. Storage is separate in both modes: 500 GB at $0.25/GB-month is $125. Notice also that writes dominate the bill, and the GSI doubled them: a GSI projecting only the attributes it needs, or a sparse GSI (only items that have the attribute), cuts that cost directly.

Scaling behaviour differs too. Provisioned tables with auto scaling react when consumed capacity exceeds the target for two consecutive minutes, plus alarm delay — minutes, during which throttling is possible. On-demand tables, per the documentation, instantly accommodate up to double the previous peak; new tables start able to sustain 4,000 writes and 12,000 reads per second; exceeding double the previous peak within 30 minutes can throttle, so known launches should pre-warm.

7. Managed caches: ElastiCache with Valkey, Redis OSS or Memcached

A cache keeps hot data in memory so reads take a fraction of a millisecond and the database sees fewer queries (sc3 covers patterns: cache-aside, write-through, TTLs, stampedes). ElastiCache runs the engine on nodes you size, or as a serverless option billed by data stored and compute units. In 2024 Redis changed its licence away from open source, and the Linux Foundation's Valkey fork continued the BSD-licensed code; ElastiCache supports Valkey alongside Redis OSS and Memcached and prices it lower — in us-east-1 on 7 October 2026 a cache.r7g.large (13.07 GiB) node was $0.1752 an hour with Valkey against $0.219 with Redis OSS (20% less), and serverless data storage $0.084 against $0.125 per GB-hour.

The production-relevant knobs: cluster mode shards keys across node groups by hash slot so memory and throughput scale out; each shard has a primary and replicas, ideally in other zones, with automatic failover; eviction policy decides what's dropped when memory fills (for a pure cache, evict least-recently-used keys across all keys); persistence is limited — a cache is not a database, and replication is asynchronous, so a failover can lose recent writes. Where a Redis-compatible store must be durable, AWS offers MemoryDB, which logs writes durably across zones before acknowledging.

The design principle is to make the database survive the cache being empty. Measure the database's capacity against the uncached read rate; if it can't take it, add request coalescing (one fetch per key per miss storm), staggered TTLs, a warm-up procedure after failover, and replicas so a node loss doesn't empty a shard.

8. Connections from serverless and containers

Relational databases handle a limited number of connections well; PostgreSQL in particular uses a process per connection. Modern compute multiplies connections: 50 container replicas with a pool of 20 each is 1,000 connections; 500 concurrent Lambda environments with one each is 500 (cl5). RDS Proxy (or self-managed PgBouncer) sits between clients and the database, keeps a small pool of real connections and multiplexes many client connections onto them; it also holds client connections during a failover and reconnects to the new primary, shortening what applications see. The trade-off of transaction-level pooling is that session state — prepared statements, temporary tables, session variables, advisory locks — can't be relied on across transactions.

9. Managed versus self-hosted

Managed (RDS, Aurora, DynamoDB, ElastiCache)Self-hosted (EC2 or Kubernetes)
