Two lessons. First, request-priced services charge per call, so batching and long polling matter as much as the service choice: the same SQS workload is ten times cheaper batched. Second, at high steady volume a stream is an order of magnitude cheaper per event than routers and topics, because it charges for capacity and bytes, not per event. At 20 events per second, all of these cost a few dollars a month and features decide; at 2,000 per second, the bill does.
deep:
Why at-least-once is the default everywhere

Exactly-once delivery across a network is impossible to guarantee without coordination between sender and receiver: a sender that doesn't get an acknowledgement can't tell whether the message or the acknowledgement was lost, so it must either resend (risking duplicates) or not (risking loss). Managed services choose resending because losing messages is worse than duplicating them, and because duplicates can be made harmless downstream with idempotency. "Exactly-once" features — FIFO deduplication, Kafka transactions, Pub/Sub exactly-once delivery, Standard workflows — narrow the window within specific boundaries (a five-minute dedup window, a single Kafka cluster's read-process-write, one region), but the end-to-end effect is still your design.

Ordering costs parallelism

Ordering is enforced by funnelling related messages through one lane: one FIFO message group, one shard, one Kafka partition. Throughput for that key is then bounded by one lane's capacity and one consumer's processing speed, and a slow or failing message blocks everything behind it in the lane. The design question is always "ordered with respect to what?" Per customer or per account is usually enough and parallelises across customers; global order serialises the whole system and is almost never needed. When keys are skewed — one enormous customer — that customer's lane becomes the bottleneck, and the answer is sub-keys with application-level reordering, or accepting less strict order.

Push versus pull decides who absorbs bursts

SNS and EventBridge push: they deliver as fast as events arrive (up to target throttles) and retry when targets fail, so a burst lands directly on the targets. SQS and streams are pulled: consumers fetch at their own pace and the backlog absorbs the burst. Pushing into a fragile target (an HTTP endpoint, a Lambda function writing to a database) without a buffer is the common way to turn a traffic spike into an outage. Putting a queue between a push source and the work, and capping consumer concurrency, turns spikes into backlog, which is measurable and drains.

The outbox problem: publishing and committing atomically

A service that writes to its database and then publishes an event can crash between the two: the order exists but nobody hears about it, or (if publishing first) the event announces an order that was rolled back. The transactional outbox (sc11) writes the event into an outbox table in the same transaction and has a separate relay publish it; change data capture (DynamoDB Streams, PostgreSQL logical replication via Debezium or DMS) does the same by turning committed changes into events. EventBridge Pipes can consume DynamoDB Streams directly, which makes "publish exactly the committed changes" a configuration exercise on AWS.

All-to-all designs fail suddenly

The 2020 Kinesis event came from a design where every front-end server kept threads for every other front-end server: resource use per server grew with fleet size, so a small capacity addition pushed every server over a fixed OS limit at once. The same shape appears in application systems — full-mesh service discovery, every pod connecting to every broker, gossip protocols — and fails the same way: fine until a threshold, then everywhere simultaneously. Cells (independent copies of a service, each serving a slice of customers) bound the mesh size; AWS's remediation included cellularising the Kinesis front end for exactly this reason.

Backpressure has to reach the producer eventually

Buffers absorb bursts, but a sustained imbalance — producers faster than consumers for hours — only moves the problem: the backlog grows until retention deletes messages or the stream's write limits throttle producers. Healthy systems make the imbalance visible (age of oldest message, iterator age), scale consumers within downstream limits, and, when that isn't enough, push back on producers: Kinesis throttles writes above shard capacity, SQS doesn't, so producers to SQS need their own rate limits or load shedding for non-critical events. Deciding in advance which events may be dropped or sampled under pressure — analytics yes, payments no — is part of the design, not an incident decision.

Schemas are the contract between teams

Once events flow between teams, their shape is an API with many unknown consumers. Changing a field name breaks someone's rule or parser silently. Treat event schemas like APIs: version them, make changes backward compatible (add fields, never repurpose them), publish them in a registry (EventBridge schema registry, Confluent or Glue schema registries for Kafka and Kinesis), and validate in CI. Envelope fields — event ID, type, version, time, correlation ID — make idempotency, routing and tracing possible across the whole system.
prod:
Failure modes and their symptoms

Growing backlog. ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible and ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage climb on a queue; iterator age climbs on a stream. Consumers are too slow or failing. Scale consumers (within downstream limits), find hot keys or shards, and make sure retention outlasts the backlog — messages older than retention are deleted silently.

Poison messages. One message fails forever; with FIFO or streams it blocks its group or shard. Fix: low maxReceiveCount with a DLQ, partial batch responses, bisect-on-error and maximum record age for stream consumers.

Duplicate side effects. Double emails or charges after retries, redeliveries or a visibility timeout shorter than processing time. Fix: idempotency keys, longer visibility timeouts, delete only after success.

Silent drops. EventBridge or SNS gives up after its retry policy while a target is down, and nobody configured a DLQ. Fix: DLQs on every target and subscription, alarms on DLQ depth and on failed invocation metrics.

Throttled targets. A rule or subscription pushes faster than a Lambda function or API can take; retries pile up. Fix: SQS in between, concurrency caps, SNS HTTP throttle policies.

Hot shards and groups. Throughput stuck well below provisioned capacity because traffic concentrates on a few keys. Find them with per-shard metrics; re-key or split.

Regional quota cliffs. A design that works in us-east-1 fails in another region because default quotas differ: in October 2026 the SNS publish quota per account was 30,000 messages per second in us-east-1 but 1,500 in Frankfurt and 300 in many smaller regions, and SQS FIFO high-throughput limits also vary by region. Check quotas for every region you deploy to, and request increases before launch.

Cost surprises. Unbatched SQS calls, empty receives without long polling, high-volume events routed through EventBridge, per-event Standard workflows. Break the bill down by service and usage type.

What to watch

Queues: visible messages, age of oldest message, messages in flight, DLQ depth, empty receives. Topics and buses: publishes, failed deliveries, throttles, DLQ depth, invocation latency. Streams: incoming bytes and records against limits, write and read throttles, iterator age per consumer, per-shard metrics. Workflows: executions started, failed, timed out, throttled; duration per state. End to end: the age of the event when it's finally processed.

The case: Kinesis in us-east-1, 25 November 2020

AWS's summary describes Kinesis's front-end fleet: servers that authenticate requests, throttle, and route each request to the right back-end cluster using a shard map that every front-end server builds and maintains. To keep that map current, each front-end server holds operating-system threads for communicating with each of the other front-end servers. Between 2:44 and 3:47 AM PST, a relatively small amount of capacity was added to the fleet. Because every server's thread count grows with the number of servers, the addition pushed every server past the maximum number of threads allowed by an OS configuration. Servers could no longer complete their shard maps, and from about 5:15 AM PST Kinesis requests in the region began failing.

The fix — remove the added capacity, raise limits — was quick to decide and slow to apply: rebuilding shard maps loads the fleet, so servers could only be brought back at a rate of a few hundred per hour across a fleet of many thousands. Kinesis fully recovered at 10:23 PM PST, about 17 hours after errors began. Meanwhile, AWS services built on Kinesis failed in turn: Cognito (which buffers data through Kinesis) returned errors; CloudWatch couldn't process metrics and logs; EventBridge and CloudWatch Events were delayed; Lambda saw elevated errors from memory pressure caused by buffered metrics; reactive Auto Scaling policies were delayed because they depend on CloudWatch metrics; and AWS's Service Health Dashboard, which used Cognito, couldn't be updated normally. AWS's remediations: move to larger servers so the fleet needs fewer, add fine-grained alarming on thread consumption, raise the OS limit, accelerate cellularisation of the front-end fleet, and let CloudWatch keep metrics locally for hours when Kinesis is unavailable.

For a designer, it's a compact lesson in integration risk. The messaging layer is a dependency of many things you don't think of as "using Kinesis" — including monitoring and autoscaling. Fleets with all-to-all relationships hit limits suddenly. Recovery speed can be limited by the system's own need to avoid overload. Producers need local buffering and backoff, consumers need retention long enough to catch up after a day-long outage, and critical alarms need a path that doesn't share the failing dependency.
myths: FIFO queues give exactly-once processing.

SQS FIFO queues deduplicate messages with the same deduplication ID sent within a five-minute window and deliver each message group in order, but processing is still at-least-once from the consumer's point of view: if a consumer crashes after doing its work and before deleting the message, the message becomes visible again and is processed twice. Exactly-once effects still need idempotent consumers.
SNS stores messages until subscribers are ready.

SNS pushes each message to every subscription and retries on failure according to a delivery policy — for SQS and Lambda subscribers up to 100,015 attempts over 23 days, for HTTP/S endpoints by default far fewer — then discards it unless a dead-letter queue is attached. It doesn't keep a backlog for slow consumers or allow replay. The standard pattern is SNS fanning out to SQS queues, one per consumer, so each has its own durable buffer.
EventBridge is just SNS with a nicer name.

EventBridge routes events by matching their JSON content against rules, supports many target types with input transformation, can archive and replay events, and connects SaaS sources; SNS is a lower-latency, higher-throughput fan-out with simpler attribute filtering. They also price differently: in us-east-1 in October 2026, EventBridge custom events cost $1.00 per million against $0.50 per million SNS publishes. Pick by routing needs and volume.
Kinesis and SQS are interchangeable.

SQS is a queue: messages are consumed and deleted, consumers scale freely, and there's no ordering (standard) or ordering per message group (FIFO). Kinesis is a log: records stay for the retention period, are ordered per shard, can be read by several independent consumers each at its own position, and can be replayed. A queue fits task distribution; a stream fits event history that several systems process independently.
Step Functions is the natural way to orchestrate every event.

Standard workflows cost $0.025 per 1,000 state transitions in us-east-1 (October 2026). Orchestrating 5 steps for each of 5 billion events a month would cost about $657,000. Standard workflows are for long-running, auditable business processes with relatively few executions; high-volume event processing belongs in Express workflows (billed by requests and duration), plain code, or streams.
Managed messaging services can't lose messages.

They're durable for what they accept, but messages can still be dropped: SQS deletes messages older than the retention period (4 days by default, 14 at most), EventBridge drops events after its retry policy (24 hours and 185 attempts by default) unless a DLQ is set, SNS discards after its delivery policy, and Kinesis records expire after retention (24 hours by default). Every pipeline needs DLQs, alarms on their depth, and retention long enough to survive an outage of the consumer.
lab:
Goal: simulate a queue with visibility timeouts and a dead-letter queue, then a sharded stream, and see duplicates, poison messages and hot shards — Python 3.12 standard library only. About 20 minutes; no cloud account needed.

  1. Queue. Write a class with send(body), receive(now, visibility) returning messages not currently hidden (setting visible_at = now + visibility and incrementing receive_count), and delete(receipt). Add a redrive policy: on receive, if receive_count > max_receive, move to a DLQ list.
  2. Duplicates. Run two consumers in a time-stepped loop where processing takes a random 10–60 s and visibility is 30 s. Count messages processed more than once. Then set visibility to 120 s and recount.
  3. Idempotency. Add a processed set keyed by message ID; count side effects instead of processings. Duplicates should no longer produce duplicate effects.
  4. Poison. Make one message always fail. With max_receive=3, check it lands in the DLQ after three receives and that other messages keep flowing.
  5. Stream. Model a stream of 4 shards, each accepting 1,000 records per second; hash partition keys with hashlib.md5. Send 3,000 records per second with 1% of keys receiving 50% of traffic; count throttled writes per shard. Repeat with uniform keys.
  6. Costs. Reproduce the section 8 table as a function of events per second and find the rate below which the differences are under $10 a month.

What to look for: step 2 shows duplicates whenever processing exceeds the visibility timeout, and few or none at 120 s; step 3 shows that idempotency, not timeouts, is what makes effects exactly-once; step 4 shows the DLQ keeping the queue healthy; step 5 shows one shard throttling while the others idle — hot keys, not total capacity, limit streams; step 6 shows that at a few events per second every option costs about the same.

Needs an AWS account (optional): aws sqs get-queue-attributes --queue-url <url> --attribute-names ApproximateNumberOfMessages ApproximateNumberOfMessagesNotVisible RedrivePolicy VisibilityTimeout shows the backlog, in-flight count and redrive settings for a real queue.
recap: Managed integration services come in four shapes: queues (SQS) hand each message to one consumer, topics (SNS) push copies to every subscriber, event buses (EventBridge) route events by content to targets, and streams (Kinesis, managed Kafka) keep an ordered, replayable log per shard or partition.

SQS standard queues are at-least-once and unordered with nearly unlimited throughput; FIFO queues order per message group and deduplicate within five minutes, at 300 API calls per second per action by default or much more in high-throughput mode.

A received SQS message is hidden for the visibility timeout (30 s default, 12 h max) and reappears if not deleted; after maxReceiveCount receives a redrive policy moves it to a dead-letter queue; retention is 4 days by default, 14 at most; messages up to 1 MiB.
SNS fans out with retries defined per protocol and optional filtering; pair it with SQS queues so each consumer has its own buffer; SNS FIFO topics preserve order into SQS FIFO queues.

EventBridge matches events against rules and delivers to targets with retries for 24 hours and up to 185 attempts by default, plus DLQs, archives and replay; it is priced per event for routing, not for firehose volumes.

Kinesis Data Streams keeps records ordered per shard, each shard taking 1 MB/s or 1,000 records/s in and serving 2 MB/s out; consumers track their own position, so replay and several independent readers are natural; managed Kafka offers the same model with Kafka's API.

Step Functions Standard workflows run exactly-once for up to a year and bill per state transition; Express workflows run at-least-once (or at-most-once synchronously) for up to five minutes and bill by requests and duration.
Every service delivers at least once somewhere in the path, so consumers must be idempotent; ordering exists only within a message group, shard or partition key.
At 2,000 events per second the monthly cost ranges from about $139 on provisioned Kinesis to $5,256 on EventBridge, so volume decides the transport as much as features do.

Integration services are shared infrastructure: the November 2020 Kinesis outage, triggered by a small capacity addition that pushed servers past an OS thread limit, took down services built on it, including CloudWatch, Cognito and parts of EventBridge.
glossary: At-least-once delivery
A guarantee that every message is delivered one or more times; duplicates are possible, losses are not (within retention).
At-most-once delivery
A guarantee that a message is delivered zero or one times; no duplicates, but losses are possible.
Change data capture (CDC)
Turning a database's committed changes into a stream of events, for example with DynamoDB Streams or PostgreSQL logical replication.
Consumer group
In Kafka, a set of consumers that share a topic's partitions so each partition is read by exactly one member.
Content-based filtering
Delivering a message or event only to subscribers whose filter matches fields in it.
Dead-letter queue (DLQ)
A queue that receives messages or events that couldn't be processed or delivered after the allowed retries.
Deduplication ID
An identifier on an SQS FIFO message; messages with the same ID sent within five minutes are accepted but delivered only once.
Enhanced fan-out
A Kinesis feature giving each registered consumer its own 2 MB/s per shard, pushed over HTTP/2, instead of sharing the shard's read throughput.
Event bus
An EventBridge router that receives events and delivers them to targets according to rules.
Event pattern
A JSON pattern in an EventBridge rule that an event's fields must match for the rule to fire.
EventBridge Pipes
A point-to-point integration that reads from a source (a queue or stream), optionally filters and enriches, and delivers to one target.
Express workflow
A Step Functions workflow type for high-volume, short (up to five minutes) executions, billed by requests and duration.
Fan-out
Sending one message to many independent consumers.
FIFO (first in, first out)
Ordering in which items leave in the order they arrived; SQS FIFO queues and SNS FIFO topics apply it per message group.
Iterator age
For a stream consumer, how far behind the newest record its current position is, in time; the key lag metric for Kinesis.
Message group ID
The key that defines ordering in SQS FIFO queues and SNS FIFO topics: messages with the same group ID are delivered in order.
MSK (Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka)
AWS's managed Kafka service, with provisioned brokers or a serverless option.
Redrive policy
SQS configuration that moves a message to a dead-letter queue after it has been received a set number of times (maxReceiveCount).
Retention period
How long a queue or stream keeps messages or records before deleting them.
Shard
Kinesis's unit of ordering and capacity: an ordered sequence of records, written at up to 1 MB/s and read at up to 2 MB/s.
SNS (Simple Notification Service)
AWS's managed pub/sub topic service that pushes each message to every subscription.
SQS (Simple Queue Service)
AWS's managed message queue, in standard (at-least-once, unordered) and FIFO variants.
Standard workflow
A Step Functions workflow type with exactly-once execution, durable state and executions of up to a year, billed per state transition.
State transition
In Step Functions, one completed step of a workflow; the billing unit for Standard workflows.
Visibility timeout
How long a received SQS message stays hidden from other consumers; if not deleted by then, it becomes visible again.
drill:
Design: an ML feature pipeline and an order workflow on one platform

A company needs (1) clickstream events from web and mobile at 8,000 events per second (peaks 20,000), consumed by a real-time feature store, a fraud model and a daily batch export to S3, with the ability to reprocess the last 7 days after a bug fix; and (2) an order workflow — reserve stock, charge card, create shipment, send confirmation — at 50 orders per minute, where a payment can take up to 2 days to settle and every step must be auditable. Choose services for each, explain delivery and ordering guarantees, estimate monthly messaging cost for (1), and list the alarms you'd set.

Answer

(1) Clickstream: a stream. Kinesis Data Streams (or MSK) with partition key = user ID, so each user's events are ordered and load spreads across users. Provisioned sizing: 20,000 records/s at peak with ~1 KB records needs at least 20 shards for records (1,000 records/s each); use ~24 for headroom, or on-demand mode. Retention 7 days so reprocessing is a checkpoint rewind. Three consumers read independently: the feature-store updater and the fraud model with enhanced fan-out (dedicated 2 MB/s per shard each), and Firehose (or a consumer) writing to S3 for the daily export. Delivery is at-least-once to each consumer, so the feature updater uses idempotent upserts keyed by event ID. Cost (us-east-1, October 2026): 24 shards × $0.015 × 730 ≈ $263; payload units 8,000 × 2.628 million ≈ 21 billion × $0.014/M ≈ $294; retention beyond 24 h and enhanced fan-out (2 consumers × 24 shards × $0.015 × 730 ≈ $526 plus $0.013/GB read) on top — roughly $1,200–1,500 a month. Routing the same events through EventBridge would cost about $21,000 a month.

(2) Orders: Step Functions Standard. Exactly-once execution, waits of up to a year (payment settlement via a callback task token), retries with backoff on each step, catch blocks for compensation (release stock, refund), and 90 days of auditable history. 50 orders/min ≈ 2.2 million a month × ~8 transitions ≈ 17.5 million × $0.000025 ≈ $438. The order service starts executions from an outbox so no order is lost; confirmation emails go through SNS → SQS with idempotency on order ID.

Alarms: Kinesis write throttles and iterator age per consumer; Firehose delivery failures; Step Functions executions failed, timed out and throttled; age of the oldest pending payment callback; DLQ depth on every queue and target; and an end-to-end "event age at processing" metric for the feature store.
qa: E
When would you use SQS, SNS, EventBridge or Kinesis?

SQS when work items should each be processed by one of a pool of workers, with a durable buffer between producer and consumer. SNS when one message must reach several subscribers quickly — usually SQS queues, Lambda functions or HTTP endpoints. EventBridge when events from many sources must be routed to different targets by their content, with schema discovery, archives and replay, and moderate volume. Kinesis (or managed Kafka) when you need an ordered, retained log that several consumers read independently at high throughput and can replay.
Follow-up: what's the most common combination? — SNS fanning out to one SQS queue per consuming service: SNS gives fan-out, each queue gives its consumer an independent buffer, retries and a DLQ.
E
What is a visibility timeout and how do you set it?

When a consumer receives an SQS message, SQS hides it from other consumers for the visibility timeout (30 seconds by default, up to 12 hours). If the consumer deletes the message within that time, it's gone; if not — because the consumer crashed or was slow — it reappears and someone processes it again. Set it longer than the maximum processing time (AWS recommends six times the function timeout for Lambda consumers), and have long jobs extend it with ChangeMessageVisibility as they go.
Follow-up: what does a too-long timeout cost you? — Slow recovery: a message whose consumer died stays invisible for the whole timeout before anyone retries it.
E
What does a dead-letter queue protect against?

Poison messages — messages that fail every time, because they're malformed or trigger a bug. Without a DLQ, such a message is received, fails, reappears, and repeats until retention expires, consuming capacity and, in FIFO queues, blocking everything behind it in its group. A redrive policy moves it to the DLQ after maxReceiveCount receives, so the main queue keeps flowing and someone can inspect and redrive it later. Alarm on DLQ depth, because a DLQ nobody watches is just a slower way to lose data.

Follow-up: what maxReceiveCount would you choose? — Enough to ride out transient failures (say 3–5 with backoff), not so many that a poison message burns hours; for FIFO keep it low because the group is blocked meanwhile.
M
Explain the ordering and delivery guarantees of SQS standard, SQS FIFO, SNS, EventBridge and Kinesis.

SQS standard: at-least-once, best-effort ordering, nearly unlimited throughput. SQS FIFO: order within each message group, deduplication of sends within five minutes, still at-least-once processing; throughput limited per partition and by group parallelism. SNS standard: at-least-once push to every subscriber, no ordering; SNS FIFO: ordered and deduplicated into SQS FIFO queues. EventBridge: at-least-once delivery to targets, no ordering, retried for up to 24 hours by default. Kinesis: ordered within a shard (records with the same partition key), at-least-once to consumers because retries after failures re-read records; replayable within retention.

Follow-up: how do you get per-customer ordering at high throughput? — Use the customer ID as the FIFO message group ID or the Kinesis partition key: order holds per customer while different customers process in parallel.
M
Design an order-placed event flow that notifies email, inventory and analytics services.

The order service writes the order and an outbox row in one database transaction (sc11); a relay publishes the event to an SNS topic (or EventBridge bus). Each consumer has its own SQS queue subscribed to the topic, with a filter policy if it only cares about some events, a DLQ and alarms. Inventory processes from its queue idempotently using the order ID; email does the same; analytics either has a queue or reads from a stream for replayable history. A slow or failed consumer only backs up its own queue; the others are unaffected.

Follow-up: why not have the order service call the three services directly? — Synchronous calls couple availability: if email is down, orders fail or need custom retry logic; the queue gives each consumer independent failure and retry.
M
When would you choose EventBridge over SNS, and what does it cost at volume?

EventBridge when you need content-based routing on any field of the event, many target types with input transformation, events from AWS services and SaaS partners, schema discovery, or archives and replay. SNS when you need simple, fast fan-out at high volume and low cost. In us-east-1 (October 2026), EventBridge custom events were $1.00 per million and SNS publishes $0.50 per million, with deliveries to SQS and Lambda free on SNS. At 5 billion events a month that's $5,256 against $2,628 — a reason to put high-volume telemetry on a stream and keep EventBridge for business events.
Follow-up: what is EventBridge Pipes for? — Point-to-point integrations: read from SQS, a stream or a database change source, filter and enrich, and deliver to one target without writing glue code.
M
How does Kinesis Data Streams scale, and how do you size it?

In provisioned mode each shard accepts up to 1 MB/s or 1,000 records/s of writes and serves 2 MB/s of reads shared by standard consumers (up to five GetRecords calls per second); enhanced fan-out gives each registered consumer its own 2 MB/s per shard. Size by the larger of bytes and records: 2,000 records/s of 1 KB needs at least two shards for records, and peaks need more — six shards for a 3× peak. Records with the same partition key go to the same shard, so a hot key limits throughput to one shard. On-demand mode scales automatically (new streams start at 4 MB/s write, scaling much higher) and bills per GB.

Follow-up: a consumer's iterator age keeps rising. What do you do? — The consumer is falling behind: add parallelism (more shards, or Lambda's parallelization factor per shard), make processing faster, check for one hot shard, and make sure failing records aren't blocking a shard.
M
Step Functions Standard or Express — how do you choose?

Standard for long-running, low-to-moderate volume business processes where each execution matters: exactly-once execution, waits of up to a year, callbacks and human approval, full execution history for 90 days, billed $0.025 per 1,000 state transitions. Express for high-volume, short (under five minutes) event processing: at-least-once asynchronously or at-most-once synchronously, billed $1 per million requests plus duration, with history only in CloudWatch Logs. Steps in Express workflows must be idempotent.

Follow-up: what does a five-step Standard workflow cost per million executions? — Five transitions per execution (plus retries): 5 million × $0.000025 = $125, before the Lambda or other services it calls.
H
Compare the monthly cost of moving 2,000 one-kilobyte events per second through SQS, SNS to three queues, EventBridge and Kinesis.

That's about 5.26 billion events a month (us-east-1, October 2026). SQS standard at $0.40 per million requests: send, receive and delete unbatched is 15.8 billion requests ≈ $6,307; batching 10 per call cuts it to ≈ $631. SNS publishing at $0.50 per million ≈ $2,628, plus three queues' batched receives and deletes ≈ $1,261. EventBridge at $1.00 per million ≈ $5,256. Kinesis provisioned with six shards for a 3× peak: 6 × $0.015 × 730 ≈ $66 in shard-hours plus $0.014 per million 25 KB payload units ≈ $74, about $139; on-demand ≈ $831 with two consumers. For firehose telemetry, a stream is an order of magnitude cheaper; for business events at modest volume the differences are noise and features decide.

Follow-up: what assumption most changes the SQS number? — Batching and long polling: unbatched sends and empty receives multiply request counts; batching ten and waiting up to 20 seconds on receive cut requests by roughly ten times.
H
How do you build an exactly-once effect on top of at-least-once delivery?

Make the consumer idempotent: derive a stable key per message (order ID, event ID or the FIFO deduplication ID), and before applying side effects record it in a store with a conditional write — or apply the effect as an upsert keyed by it — so a second delivery is a no-op. Make downstream calls idempotent too (APIs with idempotency keys). For read-process-write pipelines on Kafka, transactions can commit consumer offsets and output atomically; on Kinesis and SQS you combine checkpointing or deletion with idempotent writes. Delete or checkpoint only after the effect is durable.

Follow-up: where can this still fail? — If the idempotency record and the side effect aren't atomic (a crash between them), or if the record expires before a late duplicate arrives; keep records longer than the maximum redelivery window.
H
Walk through the November 2020 Kinesis outage and what it teaches about integration services.

On 25 November 2020, AWS added a relatively small amount of capacity to the Kinesis front-end fleet in us-east-1 between 2:44 and 3:47 AM PST. Each front-end server keeps operating-system threads for communicating with every other front-end server, so adding servers raised the thread count on all of them, and the fleet exceeded an OS limit on threads; servers could no longer build the shard maps they need to route requests, and Kinesis requests failed from about 5:15 AM. Because rebuilding a front-end server's view loads the fleet, operators could only bring servers back at a few hundred per hour, so full recovery took until 10:23 PM PST. Services built on Kinesis were hit: Cognito, CloudWatch metrics and logs, EventBridge and CloudWatch Events delivery, Lambda (memory pressure from buffered metrics), reactive Auto Scaling, and AWS's own Service Health Dashboard updates. AWS moved to larger servers (fewer threads per fleet), added alarms on thread consumption, raised the limit and planned to cellularise the fleet. Lessons: an integration service is a shared dependency for many others, including your monitoring; all-to-all designs scale quadratically and hit limits suddenly; and recovery can be throttled by the need to avoid overloading the system itself.

Follow-up: what would you change in your own architecture? — Keep critical alarms on a path that doesn't depend on the same service, size retention so consumers can catch up after a day-long outage, and give producers local buffering and backoff.
H
How do the equivalents on Google Cloud and Azure differ?

Google Cloud Pub/Sub combines topic fan-out with per-subscription queues: each subscription gets every message, with acknowledgement deadlines (like visibility timeouts), at-least-once delivery by default, optional ordering keys and an exactly-once delivery option within a region, and replay by seeking to a timestamp; Eventarc routes events, Managed Service for Apache Kafka provides Kafka, and Workflows orchestrates. Azure Service Bus offers queues and topics with sessions for ordering, duplicate detection and dead-lettering; Event Grid routes events; Event Hubs is the partitioned stream with a Kafka-compatible endpoint; Logic Apps and Durable Functions orchestrate. The semantics — at-least-once, ordering per key, DLQs, retention — carry over; names and limits differ.
Follow-up: what's the closest thing to SNS-plus-SQS on GCP? — A Pub/Sub topic with one subscription per consumer: each subscription is its own durable queue.
