t: Observability and operations on the cloud: CloudWatch-style metrics, logs and traces, alarms, audit logs (CloudTrail), and on-call for cloud services
sum: The cloud's own telemetry and how to run services on it: CloudWatch metrics (namespaces, dimensions, resolution and rollups), alarms evaluated M out of N with missing-data rules and composite alarms, logs with retention, metric filters and query costs, traces with X-Ray and OpenTelemetry, CloudTrail management and data events and AWS Config for audit and forensics, provider health events, an observability bill worked with real cardinality numbers, and how on-call differs when part of the stack is someone else's — with Datadog's March 2023 multi-region, multi-cloud outage as the case.
prereq: sc13

SLIs and SLOs define reliability from the user's view; burn-rate alerts page on fast budget consumption; metrics, logs and traces answer different questions; cardinality drives cost; incidents end in blameless post-mortems.
cl2
Every API call is authenticated and authorised by IAM; principals are users, roles and sessions; the role session name and source identity show who acted.
cl8
EventBridge routes events, including AWS service events, to targets; SNS fans out notifications; integration services can themselves fail, as Kinesis did in 2020 taking CloudWatch with it.
cl10
Static stability, failover without control planes, and monitoring that doesn't share fate with the systems it watches.
why:
At 03:10 an on-call engineer is paged: checkout error rate 14%. The dashboards show nothing wrong with the service's instances — CPU is normal. The database's metrics look fine. Is it a bad deploy (there was one at 02:40)? A dependency? The cloud provider? The status page is green. Forty minutes later someone notices that errors are only in one availability zone, and that the provider's account-specific health feed posted a notice about network degradation in that zone at 03:04. A zonal shift fixes it in two minutes. The outage lasted 45.

The following week a security alert says an access key was used from an unknown IP address. Which data did it read? The audit trail shows the key listed buckets and changed nothing — but object-level reads were never being recorded, so nobody can say which customer exports were downloaded. The legal team assumes the worst.

And at month end, the observability bill exceeds the compute bill, because someone added the instance ID as a dimension to every custom metric on an autoscaled fleet that cycles through hundreds of instances a day.

Running services in the cloud means operating a system partly built and run by someone else. The provider produces a great deal of telemetry — metrics for every managed service, logs, audit records of every API call, configuration history, health events — and you produce your own. Turning that into fast, correct answers during incidents, and into evidence after security events, depends on knowing how the telemetry is structured, what it doesn't cover by default, how alarms actually evaluate, and what it all costs. sc13 covered the principles of SLOs, burn-rate alerting and the three pillars. This lesson is about the cloud's concrete machinery: CloudWatch metrics, alarms and logs, tracing, CloudTrail and Config, provider health events, the cost model, and on-call practices for services that depend on a provider — with Datadog's 2023 outage as a reminder that the monitoring itself can fail.
primer:
Picture a large office building's control room. Some screens come with the building: temperature in each room, lift status, door alarms, power use — installed by the landlord, reporting automatically. Others the tenant installs: sensors inside their own equipment, cameras in their own rooms. There's a visitor log at reception recording every person who enters, which door, when, and on whose authority. And there's a noticeboard from the landlord: "Lift 3 under maintenance Tuesday", "Power fault on floor 2".

The cloud equivalents. The landlord's screens are provider metrics: every managed service publishes numbers about itself to CloudWatch for free — an instance's CPU and network, a load balancer's request count and latency, a queue's depth, a function's errors and duration. The tenant's sensors are your telemetry: application metrics, logs and traces, plus anything inside the virtual machine the provider can't see, such as memory and disk space. The visitor log is CloudTrail, the audit trail of every API call: who, what, when, from where. The noticeboard is AWS Health and the status page: provider-side events, some specific to your account.

Two properties of this system shape everything else. The first is cost follows volume and cardinality: logs are billed per gigabyte ingested, metrics per distinct time series, traces per span stored, audit data per event — so how you emit telemetry is a cost decision. The second is shared fate: the monitoring system runs somewhere, and if that somewhere is the region or the vendor having a bad day, you lose visibility exactly when you need it.

Put together, these sources answer the four questions every incident and investigation asks, in order. Is something wrong for users? — symptom metrics and synthetic checks. Where is it? — metrics broken down by zone, region, endpoint and dependency, and traces of slow or failing requests. Is it us or the provider? — your deploy history against provider health events and the managed services' own metrics. Who changed what? — the audit trail and configuration history. A well-run cloud estate can answer each within minutes because the telemetry was designed for those questions in advance: the right dimensions on metrics, the right fields in logs, trace context propagated end to end, and audit logs switched on where the data is. The rest of the lesson goes through each piece of machinery with that purpose in mind.

Where the analogy breaks: the building's visitor log records people at the doors. CloudTrail by default records only the "door" events — creating, changing and deleting things — not every use of the things inside. Object reads, function invocations and item lookups are separate "data events" that you must switch on and pay for. That gap is where many security investigations come to a halt.
body:
1. Metrics: identity, resolution and retention

A CloudWatch metric is identified by a namespace (AWS/EC2, AWS/ApplicationELB, or your own such as Shop/Checkout), a metric name and up to 30 dimensions (name/value pairs such as LoadBalancer=app/prod-alb/…, AvailabilityZone=euc1-az1). From the CloudWatch documentation (October 2026), each unique combination of dimensions is a separate metric, and CloudWatch doesn't aggregate across dimensions for custom metrics — if you publish by service and endpoint, you can't later query "all endpoints" unless you also publish that combination or use metric math search expressions.

Data points have standard resolution (one minute) or, for custom metrics, high resolution (one second). Retention rolls up: points finer than 60 seconds are kept for 3 hours; one-minute points for 15 days; five-minute aggregates for 63 days; hourly aggregates for 455 days (15 months). So a graph of last quarter is hourly whatever you sent. AWS services publish many metrics free (EC2's basic metrics at five-minute resolution, one-minute with paid detailed monitoring). Custom metrics are billed per metric-month: $0.30 for the first 10,000 in us-east-1 in October 2026, falling to $0.10 and lower in higher tiers.

Ways to get application metrics in: the PutMetricData API (each call billed), the CloudWatch agent or an OpenTelemetry collector (which can also scrape Prometheus endpoints), and the embedded metric format (EMF) — structured JSON log lines from which CloudWatch extracts metrics automatically. EMF is popular in Lambda because writing a log line is cheap and synchronous-call-free:

{"_aws":{"Timestamp":1791374400000,"CloudWatchMetrics":[{"Namespace":"Shop/Checkout",
  "Dimensions":[["Service","Endpoint"]],"Metrics":[{"Name":"Latency","Unit":"Milliseconds"}]}]},
 "Service":"checkout","Endpoint":"POST /orders","Latency":182,"RequestId":"req-7f3a"}

Here RequestId is logged but isn't a dimension, so it doesn't create metrics — it's searchable in the log, which is exactly where high-cardinality fields belong.

Two blind spots catch people. The hypervisor-level EC2 metrics don't include memory or disk space; those need an agent. And percentiles: CloudWatch can compute p99 for metrics where it has raw points (and for many AWS service metrics), but averaging latency hides tails, so alarm on percentiles for latency.

2. Alarms: evaluation, missing data and composition

An alarm watches one metric (or a metric math expression) and has three evaluation settings: the period over which data is aggregated into one point, the evaluation periods N (how many recent points to look at) and datapoints to alarm M (how many of them must breach). For periods of a minute or more, alarms are evaluated every minute over a sliding window. States are OK, ALARM and INSUFFICIENT_DATA, and actions (SNS notification, autoscaling, EC2 actions, Systems Manager incidents) fire on transitions.

Missing data is the subtle part. For each alarm you choose whether periods without data are treated as breaching, not breaching, ignored (keep the current state) or missing (contributing to INSUFFICIENT_DATA). An error-count metric that's only emitted when errors occur should treat missing as not breaching; a request-count or heartbeat metric should treat missing as breaching, because silence means the service or its telemetry stopped. A service that crashes and stops emitting errors looks healthy to an error-rate alarm with the wrong setting.

Composite alarms combine others with AND, OR and NOT: page only when the error-rate alarm AND the latency alarm are both in ALARM, or suppress zone-level alarms while a deployment alarm is active. They're the main tool against alert noise. Anomaly detection alarms compare a metric with a learned band rather than a fixed threshold, useful for metrics with strong daily patterns. Prices in us-east-1 (October 2026): $0.10 per standard alarm metric per month, $0.30 for high-resolution, $0.50 per composite alarm.

For user-facing services, the alarms that page people should be SLO burn-rate alarms on error rate and latency (sc13), computed with metric math from request and error counts; resource alarms (CPU, disk, queue depth) usually create tickets, not pages, except where they predict imminent failure (disk 90% full, queue age rising).

3. Logs: groups, retention, filters and queries

CloudWatch Logs organises events into log streams (one per source, such as a container or function instance) within log groups (one per application or component), each with its own retention (from a day to never expire — the default is never, which quietly accumulates storage), encryption key and access policy. Prices in us-east-1 (October 2026): ingestion $0.50 per GB in the Standard class or $0.25 in Infrequent Access (fewer features, for logs you rarely query), storage $0.03 per GB-month, Logs Insights queries $0.005 per GB scanned.

From a log group you can: create metric filters that count or extract values from matching events into metrics; query interactively with Logs Insights; stream events through subscription filters to Lambda, Kinesis or Firehose for processing or export; and export to S3 for long-term storage and analysis with Athena. Structured JSON logs with consistent fields (timestamp, level, service, request ID, trace ID, tenant) make every one of these cheaper and more useful than free text.

A Logs Insights query to find the slowest endpoints in the last hour:

fields @timestamp, Endpoint, Latency
| filter Service = "checkout" and Latency > 1000
| stats count(*) as slow, pct(Latency, 99) as p99 by Endpoint
| sort slow desc
| limit 10

It scans every log event in the time range of the selected groups, so cost is proportional to data volume times time range: narrowing to the right log group and the last hour rather than the last week can make a query a hundred times cheaper.

4. Traces

A trace records one request's path as a tree of spans, each a timed operation with attributes (service, operation, status, database statement, queue name). The trace ID and parent span ID travel between services in headers — the W3C traceparent header for OpenTelemetry, or X-Ray's own header — and in message attributes across queues and event buses (cl8). OpenTelemetry is the vendor-neutral standard for instrumentation; AWS ships a distribution of its SDKs and collector, and X-Ray accepts OpenTelemetry data, as do third-party backends.

Tracing everything is expensive, so systems sample. Head-based sampling decides at the first service (keep 5% of requests); it's cheap but drops most failures. Tail-based sampling buffers spans in a collector and decides after the request completes (keep all errors and requests slower than 1 second, plus 1% of the rest), which captures the interesting traces at the cost of running and sizing collectors. Traces answer the question metrics can't: which hop made this request slow.

5. Audit: CloudTrail and AWS Config

CloudTrail records API calls as JSON events. A trimmed example of someone opening a security group:

{ "eventTime": "2026-10-06T14:02:11Z",
  "eventSource": "ec2.amazonaws.com",
  "eventName": "AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress",
  "awsRegion": "eu-central-1",
  "sourceIPAddress": "203.0.113.24",
  "userIdentity": { "type": "AssumedRole",
    "arn": "arn:aws:sts::111122223333:assumed-role/platform-admin/alice@example.com",
    "sessionContext": { "sourceIdentity": "alice@example.com" } },
  "requestParameters": { "groupId": "sg-0abc…",
    "ipPermissions": { "items": [ { "ipProtocol": "tcp", "fromPort": 22, "toPort": 22,
      "ipRanges": { "items": [ { "cidrIp": "0.0.0.0/0" } ] } } ] } } }

Event types matter. Management events (control-plane operations) are recorded by default; every account gets a free, searchable 90-day event history, and the first copy delivered by a trail is free. Data events (S3 object reads and writes, Lambda invocations, DynamoDB item operations and more) are off by default and cost $0.10 per 100,000 events delivered (October 2026); extra copies of management events cost $2.00 per 100,000. Network activity events for VPC endpoints and Insights (anomalies in API call rates) are further options. CloudTrail Lake stores and queries events with SQL.

The standard organisation design: an organisation trail covering all accounts and regions, delivered to an S3 bucket in a dedicated log-archive account with Object Lock and a bucket policy that only CloudTrail can write to, KMS encryption with a key in that account, log file integrity validation on (digest files let you prove logs weren't altered), and data events enabled for sensitive buckets and critical functions. Security tooling (GuardDuty, a SIEM) reads from there.

AWS Config records the configuration of resources over time as configuration items and evaluates them against rules — managed ones such as "S3 buckets block public access" or custom ones — with optional automatic remediation. CloudTrail tells you who changed the security group and when; Config shows what it looked like before and after and which resources were attached to it. Config bills per configuration item recorded and per rule evaluation, so constantly changing resources are worth scoping.

6. Provider health

AWS Health publishes events about AWS services: public events (a service issue in a region) and account-specific ones (an instance scheduled for retirement on degraded hardware, an RDS maintenance window, a notice that a zone in your account is affected by an event). Account-specific events go to EventBridge, so they can page on-call or trigger automation (for example, drain an instance scheduled for retirement). They usually arrive before the public status page is updated and say which of your resources are affected, which is far more useful during an incident than a regional status colour. Google Cloud's Personalized Service Health and Azure Service Health play the same role.

7. An observability bill, worked

A checkout service runs on 30 instances in an autoscaling group, handles 200 requests per second on average and writes one structured log line of about 1 KB per request. Monthly volumes (a 730-hour month is 2,628,000 seconds) and us-east-1 prices from October 2026:

ItemVolumeMonthly cost
Log ingestion (Standard)200 × 2,628,000 ≈ 526 M lines ≈ 500 GB500 × $0.50 = $250
Log storage, 30-day retention~500 GB on hand≈ $15
Logs Insights200 queries × 20 GB scanned4,000 GB × $0.005 = $20
Latency metric by service × 40 endpoints × 5 status classes × 30 instance IDs6,000 metrics6,000 × $0.30 = $1,800
Same metric without instance ID200 metrics200 × $0.30 = $60
Alarms50 standard$5
CloudTrail data events on the exports bucket50 M GetObject500 × $0.10 = $50

The instance-ID dimension is the trap: it makes the metric bill thirty times larger, and because autoscaling replaces instances, the number of distinct instance IDs over a month can be far more than 30 — each new one creates new metrics that persist. Log ingestion grows linearly with traffic; it's usually the largest line at scale, and the levers are log level, sampling of successful requests, the Infrequent Access class for rarely queried logs, and retention.

8. On-call for services that run on a provider

On-call in the cloud adds one recurring question to every incident: is this us or them? A practical sequence:

  1. Scope by dimension. Break the symptom down by zone, region, endpoint, dependency and deployment version. Errors in one zone suggest a zonal provider issue or a zone-local dependency; errors starting at a deploy suggest you; errors in calls to one managed service suggest that service.
  2. Check provider signals. Account-specific Health events, the service's own metrics (throttles, 5xx from the AWS API), and whether other teams see the same.
  3. Mitigate first. Roll back the deploy, zonal-shift away from a bad zone, fail over, shed load with feature flags — whichever applies — before root cause is known.
  4. Escalate to the provider with evidence: request IDs, resource IDs, timestamps, regions and zones (with AZ IDs), and impact. Support plans determine response times; know yours before you need it.
  5. Learn. The post-mortem separates the provider's fault from your design choices: a zone failure is theirs; being unable to survive one is yours.
deep:
Cardinality is the cost model of every metrics system

Whether it's CloudWatch, Prometheus or a vendor, metrics systems store and index one time series per unique label combination, so cost and query speed scale with cardinality, not with event volume. A metric with labels of 10, 40 and 5 values has up to 2,000 series; adding a user ID with 100,000 values makes it 200 million. The discipline is to use metrics for bounded dimensions that you alarm or aggregate on, and to push unbounded identifiers into logs and traces where they're stored per event and queried on demand. Autoscaling, Kubernetes pod names and container IDs are the common accidental sources of cardinality, because they create new values continuously.

Alerts on symptoms, dashboards for causes

Paging on causes (CPU above 80%, a queue above 1,000) produces many pages that don't matter and misses failures nobody predicted; paging on symptoms (users' requests failing or slow, measured against an SLO) catches whatever breaks and ignores what doesn't hurt. In the cloud this matters more because many causes are the provider's and outside your control, while symptoms are always yours. Resource metrics still matter: they're the dashboards on-call uses to find the cause once a symptom alert fires, and the tickets that prevent tomorrow's incident.

Telemetry pipelines need backpressure and isolation

Logging and metrics agents run on the same hosts as applications. If the telemetry backend slows down, agents buffer, then use memory and disk, then — if poorly configured — block application threads writing logs or crash hosts with full disks. Good pipelines bound their buffers, drop or sample under pressure (debug logs first), and never make application requests wait on telemetry delivery. In serverless, writing logs to stdout keeps delivery out of the request path; in containers, sidecar or node-level collectors isolate it.

Audit logs are evidence, which changes how they're stored

Operational logs help you debug; audit logs may be used to prove what happened to regulators, courts or customers. That requires completeness (all accounts, all regions, data events where data matters), integrity (CloudTrail's digest files, chained by hash, show tampering; Object Lock prevents deletion), retention matched to obligations (often a year or more) and access control so the people investigated can't edit the record. It also requires being able to query years of events quickly when needed, which is why teams load trails into a lake (Athena, CloudTrail Lake, a SIEM) rather than reading JSON files from S3 during an incident.

Correlated failures hide in shared configuration

Datadog's regions were architecturally independent — separate infrastructure, separate cloud providers — yet failed within an hour of each other because they shared an operating-system default: an automatic security-update window from 06:00 to 07:00 UTC. The same pattern appears with certificates that expire at the same moment everywhere, global configuration pushes, feature flags, base images, and scheduled jobs. Finding these common modes is an audit exercise: list everything that changes all regions at once and stagger it, canary it or remove it.

Sampling decides what you can know later

Every telemetry system samples somewhere: traces at the edge or in a collector, logs by level or by rate, metrics by aggregation into one-minute or one-hour points. Each choice deletes information you might need in a future investigation, so it should be deliberate. A useful rule is to keep everything about failures and outliers (all error traces, all slow requests, all audit events for sensitive data) and sample the boring majority. Long-term retention follows the same logic: aggregated metrics for capacity trends, raw logs for weeks, audit trails for years. Writing these choices down per signal — what's kept, for how long, at what fidelity — turns "we don't have that data" from an incident-time surprise into a known, accepted trade-off.

Observability for AI workloads adds token-level telemetry

LLM-backed services need the usual metrics plus their own: tokens in and out per request, time to first token and inter-token latency, model and prompt versions, cache hit rates, tool calls, refusal and guardrail events, and cost per request. OpenTelemetry's generative-AI semantic conventions define standard attributes for these spans. The cardinality warnings apply with force — prompt text and user IDs belong in sampled traces or logs with access controls, not in metric dimensions — and the privacy rules from au12 and ae5 apply to what's logged at all.
prod:
Failure modes and their symptoms

Silent services. A component stops emitting metrics; error alarms stay green. Fix: heartbeat and request-count alarms with missing data as breaching, and synthetic checks.

Alert fatigue. Dozens of resource alarms page nightly; real incidents are missed. Fix: page on SLO burn rates and composite alarms; demote resource alarms to tickets; review every page in a weekly on-call handover.

Cardinality bill shock. Custom metrics with instance, pod or user IDs as dimensions. Fix: remove unbounded dimensions, use EMF with high-cardinality fields as properties, not dimensions.

Log cost runaway. A debug flag left on, a retry loop logging stack traces, a chatty library. Fix: per-group ingestion alarms, sampling, log levels controlled by configuration, retention policies on every group.

Missing audit data. A breach investigation can't answer what was read because data events or S3 access logs were never enabled; a region nobody uses wasn't covered by the trail. Fix: organisation trail across all regions, data events for sensitive resources, periodic checks that logging is still on (attackers turn it off — alert on StopLogging and DeleteTrail).

Monitoring that shares fate. The region's CloudWatch is degraded during a regional event, or the observability vendor is down. Fix: cross-region synthetic checks and a minimal independent alerting path.

Time and clocks. Metrics with wrong timestamps (clock skew, batch publishing) put alarms into INSUFFICIENT_DATA or delay them. Use NTP (the Amazon Time Sync Service) and publish with current timestamps.

What good looks like

Every user-facing service has SLO alerts and a dashboard broken down by zone, region and dependency; every log group has retention; every account is in the organisation trail with data events for sensitive stores; Health events reach on-call; synthetic checks run from outside the region; observability spend is tracked per team; and game days include "monitoring is down" as a scenario.

The case: Datadog, 8 March 2023

Datadog's post-mortem describes how, at 06:00 UTC on 8 March 2023, a security update to systemd was installed automatically on many of its Ubuntu hosts through a legacy unattended-upgrades channel that was still enabled in the base image. Installing the update restarted systemd-networkd, and on restart it removed network routes that had been added by Cilium, the container networking plugin Datadog uses in Kubernetes. Nodes lost connectivity and dropped out of their clusters. Because the operating system's default window for automatic installation was 06:00 to 07:00 UTC, the update hit tens of thousands of nodes in five Datadog regions (US1, EU1, US3, US4 and US5) — running on three different cloud providers — at nearly the same time.

For customers, Datadog's web application and APIs were unavailable or degraded, monitors were not evaluating or alerting, and data ingestion was disrupted. Datadog posted its first public notice at 06:31 UTC; web access was restored at 09:13 UTC; the first major service was fully operational again at 16:44 UTC; all services were operational on 9 March at 08:58 UTC; and historical data backfill completed on 10 March at 06:25 UTC. The response involved some 10 senior engineering leaders, around 70 incident commanders and a pool of 450–750 responders across four shifts. Datadog disabled the legacy update channel across its fleet, configured systemd-networkd so that restarts don't remove routes it didn't create, and audited for other common-mode risks.

Two lessons transfer directly. First, regions and clouds are only independent if nothing changes them all at once; a default time window in an OS image was a hidden global switch. Second, every customer whose alerting lived entirely in Datadog lost it for hours — a reminder that the observability system is a dependency with its own failure modes, and that the most critical alerts deserve an independent path.
myths: CloudWatch shows memory and disk usage for my EC2 instances out of the box.

EC2's built-in metrics come from the hypervisor: CPU, network, disk I/O and status checks. The hypervisor can't see inside the guest operating system, so memory use, disk space and process-level metrics need an agent (the CloudWatch agent or an OpenTelemetry collector) running on the instance. Teams discover this when an instance runs out of disk and no alarm fired.
More dimensions on a metric just make it more useful.

Every unique combination of dimension values is a separate metric, billed separately. A latency metric with service, endpoint (40 values), status class (5) and instance ID (30) is 6,000 metrics — at $0.30 each per month for the first 10,000 in us-east-1 (October 2026), about $1,800 a month for one measurement. Drop instance ID and it's 200 metrics, $60. High-cardinality detail belongs in logs or traces, queried when needed.
CloudTrail records everything that happens in my account.

A trail records management events (control-plane calls like CreateBucket, RunInstances, PutRolePolicy) by default. Data events — S3 object reads and writes, Lambda invocations, DynamoDB item operations — are not recorded unless you enable them, and they're billed per event. Many breach investigations stall because nobody can say which objects were read: the data events were never on.
An alarm that didn't fire means nothing was wrong.

Alarms only see their metric, through their configuration. A metric that stops arriving (the agent died, the service stopped emitting) puts the alarm into INSUFFICIENT_DATA, which by default triggers nothing; with missing data treated as 'not breaching', a dead service can look perfectly healthy. Decide missing-data behaviour per alarm, and alarm separately on the absence of heartbeats.
The provider's status page tells me whether it's their problem.

Provider status pages are updated by humans after investigation and often lag the start of an event by tens of minutes; in AWS's 2017 and 2021 events the dashboard itself was impaired. Your own per-region, per-service error metrics and the account-specific AWS Health events arrive sooner. The status page confirms; your telemetry detects.
Using a third-party observability vendor removes the risk of monitoring failing with production.

It moves the shared fate elsewhere. Datadog's March 2023 outage left its customers without dashboards and alerts for hours, on the same day their own systems might have needed them. Critical alerting should have a fallback path — a few provider-native alarms, synthetic checks from an independent service — so that losing one observability system doesn't leave you blind.
lab:
Goal: implement CloudWatch-style alarm evaluation, a cardinality and cost estimator, and a tiny CloudTrail-style investigation — Python 3.12 standard library only. About 20 minutes; no cloud account needed.

  1. Alarm engine. Write evaluate(points, threshold, m, n, missing) where points is a list of floats or None; treat None per missing in {"breaching", "notBreaching", "ignore", "missing"} and return the state after each minute. Reproduce the figure (breaches at minutes 2, 6, 8, 9, 10; alarm at minute 10 for 3 of 5).
  2. Silent failure. Feed an error-count series that stops (all None) after minute 20. Compare states for "notBreaching" and "breaching", then add a request-count heartbeat alarm.
  3. Cardinality. Write series(dims) = product of distinct values; compute monthly cost at $0.30 per metric for the first 10,000 and $0.10 after for the lesson's metric with and without instance ID. Then simulate an autoscaling fleet replacing 10% of 30 instances per hour for a month and count distinct instance IDs.
  4. Logs. Write log_cost(rps, bytes_per_line, retention_days) using $0.50/GB ingestion and $0.03/GB-month storage, and reproduce the table.
  5. Investigation. Generate 10,000 fake CloudTrail-like events (JSON dicts with eventName, userIdentity.arn, sourceIPAddress, requestParameters.key) including 40 GetObject events by a leaked role from one IP. Write queries with list comprehensions: all actions by that role, distinct objects read, first and last time seen.

What to look for: step 2 shows the dead service staying OK with notBreaching — and the heartbeat catching it; step 3 shows 6,000 versus 200 metrics and, with fleet churn, thousands of distinct instance IDs in a month (2,190 replacements at 10% per hour) — the bill multiplies; step 5 shows how quickly an investigation goes when object-level events exist, and what you'd be unable to answer without them.

Needs an AWS account (optional): aws cloudtrail lookup-events --lookup-attributes AttributeKey=EventName,AttributeValue=AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress --max-results 5 searches the free 90-day management event history.
recap: Cloud observability combines provider telemetry (service metrics, logs, health events, audit trails) with your own (application metrics, logs, traces) routed into one place where alarms and dashboards live.

A CloudWatch metric is identified by namespace, name and dimensions; every dimension combination is a separate billed metric; standard resolution is one minute, high resolution one second, and data rolls up to 5-minute points after 15 days and hourly after 63 days, kept 15 months.

Alarms evaluate M breaching data points out of the last N periods, with explicit treatment of missing data; composite alarms combine alarms to cut noise; alarm actions notify through SNS, trigger autoscaling or start automation.

Logs land in log groups with retention you set; metric filters and the embedded metric format turn log lines into metrics; Logs Insights queries are billed per GB scanned; ingestion is usually the largest observability cost.
Traces follow a request across services with propagated context; X-Ray and OpenTelemetry (through the AWS Distro or collectors) record spans, and sampling keeps cost bounded.

CloudTrail records management events by default and data events when enabled; organisation trails delivered to a locked bucket in a separate account are the audit and forensics backbone; AWS Config records resource configuration over time.
AWS Health and provider status show provider-side events; account-specific Health events through EventBridge reach on-call faster than status pages.

On-call for cloud services means distinguishing your fault from the provider's quickly — per-zone and per-region error metrics, synthetic probes from outside, Health events — and having runbooks that work when the provider is degraded.

Observability must not share fate with what it watches: monitoring in another region or provider for critical alerts, heartbeat alarms, and a fallback when the observability vendor fails, as Datadog's customers learned in March 2023.
glossary: AWS Config
A service that records the configuration of resources over time and evaluates them against rules, answering 'what did this look like last Tuesday?'
AWS Health
The source of provider-side events (service issues, scheduled maintenance, account-specific notices), available in a dashboard, an API and EventBridge.
Cardinality
The number of distinct values (or value combinations) a metric's dimensions or labels take; each combination is a separate time series.
CloudTrail
AWS's audit log of API calls: who called what, from where, when, with which parameters and result.
CloudWatch
AWS's monitoring service for metrics, alarms, logs, dashboards and (with related features) traces and synthetic checks.
Composite alarm
An alarm whose state is a Boolean expression of other alarms' states, used to reduce noise and page only on meaningful combinations.
Data event
A CloudTrail record of a data-plane operation such as an S3 GetObject or a Lambda invocation; off by default and billed per event.
Datapoints to alarm
The M in an 'M out of N' alarm: how many of the last N periods must breach for the alarm to fire.
Dimension
A name/value pair that is part of a CloudWatch metric's identity, such as InstanceId=i-0abc.
Embedded metric format (EMF)
A JSON log structure from which CloudWatch extracts metrics automatically, so applications emit metrics by writing logs.
Heartbeat alarm
An alarm that fires when an expected signal stops arriving, catching silent failures.
High-resolution metric
A custom metric stored at one-second granularity, retained at that resolution for three hours.
Log group
A CloudWatch Logs container for log streams with shared retention, encryption and access settings.
Management event
A CloudTrail record of a control-plane operation, such as creating, modifying or deleting a resource.
Metric filter
A pattern on a log group that turns matching log events into a CloudWatch metric.
Missing data treatment
How an alarm treats periods with no data points: as breaching, not breaching, ignored or missing.
Namespace
A container that isolates CloudWatch metrics, such as AWS/EC2 or a custom MyApp/Orders.
NTP (Network Time Protocol)
The protocol that keeps machine clocks synchronised; accurate timestamps matter for metrics and alarms.
OpenTelemetry (OTel)
The open standard and tooling for producing and exporting metrics, logs and traces, supported by every major cloud and vendor.
Organisation trail
A CloudTrail trail created in the management account that records events from every account in an AWS organisation.
SIEM (security information and event management)
A system that collects security logs from many sources, correlates them and raises alerts for investigation.
SLI / SLO
Service level indicator (a measured property such as the share of successful requests) and service level objective (its target); see sc13.
Span
One timed operation within a trace, such as a database call, with attributes and a parent span.
Synthetic monitoring
Scripted requests from outside (for example CloudWatch Synthetics canaries) that test a service the way users would.
Trace
The set of spans recording one request's path through a distributed system, linked by a propagated trace ID.
W3C traceparent
The standard HTTP header carrying a trace ID and parent span ID between services.
X-Ray
AWS's distributed tracing service, now ingesting OpenTelemetry data and integrated with CloudWatch.
drill:
Diagnose and design: "we didn't know until customers told us"

An API team on AWS had a 50-minute outage. Timeline: 14:00 deploy of version 412 to all three zones at once; 14:05 a configuration error makes the service return HTTP 200 with an empty body for 60% of requests; 14:20 the service's error-rate alarm (5xx count, missing data as not breaching) is still OK; the CPU alarm is OK; 14:48 a customer tweets; 14:50 rollback. Their observability: CloudWatch dashboards of CPU and 5xx, logs in Standard class with no retention set, a custom latency metric with dimensions service, endpoint and pod name, and a third-party vendor for traces. Explain why nothing alerted, and redesign their alerting and observability (including cost) so this is caught within five minutes.

Answer

Why nothing fired. The failure produced 200s, so 5xx alarms saw nothing; CPU was normal; there was no measure of correctness. Nothing checked what users actually got.

Detection. (1) Synthetic canaries every minute from another region that call the main endpoints and assert on the response body (non-empty, expected fields) — this alone would have paged by ~14:07. (2) An application-level success SLI: the service emits, via EMF, a count of "valid responses" and "invalid responses" (empty body, schema validation failures) by endpoint; a burn-rate alarm on the invalid ratio. (3) Business metrics with anomaly detection (orders per minute) as a backstop.

Deploys. Deploy zone by zone (or by cell) with automatic rollback on the canary and SLI alarms; a 14:00 deploy to all zones at once is why 60% of all traffic was affected.

Alarm hygiene. Add request-count heartbeats with missing data as breaching; use composite alarms so a deploy-in-progress flag doesn't suppress real pages.

Cost and data. Remove pod name from the latency metric's dimensions (pods churn on every deploy, creating new metrics each time); keep pod and request IDs as log fields. Set log retention (30 days hot, export to S3 for longer), and move verbose logs to the Infrequent Access class. Keep traces in the vendor, but make sure the canaries and the SLI burn-rate alarm page through a path that doesn't depend on that vendor.
qa: E
What's the difference between metrics, logs and traces, and what does the cloud give you of each by default?

Metrics are numbers over time, cheap to store and fast to alert on; logs are detailed event records for investigation; traces follow single requests across services to show where time went. By default AWS services publish metrics to CloudWatch (EC2 CPU and network, load-balancer request counts and latencies, Lambda invocations and errors, RDS CPU and connections), many services can send logs (Lambda automatically, others when configured), and CloudTrail records API activity. Application metrics, guest-OS metrics such as memory and disk, application logs and traces need agents, SDKs or OpenTelemetry instrumentation.

Follow-up: which of the three would you use to find why p99 latency rose for one customer? — Traces (filtered to that customer) to see which span grew, then logs for the slow spans; the metric only told you that it rose.
E
How does a CloudWatch alarm decide to fire?

Every period (say 60 seconds) the metric is aggregated into one data point with a statistic (average, p99, sum). The alarm looks at the last N data points (evaluation periods) and goes to ALARM if at least M of them (datapoints to alarm) breach the threshold, then performs its actions — an SNS notification, an autoscaling policy, a Systems Manager action. Periods without data are handled by the missing-data setting. Actions run on state changes, not continuously.

Follow-up: why use 3 out of 5 rather than 1 out of 1? — To avoid paging on single noisy data points while still catching sustained problems quickly; it trades a little detection time for far fewer false alarms.
E
What does CloudTrail record, and how would you set it up for an organisation?

CloudTrail records API calls — who (principal, session, source identity), what (event name and parameters), when, from where (IP, VPC endpoint, user agent) and the result. The 90-day event history of management events is free in every account. For an organisation, create an organisation trail from the management or delegated admin account covering all accounts and regions, deliver to an S3 bucket in a dedicated log-archive account with Object Lock and a restrictive bucket policy, enable log file integrity validation, and enable data events selectively for sensitive buckets and functions.
Follow-up: why a separate account? — An attacker who compromises a workload account can't delete or alter the logs that record what they did.
M
How do dimensions drive CloudWatch cost, and how do you design metrics to control it?

Each unique dimension combination is a separate metric billed per month: in us-east-1 in October 2026, $0.30 per metric for the first 10,000, then $0.10. A latency metric by service, 40 endpoints, 5 status classes and 30 instance IDs is 6,000 metrics, about $1,800 a month; dropping instance ID leaves 200 metrics, $60. Design dimensions for questions you alarm and graph on (service, endpoint, status, zone), keep unbounded values (user IDs, request IDs, instance IDs in autoscaled fleets) out, and put them in logs or traces. Autoscaling makes this worse because every new instance ID creates new metrics that persist for 15 months.

Follow-up: how do you still investigate one bad instance? — Use the provider's per-instance metrics, which are free, or query logs with the instance ID as a field; aggregate custom metrics at the service level.
M
How should alarms treat missing data, and why does it matter?

Missing data means the metric didn't arrive for a period: the service may be idle, or dead, or the agent broke. Options are to treat it as breaching (good for heartbeats and 'should always have traffic' metrics), not breaching (good for error counts that are naturally absent when there are no errors), ignore it (keep the current state), or missing (alarm goes to INSUFFICIENT_DATA once there's not enough data). The trap is error-rate alarms that treat missing as not breaching on a service that stopped emitting: everything looks green while nothing works. Pair such alarms with a heartbeat or request-count alarm that treats missing as breaching.

Follow-up: what's a heartbeat alarm for a batch job? — A metric the job emits on success, with an alarm whose evaluation window is slightly longer than the schedule and missing data treated as breaching.
M
What would you include in on-call for a service running on AWS?

SLO-based alerts on user-facing symptoms (error rate and latency burn rates, sc13) rather than every resource metric; per-zone and per-region breakdowns so you can tell a zone problem from a deploy; synthetic canaries from outside the region; AWS Health events for your account routed via EventBridge to the on-call channel; runbooks that cover provider degradation (zonal shift, failover, feature flags to shed load); access that works when SSO or the console is impaired; and a clear path to open a support case with the right severity and evidence. After incidents, post-mortems that separate provider causes from your own design choices.

Follow-up: how do you decide whether it's you or the provider? — Check whether errors are concentrated in one zone or one service dependency, whether they started with your last deploy, and whether Health events or other teams see the same; your per-dimension metrics answer faster than the status page.
M
How do traces work across a serverless and queue-based system?

Each request gets a trace ID at the edge (API Gateway or the load balancer, or the first instrumented service). Every service creates spans for its work and propagates the trace context in outgoing calls — HTTP headers (W3C traceparent or X-Ray's header), and message attributes for SQS, SNS and EventBridge so consumers continue the same trace. The tracing backend (X-Ray, which now accepts OpenTelemetry data, or a vendor) assembles spans into a trace and service map. Sampling keeps cost down: head sampling decides at the start; tail sampling keeps slow or failed traces after seeing them, which needs a collector that buffers spans.

Follow-up: what breaks traces most often? — A hop that doesn't propagate context: a queue consumer that starts a new trace, a library without instrumentation, or a batch that mixes messages from many traces.
M
What is AWS Config for, compared with CloudTrail?

CloudTrail answers 'who did what, when' — API calls. Config answers 'what did this resource look like at time T, and what changed' — it records configuration items for resources (a security group's rules, a bucket's policy) over time, with relationships, and evaluates them against rules (managed or custom) such as 'S3 buckets must block public access' or 'EBS volumes must be encrypted', with optional automatic remediation. Together they reconstruct incidents: Config shows the security group became open at 14:02, CloudTrail shows which role called AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress.

Follow-up: what does Config cost you to watch out for? — It bills per configuration item recorded; resources that change constantly (autoscaling instances, network interfaces) can generate large bills, so scope recording or use periodic recording for noisy types.
H
Estimate the monthly observability bill for a service and show where to cut it.

A service on 30 instances handles 200 requests per second and logs one 1 KB line per request: 200 × 2.628 million seconds ≈ 526 million lines ≈ 500 GB a month. In us-east-1 (October 2026): Standard log ingestion at $0.50/GB ≈ $250, storage at $0.03/GB-month growing with retention, Logs Insights at $0.005 per GB scanned (200 queries over 20 GB ≈ $20). Custom latency metrics with instance ID as a dimension: 6,000 metrics ≈ $1,800; without it ≈ $60. Fifty standard alarms at $0.10 ≈ $5. CloudTrail data events on a bucket with 50 million GETs ≈ $50. Cuts: remove high-cardinality dimensions, sample or downgrade debug logs, use the Infrequent Access log class ($0.25/GB) for logs you rarely query, set retention, and query narrower time ranges.
Follow-up: which number grows fastest as the business grows? — Log ingestion, linearly with traffic; metrics grow with cardinality, which grows with fleet churn if instance IDs leak into dimensions.
H
Walk through Datadog's March 2023 outage and what it means for your monitoring design.

On 8 March 2023 at 06:00 UTC, a security update to systemd was applied automatically through a legacy unattended-upgrade channel on Datadog's Ubuntu hosts. Restarting systemd-networkd removed routes managed by Cilium, Datadog's container networking, taking nodes offline. The OS default window for automatic installation was 06:00–07:00 UTC, so it hit tens of thousands of nodes across five Datadog regions on three cloud providers at nearly the same time, despite those regions being architecturally independent. Customers lost the web UI, monitors weren't evaluating or alerting, and ingestion was disrupted; web access returned at 09:13 UTC, services came back over the following day, and backfill completed on 10 March. Datadog disabled the legacy channel, configured systemd-networkd to preserve routes and audited for similar risks. For you: your monitoring vendor is a dependency that can fail while you need it; keep a minimal set of critical alarms on an independent path (provider-native alarms or a second service) and synthetic checks that page through a different route.

Follow-up: what's the general lesson about 'independent' regions? — Shared configuration and shared timing (an OS default window, a global config push, a certificate expiry) correlate failures across regions and even clouds; stagger changes and audit for common modes.
H
An S3 bucket of customer exports may have been accessed by a leaked key. How do you investigate with cloud telemetry?

Identify the key's principal (IAM user or role) and its activity window from CloudTrail management events in all regions: GetCallerIdentity calls, ListBuckets, policy or key changes, new users or roles created (persistence). Object-level reads appear only if S3 data events were enabled for that bucket; if they were, query them (CloudTrail Lake or Athena over the trail's S3 logs) for GetObject by that principal and list the keys read. If not, S3 server access logs (if enabled) are the fallback; otherwise you can't say what was read and must treat the bucket as exposed. Check source IPs and VPC endpoint IDs to see whether the calls came from outside your network, and Config history for policy changes. Then contain: deactivate the key, revoke sessions, rotate, and enable data events going forward.

Follow-up: why do teams leave data events off? — Cost: they're billed per event ($0.10 per 100,000 in October 2026), so a bucket with billions of reads is expensive to log fully; enable them at least for buckets holding sensitive data.
H
How would you design observability so it still works during a regional outage?

Separate the alerting path from the region and services it watches: synthetic canaries running in another region (or another provider) hitting user-facing endpoints, a small set of critical alarms evaluated outside the primary region, paging through a service that doesn't depend on the primary region, and dashboards that can read cross-region. Buffer telemetry at the source so a degraded collector doesn't block applications. Keep runbooks and break-glass credentials accessible without the region's SSO. Recognise that CloudWatch in a region shares fate with that region (the 2020 Kinesis event degraded CloudWatch in us-east-1) and that a third-party vendor shares fate with its own infrastructure. Test it in game days by blocking the primary region's monitoring and checking the pages still arrive.

Follow-up: what's the cheapest piece with the biggest payoff? — External synthetic checks of the main user journeys, paging through an independent route; they detect almost every user-visible outage regardless of what else failed.

t: Cost and FinOps: pricing models (on-demand, reserved, savings plans, spot), hidden costs (egress, NAT, cross-AZ, idle), tagging and allocation, and a cost estimate for a real architecture
sum: How cloud bills are built and controlled: the pricing models and their break-even utilisations worked from the October 2026 price files, how commitments are sized from an hourly usage curve, the costs that hide in egress, NAT, cross-zone traffic, public IPv4, idle and forgotten resources, tagging, accounts and the cost-and-usage data used to allocate spend and compute unit costs, the FinOps operating loop, and a line-by-line monthly bill for a small production web app — with 37signals' cloud exit as the case for when renting stops making sense.
prereq: cl3
Every network path has a per-GB price: free in a zone, $0.01 out plus $0.01 in across zones, NAT and Transit Gateway processing, $0.09/GB internet egress after the first 100 GB a month.
cl4
On-demand, commitment and spot are three ways to buy the same capacity; fleets are sized from CPU per request, utilisation targets and zone headroom.
cl6
Storage classes trade price per GB for minimum durations, minimum object sizes, retrieval and transition fees; requests are billed separately.
ae2
LLM bills are built from tokens times prices with caching, batching and routing as levers; the same unit-economics thinking applies to cloud infrastructure.
why:
A startup's AWS bill is $9,000 in January and $31,000 in June. Nobody can say why. The finance lead asks engineering; engineering points at the growth in users; the CEO notices users only doubled. When someone finally opens the detailed billing data they find: a staging environment with production-sized instances running 24/7 since February; $4,100 a month of NAT gateway processing from a data pipeline reading S3 through NAT; $2,300 of cross-zone traffic from a Kafka cluster whose consumers ignore zones; 38 TB of debug logs kept forever; an expired three-year reservation that nobody renewed, so the database fleet quietly moved to on-demand rates; and a GPU instance someone launched for an experiment in March and forgot.

None of these needed clever optimisation. They needed someone to see the bill in a form engineers understand, to know which team owned each line, and to understand how cloud prices work: what's billed per hour versus per gigabyte versus per request, which data paths cost money, and what commitments do. The cloud's pricing model is the source of its flexibility — pay only for what you use — and, without discipline, the reason bills grow faster than businesses.

The track has priced components along the way: network paths in cl3, compute options in cl4, functions in cl5, storage classes in cl6, databases in cl7, messaging in cl8, DR in cl10, observability in cl11. This lesson pulls them together into how bills are structured and managed: the purchasing models and how to size commitments, the hidden costs, tagging and allocation, the billing data and tools, the FinOps practice that makes engineers accountable, and a complete monthly estimate for a small production web app with every price taken from AWS's price files on 7 October 2026. The case is 37signals, whose move off AWS is the best-documented example of when renting stops being the cheap option.
primer:
Think about running a cloud estate like running a fleet of rental cars for a company.

Every car is billed by the hour, but there's more on the invoice: fuel by the litre, tolls on certain roads, a parking fee for every car whether it moves or not, a charge every time a car leaves the city, a fee for each extra key. Drivers choose routes and cars; finance pays the invoice a month later. If drivers never see the invoice, nobody notices the car that's been parked at an airport since February, the delivery van taking the toll road every trip when a free road runs parallel, or the luxury saloon booked for errands. And you can negotiate: book a car for a year and the hourly rate drops by a third — worth it for the car that's out every day, wasteful for the one used on Fridays.

The cloud equivalents. Hourly rates are instance-hours, database-hours, load balancer-hours. Fuel and tolls are usage charges: gigabytes stored, requests made, and above all bytes moved across billed boundaries — out to the internet, between regions, between zones, through NAT gateways. Parking fees are things billed just for existing: public IP addresses, unattached volumes, idle load balancers, snapshots. Year-long bookings are commitments: Savings Plans and reserved instances. Standby cars at a steep discount that can be recalled are spot capacity.

Two levers control every bill. Usage is decided by architecture and operations: which instance types, how many, how traffic flows, what's kept and for how long. Rate is decided by purchasing: on-demand, commitments, spot, negotiated discounts. Engineers own the first and should influence the second. The discipline that makes both happen continuously — visibility per team, ownership, unit costs, budgets and alerts — is called FinOps.

The order in which to pull the levers matters. Purchasing discounts are tempting because they need no engineering work, but committing to waste locks the waste in for a year or three. The usual sequence is: first make costs visible and owned; then remove what shouldn't exist (idle, orphaned, over-retained); then fix architecture that moves or stores more than it needs; then rightsize what remains; and only then commit to the steady baseline that's left. Each step makes the next one more accurate, and the final commitment covers a smaller, cleaner footprint.

Where the analogy breaks: a fleet manager can see every car on a map. In the cloud, resources multiply silently through automation — autoscaling, IaC, CI pipelines, experiments — across many accounts and regions, and a single line of code can create a cost that runs for years. Visibility has to be designed in, through account structure, tags and billing data, because nobody can see it by looking around.
body:
1. How a cloud bill is built

Every line on a cloud bill is a rate times a quantity, identified by a usage type. In AWS's Cost and Usage Report you'll see lines like BoxUsage:m7g.large (instance-hours), EBS:VolumeUsage.gp3 (GB-months), DataTransfer-Out-Bytes (GB to the internet), DataTransfer-Regional-Bytes (cross-zone GB), NatGateway-Hours and NatGateway-Bytes, Requests-Tier1 (S3 PUTs), TimedStorage-ByteHrs (S3 storage). The units fall into a few families:

  • Capacity-time: instance-, node-, database- and load-balancer-hours (per second for many), provisioned IOPS-months, DynamoDB provisioned capacity-hours. Billed whether used or not.
  • Storage-time: GB-months of volumes, objects, snapshots, logs, backups. Billed for what's kept.
  • Requests: per million API calls, events, messages, function invocations; per GB-second for functions.
  • Data movement: per GB out to the internet, between regions, between zones, through NAT, Transit Gateway or endpoints.
  • Existence fees: public IPv4 addresses ($0.005 an hour each, about $3.65 a month, in October 2026), KMS keys ($1 a month each), secrets ($0.40 a month each), hosted zones.
  • Percentages: support plans billed as a percentage of spend; marketplace software.

Because the pricing model is granular, an architecture's cost is predictable if you can estimate its usage — which is what every worked example in this track has done. It's also why cost surprises are almost always usage surprises: something running, moving or storing more than anyone thought.

2. Purchasing models and their break-even arithmetic

The same capacity can be bought several ways. Rates below are from AWS's EC2 and Savings Plans price files for us-east-1, fetched 7 October 2026, for an m7g.large (2 vCPUs, 8 GiB, Linux):

Option$/hourDiscount vs on-demandBreak-even utilisationFlexibility
On-demand0.0816——any time
Compute Savings Plan, 1 yr, no upfront0.059927%73%any family, size, region; also Fargate and Lambda
EC2 Instance Savings Plan, 1 yr, no upfront0.054034%66%one family in one region, any size
Compute Savings Plan, 3 yr, no upfront0.041449%51%as above, three years
EC2 Instance Savings Plan, 3 yr, no upfront0.037055%45%as above, three years
Spotvaries by poolup to 90% (AWS)—interruptible with 2 minutes' notice

AWS's own maximums are "up to 66%" for Compute Savings Plans and "up to 72%" for EC2 Instance Savings Plans across all instance types and terms; the m7g.large figures show typical values. The break-even utilisation is the committed rate divided by on-demand: an EC2 Instance Savings Plan at $0.054 pays off if, without it, you'd have run that capacity at least 66% of the hours. Savings Plans are commitments of dollars per hour, not instances: a plan of $2.16 an hour covers 40 m7g.large instances at the plan rate, or a mix of eligible usage, and any usage beyond it is on demand.

The same pattern applies elsewhere. Compute Savings Plans also discount Fargate (Arm vCPU-hour $0.0255 on a one-year plan against $0.03238 on demand, 21% off) and Lambda (Arm GB-second $0.0000117 against $0.0000133334, 12% off). Databases use reserved DB instances: a db.t4g.medium PostgreSQL Multi-AZ instance was $0.129 an hour on demand and $0.093 on a one-year no-upfront reservation (28% off), or $758 paid upfront for the year (about $0.087 an hour, 33% off). GPU instances show the largest absolute stakes: a p5.48xlarge was $55.04 an hour on demand, $34.68 on a one-year EC2 Instance Savings Plan and $23.78 on three years (cl14).

Sizing commitments. Plot hourly eligible usage over the last few months. The floor — the level usage rarely drops below — is safe to commit to: every committed hour gets used. Above the floor, each extra committed unit is used only in the hours when demand reaches it; it's worth buying only if that's more than the break-even fraction of hours.

Two operating habits keep commitments healthy: laddering (buying in tranches every month or quarter so they expire gradually and track growth), and monitoring utilisation (how much of what you bought is used — below 95% means you over-committed) and coverage (how much eligible usage is covered — low coverage on steady workloads means money left on the table). An expired commitment silently reverts usage to on-demand rates; renewal is a calendar event someone must own.

3. The hidden costs

The lines that surprise teams, with October 2026 us-east-1 prices from earlier lessons:

CostRateHow it hidesFix
Internet egress$0.09/GB after 100 GB free, falling to $0.05 above 150 TBgrows with users and API payload sizeCDN, compression, smaller payloads
Cross-zone traffic$0.01/GB each wayload balancers, replicas and clients in different zoneszone-aware routing (cl3)
NAT gateway$0.045/hour + $0.045/GBS3, DynamoDB, ECR pulls going through NATgateway and interface endpoints
Inter-region$0.02/GB (us-east-1 → us-west-2)replication, cross-region callsreplicate only what DR needs
Public IPv4$0.005/hour eachevery instance, load balancer node and NAT with a public addressprivate subnets, fewer public endpoints, IPv6
Idle resourcesfull pricedev environments at night, unattached volumes, idle databasesschedules, clean-up automation
Storage accretionper GB-monthsnapshots, versions, logs and backups kept foreverlifecycle rules, retention policies
Request volumeper million callschatty S3 access, KMS without bucket keys, unbatched queuesbatching, caching, packing (cl6, cl8)
Observabilityper GB and per metricdebug logs, high-cardinality metricssampling, dimensions, retention (cl11)

Scheduling non-production environments is the simplest large win: running dev and staging 12 hours on weekdays instead of 24×7 uses 60 of 168 hours, cutting their compute by about 64%.

4. Tagging, accounts and allocation

To manage costs you must attribute them to owners. Two mechanisms do this.

Accounts are the strongest boundary. Everything in an account is billed to it, including untaggable charges like data transfer and support. An account structure of one account per team or product per environment (cl13) makes most allocation automatic.

Tags refine it: key/value pairs on resources such as team=checkout, service=orders-api, env=prod, cost-center=4120. For tags to appear in billing data, user-defined keys must be activated as cost allocation tags in the billing console, and they apply only from activation onward — a common reason teams can't explain last quarter. Enforcement keeps them consistent: tag policies in AWS Organizations standardise keys and allowed values; IaC policy checks (cl9) reject untagged resources; Config rules find stragglers.

Shared costs need explicit rules. A shared Kubernetes cluster's nodes are allocated by each namespace's requested CPU and memory over time (AWS's split cost allocation data puts this into the CUR for EKS and ECS); NAT gateways and Transit Gateways by bytes per account or a fixed share; support plans and enterprise discounts proportionally to spend. The rule matters less than its being written down and stable, so teams can reason about their numbers.

Allocation enables two practices: showback, where teams see their costs, and chargeback, where their budgets pay for them. Showback is usually where to start; chargeback changes behaviour faster but needs trusted data.

5. Billing data and tools

The source of truth is the Cost and Usage Report (CUR), delivered through AWS Data Exports to an S3 bucket: hourly or daily line items with account, service, usage type, operation, resource ID, tags, rates, amortised and net costs, and commitment details. Data Exports can also produce the FOCUS format, the FinOps Foundation's open specification for billing data, so the same queries work across providers; the FOCUS site lists 1.4 as the current version in October 2026, with AWS, Azure and Google Cloud among providers generating FOCUS data. Teams load the CUR into Athena or a warehouse and build dashboards on it.

On top sit the native tools: Cost Explorer for interactive breakdowns and commitment recommendations; Budgets for alerts when actual or forecast spend crosses a threshold per account, tag or service, with optional actions; Cost Anomaly Detection, which learns spend patterns per service or account and alerts on unusual increases; and Compute Optimizer for rightsizing recommendations from utilisation. A typical CUR query to find the top cost growths by usage type between two months:

SELECT line_item_usage_type,
       SUM(CASE WHEN month = '2026-08' THEN line_item_unblended_cost END) AS aug,
       SUM(CASE WHEN month = '2026-09' THEN line_item_unblended_cost END) AS sep
FROM cur
GROUP BY line_item_usage_type
ORDER BY sep - aug DESC
LIMIT 15;

6. A small production web app, priced line by line

The architecture: a web application on two m7g.large instances in two availability zones behind an internet-facing Application Load Balancer; an RDS PostgreSQL db.t4g.medium database in Multi-AZ mode with 100 GB of gp3 storage; private subnets with one NAT gateway per zone; 500 GB a month of responses to users over the internet; 200 GB a month of outbound calls through NAT (package updates, third-party APIs, S3 without an endpoint); 100 GB in S3; 20 GB of logs a month; one Route 53 hosted zone with 10 million queries. All prices are us-east-1 from the AWS price list and pricing pages on 7 October 2026, for a 730-hour month, before taxes and free-tier credits.

LineCalculationMonthly
EC2 instances2 × $0.0816 × 730$119.14
EBS gp3 root volumes2 × 30 GB × $0.08$4.80
Application Load Balancer$0.0225 × 730 + ~1 LCU × $0.008 × 730$22.27
ALB public IPv4 (one per zone)2 × $0.005 × 730$7.30
RDS db.t4g.medium Multi-AZ$0.129 × 730$94.17
RDS gp3 storage, Multi-AZ100 GB × $0.23$23.00
NAT gateway hours2 × $0.045 × 730$65.70
NAT data processing200 GB × $0.045$9.00
NAT Elastic IPs2 × $0.005 × 730$7.30
Internet egress(500 − 100 free) GB × $0.09$36.00
S3 Standard100 GB × $0.023$2.30
CloudWatch Logs(20 − 5 free) GB × $0.50 + 20 GB × $0.03$8.10
