Total≈ $403.58

Read it as an engineer. Compute and database are about 59% — expected. The NAT gateways, their processing and their addresses cost $82, about 20% — more than twice the internet egress — and they exist so two instances can make outbound calls. Public IPv4 addresses alone are $14.60. Options, with their trade-offs:

  • Commitments: a one-year Compute Savings Plan on the two instances saves 2 × ($0.0816 − $0.0599) × 730 ≈ $31.68 a month; a one-year no-upfront reserved DB instance saves ($0.129 − $0.093) × 730 ≈ $26.28. Together about $58, 14% of the bill, with no architectural change, if the app will run all year.
  • NAT: a gateway endpoint for S3 removes that share of NAT processing for free; one NAT gateway instead of two saves $36.50 a month but loses outbound access if its zone fails (cl3) — acceptable for some apps, not others. The regional NAT gateway mode bills per zone it's active in, so it doesn't save the hourly charge.
  • Egress: a CDN in front of static assets reduces origin egress and often costs less per GB at volume.
  • Database: Multi-AZ doubles the instance and storage price; it's the price of minutes rather than hours of recovery after a zone failure (cl7, cl10). Keep it for production; drop it in staging.

The same app on serverless (Lambda, API Gateway, DynamoDB on-demand) might cost less than $50 a month at low traffic and more at high traffic (cl5); on a single instance with a local database, under $50, with no zone resilience. Cost estimates are most useful exactly like this: as a comparison between designs with explicit trade-offs.

7. The FinOps loop

The FinOps Foundation describes the practice as a cycle of three phases, run continuously:

  1. Inform: allocate costs to owners, publish dashboards per team with daily spend, trends and unit costs, forecast, and benchmark.
  2. Optimise: rightsize, schedule, remove idle resources, fix architectural waste (data movement, storage retention), buy and manage commitments, use spot where safe.
  3. Operate: budgets and anomaly alerts routed to owners, cost reviews in architecture and launch processes, policies that enforce tags and prevent expensive mistakes, and regular reporting of unit costs to leadership.

The organisational shape that works: a small central team owning tooling, data, commitments and negotiations, and engineering teams owning their own usage and responding to their own anomalies. The metric to watch isn't total spend — that should grow with the business — but unit cost: dollars per thousand requests, per active customer, per inference, per training run.
deep:
Why cloud prices are shaped the way they are

Prices reflect the provider's cost structure and incentives. Ingress is free because it fills network capacity that's otherwise idle and brings data (and workloads) in; egress is charged because it consumes transit and makes leaving costly. Cross-zone traffic is charged because it crosses metro fibre between buildings. Commitment discounts exist because predictable demand lets the provider plan capacity and lowers its cost of capital. Spot is cheap because unsold capacity earns nothing. Reading prices this way predicts which designs will be cheap — stay in a zone, keep data where compute is, commit to the predictable, flex on spot — and which will be expensive.

Commitments are a financial instrument, managed like a portfolio

A portfolio of Savings Plans and reservations has terms, exposure and risk. Over-commitment is a loss you can't undo (unused hours are gone; some reserved instances can be sold on a marketplace, Savings Plans can't). Under-commitment is a smaller, recoverable loss. The trade between one- and three-year terms is a bet on stability: three years nearly halves the rate for m7g but locks in architecture and region assumptions. Mature teams buy in tranches, keep a target coverage (say 70–80% of steady usage) rather than 100%, prefer flexible instruments when change is likely (Graviton migrations, containerisation, region moves), and track utilisation and coverage monthly like any other financial position.

Unit economics connect engineering to the business model

A rising bill is good news if revenue rises faster; a flat bill is bad news if usage collapsed. Unit costs make the comparison: cost per thousand API requests, per customer per month, per gigabyte processed, per model inference. They also expose architecture decisions: a feature whose unit cost is above its revenue per unit is a problem regardless of the total. For AI products, where GPU and model-API costs scale with usage (ae2, cl14), unit economics often determine pricing, rate limits and which model serves which customers.

Discounts beyond list prices

Large customers rarely pay list price for everything. Enterprise agreements trade spend commitments over years for percentage discounts across services; private pricing exists for specific high-volume services such as data transfer; credits come with migrations and startup programmes. These change the economics of build-versus-buy and of multi-cloud. They also create lock-in in the other direction: a spend commitment to one provider makes moving workloads elsewhere financially painful until it ends — as 37signals' four-year S3 commitment kept its storage in AWS long after compute had left.

The real comparison with owning hardware

On-premises or colocation costs include hardware amortised over three to six years, data-centre space, power and cooling, network transit, spares, staff time for procurement, installation, repair and refresh, and the capital tied up. The cloud's price includes all of that plus managed services, elasticity, global reach and speed. For a steady, predictable workload running all year at high utilisation, the hardware path often wins by a large factor, as 37signals' numbers show; for variable, growing or experimental workloads, or for teams that rely on managed services, the cloud usually wins once staff costs are counted. The honest analysis models both, including the transition cost and the value of options you give up.

Forecasting is a modelling problem, not an extrapolation

Next quarter's bill is driven by business drivers — users, requests, data ingested, models trained — multiplied by unit costs, plus planned changes (a new region, a migration, a commitment expiring). Straight-line extrapolation of last quarter's total misses all of them. A driver-based forecast (requests per month × cost per thousand requests, terabytes ingested × storage and processing cost per terabyte) is both more accurate and more useful, because when it's wrong it tells you which driver or unit cost moved. It also turns capacity and commitment planning into the same exercise: the forecast floor is what you commit to.

Cost is a non-functional requirement with trade-offs against the others

Many cost optimisations trade against reliability or latency: one NAT gateway instead of three, single-AZ databases, spot for serving, aggressive scale-in, cold storage tiers. Each is a legitimate choice for some systems and an outage waiting to happen for others. Senior engineers make the trade explicit — what reliability does this buy, at what price per month — and record it, rather than letting cost cutting and resilience work undo each other in alternating quarters.
prod:
Failure modes and their symptoms

Runaway resources. A loop in automation creates instances, a misconfigured autoscaler scales to its maximum, a forgotten GPU instance runs for months. Symptoms: a step change in daily cost for one usage type. Detection: Cost Anomaly Detection, daily per-account dashboards, budgets with forecast alerts.

Expired commitments. Same usage, higher bill, starting on an anniversary date. Track expiry dates and coverage; set calendar ownership.

Unowned spend. Untagged resources in shared accounts; nobody responds to anomalies. Enforce tagging in IaC, use accounts per team, and assign every account an owner.

Data movement creep. A new feature makes cross-region calls or streams data out; DataTransfer lines climb steadily. Review data flows in design reviews; alert on transfer usage types.

Storage accretion. Logs with no retention, snapshots without lifecycle, versioned buckets without noncurrent expiry. Default retention policies in IaC modules.

Optimisations that break things. A scheduler stops a "dev" database that production depended on; a cost cut removes the zone redundancy that would have prevented next month's outage. Tag criticality, notify before deleting, and review cost changes like other changes.

What to measure

Daily spend by account, team and service; unit costs; commitment utilisation and coverage; percentage of spend allocated to an owner; top idle resources and their cost; anomaly count and time to resolve; spend on data transfer by usage type; forecast versus budget.

The case: 37signals leaves the cloud

37signals, the company behind Basecamp and HEY, published its reasoning and numbers as it moved off AWS. In an October 2024 post, its co-owner and CTO David Heinemeier Hansson reported that seven cloud applications, including HEY, had been moved from AWS to the company's own hardware the previous summer. The cloud bill had fallen from a run rate of $3.2 million a year to $1.3 million. The new Dell hardware cost about $700,000 and was, he wrote, entirely recouped during 2023 as long-term cloud commitments rolled off, and the team managing everything was the same size — no additional hires were needed. The original estimate of $7 million saved over five years had risen to well over $10 million.

The remaining $1.3 million was S3. The post explains that while compute and managed database and search services had been on one-year commitments, file storage was locked into a four-year contract from 2021 that ran until summer 2025 — "still well over a million dollars" a year even after the commitment discounts — for almost 10 petabytes of data, much of it stored in duplicate across regions. The plan was to move to a dual-data-centre Pure Storage setup with 18 petabytes of capacity, costing about one year of S3 fees for the initial hardware and fitting in the company's existing racks and power. AWS's policy, announced in March 2024, of waiving data-transfer-out charges for customers leaving AWS entirely (on request, now with 90 days to complete the move) removed what would otherwise have been a large egress bill for the migration.

What makes the case useful is that it's specific. 37signals' workloads are steady and predictable, the company had operations skills and existing data-centre space, and it didn't depend heavily on managed services it would have to rebuild. Under those conditions, buying hardware once and running it for years beat renting the same capacity by a wide margin. Most teams don't share all of those conditions; the transferable lesson is the method — know your steady baseline, know what you pay per unit of it, know what your commitments lock in and when, and decide with numbers.
myths: Reserved capacity always saves money.

A commitment is a promise to pay for a level of usage whether or not you use it. A one-year, no-upfront EC2 Instance Savings Plan for an m7g.large cost $0.054 an hour against $0.0816 on demand in us-east-1 (October 2026) — cheaper only if the instance would otherwise run more than about 66% of the hours. Commit to the floor of your usage, not the average or the peak, or you pay for idle commitment.
The biggest line on the bill is compute, so that's where to optimise.

Often, but the fastest savings are usually in lines nobody owns: NAT gateways processing traffic that should use free endpoints, cross-zone chatter, idle load balancers and unattached volumes, snapshots and logs kept forever, public IPv4 addresses, and data transfer. In the small web app worked in this lesson, NAT gateways and their addresses were about a fifth of the bill.
Tagging everything solves cost allocation.

Tags only allocate what can be tagged, only after the tag is activated for cost allocation (and only from then on), and only if they're applied consistently. Shared costs — NAT gateways, Transit Gateways, support plans, data transfer, a shared cluster — need an explicit split rule. Accounts per team or product give cleaner allocation than tags, and enforcement (tag policies, IaC checks) matters more than the tagging scheme.
Spot is free money.

Spot prices are low because capacity can be reclaimed with two minutes' notice. Workloads that can't checkpoint, drain or retry pay in failed jobs, wasted partial work and engineering time. Spot saves money for diversified, interruption-tolerant fleets; for others it's an outage generator.
The cloud is always cheaper than owning hardware.

The cloud is cheaper when it converts fixed costs to variable ones you actually vary, or buys you speed and managed services you'd otherwise build. For large, steady, predictable workloads with in-house operations skills, owning or leasing hardware can be much cheaper: 37signals reported cutting its annual cloud bill from $3.2 million to $1.3 million with about $700,000 of hardware, recouped within the year, before moving storage too.
FinOps is the finance team's job.

Finance can report the bill; only engineers can change it, because architecture, instance choice, scaling and data movement decide cost. FinOps works when engineering teams see their own spend and unit costs in near real time, own budgets and anomalies, and treat cost as a non-functional requirement alongside latency and reliability.
lab:
Goal: build a cloud cost calculator and a commitment optimiser in Python 3.12 (standard library only), and reproduce the lesson's numbers. About 20 minutes; no cloud account needed.

  1. Price book. A dict of the October 2026 us-east-1 rates used in this lesson (EC2, Savings Plans, RDS on-demand and reserved, ALB, NAT, IPv4, egress tiers, S3, logs, Route 53). Mark each with its source and date.
  2. Bill. Write bill(architecture) where the architecture is a dict of quantities (instances, GB, hours, requests) and return line items and a total. Reproduce section 6's table to the cent.
  3. Egress tiers. Implement the tiered internet egress (100 GB free; $0.09 to 10 TB; $0.085 to 50 TB; $0.07 to 150 TB; $0.05 beyond) and price 1 TB, 60 TB and 500 TB a month.
  4. Commitment optimiser. Generate 60 days of hourly demand between 40 and 100 instances with a daily cycle. For commitments from 0 to 100 instances, compute monthly cost = commitment × plan rate × 730 + on-demand for usage above it. Find the minimum for the 1-year EC2 Instance plan ($0.054) and the Compute plan ($0.0599).
  5. Break-even. For each plan, compute rate ÷ on-demand and check that the optimal commitment level is where demand exceeds that level for about that share of hours.
  6. Schedules. Price a dev environment (the same app without Multi-AZ) running 24×7 versus 12 hours on weekdays.

What to look for: step 2 gives ≈ $403.58 with NAT ≈ $82 (20%); step 3 shows the falling marginal rate; step 4 finds an optimum near the level demand exceeds about two-thirds of the time for the EC2 Instance plan and slightly lower for the Compute plan — more commitment above that costs more than it saves; step 6 shows about a 64% saving on compute from a simple schedule.

Needs an AWS account (optional): aws ce get-cost-and-usage --time-period Start=2026-09-01,End=2026-10-01 --granularity MONTHLY --metrics UnblendedCost --group-by Type=DIMENSION,Key=USAGE_TYPE lists last month's cost by usage type — the first place to look for NAT, transfer and idle surprises.
recap: A cloud bill is a sum of rates times usage: instance-hours, GB-months, requests, GB transferred, units of capacity; architecture decides the usage and purchasing decides the rates.

On-demand has no commitment; Savings Plans and reserved instances trade a one- or three-year commitment for discounts (Compute Savings Plans up to 66%, EC2 Instance Savings Plans up to 72% per AWS); spot gives up to 90% off for interruptible capacity.

A commitment pays off when expected utilisation exceeds its price ratio to on-demand — about 66% for a one-year EC2 Instance Savings Plan on an m7g.large in October 2026 — so commitments should cover the steady floor of an hourly usage curve.

Hidden costs live in data movement (internet egress, cross-zone traffic, NAT and Transit Gateway processing, inter-region replication), public IPv4 addresses, idle and orphaned resources, over-retained storage and logs, and request-priced services at high volume.
Allocation needs structure: an account per team or environment, consistent tags activated as cost allocation tags, tag policies and IaC checks, and explicit rules for splitting shared costs.
The Cost and Usage Report (via AWS Data Exports, also in the FOCUS format) is the source of truth; Cost Explorer, Budgets and Cost Anomaly Detection sit on top of it.
Unit economics — cost per request, per customer, per training run — connects spend to the business and shows whether efficiency is improving as you grow.
FinOps runs a loop: inform (visibility and allocation), optimise (rightsizing, commitments, architecture), operate (budgets, anomaly response, accountability), with engineers owning the decisions.
A small production web app in us-east-1 cost about $400 a month in this lesson's estimate, with NAT about 20% and commitments able to cut compute and database costs by roughly a quarter to a third.

Repatriation can win for large, steady workloads with operations skills, as 37signals showed; the cloud's value is elasticity, managed services and speed, which you should be using if you're paying for them.
glossary: Amortised cost
Spreading upfront commitment payments evenly over the commitment term so monthly costs reflect actual usage periods.
Blended / unblended cost
Unblended is each line at its actual rate; blended averages rates across an organisation; amortised spreads commitments.
Break-even utilisation
The fraction of hours a resource must run for a commitment to cost less than on-demand: commitment rate ÷ on-demand rate.
CDN (content delivery network)
Edge caches near users that serve content and reduce origin egress (net12).
Chargeback / showback
Billing teams for the cloud costs they generate (chargeback) or just showing them (showback).
Commitment coverage
The share of eligible usage paid at commitment rates rather than on-demand.
Commitment utilisation
The share of a purchased commitment actually used; unused commitment is pure waste.
Cost allocation tag
A resource tag activated in billing so that costs can be grouped by its values; applies only from activation onward.
Cost and Usage Report (CUR)
AWS's most detailed billing dataset, hourly or daily line items for every resource and charge, delivered to S3 through Data Exports.
Cost Anomaly Detection
An AWS service that learns spending patterns and alerts on unexpected increases.
Data movement
Billed transfer of bytes across boundaries: to the internet, between regions or zones, or through NAT, Transit Gateway and endpoints.
Egress
Data leaving a provider's network (to the internet) or a region; usually billed per GB, while ingress is usually free.
FinOps
The practice of managing cloud costs through collaboration between engineering, finance and business, with engineers accountable for usage.
FOCUS
The FinOps Open Cost and Usage Specification, an open standard format for billing data across clouds and SaaS (version 1.4 current in October 2026).
Idle resource
Something billed but doing no useful work: stopped-but-allocated volumes, unused load balancers, idle databases, unattached IP addresses.
LCU (load balancer capacity unit)
The usage measure Application Load Balancers are billed by, based on the largest of new connections, active connections, bytes processed and rule evaluations.
NAT gateway
The managed service that lets private-subnet resources reach the internet, billed per hour and per GB processed (cl3).
On-demand
Paying list price per second or hour with no commitment.
Reserved instance (RI)
A commitment to a specific instance type (or family) in a region for one or three years, at a discount; still used for databases and some services.
Rightsizing
Changing a resource's size or type to match its actual utilisation.
Savings Plan
A commitment to spend a fixed dollar amount per hour on compute for one or three years, applied automatically to matching usage at discounted rates.
Spot
Spare capacity sold at a variable discount that can be reclaimed with short notice.
Tag policy
An AWS Organizations policy that enforces tag keys and allowed values across accounts.
Unit cost
Cost divided by a business measure, such as dollars per thousand requests, per active customer or per training run.
drill:
Estimate and decide: the ML platform's bill

An ML team's monthly AWS spend is $84,000. The breakdown: 6 × p5.48xlarge for training at about 40% average utilisation, on demand ($55.04/hour each); an inference fleet of 12 g6e.xlarge running 24×7 on demand ($1.861/hour); an EKS cluster of 30 m7i.xlarge on demand for data processing at 25% average CPU; 400 TB in S3 Standard, 300 TB of which hasn't been read in 90 days; $3,900 of NAT processing; $2,600 of cross-zone transfer. Leadership asks for 30% savings without harming the roadmap. Propose a plan with estimated savings and risks, using October 2026 us-east-1 prices from this track.

Answer

Training GPUs (biggest line). 6 × $55.04 × 730 ≈ $241,000 if always on — so at $84k total they're clearly not running all month; at 40% utilisation of the hours they're up, the fix is scheduling and packing rather than commitment. Run jobs through a queue that launches capacity only when jobs exist (or capacity blocks for planned runs), and use spot with checkpointing for fault-tolerant runs (cl14). A three-year Instance Savings Plan ($23.78/hour) only pays if the team will keep p5 capacity busy more than about 43% of hours for three years — unlikely to be justified at 40% today.

Inference. 12 × $1.861 × 730 ≈ $16,300. Steady 24×7: a one-year EC2 Instance Savings Plan at $1.172 (37% off) saves ≈ $6,000 a month if the fleet's floor is 12; Compute plan at $1.407 saves ≈ $4,000 with more flexibility. Also check utilisation and batching before committing.

Data processing cluster. 30 × $0.2016 × 730 ≈ $4,415 at 25% CPU. Rightsize (Karpenter consolidation, smaller or Graviton nodes) and run batch on spot: plausibly halve it, ≈ $2,200 saved.

S3. 300 TB untouched for 90 days: Standard ≈ 307,200 GB × $0.023 ≈ $7,066 a month; Glacier Instant Retrieval at $0.004 ≈ $1,229 — ≈ $5,800 a month saved if objects are large enough (check average size; cl6) and reads stay rare.

NAT and cross-zone. Gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB (most of the $3,900 if it's dataset reads), zone-aware routing for the cross-zone traffic: ≈ $4,000–5,000 together.

Total: inference commitment ~$6,000, cluster ~$2,200, S3 ~$5,800, network ~$4,500, plus GPU scheduling and spot (likely the largest, perhaps $10,000+) — comfortably above $25,000 (30%) without slowing the roadmap. Risks: spot interruptions on training without good checkpointing, over-committing inference if traffic shifts to a new model or instance type (prefer Compute plans or shorter ladders), and archived data unexpectedly needed for retraining (retrieval fees). Track unit costs — cost per training run and per thousand inferences — to show the gains held.
qa: E
What are the main ways to pay for cloud compute, and when do you use each?

On-demand: list price, no commitment; for spiky, new or short-lived workloads. Commitments — Savings Plans (a dollars-per-hour commitment for one or three years, applied automatically; Compute Savings Plans cover EC2, Fargate and Lambda across families and regions, EC2 Instance Savings Plans give deeper discounts for one family in one region) and reserved instances (still the main option for RDS, ElastiCache and some others): for the steady baseline. Spot: spare capacity at up to 90% off with two minutes' interruption notice, for fault-tolerant work. Most estates combine all three.

Follow-up: Compute or EC2 Instance Savings Plan? — EC2 Instance plans are cheaper but lock you to a family and region; Compute plans cost more but survive migrations to Graviton, Fargate or another region, which is often worth the difference.
E
What hidden costs show up on cloud bills?

Data transfer out to the internet ($0.09/GB after the first 100 GB a month in us-east-1, October 2026), cross-zone traffic ($0.01 each way per GB), NAT gateway hours and per-GB processing, Transit Gateway processing, inter-region replication, public IPv4 addresses ($0.005 per hour each), idle and orphaned resources (unattached volumes, old snapshots, idle load balancers, forgotten dev environments), log ingestion and indefinite retention, request charges on high-volume services, and support plans priced as a percentage of spend.
Follow-up: which is easiest to fix? — Usually NAT processing of S3 or DynamoDB traffic (add free gateway endpoints) and storage retention (lifecycle rules, log retention settings).
E
Why does tagging matter, and what goes wrong with it?

Tags let you group costs by team, service, environment or customer, which is how you find owners and compute unit costs. What goes wrong: tags aren't applied consistently (different spellings, missing on resources created by hand), user-defined tags aren't activated as cost allocation tags (and activation isn't retroactive), some charges can't be tagged (data transfer, some shared services), and shared resources need split rules. Fix with accounts per team and environment as the primary boundary, tags as the secondary, tag policies in Organizations and policy checks in IaC.

Follow-up: how would you allocate a shared EKS cluster? — By requested CPU and memory per namespace or label over time (tools like Kubecost or split cost allocation data in the CUR), plus a rule for idle cluster capacity.
M
How do you decide how much compute to commit to?

Look at hourly usage over the last few months (from the CUR or Cost Explorer) and find the level that usage almost never drops below — the floor. Commit near that floor, because commitment below usage is always used, while commitment above it is paid for idle. Check the break-even: a commitment at rate c against on-demand rate o pays off if the covered usage runs more than c/o of the time — for an m7g.large in October 2026, 0.054/0.0816 ≈ 66% for a one-year EC2 Instance Savings Plan, 0.0599/0.0816 ≈ 73% for a Compute Savings Plan. Ladder purchases (commit in tranches every quarter) so commitments track growth and expire gradually.

Follow-up: what happens if you migrate to Graviton mid-term with an EC2 Instance Savings Plan for m7i? — The plan keeps charging for the m7i family commitment; the new Graviton usage runs on demand until the plan expires, which is why Compute Savings Plans suit teams expecting change.
M
Estimate the monthly bill for a small production web app.

Two m7g.large instances across two zones ($119), their gp3 volumes ($5), an Application Load Balancer ($16 plus about $6 of capacity units) with two public IPv4 addresses ($7), RDS PostgreSQL db.t4g.medium Multi-AZ ($94) with 100 GB gp3 ($23), two NAT gateways ($66) processing 200 GB ($9) with two Elastic IPs ($7), 500 GB a month to the internet ($36 after the free 100 GB), 100 GB in S3 ($2), 20 GB of logs ($8) and Route 53 ($5): about $404 a month in us-east-1 at October 2026 prices. NAT and its addresses are about 20% of it; compute and database about 55%.

Follow-up: what would you change first? — Add S3 and DynamoDB gateway endpoints, consider one NAT gateway (accepting the zone risk) or IPv6 egress for some traffic, then commit: a one-year Compute Savings Plan on the instances and a reserved DB instance cut about $58 a month together.
M
What is FinOps, and how would you set it up in an engineering organisation?

FinOps is the practice of making cloud spend visible, owned and optimised, with engineers accountable for the usage they create. Setup: accounts per team and environment; tagging standards enforced in IaC; the CUR exported to a queryable store with dashboards per team showing spend, trend and unit cost; budgets and anomaly alerts routed to the owning team; a central function that manages commitments and negotiates discounts; regular reviews of the top savings opportunities; and cost as a design criterion in architecture reviews. The FinOps Foundation frames it as a loop of inform, optimise and operate.

Follow-up: what metric shows FinOps is working? — Unit cost (dollars per request, per customer, per model inference) trending down or flat while usage grows, not total spend, which should grow with the business.
M
Where does data transfer cost come from, and how do you reduce it?

From bytes crossing billed boundaries: to the internet (largest per GB), between regions, between zones, and through NAT gateways, Transit Gateways and interface endpoints. Reduce it by keeping traffic zone-local (zone-aware routing, replicas per zone), using gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB, putting a CDN in front of internet-facing content (cheaper egress at volume plus caching), compressing payloads, avoiding chatty cross-region designs, and placing compute next to data rather than moving data to compute.

Follow-up: why is moving a 500 TB dataset to another provider expensive even if storage is cheaper there? — Egress: at $0.09–0.05/GB tiers it's tens of thousands of dollars, plus weeks of transfer; AWS now waives egress for customers leaving AWS entirely, on request and within 90 days, but not for ongoing multi-cloud traffic.
M
How do you find and remove idle resources safely?

Inventory with tags, Config and Cost Explorer: unattached EBS volumes, snapshots older than retention, idle load balancers (no requests for weeks), stopped instances with attached volumes, unused Elastic IPs, idle RDS instances (no connections), oversized instances at under 10% CPU, dev environments running nights and weekends. Confirm ownership through tags or account, notify owners with a deadline, snapshot before deleting stateful things, and automate schedules (stop dev at night, which cuts their compute by about 65% for a 12-hour weekday schedule). Make it routine rather than a quarterly clean-up.
Follow-up: what's the risk? — Deleting something that looked idle but isn't (a DR replica, a quarterly batch database); ownership tags and a notify-then-delete process prevent it.
H
Compare on-demand, Savings Plans and spot for a fleet whose hourly demand varies between 40 and 100 m7g.large-equivalents.

Commit to the floor: about 40 instances' worth on a one-year plan. At October 2026 us-east-1 rates, 40 × 730 × $0.054 ≈ $1,577 a month on an EC2 Instance Savings Plan versus $2,383 on demand for the same hours. Above the floor, demand averages perhaps 30 more instances: if the workload tolerates interruption, run that on spot with a diversified fleet; otherwise on demand (30 × 730 × $0.0816 ≈ $1,787). Committing to 70 instead of 40 would pay for 30 instances' commitment even in hours when only 40 are needed; whether it's worth it depends on how many hours demand is above 66% of the extra commitment — compute it from the hourly curve rather than guessing.

Follow-up: how do you handle growth? — Re-evaluate quarterly and add commitment tranches as the floor rises; let older tranches expire on a staggered schedule so you're never locked into a large commitment at once.
H
Your cloud bill jumped 35% month over month. Walk through the investigation.

Start in the CUR or Cost Explorer: break the increase down by account, service, usage type and region, and compare daily to find when it started. Typical culprits by usage type: DataTransfer-Out-Bytes or Regional-Bytes (a new feature moving data, a misrouted path), NatGateway-Bytes (traffic that should use endpoints), BoxUsage of a new instance type (a scaled-up or forgotten fleet), API requests (S3, KMS, CloudWatch PutMetricData from new instrumentation), log ingestion, or commitments expiring (same usage, higher rates). Correlate the start time with deploys and IaC changes, find the owner by tag or account, fix, and add an anomaly alert and a budget so the next one is caught in a day, not a month.
Follow-up: what's the cheapest early-warning mechanism? — Cost Anomaly Detection monitors per service and account, routed to the owning team's channel, plus daily cost dashboards per team.
H
When does leaving the cloud make financial sense? Use a real case.

When workloads are large, steady and predictable, the team can operate hardware, and the managed services and elasticity being paid for aren't needed. 37signals reported in October 2024 that moving seven applications, including HEY, from AWS to its own hardware cut its cloud bill from $3.2 million a year to $1.3 million, with about $700,000 of Dell hardware recouped within 2023, the same team running it, and total projected savings above $10 million over five years once it also moved almost 10 petabytes off S3 (where a four-year storage commitment from 2021 ran to summer 2025) to an 18-petabyte Pure Storage setup costing about one year of S3 fees. Counter-cases: spiky or fast-growing workloads, heavy use of managed services, global footprints, small teams. The honest analysis includes staff, data-centre space and power, hardware refresh, lost elasticity and egress for the move (AWS waives it for customers leaving, on request).

Follow-up: what would you try before leaving? — Commitments, Graviton, rightsizing, storage tiering, architecture fixes for data transfer, and negotiated enterprise discounts; many teams find 30–50% inside the cloud first.
H
How do you build unit economics for an AI product on the cloud?

Define units the business recognises — cost per thousand inference requests, per active customer per month, per fine-tuning run — and attribute costs to them: GPU instance-hours (by tag, namespace or job ID), model API spend (ae2), storage and data transfer for datasets and checkpoints, and shared platform costs allocated by usage share. Track them over time against usage: falling unit costs mean efficiency improvements (batching, quantisation, caching, better utilisation) are working. Make them visible per team and per feature, because a feature with negative margin at scale is a product decision, not just an infrastructure one.

Follow-up: what's the hardest cost to attribute? — Shared, idle GPU capacity kept for latency or availability; allocate it explicitly as a reliability cost to the services that require it, so its owners see it.

t: Cloud security and governance: account and organisation structure, guardrails (SCPs and RCPs), encryption and KMS, secrets, network isolation, compliance basics, and common breach patterns
sum: How organisations keep many cloud accounts safe by construction: a multi-account landing zone and why accounts are the strongest boundary, preventive guardrails (SCPs, RCPs, Block Public Access, data perimeters) and detective controls (CloudTrail, Config, GuardDuty, Security Hub), encryption defaults and KMS key policies across accounts, secrets and network isolation in practice, compliance frameworks and the shared-responsibility evidence behind them, and the breach patterns that keep recurring — leaked keys exploited within minutes, public buckets, over-broad roles — with the 2025 'Codefinger' SSE-C ransomware and S3's 2026 change of default as the case.
