IAM evaluates every call with explicit-deny-wins logic; SCPs and RCPs are guardrails that cap but never grant; condition keys like aws:PrincipalOrgID and aws:SourceVpce express perimeters.
au10
Workloads should get short-lived credentials through federation, not static keys; IMDSv2 blocks the SSRF path used in the Capital One breach.
au11
Secrets belong in a secret manager with rotation; KMS envelope encryption protects data keys with master keys that never leave the service; leaked-key response is a playbook.
net14
Segmentation, least-privilege network paths, egress control, WAF and DDoS protection, and zero trust replacing network position with identity.
cl11
CloudTrail organisation trails in a log-archive account, data events for sensitive stores, AWS Config history and rules, and Health and security findings routed to on-call.
why:
A fast-growing company has one AWS account. Everyone has administrator access because it was easiest. CI deploys with an IAM user's access key stored in the CI system's settings. A data scientist creates a bucket for a partner, makes it public "for a day" to share a file, and forgets. A developer copies the CI key into a test script and pushes it to a public repository on a Friday evening.

Within minutes, automated scanners find the key. By Saturday morning there are 40 large instances mining cryptocurrency in eight regions the company never uses; the bill alert fires on Monday. Investigating, the security engineer discovers that CloudTrail was only enabled in one region, that the public bucket contained a customer export, and that the key could also read and write every bucket in the account. Nobody can say what was copied. A month later, a different set of stolen credentials is used to re-encrypt production objects with an attacker's key and schedule them for deletion in seven days.

None of this required the attacker to break anything. Every step used legitimate APIs with legitimate credentials against configurations nobody had chosen deliberately. That's the shape of most cloud security incidents: failures on the customer's side of the shared-responsibility line (cl1), multiplied by flat structures in which one credential reaches everything.

The track has covered the parts: IAM evaluation and least privilege (cl2), workload identity and secrets (au10, au11), network segmentation (cl3, net14), logging (cl11). This lesson is about governance at scale — how organisations make the safe configuration the default for hundreds of accounts. It covers the multi-account landing zone, preventive guardrails (SCPs, RCPs, Block Public Access, data perimeters) and detective controls, encryption and KMS key policies across accounts, secrets and network isolation in practice, compliance frameworks and evidence, and the breach patterns that keep recurring. The case is the 2025 Codefinger campaign, which held S3 data to ransom with nothing but leaked credentials and an encryption feature, and S3's decision to switch that feature off by default in 2026.
primer:
Think of cloud governance as city planning rather than locking individual doors.

You could secure a city by inspecting every building as it's built and hoping each owner locks up. Or you can zone the city: industrial here, residential there, a vault district with one gate; building codes that make every new building fire-resistant whatever the architect prefers; laws that apply everywhere (no building may be taller than the airport's flight path allows); CCTV on every main road recording who went where; and an emergency service that knows the map. Individual owners still lock their doors, but the city is safe even when some forget.

In the cloud: zoning is the account structure — separate accounts for production, development, security tooling and logs, grouped into organisational units. Building codes are preventive guardrails applied centrally: SCPs that cap what anyone in an account can do, RCPs that cap what can be done to resources, Block Public Access, encryption by default. CCTV is detective control: CloudTrail recording every call into an archive nobody in the workload accounts can alter, Config recording every configuration, GuardDuty watching for signs of attack. Emergency services are incident response: runbooks, quarantine, immutable backups.

This structure changes what security work looks like. Instead of reviewing every bucket, the platform team ensures no bucket in the organisation can become public. Instead of trusting every team to enable logging, the organisation trail records every account. Instead of hoping nobody uses an unapproved region, an SCP makes those regions unusable. Teams get freedom inside the boundaries; the boundaries are maintained centrally and changed through review.

The economics favour this approach. A breach investigation in a flat, unlogged account costs weeks of engineering and often ends with the answer that nobody can tell what was accessed, which regulators and customers read as everything. The same incident in a governed organisation is usually smaller (the credential reached one account), shorter (the trail shows exactly what it did) and recoverable (backups sat outside its reach). The controls in this lesson cost little to run once built; the expensive part is building them before the first incident rather than after it.

Where the analogy breaks: a city's building codes are inspected when a building is constructed. Cloud resources are created, changed and destroyed thousands of times a day, by automation as much as by people, and attackers use the same APIs as everyone else. Controls therefore have to act at API-call time (guardrails evaluated on every request) and continuously afterwards (detection on every change), not at a one-off inspection.
body:
1. Accounts and the landing zone

An AWS organisation groups accounts under a management account, arranged in organisational units (OUs). AWS's multi-account whitepaper and Control Tower's default landing zone converge on a structure like the diagram: a Security OU with a log archive account (receives organisation-wide CloudTrail, Config and other logs, in immutable storage) and an audit or security-tooling account (delegated administrator for GuardDuty, Security Hub, Access Analyzer, Config aggregation); an Infrastructure OU for shared networking (Transit Gateway, central egress and inspection, cl3) and shared services; Workloads OUs split by environment, with an account per team or product per environment; a Sandbox OU for experiments, with budgets and no connectivity to production; and a Suspended OU for accounts being retired.

Why accounts and not just IAM policies inside one account? Because the account is the boundary for nearly everything: IAM principals and their default reach, service quotas, billing and cost allocation (cl12), resource visibility, and the scope of most mistakes. A developer with administrator rights in orders-dev can't affect orders-prod at all unless a cross-account role says so, and that role can be audited. The cost of many accounts is managing them — which is what landing-zone tooling (Control Tower, account factories in IaC) automates: new accounts arrive with the baseline network, logging, guardrails, SSO access and budgets already in place.

The management account deserves special handling: SCPs don't apply to it, and it can change everything in the organisation. Run nothing there except organisation administration and billing, protect its root user with MFA hardware, and keep access to a few people.

2. Preventive guardrails

Service control policies (SCPs) cap the permissions of every principal in the accounts they're attached to, through the evaluation logic in cl2. A baseline set, attached at the root and inherited:

{ "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    { "Sid": "NoLeavingOrg", "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": "organizations:LeaveOrganization", "Resource": "*" },
    { "Sid": "ProtectAuditTrail", "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": ["cloudtrail:StopLogging", "cloudtrail:DeleteTrail", "cloudtrail:UpdateTrail",
                 "config:StopConfigurationRecorder", "config:DeleteConfigurationRecorder",
                 "guardduty:DeleteDetector", "guardduty:DisassociateFromMasterAccount"],
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": { "ArnNotLike": { "aws:PrincipalArn": "arn:aws:iam::*:role/SecurityAdmin" } } },
    { "Sid": "NoIamUserKeys", "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": ["iam:CreateUser", "iam:CreateAccessKey"], "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": { "ArnNotLike": { "aws:PrincipalArn": "arn:aws:iam::*:role/BreakGlass" } } },
    { "Sid": "RequireImdsV2", "Effect": "Deny", "Action": "ec2:RunInstances",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:ec2:*:*:instance/*",
      "Condition": { "StringNotEquals": { "ec2:MetadataHttpTokens": "required" } } }
  ] }

plus the region guardrail from cl2 and, for production OUs, denies on deleting KMS keys, disabling EBS default encryption, and using SSE-C (section 6). SCPs are tested in a staging OU first, because a mistake can lock an entire OU out of a service.

Resource control policies (RCPs) are the resource-side counterpart: attached to OUs or accounts, they cap what can be done to resources in them, whoever calls — including principals outside your organisation, which SCPs can't reach. The classic RCP denies access to the organisation's S3 buckets, KMS keys, SQS queues and Secrets Manager secrets unless the caller is in the organisation or is an AWS service acting on your behalf. That turns a misconfigured bucket policy granting access to "*" into a denied request.

S3 Block Public Access, set at the account or organisation level, overrides any policy or ACL that would make a bucket public; S3 applies the most restrictive combination of organisation, account, bucket and access-point settings, and new buckets block public access by default. Default encryption: S3 encrypts every new object (SSE-S3) by default since January 2023, and EBS encryption by default can be enabled per region so every new volume and snapshot is encrypted, with an SCP preventing anyone from turning it off.

Guardrails extend into the delivery pipeline: IaC policy checks (cl9) reject resources that would be caught later anyway, so developers learn at pull-request time rather than from a denied API call.

3. Data perimeters

A data perimeter combines these into three statements, each enforced with condition keys from cl2:

PerimeterStatementEnforced byStops
IdentityOnly our identities (and AWS services acting for us) can access our resourcesRCPs and resource policies: deny unless aws:PrincipalOrgID = our org, with aws:PrincipalIsAWSService exceptionsmisconfigured public or cross-account grants
ResourceOur identities can access only our resourcesSCPs: deny unless aws:ResourceOrgID = our org (exceptions for AWS-owned resources)exfiltration to an attacker's bucket with stolen credentials
NetworkOur credentials work only from our networksSCPs and resource policies: deny unless aws:SourceVpce/aws:SourceIp match, or aws:ViaAWSServiceuse of leaked credentials from the internet

The network perimeter is the most powerful against leaked credentials and the hardest to roll out, because many legitimate paths (developers on laptops, SaaS integrations, AWS services) must be accounted for. Teams start with the identity perimeter on sensitive data stores, run the others in audit mode using Access Analyzer and CloudTrail to find legitimate exceptions, then enforce.

4. Detective controls

Prevention misses things; detection finds them. The organisation-wide set:

  • CloudTrail organisation trail to the log archive (cl11), with data events on sensitive buckets, and alerts on high-risk events: root sign-in, StopLogging, CreateAccessKey, PutBucketPolicy granting public access, KMS ScheduleKeyDeletion.
  • AWS Config with conformance packs (collections of rules mapped to frameworks), aggregated across accounts: unencrypted volumes, open security groups, buckets without Block Public Access, IAM users with old keys.
  • GuardDuty, which analyses CloudTrail, VPC flow, DNS and other telemetry for signs of compromise: credentials used from unusual locations or Tor, instance credentials used outside the instance, crypto-mining DNS lookups, anomalous S3 access.
  • IAM Access Analyzer for resources and roles accessible from outside the organisation, and unused access.
  • Macie to find personal or sensitive data in S3, which tells you which buckets deserve the strictest controls.
  • Security Hub to aggregate findings and score accounts against standards such as AWS Foundational Security Best Practices or CIS benchmarks.

Detection is only as good as response. Findings route by account owner to the team's channel with severity; high-severity findings page; some are auto-remediated (re-enable Block Public Access, quarantine an instance by swapping its security group). The test of the system is how many minutes pass between a dangerous change and someone acting on it.

5. Encryption and key management

Encryption at rest on AWS is server-side and transparent: the service encrypts data with a data key and protects the data key with a KMS key (envelope encryption, au11). The choices are which key and who controls it:

OptionWho controls the keyAuditUse
SSE-S3 / AWS-owned keysthe serviceno per-use recorddefault protection against media loss
AWS-managed KMS keysAWS, in your accountkey use in CloudTrailbasic separation, no custom policy
Customer-managed KMS keysyou: key policy, rotation, disableevery use in CloudTrailsensitive data, cross-account sharing, crypto-shredding
Imported key material / external key storesyou, partly outside AWSas aboveregulatory requirements to hold keys

Customer-managed keys matter because they add a second, separately controlled permission: reading an object needs both s3:GetObject and kms:Decrypt on its key. A key's key policy is a resource policy that must allow a principal — directly, or by delegating to the account's IAM policies — before anyone can use the key; an IAM policy alone isn't enough. Cross-account use needs both sides: the key policy in the key's account names the other account or role, and the other account's IAM policy allows the KMS actions on the key's ARN. This is also how backups are protected (cl10): copies in the backup account are re-encrypted with a key owned there, so production credentials can't decrypt or destroy them.

The key is also a kill switch. Disabling it, or deleting it after the mandatory waiting period (7 to 30 days), makes everything under it unreadable — useful for crypto-shredding data you must destroy, catastrophic if an attacker does it. Protect key deletion and policy changes with SCPs and alerts.

In transit, AWS APIs use TLS; enforce it on resources with policies (aws:SecureTransport, cl2) and between your services with TLS or a mesh (net9, au10).

6. Secrets and SSE-C

Secrets follow au11: stored in Secrets Manager or Parameter Store with KMS encryption, fetched at runtime by workload roles, rotated automatically where possible, never in code, images, environment files or IaC state. Governance adds organisation-wide checks: secret scanning on repositories and CI logs, Config rules for secrets without rotation, and SCPs that deny creating IAM user access keys at all.

SSE-C is worth singling out because of how it was abused. With server-side encryption with customer-provided keys, the caller sends a 256-bit key with each PUT and GET; S3 uses it to encrypt the object and discards it, storing only a hash to validate later requests. Few applications need it now that customer-managed KMS keys exist — AWS's own announcement says there's no practical security benefit left — but it gives anyone who can write objects the ability to make them unreadable to everyone else. In response to its abuse, S3 began blocking SSE-C by default in April 2026 for all new general-purpose buckets and for existing buckets in accounts with no SSE-C-encrypted objects; applications that need it must enable it explicitly per bucket. For older buckets, a bucket policy or SCP denying requests that carry the SSE-C algorithm header closes the path.

7. Network isolation in practice

Network controls (cl3, net14) are a second layer behind identity, not a replacement. The baseline: data stores in private subnets with no public endpoints; inbound internet traffic only through load balancers and WAF; egress through NAT or, better, inspected egress with allow-lists, and VPC endpoints with endpoint policies for AWS services so even S3 traffic is restricted to your buckets; no SSH or RDP open anywhere — administrative sessions through Systems Manager Session Manager or EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint, authorised by IAM and recorded; and for the most sensitive environments, no internet egress at all. Network isolation also makes the network perimeter in section 3 possible, because requests from your workloads arrive through known endpoints.

8. Compliance basics

Compliance frameworks express control objectives; clouds help you meet them but don't meet them for you. The provider's side is documented in independent audit reports (SOC 1, SOC 2 and SOC 3, ISO 27001 and related standards, PCI DSS for card data, FedRAMP for US government, and region- or sector-specific schemes), downloadable from AWS Artifact and equivalents; regulated data may need contracts such as a HIPAA business associate addendum, and services must be in scope for the framework. Your side is shown by the controls in this lesson and evidence that they operate continuously: Config conformance packs and Security Hub standards mapped to the framework, CloudTrail and Config history, IaC and change records, access reviews, backup and restore tests, and incident-response exercises. Data-residency rules (cl1) shape which regions and services are allowed; they're enforced with region SCPs and by checking which features replicate data elsewhere.
deep:
Why accounts beat policies as a boundary

Inside one account, isolation between teams relies on every IAM policy being right: resource ARNs scoped, wildcards avoided, PassRole restricted (cl2). One mistake — or one compromised role with broad permissions — crosses every internal boundary. Between accounts, the default is no access: a principal in one account can touch another account's resources only if both sides explicitly allow it, and SCPs can forbid even that. Mistakes inside an account stay inside it. The trade-off is operational overhead (networking between accounts, cross-account roles, shared services), which is why account vending and landing-zone automation are core platform investments rather than conveniences.

Guardrails need their own change management

An SCP is code that applies to hundreds of accounts at once. A typo can deny a service organisation-wide; an over-broad condition can lock teams out of incident response. Mature organisations treat guardrails like production code: in version control, reviewed, tested against representative principals with the policy simulator or test accounts, rolled out to a staging OU, then progressively wider, with a documented emergency path (a break-glass role exempt from most guardrails, itself monitored and rarely used). The same applies to RCPs and organisation-wide Block Public Access, which can break legitimate integrations if applied without discovery.

Detection engineering is about signal, not volume

Turning on every detector produces thousands of findings, most low-value, and teams learn to ignore them. Effective programmes choose a small set of high-signal detections tied to the threat model — root use, logging disabled, credentials used from unusual places, public access granted, keys scheduled for deletion, mass object rewrites — with clear owners and runbooks, then widen. Every finding should end in one of three outcomes: fixed, accepted with a recorded reason and expiry, or turned into a preventive control so it can't recur.

Ransomware in the cloud attacks recoverability

On-premises ransomware encrypts disks; cloud ransomware uses the cloud's own APIs: re-encrypting objects with attacker keys (SSE-C), scheduling KMS key deletion, deleting snapshots and backups, setting lifecycle expiry, or simply exfiltrating and threatening publication. The defences are therefore about making destruction impossible for the credentials an attacker is likely to get: backups and copies in a separate account with locked retention (cl10), Object Lock on critical buckets, SCPs that deny key deletion and SSE-C, no long-term keys, and alerts on bulk destructive patterns. A useful exercise is to ask, for each critical dataset: which single role, if stolen, could make this data unrecoverable? If the answer isn't "none", the design isn't finished.

Third-party access is part of the perimeter

Monitoring vendors, CI/CD platforms, cost tools and security scanners all hold roles in your accounts. Each is a path an attacker can use if the vendor is compromised (the 2022 theft of OAuth tokens issued to Heroku and Travis CI, covered in the auth track, and CircleCI in au11). Controls: roles per vendor with least privilege and external IDs (cl2), OIDC federation rather than stored keys for CI, Access Analyzer findings for every external principal, and periodic reviews that remove unused integrations. RCPs and the identity perimeter must explicitly carve out these vendors, which also documents them.

Identity is the new perimeter, but networks still matter

Zero-trust thinking (net14) says every request should be authenticated and authorised on its own merits, not trusted for coming from inside a network. Cloud IAM is built that way: every API call carries a signed identity. But identity alone doesn't stop a stolen credential used from an attacker's laptop; network conditions do. The strongest cloud designs combine both — identity on every call, plus perimeters that make credentials useless outside expected networks — and treat them as complementary layers rather than competing philosophies.

Security and cost governance share machinery

The same organisation structure, tags, Config rules and IaC policy checks that enforce security also enforce cost controls (cl12) and reliability standards (cl10). Platform teams that build one governance pipeline — policies as code, evaluated in CI and continuously in accounts, with findings routed to owners — get all three for the price of one, and avoid teams facing three different review processes.
prod:
Recurring breach patterns and their signatures

Leaked long-term keys. Signature: API calls from unfamiliar IPs or regions, GetCallerIdentity and enumeration calls, new IAM users or keys, large instances launched in unused regions. Unit 42's 2023 research saw exposed keys used within five minutes; AWS's quarantine policy arrived within about two minutes in that research but only limits some actions. Prevention: no IAM user keys, secret scanning, region SCPs.

Public storage. Signature: anonymous GetObject in S3 access logs or data events, Access Analyzer public findings. Prevention: organisation-level Block Public Access, identity-perimeter RCPs, CloudFront with origin access control for genuinely public content.

Application-to-credentials chains. SSRF to instance metadata (au10's Capital One analysis), code execution in a container with a broad role, CI pipelines with admin roles. Signature: instance or task credentials used from outside their compute, unusual API patterns from workload roles. Prevention: IMDSv2, least-privilege workload roles, network perimeter.

Destructive actions. Mass PutObject with SSE-C, lifecycle rules expiring buckets, ScheduleKeyDeletion, DeleteSnapshot sprees. Prevention: SCPs, immutable backups elsewhere, alerts on these specific events.

Disabled visibility. StopLogging, deleted GuardDuty detectors, removed Config recorders. Prevention: SCPs protecting them; detection on any attempt.

Response essentials

A rehearsed runbook per pattern: who decides, how to deactivate keys and revoke role sessions (a deny on tokens issued before now, cl2), how to isolate instances (swap security groups, snapshot for forensics), where logs are and who can query them, how to restore from immutable backups, and who notifies customers and regulators within required timeframes. Pre-provisioned forensic tooling and access in the security account, and a break-glass path that works when SSO is the thing compromised.

What to measure

Count of IAM users with active keys (target zero) and key age; accounts outside the landing zone or missing baseline controls; Security Hub score per account; open high-severity findings and their age; external-access findings; buckets with sensitive data and their controls; time from dangerous change to detection and to remediation; last tested restore of each critical dataset from the backup account.

The case: Codefinger and S3's change of default

On 13 January 2025, the security firm Halcyon published research on a group it named Codefinger running ransomware against Amazon S3. The attack needed no AWS vulnerability. Using compromised AWS credentials that had s3:GetObject and s3:PutObject permissions, the attackers rewrote victims' objects using SSE-C, supplying an AES-256 key they had generated themselves. Because S3 doesn't store SSE-C keys — CloudTrail records only an HMAC of the key — the data could not be decrypted without the attackers' key. They then applied lifecycle rules to delete the encrypted objects within seven days and left ransom notes, adding time pressure. Analyses by Arctic Wolf and others relayed AWS's guidance: restrict SSE-C through policy conditions where it isn't needed, avoid long-term credentials and rotate any exposed ones, enable logging that would show bulk encryption and lifecycle changes, and keep credentials out of code.

AWS then changed the default. Its storage blog gave advance notice, and in April 2026 S3 blocked SSE-C for new writes by default on all new general-purpose buckets and on existing buckets in accounts with no SSE-C-encrypted objects; requests specifying SSE-C on such buckets are rejected with 403, and the small number of applications that need SSE-C must enable it per bucket. AWS's stated reason is that customer-managed KMS keys provide the control SSE-C once offered, so its remaining practical use was mostly as a weapon.

The case teaches governance more than cryptography. The initial access was ordinary — leaked credentials. The damage came from permissions broader than any workload needed and from a feature no workload used. The controls that would have stopped it are the ones in this lesson: no long-term keys, least privilege on write paths, a guardrail removing an unused dangerous capability, immutable backups in another account, and alerts on destructive bulk actions. And the provider's response — making the safe configuration the default — is exactly what a platform team should do inside its own organisation whenever an incident reveals a capability nobody needs.
myths: Encryption at rest protects our data from attackers.

Encryption at rest protects against someone obtaining the physical media or a raw snapshot without key access. An attacker with valid credentials that allow s3:GetObject and kms:Decrypt reads plaintext, because the service decrypts transparently for authorised callers. What protects data is who can call the APIs — IAM, key policies, perimeters — and encryption's real security value is the extra, separately controlled permission on the key.
A single well-secured account is simpler and just as safe as many accounts.

Accounts are the hardest isolation boundary the cloud offers: separate IAM, separate quotas, separate billing, separate blast radius. In one account, every role, every developer mistake and every compromised workload sits next to production data, and policies must carve out exceptions forever. Multi-account landing zones let guardrails apply by organisational unit and make 'dev can't touch prod' a structural fact rather than a policy hope.
Making a bucket private is enough to keep it private.

Public exposure can return through many paths: a later bucket policy edit, an ACL on an object, an access point, a presigned URL, a cross-account grant, a CDN origin misconfiguration. Block Public Access at the account (or organisation) level stops policies and ACLs from making buckets public at all, regardless of who edits them later, and resource control policies can deny access from outside the organisation.
Cloud breaches mostly come from sophisticated exploits of the provider.

The common patterns are mundane and on the customer side of the shared-responsibility line: leaked long-term access keys (Unit 42 observed keys pushed to public GitHub being used within five minutes), publicly readable storage, over-broad roles reached through application bugs, missing logging. Provider-side vulnerabilities exist and get fixed; most incidents are configuration and credential failures.
Compliance certification means we're secure.

A provider's SOC 2, ISO 27001 or PCI DSS reports cover the provider's controls for its services — its side of the shared-responsibility model. Your certification covers your controls, assessed at a point in time against a framework's requirements. Both are useful evidence; neither proves that today's configuration is safe, which is why continuous controls (guardrails, Config rules, findings) matter more than the audit.
Guardrails slow teams down, so platform teams should keep them minimal.

Badly designed guardrails do. Well-designed ones remove whole categories of mistakes — no public buckets, no unencrypted volumes, no leaving the organisation, no disabling logs — so teams can move fast inside them without security reviews for every change. The trick is to block what's never legitimate, detect what's sometimes legitimate, and give teams a paved path that's easier than working around either.
lab:
Goal: build a small "governance scanner" over a simulated organisation and an exposure-path checker — Python 3.12 standard library only. About 20 minutes; no cloud account needed.

  1. Model. Represent an organisation as JSON: OUs with attached guardrail flags (block_public, require_imdsv2, deny_regions, deny_sse_c), accounts in OUs, and resources per account (buckets with policy, BPA flags, encryption type, versioning, object lock; IAM users with key ages; roles with trust principals and permissions; KMS keys with policies).
  2. Rules. Write checks returning findings with severity: IAM user keys older than 90 days or present at all in prod; bucket public (policy Principal "*" without org condition, and no effective Block Public Access after combining OU, account and bucket settings — most restrictive wins); buckets with sensitive tag but no CMK; prod buckets without versioning or Object Lock; trust policies with Principal "*" and no org condition; SSE-C allowed on prod buckets.
  3. Inheritance. Implement effective guardrails as the union of flags from root to account, and show that moving an account from the Sandbox OU to the Prod OU changes its findings without touching the account.
  4. Exposure paths. Given "a leaked credential for role X", compute which buckets it could read, write or make unreadable (write + SSE-C allowed, or kms:ScheduleKeyDeletion on their key), and which backups survive (copies in another account with locked retention).
  5. Report. Print findings by account and severity, and a one-line answer per critical dataset to "which single role could make this unrecoverable?"

What to look for: step 3 shows why OU placement is the security architecture; step 4 reproduces the Codefinger chain in miniature — a role with PutObject on a prod bucket and SSE-C allowed can destroy data unless a backup lives elsewhere; step 5's question should return "none" for every critical dataset once guardrails and cross-account backups are in place.

Needs an AWS account (optional): aws s3control get-public-access-block --account-id <id> shows the account-level Block Public Access settings; aws organizations list-policies-for-target --target-id <ou-or-account> --filter SERVICE_CONTROL_POLICY lists SCPs attached at that level.
recap: Security in the cloud is the customer's side of the shared-responsibility model: identities, permissions, network exposure, data protection, logging and configuration.

A landing zone organises accounts into organisational units — security (log archive, audit), infrastructure, workloads by environment, sandbox — because accounts are the strongest isolation, quota and billing boundary.

Preventive guardrails stop bad states from existing: SCPs cap what principals can do, RCPs cap what can be done to resources, Block Public Access stops public buckets, and data-perimeter conditions keep identities, resources and networks inside the organisation.

Detective controls find what prevention misses: organisation CloudTrail in an immutable log archive, AWS Config rules, GuardDuty threat detection, Security Hub aggregation, Macie for sensitive data, Access Analyzer for external access.

Encryption is on by default for S3 and can be for EBS; customer-managed KMS keys add a separately controlled permission, an audit trail of key use and the ability to revoke access, and their key policies must explicitly grant cross-account use.

Secrets belong in a secret manager with workloads fetching them at runtime through their roles; network isolation keeps data stores private, egress controlled and administrative access through identity-based sessions rather than open ports.
Compliance frameworks map to controls; the provider's attestations cover its side, yours must show continuous enforcement and evidence for your side.

Recurring breach patterns are leaked long-term keys (exploited within minutes), public storage, over-privileged roles reached via application bugs, disabled or missing logs, and destructive actions by compromised credentials, as in the 2025 Codefinger SSE-C ransomware.
Response depends on preparation: key quarantine and session revocation, immutable logs and backups in another account, and runbooks rehearsed before the incident.
glossary: Access Analyzer
An IAM feature that finds resources and roles accessible from outside your organisation (or account), unused access, and validates policies.
Block Public Access (BPA)
S3 settings at organisation, account, bucket or access-point level that override any policy or ACL granting public access.
Control Tower
An AWS service that sets up and governs a multi-account landing zone with predefined accounts, OUs and controls.
Customer-managed key (CMK)
A KMS key you create and control, with its own key policy, rotation and audit trail, as opposed to an AWS-managed key.
Data perimeter
A set of guardrails ensuring that only trusted identities access trusted resources from expected networks, built from SCPs, RCPs and resource policies.
Defence in depth
Layering independent controls so that one failure doesn't expose the asset.
Detective control
A control that finds and alerts on problems after they occur, such as a Config rule or a GuardDuty finding.
GuardDuty
AWS's threat-detection service that analyses CloudTrail, VPC flow, DNS and other telemetry for signs of compromise.
HIPAA
The US law governing protected health information; cloud use requires in-scope services and a business associate addendum.
Key policy
The resource policy on a KMS key; it must allow a principal (directly or by delegating to IAM) before anyone can use the key.
Landing zone
A pre-configured, secure multi-account environment with standard accounts, network, logging and guardrails.
Log archive account
A dedicated account that receives organisation-wide logs in immutable storage, readable by few and writable only by logging services.
Macie
An AWS service that discovers and classifies sensitive data such as personal information in S3.
Organisational unit (OU)
A group of accounts in AWS Organizations to which policies can be attached.
Preventive control
A control that stops a bad action or state from occurring, such as an SCP deny or Block Public Access.
Quarantine policy
An AWS-managed policy (AWSCompromisedKeyQuarantine) that AWS may attach to an exposed IAM user to block high-risk actions.
RCP (resource control policy)
An AWS Organizations guardrail that caps what may be done to resources in the attached accounts, whoever the caller is.
SCP (service control policy)
An AWS Organizations guardrail that caps what principals in the attached accounts may do (cl2).
Security Hub
An AWS service that aggregates findings from security services and checks accounts against standards such as the Foundational Security Best Practices.
SOC 2 / ISO 27001 / PCI DSS
Common security attestation and certification frameworks: service-organisation controls reports, an information-security management standard, and the card-payment data standard.
SSE-C
S3 server-side encryption with customer-provided keys: the caller sends the key with each request and S3 doesn't store it.
SSE-KMS / SSE-S3
S3 server-side encryption with KMS keys (auditable, policy-controlled) or with S3-managed keys (the default since January 2023).
SSRF (server-side request forgery)
A bug that lets an attacker make a server send requests on their behalf, for example to the instance metadata endpoint (au10).
Tag policy / backup policy
AWS Organizations policy types that standardise tags or backup plans across accounts.
WAF (web application firewall)
A filter in front of web applications that blocks malicious requests by rules (net14).
drill:
Review: a startup's first security baseline

A 60-person startup runs everything in two AWS accounts (prod and dev) created by the CTO, who uses the root user for billing. Findings from a review: 14 IAM users with access keys (oldest 3 years), including one used by CI; CloudTrail enabled only in us-east-1 in prod; no organisation; S3 buckets in prod include one with a policy allowing "Principal": "*" for s3:GetObject on exports/*; RDS and S3 encrypted with AWS-managed keys; backups are RDS automated snapshots in the same account; developers SSH into prod instances through a security group open to 0.0.0.0/0 on port 22. Prioritise the fixes for the next 30 days and sketch the target state.

Answer

Week 1 — stop the bleeding. (1) The public exports/* grant: remove it, turn on account-level Block Public Access, check access logs or data events for past anonymous reads and treat the data as exposed if none exist. (2) Port 22 open to the world: close it; move to Session Manager. (3) Root user: enable hardware MFA, remove any root access keys, stop using it for billing (create a billing role). (4) CloudTrail: a multi-region trail in both accounts now; alert on root sign-in and StopLogging.

Weeks 2–3 — remove long-term credentials. Replace CI's IAM user with OIDC federation to a deploy role per account (cl2, au10). Move humans to IAM Identity Center with MFA and permission sets; deactivate and delete the 13 other users' keys after checking CloudTrail for their use. Add secret scanning to repositories.

Weeks 3–4 — structure and recoverability. Create an AWS organisation (new management account; move prod and dev in), add log-archive and security accounts, an organisation trail to an Object Lock bucket, GuardDuty and Security Hub with delegated admin. Baseline SCPs: no leaving org, protect logging, approved regions, no IAM user keys, IMDSv2, no SSE-C in prod. Backups: AWS Backup copies of RDS and critical S3 data to a backup account with Vault Lock and a key owned there.

Target state (next quarter). Accounts per team and environment via an account factory; RCP identity perimeter on sensitive buckets; customer-managed KMS keys for sensitive data with tight key policies; Config conformance packs; restore tests; a short incident-response runbook rehearsed once. The single question to answer for each critical dataset: which stolen credential could make it unrecoverable — and the answer should be none.
qa: E
Why use multiple AWS accounts, and how would you organise them?

Accounts are the strongest isolation boundary: separate IAM, quotas, billing and blast radius, and a compromised workload or a mistake in one can't directly affect another. A typical landing zone has the management account (only organisation administration), a Security OU with a log-archive account and an audit/security-tooling account, an Infrastructure OU with shared networking and services, Workloads OUs split by environment (prod, non-prod) with an account per team or product, a Sandbox OU for experiments with tight budgets, and a Suspended OU for accounts being closed. Guardrails attach by OU.
Follow-up: why keep workloads out of the management account? — SCPs don't apply to it, and it controls the whole organisation; anything running there has the highest possible blast radius.
E
What's the difference between preventive and detective controls in the cloud? Give examples.

Preventive controls stop a bad state from existing: an SCP denying CloudTrail StopLogging, account-level S3 Block Public Access, an RCP denying access to resources from outside the organisation, IaC policy checks that reject unencrypted volumes. Detective controls find bad states or activity after the fact: AWS Config rules flagging unencrypted volumes, GuardDuty detecting credential misuse or crypto-mining, Access Analyzer finding external access, CloudTrail alerts on root sign-in. Use preventive controls for things that are never legitimate and detective controls for things that sometimes are.

Follow-up: why not make everything preventive? — Some states are legitimate in context (a public bucket for a static website, a temporary open port in a lab), and over-broad preventive controls push teams to work around them.
E
What does S3 Block Public Access do?

Four settings that override any bucket policy, access point policy or ACL granting public access: block new public ACLs, ignore existing public ACLs, block public bucket policies, and restrict access to buckets with public policies to the owner account and AWS services. They apply at bucket, account or organisation level, and S3 enforces the most restrictive combination. New buckets have public access blocked by default. Turning them on at the account or organisation level means nobody can make a bucket public by editing its policy later.
Follow-up: how do you host a public static website then? — Keep the bucket private and serve it through CloudFront with origin access control, so only the CDN can read the bucket.
M
How do customer-managed KMS keys work across accounts, and why use them?

A KMS key's key policy is a resource policy that must allow a principal (or delegate to the account's IAM policies) before anyone can use the key — unlike most resources, an IAM policy alone isn't enough. For cross-account use, the key policy in the key's account must allow the other account (or a role in it), and that account's IAM policy must allow kms:Decrypt on the key ARN. Customer-managed keys add a separately controlled permission on top of data access, a CloudTrail record of every use, rotation, and a kill switch: disabling the key or removing a grant cuts off decryption everywhere. They cost $1 per key per month plus requests (au11).

Follow-up: what's the danger of the kill switch? — Disabling or scheduling deletion of a key makes all data under it unreadable, including backups; attackers can use this as ransomware, so key deletion should be guarded by SCPs and the deletion waiting period.
M
What is a data perimeter, and how do you implement it on AWS?

A set of guardrails ensuring that only your identities access your resources, from your networks. Identity perimeter: resource policies and RCPs deny access unless aws:PrincipalOrgID is your organisation (with exceptions for AWS service principals). Resource perimeter: SCPs deny your principals access to resources outside the organisation (aws:ResourceOrgID), which stops exfiltration to an attacker's bucket. Network perimeter: policies deny use of credentials unless the request comes through your VPC endpoints or IP ranges (aws:SourceVpce, aws:SourceIp, aws:ViaAWSService). Together they turn leaked credentials or a misconfigured policy from a breach into denied requests.

Follow-up: what breaks when you roll this out? — AWS services that access your resources on your behalf and third-party integrations; roll out in audit mode first (use Access Analyzer and CloudTrail to find legitimate external access), then add explicit exceptions.
M
A developer's access key was pushed to a public repository. What happens next and what do you do?

Automated scanners find exposed AWS keys within minutes — Unit 42's 2023 EleKtra-Leak research observed exposed keys used within five minutes, mostly to launch large instances for crypto-mining in many regions. AWS also scans public GitHub and may attach the AWSCompromisedKeyQuarantine policy, which in that research happened within about two minutes but restricts only some actions. Response: deactivate the key immediately; review CloudTrail across all regions for its use (and for new users, keys, roles or policy changes the attacker created for persistence); terminate unknown resources; revoke sessions of any roles it assumed; rotate anything it could read; then fix the cause — replace IAM user keys with federated, short-lived credentials and add secret scanning to commits.
Follow-up: why check all regions? — Attackers launch resources in regions you don't use precisely because nobody watches them; an SCP denying unused regions prevents that whole class.
M
What would you put in a baseline set of SCPs for an organisation?

Deny leaving the organisation; deny disabling or deleting CloudTrail, Config, GuardDuty and Security Hub, and modifying the log-archive bucket; deny actions in unapproved regions (with exemptions for global services); deny root-user actions in member accounts; deny creating IAM users and access keys except for a break-glass role; require IMDSv2 for new instances; deny disabling EBS default encryption and S3 account-level Block Public Access; deny KMS key deletion except by a security role. Test them in a staging OU first, because an SCP mistake can lock out a whole OU.

Follow-up: deny lists or allow lists? — Deny lists on top of FullAWSAccess are easier to maintain and less likely to break new services; allow lists are tighter but need updating as teams adopt services.
M
How do you keep administrative access to instances secure without opening SSH?

Remove inbound SSH and RDP from security groups entirely and use an identity-based session service: AWS Systems Manager Session Manager (or EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint) opens shell sessions through the agent and AWS APIs, authorised by IAM, recorded in CloudTrail with optional session logging, no bastion hosts or keys to manage. Combine with just-in-time access (time-bound permissions) for production. This removes a whole attack surface — internet-exposed management ports — and gives an audit trail of every session.

Follow-up: what about databases? — Use IAM database authentication or short-lived credentials from a secrets manager through a role, and reach them from a session or a private connection, not a public endpoint.
H
Walk through the Codefinger SSE-C ransomware and how you would prevent it.

In January 2025, Halcyon reported a group using compromised AWS credentials with s3:GetObject and s3:PutObject permissions to rewrite victims' objects using SSE-C — server-side encryption with a customer-provided AES-256 key that the attacker generated. S3 doesn't store SSE-C keys (CloudTrail logs only an HMAC), so without the attacker's key the data can't be decrypted. The attackers set lifecycle rules to delete the objects within seven days and left ransom notes. No AWS vulnerability was involved. Prevention: no long-term access keys (the credentials were leaked keys); deny SSE-C where it isn't needed — AWS's guidance was an IAM or bucket-policy condition on the SSE-C algorithm header, and from April 2026 S3 disables SSE-C by default on new general-purpose buckets and on existing buckets with no SSE-C objects; versioning plus Object Lock or AWS Backup copies in another account so originals survive; and alerts on unusual bulk PutObject with SSE-C or lifecycle changes.

Follow-up: why doesn't versioning alone save you? — An attacker with enough permissions can delete versions or set lifecycle rules that expire them; immutability (Object Lock compliance mode) or copies the attacker's credentials can't reach are what survive.
H
Design security controls for a new ML platform account that holds customer data for fine-tuning.

Place it in the production workloads OU with the baseline SCPs. Data: S3 buckets with Block Public Access, SSE-KMS with a customer-managed key whose policy allows only the training and pipeline roles, bucket policies requiring access via the VPC endpoint and from the organisation, versioning and Object Lock for the canonical datasets, Macie classification, and CloudTrail data events on those buckets. Compute: training jobs in private subnets with no internet egress except through an inspected proxy or endpoints, roles per job with least privilege, IMDSv2, no long-term keys. Models and checkpoints: separate buckets, same controls, with promotion to serving through a pipeline. People: SSO with MFA, read-only by default, just-in-time elevation. Detection: GuardDuty, Security Hub, Access Analyzer; alerts on access to the data buckets from unusual principals. Compliance: records of where personal data is and who accessed it, retention and deletion procedures.

Follow-up: what's the most likely real-world failure here? — A notebook or experiment environment with broad roles and internet access copying data out; isolate experimentation in its own account with synthetic or minimised data.
H
How do compliance frameworks map onto cloud controls, and where does the provider's certification stop?

Frameworks (SOC 2, ISO 27001, PCI DSS, HIPAA, FedRAMP, the EU's DORA for financial services) define control objectives: access control, logging, encryption, change management, vulnerability management, incident response, vendor management, data residency. The provider's attestations, available through AWS Artifact and equivalents, cover the provider's controls for in-scope services — the physical and infrastructure side. Your audit covers your configuration and processes: IAM, network, encryption choices, logging, backups, change control, plus contracts such as a HIPAA business associate addendum for regulated health data. Continuous evidence comes from guardrails, Config conformance packs and Security Hub standards mapped to the framework, IaC history and CloudTrail.

Follow-up: why does data residency complicate things? — It constrains which regions (and sometimes which services and support paths) you may use, and global services or replication features can move data across borders unless restricted by policy.
H
Contrast the main cloud breach patterns with the controls that stop each.

Leaked long-term keys → no IAM user keys (federation, short-lived credentials), secret scanning, region-deny SCPs, anomaly detection. Public storage → account/organisation Block Public Access, RCP data perimeter, Access Analyzer. SSRF to instance metadata and over-broad instance roles (Capital One, au10) → IMDSv2, least-privilege roles, egress control. Over-privileged CI and third-party roles → OIDC federation with subject conditions, external IDs, scoped roles. Destructive actions (ransomware via SSE-C, deleting backups, disabling keys) → immutable backups in another account, SCPs on key deletion and SSE-C, Object Lock. Logging disabled to hide activity → SCPs protecting CloudTrail and Config, organisation trails, alerts on StopLogging. Most real incidents chain two or three of these, so defence in depth matters more than any single control.
Follow-up: which one control gives the most protection per hour of work? — Eliminating long-term access keys; it removes the most common initial access path outright.
refs: Ransomware campaign encrypting Amazon S3 buckets using SSE-C (Arctic Wolf, January 2025)
The case: Codefinger's use of leaked credentials, attacker-supplied SSE-C keys and seven-day lifecycle deletion, with mitigations.
Advanced notice: Amazon S3 to disable the use of SSE-C encryption by default (AWS Storage Blog)
Why and how S3 blocks SSE-C by default for new buckets and existing buckets without SSE-C data from April 2026.
EleKtra-Leak: cryptojacking with exposed IAM keys (Unit 42, October 2023)
Exposed AWS keys on GitHub used within five minutes; AWS quarantine within about two.
Organizing your AWS environment using multiple accounts (whitepaper)
Recommended OUs, accounts and guardrails for a landing zone.
Blocking public access to your Amazon S3 storage
The four settings, organisation/account/bucket levels and what S3 considers public.
Example guardrails and guidance for testing SCPs safely.
Building a data perimeter on AWS (whitepaper)
Identity, resource and network perimeters with SCPs, RCPs and resource policies.
How key policies, IAM policies and grants combine, including cross-account access.

t: ML and LLM workloads on the cloud: GPU instances and capacity, managed ML platforms, managed LLM APIs, data locality, quotas, and a GPU cost estimate
sum: Running training, fine-tuning and inference on cloud GPUs: the instance families from L4 to B300 with October 2026 prices, why capacity rather than price is often the constraint and the ways to get it (on-demand, capacity reservations, Capacity Blocks, commitments, spot), managed ML platforms (SageMaker AI, Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, Azure Machine Learning) and their premium, managed LLM APIs (Bedrock, Google's model APIs, Microsoft Foundry with Azure OpenAI) with quotas and cross-region inference, data locality and residency, a fine-tuning run costed on-demand versus spot with interruptions, and the architecture of an ML platform — with Berkeley's 'Can't Be Late' study of spot under deadlines as the case.
prereq: gpu12
Choosing accelerators by fit (memory), bottleneck (FLOPs, bandwidth, interconnect) and cost per useful unit; training cost from FLOPs ÷ (peak × utilisation); build, rent or call an API.
ae2
LLM API bills are tokens × prices, with caching, batching and routing as levers, and a crossover where self-hosting becomes cheaper at steady high volume.
k8s14
GPUs reach containers through drivers and device plugins; gang scheduling and queues for training; serving autoscaled on queue depth or GPU signals; cold starts dominated by image and weight loading.
cl4
Instance families and pricing models; spot capacity with two-minute notice; capacity is finite per zone and type.
cl6
Datasets as large shards in S3, checkpoints written in parallel with a manifest, weights staged on local NVMe for fast loading.
cl12
Commitments pay off above their price ratio to on-demand; cost per unit of work is the metric to manage.
why:
An AI team gets approval to fine-tune an open model for a customer-support product. They write the training script, open the cloud console and try to launch an 8-GPU H100 instance. The request fails: their account's quota for that instance family is zero. They request an increase; it takes days. When it arrives, launches fail with "insufficient capacity" in their region's zones. They try spot instead, get capacity in another region, copy their 30 TB dataset across (paying for the transfer), and start training — which is interrupted four times in the first night, each time losing an hour and a half of work because checkpoints were every two hours. The run that was budgeted at $5,000 costs $9,000 and finishes a week late.

Then they serve the model. Each inference instance holds one GPU and runs at 15% utilisation outside office hours. Meanwhile another team ships a feature on a managed LLM API, hits the per-region tokens-per-minute quota on launch day, enables cross-region inference to get more throughput — and the compliance team discovers that requests from EU customers are now being processed in other regions within the geography the team picked, which nobody had checked against the contract.

ML and LLM workloads are where the cloud's assumptions bend. Compute is scarce and expensive rather than plentiful and cheap; capacity has to be planned and booked; utilisation matters more than hourly price; data is large enough that its location dictates where compute can run; and managed AI services come with quotas and data-routing options that are as much legal decisions as technical ones. gpu12 taught how to choose accelerators and estimate cost from first principles, ae2 how LLM API bills work, and k8s14 how GPUs are scheduled in Kubernetes. This lesson is about the cloud layer around them: the GPU instance families and prices, the ways to get capacity, managed ML platforms, managed LLM APIs, data locality and residency, quotas, and a fine-tuning run costed on-demand versus spot. The case is a Berkeley study of how to use spot capacity without missing deadlines.
primer:
Think of cloud GPUs as hiring specialist heavy machinery for a construction project, rather than renting ordinary vans.

Vans are everywhere: you call, one arrives, you pay by the hour. Cranes are different. There are few of them, everyone wants them at the same time, and the big ones must be booked weeks ahead, delivered to your site and set up next to each other. You can book a crane for a specific fortnight at a fixed price (a reservation), sign a year-long contract at a discount (a commitment), or take one on standby at a steep discount on the condition that it can be pulled away for another job with two minutes' warning (spot). You can also hire a crew that brings its own crane and operates it for you (a managed ML platform), or skip the crane entirely and buy finished components from a factory (a managed model API).

A crane that sits idle still bills by the hour, so the plan matters: have the materials on site before the crane arrives (data in the same region, staged fast), keep it busy (high utilisation), and make sure that if it's pulled away mid-lift you don't lose the whole day's work (checkpoints). And some materials can't legally leave the country they're in, so you hire cranes where the materials are (data residency).

The two numbers to keep in mind throughout are cost per useful unit of work — per training run, per million tokens served — rather than cost per hour, and utilisation, which converts one into the other. A cheaper GPU-hour that sits idle half the time is more expensive than a dearer one kept busy.

The work also splits into phases with very different needs. Experimentation is bursty, small and tolerant of interruption: a few GPUs for hours, ideal for spot or short on-demand use, with notebooks that must be shut down when idle. Training and fine-tuning are large, planned and deadline-bound: many GPUs together for days, which is where capacity reservations and careful checkpointing pay off. Serving is continuous and latency-sensitive: a steady baseline worth committing to, peaks worth autoscaling, and a choice between running models yourself and calling someone else's. Most cost and reliability problems come from buying capacity for one phase the way you'd buy it for another — reserving GPUs for experiments, or running a deadline-critical training job on hope.

Where the analogy breaks: cranes don't get faster every year. GPUs do, and the newest generation is both the scarcest and often the cheapest per unit of work. Capacity planning in the cloud is therefore also a bet on which hardware to target, and commitments longer than a hardware generation carry the risk of paying for yesterday's chips.
body:
1. The GPU instance families

AWS's accelerated instances fall into two broad groups. Inference and light training (the g family): one to eight GPUs per instance, PCIe-attached, good price per GPU. Large-scale training and heavy inference (the p family): eight GPUs connected by NVLink inside the instance and EFA networking between instances. AWS also offers its own accelerators, Trainium (trn) for training and Inferentia (inf) for inference, programmed through the Neuron SDK. On-demand Linux prices in us-east-1 from the AWS price list on 7 October 2026:

InstanceAcceleratorsGPU memory$/hour$/GPU-hourTypical use
g6.xlarge1 × NVIDIA L424 GB0.80480.80small-model inference
g5.xlarge1 × NVIDIA A10G24 GB1.0061.01inference (older)
g6e.xlarge1 × NVIDIA L40S48 GB1.8611.867–13B inference, fine-tuning small models
g6e.12xlarge4 × L40S192 GB10.492.62larger-model inference
p4d.24xlarge8 × A100 40 GB320 GB21.962.74training (previous generation)
p5.48xlarge8 × H100640 GB55.046.88training, large-model inference
p5en.48xlarge8 × H2001,128 GB63.307.91memory-hungry training and inference
p6-b200.48xlarge8 × B200≈1.4 TB113.9314.24frontier training
p6-b300.48xlarge8 × B300≈2.1 TB142.4217.80frontier training and inference
trn1.32xlarge16 × Trainium512 GB21.50—training on Neuron
inf2.xlarge1 × Inferentia232 GB0.7582—inference on Neuron

Prices differ by region (a p5.48xlarge was $66.05 in Mumbai, $68.80 in Tokyo and $92.47 in São Paulo the same day; cl1), and not every type is offered everywhere. The price per GPU-hour rises with each generation, but so does work per hour; gpu12 shows how to compare by cost per token or per training run rather than per hour. Inside the instance, the details that decide performance — GPU memory and bandwidth, NVLink between GPUs, EFA bandwidth between instances, local NVMe for staging data and checkpoints — matter more than the vCPU count.

2. Capacity: quotas, availability and placement

Three separate things stand between you and running GPUs:

  • Quota. EC2 limits on-demand and spot usage per instance family group in vCPUs per region. A p5.48xlarge has 192 vCPUs, so running four needs a quota of 768 for that group. New accounts frequently start at zero for P instances; increases are requested through Service Quotas and may take time or require usage history. Request them weeks before you need them, in every region you might use.
  • Availability. Even with quota, a zone may have no free hosts of that type, and RunInstances fails with an insufficient-capacity error. For large GPU types this is common.
  • Placement. Distributed training needs instances close together on a fast network. AWS's UltraClusters provide non-blocking, petabit-scale networking; capacity reserved through Capacity Blocks is placed inside them automatically.

The ways to obtain capacity, from most flexible to most certain:

MechanismGuaranteePricingFits
On-demandnonelist price, per secondshort experiments when available
Spotnone; reclaimed with 2 minutes' noticevariable discount by poolcheckpointed, deadline-tolerant work
Savings Plansnone (discount only)p5.48xlarge $34.68/h on a 1-year EC2 Instance plan, $23.78 on 3 yearssteady, long-lived usage
On-demand capacity reservationcapacity in a zone while reservedon-demand rate, paid whether used or notsteady inference, critical baselines
Capacity Blocks for MLa fixed future windowdynamic price, paid upfrontplanned training and fine-tuning runs

Capacity Blocks deserve detail because they were designed for exactly this problem. Per the EC2 documentation (October 2026): you can see available future capacity and reserve a block of GPU instances — up to 64 instances per block and 256 across blocks for an organisation on any date — starting as soon as 30 minutes later or up to eight weeks ahead, for days or weeks. Instances are placed in UltraClusters; blocks can't be cancelled; instances must target the reservation ID; instances in a block don't count against on-demand quotas; and blocks end at 11:30 UTC on the final day, with instance termination starting at 11:00 — so jobs must checkpoint before then. They're available for P5, P5e, P5en, P6, P4d and Trainium types in selected regions.

3. Managed ML platforms

Each provider offers a platform that wraps capacity in ML-specific services: SageMaker AI on AWS, the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform on Google Cloud (Vertex AI until its rename at Cloud Next 2026), and Azure Machine Learning (with Microsoft Foundry for generative AI). The common services:

  • Training jobs. Submit a container, a data location, an instance type and count; the platform provisions, runs, retries and shuts down. Managed spot training runs on spot capacity and resumes from checkpoints written to S3 after interruptions.
  • Resilient clusters for long, large jobs (SageMaker HyperPod): persistent clusters with health checks on GPUs and networking, automatic replacement of failed nodes, and job auto-resume — addressing the reality that large GPU fleets fail regularly.
  • Notebooks and development environments with managed images.
  • Model registry and pipelines for versioning, approval and promotion.
  • Inference endpoints: real-time (autoscaled instances), serverless, asynchronous (queued requests for long inferences) and batch transform.

The trade is a premium per instance-hour for these services. From the SageMaker and EC2 price lists in us-east-1 on 7 October 2026: an ml.p5.48xlarge training instance cost $63.296 an hour against $55.04 for the equivalent EC2 instance (15% more); ml.g6e.xlarge $2.61 against $1.861 (40% more); ml.g5.xlarge $1.408 against $1.006 (40% more). For teams without a platform team, the premium buys a great deal; teams already running Kubernetes with GPU scheduling, queues and serving (k8s14) often run on EC2 or EKS directly and pay the raw instance price.

4. Managed LLM APIs

The other path skips GPUs entirely. Amazon Bedrock, Google's model APIs on the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, and Microsoft Foundry Models (which include Azure OpenAI) offer hosted models — the providers' own and third-party ones — through APIs billed per input and output token, with options for batch processing at lower prices for supported models and provisioned throughput (dedicated model capacity bought for a term) for guaranteed performance. ae2 covers the token economics; the cloud-specific concerns are these:

  • Quotas. Per account, per region, per model limits on requests and tokens per minute. Launches need quota increases planned like GPU quotas.
  • Cross-region routing. Bedrock's cross-region inference routes requests to other regions to find capacity. Per the Bedrock documentation (October 2026), geographic inference profiles keep processing within a geography such as the US, EU or APAC, while global profiles may route to any supported commercial region, at about 10% lower cost; CloudTrail in the source region records where each request was processed; and region-restricting SCPs must allow the destination regions (or, for global profiles, a documented special value), or requests fail. Azure OpenAI offers analogous global, data-zone and regional deployment types.
  • Data handling. Providers document whether prompts and outputs are stored or used for training (for the major enterprise offerings, by default they aren't used to train the provider's models) — but this must be checked per service and model against your obligations.
  • Private connectivity and identity. Calls can go through VPC interface endpoints (cl3) and are authorised by IAM (cl2), so model access follows the same governance as other services (cl13).

5. Data locality and residency

ML workloads move more data than most: training sets of terabytes to petabytes, checkpoints of hundreds of gigabytes per save (cl6), model weights of tens to hundreds of gigabytes per instance start. Every byte that crosses a region boundary costs money ($0.02/GB from us-east-1 to us-west-2 in October 2026) and time, and every byte that leaves the cloud costs more (cl3, cl12). The rules:

  1. Put GPUs in the region where the data lives, and read it through S3 gateway endpoints so it never touches NAT.
  2. If you must chase capacity in another region, weigh the one-time copy (a 50 TB dataset is about $1,024 per copy, plus storage) against the compute saved; it pays for a large one-off run, rarely for recurring training.
  3. Serve models in the regions where users are, which may differ from training; copy the model artefact (small) rather than moving traffic (large and latency-sensitive).
  4. Apply residency requirements to every stage: training data, checkpoints, logs and traces with prompts, inference processing location (including cross-region routing), and backups.

A useful habit is to write down, for each model-dependent feature, which path it uses and why: the model, the provider or instance type, the region and routing, the quota or capacity it relies on, and the fallback if that capacity disappears. That one page answers most of the questions a security review, a cost review and an incident commander will ask.

6. A fine-tuning run, costed

A team plans a full fine-tune (continued training) of an 8-billion-parameter model on 20 billion tokens using p5.48xlarge instances (8 × H100). Following gpu3 and gpu12:

  • Compute. Training FLOPs ≈ 6 × parameters × tokens = 6 × 8×10⁹ × 20×10⁹ = 9.6×10²⁰.
  • Throughput per GPU. An H100 SXM's dense BF16 peak is about 989 TFLOPS; assume 40% model FLOPs utilisation (MFU), so about 396 TFLOPS of useful work per GPU.
  • Time. 9.6×10²⁰ ÷ 3.96×10¹⁴ ≈ 2.43 million GPU-seconds ≈ 674 GPU-hours ≈ 84.3 instance-hours of p5.48xlarge.

Price it four ways with October 2026 rates:
