The spot line needs its assumptions spelled out. With checkpoints every 30 minutes, an interruption loses on average 15 minutes of work since the last checkpoint plus about 15 minutes to get capacity back and restore: half an hour. With one interruption every six hours of running, 84.3 hours sees about 14 interruptions and 7 extra hours. And the spot prices are a snapshot from AWS's published spot price data on 7 October 2026: $31.30 an hour for p5.48xlarge in us-west-2, but $57.76 in us-east-1 — above on-demand that day — which is exactly why "use spot" isn't a rule but a measurement. If the dataset lives in us-east-1, add about $20 per TB copied to us-west-2.

Three further adjustments matter more than the purchasing choice. MFU: at 25% the run needs 60% more hours; at 50% it needs 20% fewer — measure on a short run before booking capacity. Parallelism: eight instances would finish in about 10.5 hours of wall time if scaling efficiency holds, at roughly the same total cost — useful for deadlines and for fitting inside a Capacity Block window. Overheads: evaluation runs, failed starts, data preparation and checkpoint uploads typically add 10–20%.
deep:
Utilisation is the cost lever that dominates

Every GPU-hour billed but not spent on useful computation is waste: idle time between jobs, data-loading stalls, checkpoint pauses, communication waiting in distributed training, low batch sizes in serving, and notebooks left running. For a p5 fleet at $55 an hour per instance, raising effective utilisation from 40% to 60% saves a third of the bill — more than any commitment. The tools are scheduling (queues that keep GPUs fed with jobs), input pipelines that stream from S3 fast enough (cl6), asynchronous checkpointing, batching and continuous batching for inference (gpu10), and automatic shutdown of interactive environments. Measuring GPU utilisation and MFU per job and per team, alongside cost, is what makes these visible (cl11, cl12).

GPU fleets fail often, so resilience is a design input

Large training jobs span hundreds or thousands of GPUs for weeks, and the probability that some GPU, NIC, cable or host fails during that time approaches certainty. Jobs must checkpoint frequently, detect failures quickly (stragglers, NaNs, hung collectives), replace nodes and resume automatically. Managed clusters (SageMaker HyperPod) and Kubernetes operators for training both build this in. Checkpoint frequency follows the same optimisation as in cl6 — the interval near √(2 × checkpoint cost × mean time between failures) — and spot interruptions simply add another failure source with a shorter mean time between failures.

Spot for GPUs is a portfolio and a scheduling problem

Spot capacity for large GPU instances is scarce and correlated: when demand rises, whole pools are reclaimed together, and prices in busy regions can sit near or above on-demand. Using it well means diversifying across zones and regions (and instance types, if the code tolerates it), checkpointing frequently, and treating the deadline explicitly: run on spot while you're ahead of schedule, fall back to on-demand or reserved capacity when you're behind. That is precisely the policy the 'Can't Be Late' study formalised, and tools like SkyPilot implement across clouds. The data-gravity cost of chasing spot across regions has to be in the same calculation.

Model APIs shift risk from capacity to quotas and terms

With a managed LLM API, you don't plan GPU capacity, but you inherit the provider's: quotas per model per region, throttling under shared load, model deprecation schedules, price changes, and data-handling terms. Production designs treat the model API like any critical dependency (cl10): quotas raised and monitored, client-side rate limiting and backoff, a fallback model or provider for degradation, cross-region profiles chosen with residency in mind, and contractual review of retention and training-use terms. Provisioned throughput turns the quota risk back into a capacity purchase, with its own utilisation question.

Inference economics flip with scale

At low or spiky volume, per-token APIs or serverless inference are cheapest because you pay nothing idle. At steady high volume, dedicated GPUs with good batching win because cost per token falls with utilisation (ae2 computes the crossover). In the cloud the crossover also depends on capacity guarantees (reservations or commitments for the steady baseline), on model choice (a fine-tuned small open model on L40S versus a large proprietary model via API) and on the engineering cost of running a serving stack. Many mature teams end up hybrid: self-hosted for the high-volume core, APIs for long-tail features, spikes and the newest models.

Commitments meet fast-moving hardware

A three-year commitment on p5 halves the hourly rate, but GPU generations turn over in roughly two years and each new one delivers more work per dollar. Committing long to the current generation risks paying for capacity that's no longer the best choice before the term ends, while committing short or not at all risks having no capacity. Teams handle this by committing only to the steady inference baseline they're confident about, preferring flexible instruments (Compute Savings Plans that move across instance families) over family-specific ones, and buying training capacity per run with Capacity Blocks rather than by the year.

Governance applies with extra force

ML platforms concentrate sensitive data (training sets with personal data, proprietary corpora), valuable artefacts (model weights) and expensive resources (GPUs that crypto-miners love — cl13's leaked-key pattern). The landing-zone controls all apply: separate accounts for experimentation, training and serving; datasets and weights encrypted with keys whose policies name only the roles that need them; no internet egress from training jobs except through controlled paths; region guardrails compatible with cross-region inference choices; and cost allocation per team and job so idle GPUs have owners.
prod:
Failure modes and their symptoms

Capacity unavailable. Launches fail with insufficient capacity or quota errors on the day training should start. Fix: quotas raised in advance in several regions; Capacity Blocks booked for planned runs; a fallback instance type or region with data already there.

Interrupted training losing hours. Spot reclaims or node failures with infrequent checkpoints. Fix: checkpoint intervals sized to failure rates, asynchronous checkpoint writes, automatic resume, and a deadline-aware fallback to on-demand.

Capacity Block ends mid-run. Termination starts at 11:00 UTC on the block's last day. Fix: schedule the final checkpoint before then, size runs to the window, or extend the block in advance where possible.

GPUs starved by data. Low GPU utilisation with high input-pipeline wait. Fix: sharded datasets, parallel S3 reads, local NVMe caches or FSx for Lustre (cl6).

Idle GPU spend. Notebooks, endpoints and dev instances running nights and weekends. Fix: auto-shutdown, schedules, per-owner dashboards (cl12).

API throttling at launch. Tokens-per-minute quotas hit on a model API. Fix: quota planning, cross-region profiles where allowed, provisioned throughput, client-side rate limits and fallbacks.

Residency surprises. Inference or logs processed outside an allowed geography after enabling a routing feature. Fix: residency review of every routing and replication option; SCPs aligned with the chosen profiles; CloudTrail checks of the processing region.

Cost shocks. A forgotten p5 instance at $1,321 a day, or a misconfigured autoscaler. Fix: budgets and anomaly detection per GPU account, SCPs limiting GPU instance types to approved accounts.

What to measure

GPU utilisation and MFU per job; cost per training run and per million tokens served; time to capacity (from request to running); interruption rate and lost GPU-hours; checkpoint duration; model API throttles and latency per region; quota headroom; and spend on idle GPU resources.

The case: 'Can't Be Late' (NSDI 2024)

Zhanghao Wu, Wei-Lin Chiang, Ziming Mao, Zongheng Yang, Eric Friedman, Scott Shenker and Ion Stoica, from UC Berkeley and ICSI, studied a practical question: how to use cheap but interruptible spot instances for jobs that must finish by a deadline, such as a training run due before a product review. Their setting includes the realities this lesson describes: spot capacity appears and disappears unpredictably, each switch between instances costs a changeover delay, and on-demand capacity is the safe but expensive fallback. They collected three months of real spot availability traces on AWS and released them for others to use.

The obvious strategy — use spot whenever available, and switch to on-demand only when the remaining time is just enough to finish there — performs poorly in bad cases, because it waits too long and ends up paying for long on-demand stretches. The paper's Uniform Progress policy instead compares actual progress with a straight line from start to deadline: when the job is ahead of that line, it uses spot (or waits for spot); when it falls behind, it uses on-demand until it catches up. It needs no parameters and no assumptions about spot availability. In their evaluation it closed the gap between the greedy policy and the theoretical optimum by about 2× in both average and bad cases, and in real deployments saved 27–84% of cost across representative workloads and deadlines while meeting them.

The lesson generalises beyond the algorithm. Spot is not a purchasing setting but a scheduling problem with an explicit fallback; the deadline is an input to the cost; and the savings depend on how much slack you give the scheduler. The same group's open-source SkyPilot project implements this kind of policy across regions and clouds — which brings back the data-locality question every time it moves a job.
myths: If I can pay for GPUs, the cloud will give me GPUs.

For the newest accelerators, capacity is the binding constraint. On-demand launches of 8-GPU instances often fail with insufficient capacity, new accounts usually have GPU quotas of zero, and large clusters need reserved capacity placed close together. Teams plan GPU capacity like a supply chain — quotas raised in advance, Capacity Blocks or reservations for training windows, commitments for steady inference — rather than assuming elasticity.
Spot GPUs are always the cheapest option.

Spot prices for scarce GPUs vary by region and zone and can sit close to — in AWS's published spot price snapshot for 7 October 2026, even above — on-demand in a busy region: p5.48xlarge showed $57.76 an hour in us-east-1 against $55.04 on demand, while us-west-2 showed $31.30. Interruptions also add lost work and restart time, and capacity for 8-GPU instances can vanish for hours. Spot is a good deal for checkpointed, deadline-tolerant work in regions where it's actually discounted.
Managed ML platforms are just a markup on the same instances.

They are a markup — in us-east-1 in October 2026 an ml.p5.48xlarge training instance on SageMaker cost $63.296 an hour against $55.04 for the EC2 p5.48xlarge, about 15% more — but they bundle job scheduling, retries, managed spot with checkpoint restore, cluster health checks and automatic node replacement, experiment tracking, model registry and endpoints. Whether that's worth it depends on how much of it you'd otherwise build and run yourself.
Calling a managed LLM API means my data stays in my region.

It depends on configuration. Cross-region inference on Bedrock routes requests to other regions — within a geography such as the US or EU for geographic profiles, anywhere for global profiles — and Azure OpenAI deployments can be global, data-zone or regional. If data residency matters, choose regional or geography-bounded options deliberately, check the provider's data-handling terms, and make sure SCPs that restrict regions allow exactly the regions the profile uses.
Utilisation doesn't matter much because the cloud is pay-as-you-go.

GPUs are billed per instance-hour whether the GPUs are busy or not. An 8-GPU instance at $55 an hour that spends half its time waiting on data loading, checkpoint writes or idle between jobs doubles the cost of the work done. Model FLOPs utilisation, input pipeline throughput and scheduling efficiency are cost levers as large as the pricing model.
Moving training to the region with the cheapest GPUs always saves money.

Data has to follow. Copying a 50 TB dataset from us-east-1 to us-west-2 costs about $1,024 in inter-region transfer (at $0.02/GB) and doubles storage while both copies exist; serving models in a different region from users adds latency and egress; and residency rules may forbid it. Cheap compute far from data is often a false saving for repeated workloads, and a real one for one-off large runs.
lab:
Goal: build a GPU training cost estimator and a spot-versus-on-demand deadline simulator in Python 3.12 (standard library only), and reproduce the lesson's numbers. About 25 minutes; no cloud account needed.

  1. Estimator. Write train_hours(params, tokens, peak_tflops, mfu, gpus_per_instance) returning GPU-hours and instance-hours (FLOPs = 6 × params × tokens). Check 8×10⁹ parameters, 20×10⁹ tokens, 989 TFLOPS, 40% MFU, 8 GPUs → about 674 GPU-hours and 84.3 instance-hours.
  2. Pricing. Price it with the October 2026 rates from the lesson (EC2 on-demand, SageMaker, the two spot snapshots, the 1-year Savings Plan rate). Then vary MFU from 25% to 55% and print the on-demand cost curve.
  3. Interruptions. Simulate spot with interruptions arriving as a Poisson process (mean time between interruptions 6 h), checkpoint interval C, restore time 15 min; compute expected total hours for C = 15, 30, 60 and 120 minutes, including checkpoint cost of 2 minutes each. Find the best C and compare with √(2 × checkpoint cost × MTBI).
  4. Deadline policies. Generate a spot-availability trace in 10-minute steps (a two-state Markov chain: available stays available with probability 0.95, unavailable stays unavailable with 0.9). For a job of 84 hours with a deadline of 120 hours, implement (a) greedy: spot when available, switch to on-demand when remaining slack equals the remaining work; (b) uniform progress: spot when progress is ahead of the straight line to the deadline, on-demand otherwise. Add a 15-minute changeover delay on every switch. Run 500 traces and report mean cost, worst-case cost and missed deadlines.
  5. Data gravity. Add the cost of copying a dataset of D TB at $0.02/GB when spot is used in another region, and find the dataset size at which spot in us-west-2 stops being cheaper than on-demand in us-east-1 for this run.

What to look for: step 2 shows MFU swinging the cost by roughly 2×; step 3 finds an optimum checkpoint interval of tens of minutes, near the square-root rule; step 4 should show both policies meeting deadlines on most traces, with uniform progress cheaper in the bad ones — the paper's result in miniature; step 5 shows the break-even dataset size (about 87 TB for the numbers here, since the spot saving of about $1,780 equals $20.48 per TB copied), which is why cheap compute far from data is often a false saving.

Needs an AWS account (optional): aws ec2 describe-capacity-block-offerings --instance-type p5.48xlarge --instance-count 2 --capacity-duration-hours 48 lists available Capacity Block windows and their upfront prices; aws service-quotas get-service-quota --service-code ec2 --quota-code L-417A185B shows the on-demand P-instance vCPU quota.
recap: Cloud GPU families range from inference-oriented L4 and L40S instances (g6, g6e) to 8-GPU training instances with H100, H200, B200 and B300 (p5, p5e/p5en, p6), plus AWS's Trainium and Inferentia; prices in us-east-1 ran from about $0.80 an hour for one L4 to $142 an hour for eight B300s in October 2026.
Capacity is the constraint for frontier GPUs: quotas start low, on-demand launches can fail, and large jobs need instances placed together with fast interconnect.

Capacity options trade cost against certainty: on-demand (flexible, may be unavailable), on-demand capacity reservations (guaranteed, paid while idle), Capacity Blocks for ML (reserved for days to weeks, up to 64 instances per block, booked up to eight weeks ahead), Savings Plans for steady use, and spot for interruptible work.

Managed ML platforms (SageMaker AI, Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform — formerly Vertex AI — and Azure Machine Learning) add training job orchestration, managed spot with checkpoint restore, resilient clusters, registries and endpoints for a premium over raw instances.

Managed LLM APIs (Bedrock, Google's model APIs, Microsoft Foundry Models including Azure OpenAI) bill per token or per provisioned throughput unit, enforce per-model regional quotas, and offer cross-region routing whose geography you must choose for residency.
Keep data, compute and serving close: transfer between regions and to the internet costs money and latency, and residency rules may constrain where data and inference can run.

Training cost ≈ 6 × parameters × tokens ÷ (peak FLOPs × utilisation) GPU-seconds, converted to instance-hours and priced; a full fine-tune of an 8B model on 20B tokens is about 670 H100 GPU-hours, roughly $4,600 on-demand on p5 in October 2026.

Spot is worth it when it's truly discounted in the chosen region, jobs checkpoint frequently and the deadline has slack; Berkeley's 'Can't Be Late' showed a simple policy that falls back to on-demand to meet deadlines saved 27–84% on real workloads.

An ML platform on the cloud is mostly the earlier topics applied: accounts and guardrails, private networks with endpoints, S3 for data and checkpoints, IaC, observability with GPU metrics, cost allocation per team and job, and DR for models and data.

drill:
Plan: capacity and cost for a quarter of ML work

A team's plan for the next quarter: (1) two fine-tuning runs of a 70B model with LoRA, each estimated at 1,500 H100 GPU-hours, needed by fixed review dates in weeks 5 and 11; (2) about 3,000 GPU-hours of exploratory experiments on 1–8 GPUs, with no deadlines; (3) serving their current 8B model to an internal product at a steady 300 requests per second during business hours and 50 at night, which needs about 6 L40S GPUs at peak and 1 at night; (4) a new feature on a managed LLM API expected to need 2 million tokens per minute at peak, for EU users. Their account has zero P-instance quota, data is in eu-west-1, and contracts require EU processing. Propose capacity sources, an estimated compute budget using this lesson's prices (treat eu-west-1 prices as roughly us-east-1's for estimation and say so), and the risks.

Answer

(1) Deadline runs: Capacity Blocks. 1,500 GPU-hours ≈ 188 p5.48xlarge instance-hours each. Book a block of e.g. 4 instances for ~2.5 days in an EU region that offers them (check the supported-regions table — eu-west-1 isn't listed for Capacity Blocks in October 2026, so use an EU region that is, such as eu-north-1 or eu-west-2, and copy the data inside the EU), timed to finish a few days before each review. Compute at roughly on-demand-level prices: 188 × ~$55 ≈ $10,300 per run, $20,700 for both (block prices are dynamic — get quotes). Checkpoint before the block's 11:00 UTC termination.

(2) Experiments: spot plus small on-demand. 3,000 GPU-hours, mostly on g6e (L40S) and occasional p5. On g6e.xlarge at $1.861 on demand ≈ $5,600; spot where discounted could halve it. Request P quota now (it's zero) so on-demand fallbacks are possible.

(3) Serving: reserved baseline plus on-demand peak. 1 GPU always on, 5 more for ~10 business hours on 22 days. Baseline on a 1-year Savings Plan for g6e.xlarge (≈ $1.172/h) ≈ $855/month; peak 5 × 220 h × $1.861 ≈ $2,047/month on demand; about $8,700 for the quarter. Autoscale on queue depth; weights on NVMe for fast scale-out (k8s14).

(4) LLM API feature: EU-bounded routing and quota. Use an EU geographic inference profile (not global) or an EU data-zone deployment, request quota for 2M tokens per minute in the EU regions involved, align SCPs to allow exactly those regions, and price tokens with ae2's method; consider provisioned throughput if peak is predictable. Verify where requests are processed in CloudTrail.

Total compute (excluding API tokens): roughly $20,700 + $5,600 + $8,700 ≈ $35,000 for the quarter. Risks: P quota and Capacity Block availability in EU regions (book early), data copies across EU regions (cost and residency paperwork), MFU lower than assumed (measure on a short run), LLM API quota approval timing, and idle notebooks — put schedules on everything interactive.
qa: E
Which cloud GPU instance would you choose for serving a 7B model, and for training a 70B model?

For serving a 7–8B model in bf16 (about 16 GB of weights plus KV cache), a single L4 (g6.xlarge, 24 GB, $0.80/hour in us-east-1 in October 2026) or L40S (g6e.xlarge, 48 GB, $1.86/hour) is usually enough, scaled out with replicas; quantised models fit more easily. Training a 70B model needs many 80 GB-plus GPUs with fast interconnect: 8-GPU H100/H200/B200 instances (p5, p5en, p6) in multiples, with EFA networking, for weeks — which makes capacity planning the first question (gpu12 covers fitting and bottlenecks).
Follow-up: what decides L4 versus L40S for serving? — Memory for weights plus KV cache at your batch size and context length, and throughput per dollar measured on your traffic, not peak specs.
E
What's the difference between using a managed LLM API and hosting a model yourself on cloud GPUs?

A managed API (Bedrock, Google's model APIs, Azure OpenAI in Microsoft Foundry) bills per token or provisioned unit, needs no capacity planning or serving stack, gives access to proprietary models, and enforces quotas per model per region. Self-hosting on GPUs gives control over models (open weights, fine-tunes), data path and latency, and can be cheaper at steady high volume, but you buy capacity by the hour whether busy or not and run the serving stack, scaling, upgrades and on-call. ae2 works the cost crossover; the cloud-specific questions are capacity, quotas, region availability and residency.

Follow-up: what would push you to self-host? — Steady high volume where per-token prices exceed GPU-hours at good utilisation, a fine-tuned open model, strict data-path requirements, or latency targets the API can't meet.
E
Why do new accounts often fail to launch GPU instances?

Two reasons. Quotas: EC2 quotas for GPU instance families (counted in vCPUs, a p5.48xlarge is 192) often start at zero or very low on new accounts and must be raised by request, which can take time and history. Capacity: even with quota, the zone may have no free capacity of that type right now, returning an insufficient-capacity error. Fixes: request quotas early, try other zones and regions, use Capacity Blocks or reservations for planned work, and keep a fallback instance type.

Follow-up: do Capacity Blocks count against on-demand quotas? — No; AWS's documentation says instances in a Capacity Block don't count against on-demand instance limits, which is one reason teams use them for planned training.
M
Compare the ways to obtain GPU capacity on AWS.

On-demand: no commitment, per-second billing, but launches may fail for scarce types. On-demand capacity reservations: guarantee capacity of a type in a zone, billed whether used or not; good for steady inference. Capacity Blocks for ML: book GPU instances (up to 64 per block, 256 across blocks per organisation per date) for a fixed window starting up to eight weeks ahead, placed in UltraClusters, paid upfront at a dynamic price, ending at 11:30 UTC on the last day with termination starting at 11:00; good for training runs. Savings Plans: discount steady usage but don't guarantee capacity (a one-year EC2 Instance plan cut p5.48xlarge from $55.04 to $34.68 an hour). Spot: deep discounts where available, interruptible, and often unavailable for large GPU instances.

Follow-up: which combination for a team with steady inference and monthly fine-tuning runs? — Reservations or commitments for the inference baseline, Capacity Blocks booked for each training window, spot for experiments with checkpointing.
M
Estimate the cost of a full fine-tune of an 8B-parameter model on 20 billion tokens.

Training FLOPs ≈ 6 × 8×10⁹ × 20×10⁹ = 9.6×10²⁰. An H100 SXM's dense BF16 peak is about 989 TFLOPS; at 40% MFU that's about 396 TFLOPS per GPU, so 9.6×10²⁰ ÷ 3.96×10¹⁴ ≈ 2.43 million GPU-seconds ≈ 674 GPU-hours ≈ 84 hours of an 8-GPU p5.48xlarge. At $55.04 an hour on demand (us-east-1, October 2026) that's about $4,640; on SageMaker training at $63.296, about $5,330; on us-west-2 spot at the $31.30 snapshot price, with 14 interruptions each costing half an hour of lost work and restart, about 91 hours and $2,860. Add 10–20% for evaluation, failed runs and data preparation, and run across several nodes to shorten wall time (eight nodes ≈ 10.5 hours) if scaling efficiency holds.

Follow-up: what's the most uncertain input? — MFU: it can be 25% or 55% depending on sequence length, parallelism and input pipeline, which moves the cost by a factor of two; measure it on a short run first.
M
What does a managed ML platform give you over raw instances?

Job-level abstractions (submit a training job with an image, data location, instance type and count; the platform provisions, runs, retries and tears down), managed spot with automatic resume from checkpoints in S3, resilient clusters that health-check GPUs and replace failed nodes (SageMaker HyperPod), experiment tracking, model registry with approval workflows, and endpoints for real-time, serverless, asynchronous and batch inference with autoscaling. You pay a premium per instance-hour (about 15% for ml.p5.48xlarge over EC2 in October 2026, more for smaller types) and accept the platform's conventions. Teams with strong Kubernetes platforms often run training and serving on EKS instead (k8s14).
Follow-up: what's the hidden cost of either path? — Idle capacity: notebooks and endpoints left running bill by the hour; both need schedules, auto-shutdown and per-team cost visibility.
M
How do quotas work for managed LLM APIs, and how do you design around them?

Providers set per-account, per-region, per-model limits on requests and tokens per minute (and per day for some models). Exceeding them returns throttling errors. Design: estimate peak tokens per minute from traffic and prompt sizes and request increases ahead of launches; use cross-region or global inference profiles where residency allows to draw on more capacity; buy provisioned throughput for guaranteed capacity on critical paths; queue and batch non-interactive work (batch APIs are discounted for many models); and implement client-side rate limiting, backoff and fallbacks to smaller models when throttled (ae2).

Follow-up: how do region-restricting SCPs interact with cross-region inference? — The SCP must allow every destination region in the inference profile (or the special unspecified region value AWS documents for global profiles), or requests fail; this is a common surprise after organisations add region guardrails.
M
Where should training data, checkpoints and models live relative to GPUs?

In the same region, ideally read through S3 gateway endpoints (no NAT charges) with datasets as large shards and checkpoints written in parallel with a manifest (cl6); a parallel file system such as FSx for Lustre linked to S3 when the framework needs POSIX paths and very high throughput. Models for serving should be stored in the serving region and staged on local NVMe. Moving training to another region for cheaper GPUs means copying data (50 TB at $0.02/GB is about $1,024 per copy) and keeping copies in sync, and may conflict with residency rules — worth it for a large one-off run, rarely for recurring jobs.

Follow-up: what if the dataset contains personal data under EU residency? — Train in an EU region, keep checkpoints and logs there, and make sure any managed services, cross-region inference profiles or replication used stay within the EU geography.
H
When is spot worth using for GPU training? Use the 'Can't Be Late' results.

Spot is worth it when it's actually discounted in the chosen region and zone, the job checkpoints frequently enough that interruptions lose minutes rather than hours, and the deadline has slack to absorb interruptions and periods with no spot capacity. Berkeley's 'Can't Be Late' (NSDI 2024) studied deadline-sensitive jobs using three months of real AWS spot availability traces. A greedy policy (use spot whenever available, switch to on-demand when the deadline is at risk) wastes money in the worst cases; their Uniform Progress policy, which tracks progress against a straight line to the deadline and falls back to on-demand only when behind, closed the gap to the optimal policy by about 2× and saved 27–84% in real workloads. The lesson: spot is a scheduling problem with an explicit on-demand fallback, not a binary choice.

Follow-up: what makes spot GPU capacity especially unreliable? — Large 8-GPU instances are scarce and correlated: when demand rises, whole pools are reclaimed together; spreading across zones and regions helps but drags data along.
H
Design the cloud architecture for a team that fine-tunes and serves open models for internal products.

Accounts: separate ml-dev, ml-train and ml-serve accounts under the workloads OU with guardrails (cl13). Data: curated datasets in S3 with SSE-KMS, access only from training roles via VPC endpoints, lineage recorded. Training: jobs submitted through a queue (SageMaker training or EKS with Kueue), capacity from Capacity Blocks for scheduled runs and spot for experiments, checkpoints to S3 with manifests, metrics on GPU utilisation and MFU. Registry: approved models with evaluation results promoted through a pipeline. Serving: vLLM-style servers on g6e or p5-class instances in an autoscaling group or EKS, weights staged to NVMe, autoscaling on queue depth and tokens per second, reservations or commitments for the baseline, and a managed API as overflow and fallback. Cross-cutting: IaC, cost allocation per team and job, observability with token-level metrics (cl11), DR for models and data (cl10).
Follow-up: what fails first in practice? — Capacity for training windows and cost visibility for idle notebooks and endpoints; book capacity early and put schedules on everything interactive.
H
Compare running inference on Bedrock, on SageMaker endpoints and on your own GPU instances.

Bedrock: per-token pricing, many proprietary and open models, no capacity management, quotas per model and region, cross-region profiles for throughput, provisioned throughput for guarantees; best for variable traffic and proprietary models. SageMaker endpoints: your model on managed instances (real-time, serverless, asynchronous or batch), autoscaling and deployment features, at a premium per instance-hour (ml.g6e.xlarge $2.61 versus $1.861 for g6e.xlarge on EC2 in us-east-1, October 2026); best for teams wanting managed serving of their own models. Own instances or EKS: lowest unit cost at steady high utilisation with full control (serving stack, batching, quantisation), but you own capacity, scaling, upgrades and on-call. Many teams combine them: self-hosted for the steady high-volume path, API for spikes and long-tail features.

Follow-up: what number decides between per-token and per-hour? — Tokens per GPU-hour at your latency target: multiply by the API's per-token price and compare with the instance's hourly price, including idle time.
H
How do the three clouds differ for ML and LLM workloads?

AWS: the broadest GPU instance range plus Trainium and Inferentia, Capacity Blocks and UltraClusters, SageMaker AI and HyperPod, and Bedrock hosting many model providers. Google Cloud: TPUs alongside NVIDIA GPUs, GKE with strong GPU and TPU scheduling, and the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform (the 2026 rename of Vertex AI) for training, serving and Gemini and partner model APIs. Azure: NVIDIA GPU VMs, Azure Machine Learning, and Microsoft Foundry, whose models include Azure OpenAI with global, data-zone and regional deployments and provisioned throughput units. The engineering patterns — capacity planning, quotas, data locality, residency, cost per unit — are the same; model availability, accelerator options and regional coverage differ and often decide the choice.

Follow-up: how do you avoid lock-in for ML workloads? — Keep training code framework-level (PyTorch, JAX), containers portable, data in open formats, and serving behind your own API gateway so the model provider can change; accept platform-specific capacity and managed features where they pay off.
